title: Prince to Madonna, Blur to Beth Orton: William Orbit’s 12 greatest recordings | Madonna | The Guardian
description: The late producer’s gift for bringing in elements from dance music’s cutting edge drew all manner of music royalty – and he often made them sound better than ever before
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: The late producer’s gift for bringing in elements from dance music’s cutting edge drew all manner of music royalty – and he often made them sound better than ever before
Content: Chill out … William Orbit.Photograph: Eva PentelView image in fullscreenChill out … William Orbit.Photograph: Eva PentelMadonnaPrince to Madonna, Blur to Beth Orton: William Orbit’s 12 greatest recordingsThe late producer’s gift for bringing in elements from dance music’s cutting edge drew all manner of music royalty – and he often made them sound better than ever beforeWilliam Orbit, pop producer for Madonna, All Saints and more, dies aged 69Alexis PetridisFri 7 Aug 2026 11.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTorch Song – Mothdoom Ecstasy (1986)William Orbit’s first band were a curious business. Torch Song had one foot in the pop mainstream – their biggest success came about when one of their tracks was featured on the soundtrack of the Tom Hanks-starring sex comedy Bachelor Party – and one in the left field: they recorded at London’s anarchist hub Centro Iberico, famed for staging gigs by Crass and Throbbing Gristle; they covered the Velvet Underground’s Venus in Furs. Mothdoom Ecstasy is very much of its time – stuttering samples, booming drums – but in its hazy synth textures and ethereal female vocals, you can definitely hear intimations of Orbit’s future approach.Prince – The Future (Remix) (1989)In the late 80s, Orbit did a series of mainstream pop remixes – for Belinda Carlisle, among others – and released the first in his series of solo Strange Cargo albums: its beatless synth-drifts and instrumental dance tracks sounded like the work of a man subconsciously waiting for acid house to happen. When it did, Orbit plunged in head first: a so-so track from Prince’s Batman soundtrack, The Future already had a distinct hint of house music about it, but Orbit’s remix – made in partnership with Mark Moore of S’Express – dragged it firmly into the centre of a sweaty rave.Bassomatic – Fascinating Rhythm (1990)Bassomatic: Fascinating Rhythm – videoAugmented by vocalist Sharon Musgrave and rapper MC Inna Onestep, Orbit’s new dance project had some odd ideas, a house version of Pink Floyd’s Set the Controls for the Heart of the Sun among them, but their big hit – Top 10 in the autumn of 1990 – was a breakbeat-fuelled, dub-tinged dance-pop anthem. Again, it sounds very much of its era 36 years on, but that’s part of its charm: Fascinating Rhythm exudes the bright-hued, saucer-eyed optimism that dance music brought to the British charts in the years immediately after the Second Summer of Love.React 2 Rhythm – Intoxication (Clubfield mix) (1991)In a sense, it’s a little cheeky including the Clubfield mix of Intoxication in a list of Orbit’s best tracks. His involvement with the music seems a little tangential – he’s credited with “vocal samples” – and besides, this version is all about Leftfield’s remix. But no survey of Orbit’s career would be complete without mention of Guerilla Records, the progressive house label he co-founded in 1990, which released Intoxication, alongside classics by Spooky, DOP and the Drum Club. And besides, it’s a total classic: any excuse to revisit its absolute beast of a rhythm track.William Orbit – Water from a Vine Leaf (1993)Orbit’s first Strange Cargo album seemed like a curio: an outlier in the pop landscape of 1987. By 1993, the project made a lot more sense. In addition, the music had developed a fresh sense of focus, as evidenced by the opening track of Strange Cargo III. With vocals by Orbit’s then-girlfriend Beth Orton, Water from a Vine Leaf was the perfect demonstration both of his ability to create a warm, cosseting, slowly drifting soundscape and of his melodic skill: it became a minor UK hit before enjoying a lengthy afterlife as a mainstay of chill-out compilations. And the Underworld remix is the perfect example of the then-emerging trio’s unique approach to dance music.One Dove – Breakdown (William Orbit Stereo Odyssey) (1993)One Dove’s Morning Dove White wasthepost-club soundtrack of 1993 – a beautiful, Andrew Weatherall-produced blur of dub, dreamy electronics and girl-group influenced heartbreak – before becoming the great lost dance album of the early 90s: all-back-to-mine ubiquity ultimately didn’t translate into chart success. It was the kind of music for which Orbit had an innate affinity: his remix of Breakdown decorated the song with strings, harp and off-beam electronics, stretching it out for nine minutes, as if he – quite understandably – didn’t want it to end.William Orbit – Barber’s Adagio for Strings (1995)William Orbit: Barber’s Adagio for Strings – videoThe most famous of Orbit’s solo albums, Pieces in a Modern Style, saw him reworking classical music at the suggestion of label boss Rob Dickins: a pretty ghastly idea on paper, but one that Orbit made work. A trance remix of Barber’s Adagio for Strings by Ferry Corsten propelled the track into the UK Top 5: ageingGatecrasher kidswould doubtless disagree, but the original, which gently warps Barber’s 1936 piece into nine minutes of soft-focus but sorrowful ambience – a distant relative of Brian Eno’s approach to Pachelbel’s Canon on Discreet Music – is better.Beth Orton – She Cries Your Name (1996)Orbit and Orton had a lengthy and fruitful musical partnership that outlasted their romantic relationship – they released a version of John Martyn’s Don’t Want to Know About Evil as Spill in 1992 and were still collaborating on Orbit’s final album, The Painter, 30 years later. Orbit recorded his own version of their co-authored song She Cries Your Name on his 1995 Strange Cargo album Hinterland, but it’s Orton’s take – the opening track on her fabulous Weatherall-produced breakthrough album Trailer Park – that’s the definitive version: careworn, misty, its sound strangely timeless.View image in fullscreenWilliam Orbit and Madonna accepting the Grammy award for best pop album for Ray of Light.Photograph: Youtube/GRAMMYMadonna – Drowned World/Substitute for Love (1998)Madonna employed Orbit as a producer and co-songwriter on 1998’s Ray of Light after being impressed by remixes he’d done of Justify My Love and Erotica. Orbit later said the singer’s demanding approach nearly “killed” him – “I was done in physically” – but the resulting album sold 16m copies, catapulted him into the premier league of pop producers, and may well be the best album to bear Madonna’s name. The five-minute opening track perfectly demonstrates how simpatico the pair were: Madonna’s voice – sounding far more intimate than usual – fits perfectly as Orbit’s musical backing continually changes shape – icy ambient, a beat with a whisper of drum’n’bass about it, guitars and a surprisingly intense climax.Blur – Tender (1999)Like Madonna,Bluremployed Orbit’s services after taking note of the remixes he’d done for their Bustin’ + Dronin’ mini-album. As with the making of Ray of Light, the sessions for 13 were an intense and occasionally punishing experience: as the band were falling apart, Albarn likened Orbit’s role to that of a “psychiatrist”. And like Ray of Light, the end result was fantastic. Tender in particular seems to alchemise the frayed, exhausted mood into something remarkable. A depiction of Albarn’s relationship with Justine Frischmann collapsing, it’s alternately shaky, despondent and powerfully robust. Whatever Orbit did in the producer/psychiatrist’s chair pulled an extraordinary song out of the band.All Saints – Pure Shores (2000)All Saints: Pure Shores – videoDanny Boyle would only include All Saints on the soundtrack of his film adaptation of Alex Garland’s The Beach if Orbit agreed to produce their track: the pressure to come up with something caused the producer to expend so much effort – he spent two months working on it – that he “totally lost sight of its potential” and became convinced the song was “a turd”. In reality, it was a triumph: a brilliant distillation of Orbit’s skill as a producer of what would then have been called “chillout” music into a perfect pop format, infinitely hipper and more sophisticated than your average British girl group track of the time. It still sounds fantastic.Madonna, drugs and helicopter-trained dogs: the dark, starry life of William OrbitRead moreU2 – Electrical Storm (William Orbit mix) (2002)There’s a distinct note of what-if about the two tracks Orbit produced for inclusion on U2’s greatest hits album, The Best of 1990-2000. It’s hard not to listen to Electrical Storm in particular and wonder why they didn’t extend their partnership and make a whole album together: perhaps because of the track’s relative failure when released as a single in the US. That notwithstanding, it feels like a perfect melding of their respective styles: the guitar is immediately recognisable as the work of the Edge, the blanket of soft electronics over which Bono sings the intro is equally obviously pure Orbit.William Orbit – Bank of Wildflowers (ft Georgia) (2022)Orbit’s mainstream success in the late 90s and early 2000s had unfortunate consequences. He became a blue-chip songwriter/producer for hire in LA, working with No Doubt, Britney Spears and Chris Brown among others, an experience he didn’t much enjoy; reuniting with Madonna on 2012’s MDNA noticeably failed to recapture the magic of Ray of Light. Returning to England, he vanished from public view, suffering a drug-induced nervous breakdown that led to him being sectioned. When he re-emerged in 2021, it was as a solo artist: a Guardian profile depicted him “fizzing with enthusiasm” about his new music, excitement borne out by his final album The Painter. Far closer to Strange Cargo than his pop smashes, Bank of Wildflowers drenches guest singer Georgia’s faintly Kate Bush-esque vocal in effects and sets it against beautiful piano arpeggios, shivering electronics and an intermittent mid-tempo house pulse, to hugely impressive effect.William Orbit’s greatest recordings – playlistSpotifyExplore more on these topicsMadonnaPrinceBlurDance musicPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A pretty easy fix’: how I rid my kitchen of plastic – and seven of the best swaps | Kitchen essentials | The Guardian
description: Worried about microplastics? Whether it’s titanium pans or loose-leaf tea, here are the changes you can make right now
Author: Rose Stokes
Headline: Worried about microplastics? Whether it’s titanium pans or loose-leaf tea, here are the changes you can make right now
Content: Simple switch: stainless steel or glass containers can help reduce plastic in everyday food storage.Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreenSimple switch: stainless steel or glass containers can help reduce plastic in everyday food storage.Photograph: GettyThe FilterKitchen essentials‘A pretty easy fix’: how I rid my kitchen of plastic – and seven of the best swapsWorried about microplastics? Whether it’s titanium pans or loose-leaf tea, here are the changes you can make right nowThe bestsustainable subscriptions for greener, easier livingRose StokesFri 7 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Jump toHow to reduce plastic in your kitchenKitchen utensilsChopping boardsStorage containersKettleTeaKids’ utensils, plates and cupsPansIt all started with a black plastic spatula. Whenan articlewent viral in 2024 for suggesting we may be unwittingly infusing our food with harmful chemicals by using one, I, along with many I know, lobbed ours into the bin (without a backup in place, to the annoyance of my partner).The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.It later transpired that the study the article was based on hadmiscalculated the dosage by a factor of 10. UK regulations also limit certain hazardous substances in plastics, meaning that risks should be lower in this country. But alas, it was too late for our poor spatula.Nevertheless, studies show that the amount ofmicroplastics found inside human bodiesis increasing rapidly, and theplastic in our kitchenis known to be a contributing factor, so I set out to minimise its presence.According to Dr Stephanie Wright, who leads the microplastics team at Imperial College London’s Environmental Research Group, I am not alone in my desire to be rid of the stuff. “Plastic is useful, but it was never designed to be in our bodies,” she says.Her belief is that any reduction in exposure is good. “We know from lots of other well-studied particles in our environment, like air pollution, that exposure to too much of any particle can be a bad thing, so reducing that burden is always going to be positive – I think the same is true for plastics.”Yet it is only once you start trying to reduce plastic use that you realise how ubiquitous it is. Wright’s advice is to focus on one of the highest priority areas – the heating of food and drink, because heat accelerates the degradation of plastic, and eating and drinking are effective ways to transport chemicals into our bodies.However, ditching plastics also poses an environmental threat, creating a conundrum for anyone wanting to reduce their plastics exposure. Rather than simply throwing away everything plastic in your kitchen, a good rule of thumb is to wait until it no longer has a use and then gradually replace items with non-plastic alternatives.With all this in mind, here are my top sevenplastic kitchen swaps.How to reduce plastic in your kitchenKitchen utensilsView image in fullscreenJoseph Joseph metal utensils£130 at Joseph Joseph£89.99 at AmazonView image in fullscreenWooden spatula£2 at ProCookView image in fullscreenSilicone spatula set£15 at ProCookJoseph Joseph’s metal utensils are a good blend of style and function, and I use them for frying. However, they won’t work if your pans have a non-stick coating. Silicone utensils are broadly accepted as a better option than hard plastic ones because silicone has much higher heat resistance, is derived primarily from quartz rather than crude oil and has higher durability (meaning it’s not likely to leach chemicals into food). I use silicone spatulas for baking because batters don’t stick to them, but I prefer wood for other cooking because it’s a natural material.Chopping boardsView image in fullscreenWooden chopping board£53 at Shinrai KnivesView image in fullscreenBamboo chopping boardset£100 at Joseph Joseph£100 at John LewisAnother place where food often comes into contact with plastic is the chopping board. This is a pretty easy fix: we got this set of bamboo chopping boards (any form of wood will work). The only downside is no longer being able to whack them in the dishwasher.Storage containersView image in fullscreenPyrex zero plastic storage containers, three£32.69 at AmazonI’ve accumulated a huge amount of plastic Tupperware over the years. I’ve replaced it with Pyrex cooking dishes with lids (and silicone seals that make them spillproof), and thesetall glass jars, which we use for storing sauces, soups and curries. For any glass storage, check it’s freezer-safe (tempered or borosilicate glass) and ensure you leave space between the containers so the glass doesn’t freeze together.KettleView image in fullscreenAscot glass kettleFrom £38.99 at AmazonView image in fullscreenAarke steel kettle£199.99 at LakelandMy plastic reduction mission gave me a good excuse to buy this lovely glass kettle from Ascot. The only downside is that the glass is very unforgiving on limescale (a big problem where we live), which means I have to stay on top of the deep cleaning. If I had a bigger budget, I’d probably go for this stainless steel Aarke one.For more, read thebest kettles to save energy and speed up your cuppa, testedTeaView image in fullscreenTea strainer£4 at John LewisView image in fullscreenBird & Blend loose-leaf tea, 50gskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion£6 at Bird & BlendView image in fullscreenHampstead Organic English Breakfast teabags£4.15 for 20 teabags at Ocado£14.95 for 4 x 20 teabags at AmazonSwitching to loose-leaf tea seemed like a lot of effort, but I resolved to do it when I learned that many teabags contain plastic fibres in the bag or seal, which release microplastics when brewed. Even options marketed as plastic-free often use PLA, a plant-based bioplastic that has still been associated withmicroplastic releaseandeffects on marine life. Trulyplastic-free optionsinclude Hampstead Organic, considered a pioneer in this area. But switching to loose-leaf has been the one change I am borderline evangelical about because the tea is so much better. We bought several in-mug metal infusers and buy loose leaf from our local Bird & Blend (it is put directly into a metal tin, no plastic wrapping).Kids’ utensils, plates and cupsView image in fullscreenBamboo baby elephant suction plate£18.99 at Bamboo Bamboo£18.99 at AmazonView image in fullscreenElk and Friends stainless steel bowls and lids, four pack£19.99 at AmazonView image in fullscreenElk and Friends stainless steel plates and lids, two pack£19.99 at AmazonView image in fullscreenMunchkin Cool Cat straw cup£18.99 at Munchkin£18.99 at AmazonView image in fullscreenMam Feel Good glass bottlesFrom £7.19 at Boots£13.99 at John LewisView image in fullscreenMoon Moon steel lunch box£23.99 at Moon Moon£23.99 at AmazonMy children’s plates and cups were mostly plastic and often lobbed in the microwave. We already had a couple of lovely bamboo plates from Bamboo Bamboo (they fight over who gets the elephant), but they can’t go in the dishwasher. To counter this, I bought a few stainless steel plates and bowls from Elk and Friends. Eating off a metal plate does have a bit of a scout-camp vibe, but the kids adjusted quickly. They come with detachable silicone suction pads in case you have a child who likes to throw food and the occasional utensil – I do, which is also why I didn’t trust the ceramic versions some of my friends have.With sippy cups and water bottles, we scaled down massively, and, after a lot of research, landed on Munchkin bottles. We removed the plastic straws, which just means they need to be tipped a bit higher, and also means we don’t spend our lives searching for transparent plastic bottle pieces after washing them. The spout is made from food-grade silicone. We don’t put hot liquid in them, but the stainless steel does keep everything very cool.Both of my children drank from plastic bottles before I gave much thought to the issue, but we recently got a couple of glass ones with silicone lids from Mam for our toddler, who is stubbornly clinging to them before bed.We also switched to stainless steel lunch boxes that double as food storage containers. Our sturdy Moon Moon ones have a removable silicone seal – though be warned that they’re no longer leakproof if you take this out.PansView image in fullscreenOur Place Titanium Propans, set of two£260 at Our Place£275 at HealfView image in fullscreenProCook Elite Tri-Ply frying panFrom £60 at ProCookMany non-stick frying pans are coated in PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene, a plastic), which can flake into food if there’s any damage to the surface. We were due an upgrade so went for these titanium Our Place pans. Instead of a traditional coating, these have a non-stick technology, NoCo, which uses a micro-textured titanium surface to stop food from sticking. We were sceptical at first but have been impressed by how effective it is, and are now able to use metal cooking utensils without worry – a bonus.Alternatively, you can choose a pan with a ceramic coating like the ProCook one, which has the same benefits and was rated the best ceramic-coated pan in the Filter’s test of thebest frying pans.For more, readhow to make your bathroom more sustainableandreaders’ favourite eco-friendly swapsRose Stokes is a journalist based in Bath who balances writing about women’s health and parenting two small humansExplore more on these topicsKitchen essentialsThe FilterHomesPfasFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A ‘Keminaissance’ for the Tories is wishful thinking – Badenoch’s Reform-lite summer will only end one way | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: Hiring a convicted antisemite as an adviser; rabble rousing at a time of violent unrest. She is still in a race to the bottom and making too many mistakes, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: Hiring a convicted antisemite as an adviser; rabble rousing at a time of violent unrest. She is still in a race to the bottom and making too many mistakes, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Kemi Badenoch visits a chemical company in Teeside, on the campaign trail for the local elections, 2 April 2026.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch visits a chemical company in Teeside, on the campaign trail for the local elections, 2 April 2026.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.OpinionKemi BadenochA ‘Keminaissance’ for the Tories is wishful thinking – Badenoch’s Reform-lite summer will only end one wayJonathan FreedlandHiring a convicted antisemite as an adviser; rabble rousing at a time of violent unrest. She is still in a race to the bottom and making too many mistakesFri 7 Aug 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTShareThe Keminaissance will be delayed. For nearly a year, Conservative optimists and a clutch of supportive pundits have been forecasting an upturn in the fortunes ofKemi Badenoch, confident that her party will emerge from the crater it fell into in 2024, overtake Reform UK to become once again the main party of the right and, who knows, maybe, with a following wind, even push Labour aside and return to government. Every sign of strength from the Tory leader – a robust conference speech here, a viral clip on social media there – has been hailed as evidence of the coming Keminaissance. On the evidence of the past week or so, we will have to wait a little longer.It’s quite true thatBadenoch’s personal ratingsare better than those of her party. True, too, that she ended a long losing streak when the Tories won a Westminster seat at the Aberdeen South byelection in June. But there is a more recent election result that should temper the boosters’ enthusiasm, along with a series of decisions that confirm that, when it comes to both strategy and judgment, Badenoch is badly lacking.Start with that contest from a week ago. For many, the standout fact of the byelection to replace Andy Burnham as mayor of Greater Manchester was that Reform came a very poor second, taking just21% of the vote to Labour’s 47%. It was indeed a crushing defeat for Nigel Farage’s party, which a matter of weeks earlier had talked up its chances of winning the mayoralty.But run your finger further down the vote tally until it finally reaches the Conservative candidate on a mere 7.7%. In all the previous mayoral contests in Greater Manchester, the Tories were in second place. This time they were fifth, behindRestore Britain, a party of the hard right that has become home to all manner of racists and white supremacists.A Tory result that bad among such a large electorate suggests not merely that Badenoch is making slow progress, but that she is moving her party backwards. When it comes to challenging Labour, other parties are either level with theConservativesor ahead of them. In that context, it seems an undeserved compliment to call Kemi Badenoch the leader of the opposition.Her strategic response to this competition on the right has been to move towards her rivals, hoping to blunt the appeal of the nationalist populist parties by matching their offer. The latest step came late on Thursday with, as the Telegraph billed it, a Tory “promise to end council housing for foreigners”. Badenoch’s pledge is to evict almost 230,000 non-EU foreign national households from their homes.Never mind that many of those turfed out will include people who, while not UK citizens, have been living, working and paying taxes in Britain for years, while others will be refugees fleeing war and persecution. Never mind that, once evicted, those families, including their children, will be rendered homeless, leaving local councils with the choice of either abandoning them to the streets or providing (much costlier) emergency accommodation. Never mind that it’s unclear who exactly would identify and locate these families, unless Badenoch plans to create a British equivalent of ICE, mounting raids, snatching terrified people from their cars and throwing them into detention. Never mind all that; Badenoch doesn’t care.So much for the policy; now consider the timing. The Tory leader decided the right moment to demand foreigners be kicked out of their homes was as theNorfolk town of Thetford entered its third night of violence and disorder, triggered by a mob surrounding the accommodation of suspected asylum seekers, some in the crowd trying to force their way in, as others threw rocks and chanted: “We want them out.” Into this tinderbox of a situation walked the Conservative party leader, clutching a petrol can.Just a day or two earlier, she had been defending the selection as a Somerset council candidate of Joshua Bonehill-Paine, a man who has served long jail sentences for, among other things, a sustained campaign of antisemitic harassment and abuse of the Jewish former MP Luciana Berger, a campaign that saw Berger branded an “evil money-grabber”, her facesuperimposed on the body of a ratand photographs of her doctored into multiple, sexualised images.Badenoch argued that Bonehill-Paine had renounced his past as a self-described “nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights” and now works to prevent others succumbing to what he calls the disease of antisemitism. In April, he publisheda lengthy accountof how he had come to see Jews as the malign, all-powerful “force operating behind events”, a text that contains some useful insights. (Among them, as my colleague Rafael Behrhas pointed out, is an arresting admission by Bonehill-Paine that, though then a full-strength neo-Nazi, he “welcomed Jeremy Corbyn’s election as Labour leader”, which should give pause to those who, at the time, so adamantly dismissed Jewish fears that Corbyn was a draw to those who hate Jews.)Though candid, the essay is not wholly reassuring. For one thing, it contains no apology to Berger or any of Bonehill-Paine’s other victims. For another, he explains that what changed him was reading the Bible and coming to realise that Jews are “God’s chosen people”. I suspect few Jews will find comfort in that. Instead, they will worry that the would-be politician has traded antisemitism for philosemitism, which means he still singles out “the Jews” rather than seeing Jews as regular people, with the right to be as ordinary and flawed as anyone else.Still, even if Bonehill-Paine’s disavowal of his past were wholly convincing and he should be regarded as fully rehabilitated, that doesn’t make it obvious that he is acceptable for public office. The bar for that is higher, a point Badenoch herself implicitly conceded when she hinted that Bonehill-Paine would not have cleared the threshold to become an MP. Serving as a councillor was different, she explained, as he would be responsible for nothing more than “parking and bins” – thereby, and at a stroke, insulting the many thousands of Conservatives who devote themselves to public service in their local communities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBonehill-Paine eventually withdrew his candidacy, but that did not draw a line under the episode. In her stubbornness, the Tory leader said the former neo-Nazi would now serve the party as an adviser, thereby giving him a role on the very national level she had earlier said was off-limits. Worsening matters still further, the shadow cabinet member Claire Coutinho posted that, while, “Luciana and others are unable to forgive Joshua, I do,” attributing this vicarious generosity of hers to her Catholic faith, and so, doubtless unconsciously, reinforcing that age-old trope of the forgiving Christian and the vengeful Jew.What a mess to have made in just a few days. If it were only tactical blunders and in-the-moment misjudgments, one might be more, er, forgiving. But the flaw is strategic. Badenoch has chosen to fight a race to the bottom against Reform, but it is a race she can never win. Farage will always be willing to go further. Take that latest proposal on housing. She would give foreign nationals six months to get out of their homes; Reform promises to boot them out in three. The penny has still not dropped that in a contest of Reform v Reform Lite, the real thing will always have the edge.All the while, as Badenoch chases after Farage supporters, moderate Tory voters grow more disenchanted. There may be room for ex-fascists in Conservative ranks, but the leader will allow no place for Conservatives who support net zero targets and do not want the UK to leave the European convention on human rights. The result is that those “blue wall”, southern Tories who defected to the Lib Dems in 2024 have every reason not to come back.So, yes, Kemi Badenoch may score a win now and then; she’s bound to land the odd blow on Burnham when normal hostilities resume in September. But a Keminaissance? For the Tories, it looks like the dark ages have a while to run yet.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Swedish gummies, Parisian linens and Moroccan mint tea: what travel experts always bring home from their trips | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Finding treasures is part of the fun of travel. Here, experts share their top tips on what to buy where
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Finding treasures is part of the fun of travel. Here, experts share their top tips on what to buy where
Content: Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kellie French/The GuardianLife and styleSwedish gummies, Parisian linens and Moroccan mint tea: what travel experts always bring home from their tripsFinding treasures is part of the fun of travel. Here, experts share their top tips on what to buy whereHannah CoatesFri 7 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.FoodSpeciality teaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: SJ Bright/AlamyThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.I love discovering local teas wherever I travel, whether it’s Moroccan mint, Japanese green or herbal blends I’ve never come across at home. I gave up coffee last year, and since then, tea – particularly matcha from Kyoto, which is really strong – has become my daily ritual.Adrienne Adhami, wellbeing coach and podcast hostSpanish olivesView image in fullscreenWhen in Spain, I always come home with Aceitunas gazpachas – these split manzanilla or hojiblanca olives are marinated with pickles and spices, and they’re completely addictive. I stock up in local organic food shops, which tend to have the best selection.Phillippa Fern Kenyon Shutes, private chefArmagnacprunesView image in fullscreenI grew up in the Gers region of south-west France, which is famous for preserving prunes in armagnac, so I always try to bring a jar of them back from the local Château de Cassaigne. They come in these lovely tall glass jars and make the most delicious after-supper treat.Patrick Williams, interior designer and founder of BerdoulatCoffee beansView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jose Antona/Getty ImagesI always start my day with a pour-over coffee, so I make sure to stock up on beans whenever I travel. I like ones from Ethiopia or Kenya, especially when they’ve been naturally fermented, as they tend to have a lovely fruitiness and acidity, with notes of strawberry, candied orange peel or pineapple.Once I get home, I freeze the beans to preserve their freshness.Patricia Zhou, choreographerMakrutlime leavesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pornsawan Baipakdee/Getty ImagesVisiting Bangkok’s many markets (there’s one for everything) is always a highlight of a trip to Thailand. Phra Khanong is where local people buy their groceries. There are no tourists, it’s very affordable and the vendors are friendly. I always pick up my annual supply of makrut lime leaves for 50 baht (about £1) there.Kash Bhattacharya, travel blogger@budgettravellerLocal spiritsView image in fullscreenI buy alcohol from pretty much every country I visit. Looking at my collection, I have gin from Eritrea and Botswana, local spirits from Tanzania, and even a bottle from Laos with some sort of worm in it. I don’t actually open a lot of them – I just love having them there as memories of different places. If I’m travelling to a big wine-producing country, such as South Africa or Italy, I always bring a special wine suitcase with me, which holds 12 bottles.Jessica Nabongo, travel writerSwedish gummiesView image in fullscreenWhenever I’m in Stockholm, I stock up on soft, chewy pick-and-mix sweets from any grocery store, such as Hemköp – they have big bins of them. Not just a packet or two – but a whole carry-on case full of them.Kate BerryExtra virgin olive oilView image in fullscreenI always come home with something edible. In Greece, Italy or Portugal, that’s usually a bottle of exceptional olive oil – often locally pressed – or a few bottles of the local wine we discovered over dinner and want to enjoy again once we’re home.Natasha ShafiMacaronsView image in fullscreenControversial opinion: Ladurée macarons, with their charming pistachio-green boxes, are not, in fact, the finest macarons in Paris. For those, head toCarette. The flavours are a little punchier (my favourite is salted caramel), the filling is more generous, and at about €3 (£2.55) apiece, they make the perfect sweet treat for the journey home.Jess Cartner-MorleyClothingChic but cheap childrenswearView image in fullscreenNowhere in the world gives you as much chic for your money as the childrenswear department at French storeMonoprix. Think Bonpoint vibes at H&M prices. When my kids were little, I’d stock up every Paris fashion week, but there are branches all over France. They also do the most beautiful paper napkins which – being inexpensive, small and lightweight – make the perfect gifts to bring home.Jess Cartner-Morley,Guardian fashion editorEvil-eye braceletsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Getty Images/iStockphotoHave you even been to Greece and not come home with at least one evil eye hanging from your wrist or ankle? I know it’s officially summer when mine is back on my arm.Lucy Williams, stylist and content creatorLuxury scarves and shirtsView image in fullscreenI always buy a scarf from Hermès and aCharvet shirtin France – plus socks fromMes Chaussettes RougesandTabio, because they personalise with embroidery.Kate Berry, US editor at Cabana magazineVintage jacketsView image in fullscreenWhenever I’m in Paris, I always make time forSkat Vintageand, if it’s the weekend, a wander around Saint-Ouen flea market. I can rarely resist a vintage silk scarf or jacket, although they’re often claimed by my daughter before they make it into my wardrobe.Natasha Shafi, CEO at Mr & Mrs SmithBeautyWhite flower oilView image in fullscreenI always pick up this oil from Hong Kong. With menthol, eucalyptus and wintergreen, it provides instant relief from headaches and insect bites, and even helps clear the sinuses. Just dot a few drops on your wrists, temples and behind the ears.Divia Thani, global editorial director at Condé Nast TravellerPudinHaraView image in fullscreenIn India,Pudin Harais a traditional ayurvedic formulation. It’s a bright green blend of mint extract and peppermint oil that works quickly to ease all kinds of tummy-related issues, from cramps and acidity to bloating and indigestion.Divia ThaniContinentalcolognesView image in fullscreenThe first time I went to Spain, I remember catching a distinctive waft of cologne whenever I passed a suit on their way into their office in Barcelona. It was different from the muscular scents of home at the time; light, summery and somewhat continental. I finally plucked up the courage to ask someone what they were wearing, and it turned out to be Nenuco Agua de Colonia. Now I buy it whenever I go to Spain and literally bathe in it because it only costs a few euros. A Spanish friend recently told me, however, that it’s mostly used for babies. In France, I always buy Le Petit Marseillais Lait shower gel for the same olfactory associations with summer beaches.Andy Pietrasik, Guardian travel editorArtisan candlesView image in fullscreenIf you’re passing through Athens, you have to pick up something from TheNaxos Apothecary. They make the most beautiful artisan candles, body products and fragrances from Greek flora.Lucy WilliamsMelatoninView image in fullscreenI stock up at a CVS pharmacy whenever I travel to the US. I’m a good sleeper, but for those rare nights when I’m not, their over-the-counter melatonin is a lifesaver. CVS is also the best place to find brilliant little beauty buys you can’t get at home – such asPacha Soap Co’s natural deodorant.Teresa Tarmey, facialistHandmade razorsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Huizeng Hu/Getty ImagesIn Italy, I always seek out the traditional men’s toiletries shops and usually come home with a handmade razor, brush or pair of scissors. Italians do things like this so well: practical, timeless and made to last.Kate BerryNatural deodorantView image in fullscreenI recently discovered the fragrance store Zielinski & Rozen in Amsterdam and fell in love with theirnatural antiperspirant. I’m drawn to the scent of essential oils, so now I always hunt one down when I come across their boutiques.Phillippa FernFrench pharmacymoisturiserView image in fullscreenFrench pharmacies are a treasure trove. I always stock up onDucray Ictyane emollient cream. It’s cheap as chips, and the one product that doesn’t leave my husband’s skin feeling tight.Teresa TarmeyColgate WispsView image in fullscreenThese littleon-the-go toothbrushesare one of my must-buys whenever I’m in the US. They’re perfect for travel.Natasha Sullivan, cabin crewHomewaresLuxurious sheetsView image in fullscreenAs soon as I set foot in Paris, I head straight toMerci. The store was the first to make washed bed linen and napkins feel truly beautiful. Over the years, I’ve slowly added to my collection, so now I’ve got almost every shade.Lucinda Chambers, co-founder of fashion curation site CollagerieVintage digestif glassesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: BT1976/Getty Images/iStockphotoI rarely come home from a trip without a tiny glass and a bottle of whatever the country is best known for. The glass usually comes from a market or dusty antique shop, and the bottle is always something local that’s hard to find at home. I last picked up aManuel Vermouthwhile in Biarritz.Kirthanaa Naidu, stylist, cook and creative producerVases and other ceramicsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Laurence LeenaertYou have to hunt around Marrakech’s souks, but that’s part of the fun. I’ve brought back beautifully coloured vases – which I use as carafes – and mugs. I loveLRNCE studio, which brings together textiles, art and ceramics, with a use of colour that feels subtle and distinctive.Lucinda ChambersJugs and bowlsView image in fullscreenKostas Depastas in his workshop in Greece.Photograph: James Strachan/Getty ImagesSifnos is known as Greece’s ceramics island, thanks to its abundant clay supply, and it is home to some incredible potteries that have been producing pieces for generations. Up in Cheronissos Bay, you’ll find Kostas Depastas, who still uses a foot-operated wheel. He brings his love of engineering to his work, cleverly designing jugs and bowls alongside simple, spiral-decorated pieces.Lucy WilliamsSilicone baking matsView image in fullscreenE Dehillerin in Paris has every kitchen tool you could possibly imagine, especially for desserts and pastry. Their own-brandsilpats(silicone baking mats) are my favourite – chic green and white. I have about 10 in different sizes.Imogen Kwok, chefAntique buttonsand basketsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Stuart Bur/Getty Images/iStockphotoI always make a point of visiting the local flea market wherever I go – I can’t resist picking up exquisitely made antique buttons to sew on to clothes, as well as old picture frames. I’ll also always find a way to bring home a couple of baskets – the safest way is in a largeplastic striped market bagwith a good shoulder strap. I love that almost every culture around the world has its own tradition of weaving with natural materials.Hikari Yokoyama, founder of design studio Naum HouseRugsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Karici/Getty ImagesWe’re often in Istanbul visiting my wife’s family, and I always make time for Şişli’s Feriköy flea market. You can find all sorts of treasures there, including beautiful rugs at incredibly affordable prices.Patrick WilliamsArt materialsView image in fullscreenIn Milan, I came acrossPellegrini Breraart shop after visiting the Pinacoteca di Brera, and now I go back every time I’m there. They have these brilliant architecture drafting stencils, which I use when putting together proposals for food installations – perfect for when I need a break from the computer.Imogen KwokSecondhand camerasView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Yoshikazu Tsuno/AFP via Getty ImagesA highlight of any Tokyo trip has to be a visit to the Akihabara district – you feel like you’ve stepped into the future. There’s an abundance of used camera shops, and at Camera Kitamura I’ve picked up a mint condition, secondhand Fujifilm X10 at half the usual price. Lemon Camera and Imtiaz’s Camera Market are also great places to hunt for a bargain.Kash BhattacharyaExplore more on these topicsLife and styleBeautyFoodHomesInteriorsShopping tripsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It might be one of the most unpopular tunes ever written!’: kids’ TV composers tell all | Television | The Guardian
description: Big cheques, standing ovations, irate adults – there are surprising sides to composing a children’s TV theme tune. From Bluey to Byker Grove, the creators of the best reveal the secrets
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: Big cheques, standing ovations, irate adults – there are surprising sides to composing a children’s TV theme tune. From Bluey to Byker Grove, the creators of the best reveal the secrets
Content: Dog whistle … Bluey is one of the biggest kids’ shows in the world today.Photograph: DisneyView image in fullscreenDog whistle … Bluey is one of the biggest kids’ shows in the world today.Photograph: DisneyTelevision‘It might be one of the most unpopular tunes ever written!’: kids’ TV composers tell allBig cheques, standing ovations, irate adults – there are surprising sides to composing a children’s TV theme tune. From Bluey to Byker Grove, the creators of the best reveal the secretsMichael HoganFri 7 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 16.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow do you write TV theme music for children? Does it make you mega-rich? And does the tune itself eventually drive you (and parents everywhere) nuts?We tracked down the creators of half-a-dozen of TV’s greatest children’s show themes in order to find out. As Bluey’s Joff Bush told us: “The key lesson is that if you’re going to write a theme tune, make sure you really like it because you’re going to hear it a helluva lot!”From nostalgic cult classics to current hits, from cartoon animals to live-action school soaps, six composers confess the secrets of kids’ TV music …‘Parents get woken up at 6am by it’View image in fullscreenOn the hoof … a demo track was used as the Peppa Pig theme for 20 years.Photograph: Album/AlamyComposerJulian NottscoresPeppa Pig, as well asWallace & Gromit,BingandBen & Holly’s Little Kingdom.It all started at the National Film andTelevisionSchool’s animation department. Two fellow students became friends: Nick Park, who did Wallace & Gromit, and Mark Baker, who did Peppa Pig. They’ve been collaborators ever since.Peppa was just another job that came along. I worked on the pilot episode for free as a favour. It wasn’t just the same theme tune as today, it was the same recording. We finally updated it last year but for two decades they used the demo version. It’s only 10 seconds long which is shorter than most title sequences. It was a challenge to write a short, sharp, catchy tune. It had to be fast and fun with a memorable melody. The gaps in it were exploited by Mark, who inserted oinking sound effects.We classical musicians tend to laugh at pop writers for only knowing three chords but Peppa has two, which is probably a musical outrage. There was zero budget, so it’s all played on synthesisers and samplers. The instrumentation which became associated with Peppa – marimbas, timpani, glockenspiel, vibraphone – were only chosen because they were the most convincing samples you could get back then.Peppa took over the world, so I hear my music all the time. I’m often in a cafe or airport and a child will be playing it on their iPad. I’m tempted to lean over and say: ‘I wrote that!’ but never have. There was a time when I couldn’t get on a train without hearing it. It’s a strange feeling. Kids watch their favourite shows on repeat, so it can drive parents mad. Toddlers work out how to switch on Peppa Pig and their parents get woken up at 6am by the theme music. It might be one of the most unpopular tunes ever written! But I’m very lucky that it’s given me financial security. Peppa Pig was like winning the lottery. It’s enabled me to sustain a career. It’s all upside and it’s marvellous.‘It was the luckiest two minutes of my life’View image in fullscreenRing of success … the cast of Saved By the Bell.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyScott Galewrote the theme song forNBC’s 1990s teen sitcom Saved Bythe Bell.I was music coordinator onThe Golden Girls. One Friday, the producer of this new teen comedy called and asked me to try out for the theme tune. My wife had left me that morning but I put down the phone, picked up my guitar and, bingo, it just poured out of me. It was the luckiest two minutes of my life. We recorded it over the weekend at my partner Rich Eames’s home studio.On Monday morning, we handed in our cassette. Little did I know that executive producer Peter Engel had told all the other prospective composers not to include “saved by the bell” in the lyrics because he wasn’t sure the name would stick. But I never got that message, so the title appeared five times in mine. Peter later admitted he was glad I didn’t get his instructions.Saved By the Bell was the first live-action Saturday morning kids’ show. Everything else was cartoons. I thought it’d be lucky to last seven episodes but it ran for four seasons. And the show, thank goodness, was heavy on music. We wrote it all. If there was a jukebox playing, we’d write the songs. The characters formed a rock group. We wrote what they played. There was something new every week.Saved By the Bell was very good to me. I still get royalties from Spain, South Africa, everywhere. Those gigs are hard to get but it’s the gift that keeps on giving. I never tire of hearing it. I’ll chance across it while channel surfing and it whisks me back to those wild times. Nearly four decades later, I still get to talk about it. It’s nothing but wonderful.‘I ended up writing songs with Ant and Dec’View image in fullscreenLimitless win … regular royalties from Byker Grove – the show that launched Ant and Dec – are a boon for theme composers the Kane Gang.Photograph: ITVMartin Brammeris the frontman of pop triothe Kane Gang, whose track became the basis of the theme tune to Byker Grove.We’d already reworked our song Small Town Creed to be the jingle for Radio 1 DJ Gary Davies’s show. The makers of this local teen drama – a sort of Geordie version of Grange Hill – asked if the Kane Gang fancied doing the theme tune. Either out of expedience or laziness, we thought: “Hang on! Maybe we can get a third version out of it.”It’s a challenge to create something impactful in 45 seconds. It became this tongue-in-cheek funk workout, a bit edgier than the average kids’ TV tune. A dozen of the cast came down to do the “Ooh, Byker Grove!” chants. That little laugh at the end was from Lyndyann Barrass, who played Spuggie. We liked it and left it in. People tend to remember that laugh. A few years ago, I got a request from another artist – Professor Green or someone – to sample it.The show ran for 18 series, so royalties make a handy annual bonus. It’s not a life-changing amount of money but it’s hard making a living in music nowadays, so sidelines that tick over are invaluable. Midway through the run, we redid it slightly. Put a funky drummer sample on it to make it more contemporary. Byker Grove led to all sorts of connections. I did some work with Donna Air’s pop duo Crush and songwriting sessions withAnt and Decas they were moving away from being PJ & Duncan. Lovely lads.I’ve written hundreds of proper songs but the Byker Grove tune always gets a reaction. I write with Olly Murs now and he flipped when he found out. Now there’s a reboot in development. It would be madness to change the theme tune, right? Fingers crossed we get the call from Ant and Dec.‘Kids are disappointed that I’m not a six-year-old girl’View image in fullscreenHeeler dealer … Daley Pearson wrote the Bluey theme tune.Photograph: Ludo StudioJoff Bushwrote the theme music and composes most of the soundtrack for globally loved animation Bluey.I met Daley Pearson [Bluey’s executive producer] when we were students. In 2017, he said: “Would you be interested in coming up to Brisbane for this side project we’ve got? It’s called Bluey, for four to six-year-olds.” I was like: “I doubt I’m the right fit but I’ll check it out.” I’ll be forever grateful that I did. I met [Bluey’s creator] Joe Brumm and we clicked. I watched the rough pilot episodes and just fell in love. I had do it.I knew exactly what the show’s sound should be. A bit hand-made with an almost chamber ensemble sound. It’s hard to describe but I could hear the chord progression in my head. When the writing’s that good, it’s relatively easy to score. Joe Brumm makes my music look better. I suggested building a library of music which we could reuse but Joe wanted something new for every episode. I was like: “That’s a lot of work!” But it became one of the beauties of Bluey.They were going to license a track for the theme tune but I said: “Can I have a go at it?” And then I had 10 goes at it! Version eight unlocked it. Now it’s hard to imagine without the theme song. It probably sounds simpler than it is. There are little details in it that only I notice. Parents tend to be more impressed than children. If I tell a kid that I write the music for the show, they’ll ask: “Are you Bluey?” “No.” “Oh, OK.” They’re disappointed that I’m a 41-year-old man, not a six-year-old girl. That keeps your ego in check.I’m fortunate that my work’s more famous than me. Bluey’s been great for opening up career opportunities and pretty lucrative. The albums have topped the charts. It’s enabled me to work on strange projects that I want to do, rather than taking adverts to pay the rent. I’m just starting on a ballet.I recently became a father and suddenly understood why dads find Bluey so emotional. I messaged Joe saying: “I get it now!” My daughter’s two and last week, she came back from daycare going: “Doo doo doo doo, Bluey and Bingo!” I was like: “Do you like that song?” She said: “It’s pretty good.” We rerecorded it last year and I got some cute photos of her conducting the orchestra. I’ll surprise her with them someday. Then again, I was singing Wagon Ride to her to help her go to sleep. She woke up, put her hand over my mouth and went: “Different music.” She’s my harshest critic.‘My fee definitely wasn’t Scrooge McDuck money’View image in fullscreenQuacked it … the DuckTales intro is known worldwide.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyPop and musical theatre songwriterMark Muellercomposed the theme tune forlate 80s Disney seriesDuckTales.I’d just had my first top 10 single, having writtenNothin’ at All by Heart. That’s how I got the meeting at Disney for DuckTales. The execs told me: “Write a radio song, not a cartoon song,” with lots of action in the lyrics they could animate to. That’s why I came up with “race cars, lasers, aeroplanes ... it’s a duck blur”. I jammed as many moving images as possible into 60 seconds.After the meeting, I drove back to my tiny apartment and wrote the song in 45 minutes on a second-hand Roland synthesiser. I was in a groove and it spilled out of me. I took the demo back to Disney and played it to them in person. They sent it all the way up to the head of the studio, who loved it. My head was spinning. Seldom does anything happen that quickly in Hollywood.There are so many hooks in DuckTales. Everything from the intro bass lick to the “d-d-dangers” were meant to worm into your brain. The “woo-hoos” fitted perfectly into three empty beats. Vanity Fair called it “history’s catchiest single minute of music”. To me, catchy isn’t a dirty word. It’s what I strive for. My initial fee was $1,250, which definitely wasn’t Scrooge McDuck money. It barely paid for a month’s rent but thankfully, the royalties were good and they keep coming in.After the show aired, I received a letter from the mother of an autistic child. She told me that she and her husband had never been able to communicate with their young son until he heard the DuckTales song. They would sing it to each other and it was the first time they truly connected. That touched me.Its global reach is heady stuff. I went to South Korea and my rather somber tour guide had it as his ringtone. A few months ago in Portugal, a strait-laced female banker launched into it. I heard it from tinny speakers on a rickshaw in London. The impact that this minute-long song had on my life is immeasurable. The experience has been a perfect whirlwind – or should I say “duck blur”?‘I got a £14,000 cheque for ringtones from Japan’View image in fullscreenDanger money … Mike Harding did well out of his kids’ TV scores.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyWriter, comedian and musicianMike Hardingcomposed the scores forDanger Mouseand its spin-offCount Duckula.“Manchester studio Cosgrove Hall Films were fans of my standup, so they asked if I had any ideas for animations. We made a pilot about a busking frog called Far-Out Fred and I did the music for The Reluctant Dragon. Then they said they’d got this mouse super-agent but it wasn’t quite working. I took a look and said: “You’re trying to make him a James Bond character, too rooted in the real world. You realise this is a mouse living in a pillar box? He can do whatever we like.”I went away and wrote some scripts. I based arch enemy Baron Greenback on this real-life nemesis of mine called Alan Greenbank and made him an evil toad. When it came to the theme music, I studied 60s spy films and wrote a pastiche. Sort of Bond meets Dick Tracy. We dragged in local session musicians and put it together.Danger Mouse became a classic of its time. David Jason and Terry Scott were terrific at the voices. The animators were amazing. It was a joy to be part of. People felt real warmth towards it. I once stood in for Seamus Heaney at short notice, giving the opening speech at an Irish school arts festival. When I said I wrote the music for Danger Mouse, the kids went wild. I got what my grandad used to call a “standing ovation”.We still get royalty cheques. The biggest was one year when we got £14,000 from Japan for ringtones. There was a CBBC remake a decade ago which went worldwide but the royalties from Kuala Lumpur are tuppence. I only get a standing ovation from old people nowadays. But I still have a T-shirt saying “The bloke who wrote the music for Danger Mouse”!Explore more on these topicsTelevisionBlueyPeppa PigAnt and DecfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Millions in England face longer waits for mental health care as NHS providers plan cuts | Mental health | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Seven in 10 survey respondents expect services to be reduced or shut, while more than half anticipate job losses
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Exclusive: Seven in 10 survey respondents expect services to be reduced or shut, while more than half anticipate job losses
Content: Demand for NHS mental health services has risen rapidly amid growing pressure on existing provision.Photograph: Roos Koole/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDemand for NHS mental health services has risen rapidly amid growing pressure on existing provision.Photograph: Roos Koole/Getty ImagesMental healthMillions in England face longer waits for mental health care as NHS providers plan cutsExclusive: Seven in 10 survey respondents expect services to be reduced or shut, while more than half anticipate job lossesAndrew GregoryHealth editorFri 7 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMillions of adults and children inEnglandface being forced to wait longer for mental health care, with more than two-thirds of NHS providers planning to cut services and half expected to axe jobs, the Guardian can reveal.With mental health services already under extraordinary pressure amid soaring demand for support, experts warned the proposed cuts – drawn up by trusts to plug holes in their finances – would also have “significant” consequences for the widerNHS, the economy and public services.Key services such as child and adolescent mental health care, talking therapies, addiction support, help for adults undergoing a mental health crisis and community programmes, including those for ethnic minorities and low-income groups, areamong those that may be affected.Seven in 10 (68%) NHS trusts providing mental health services are likely to reduce or shut some of their services in 2026-27, according to the results of a national survey conducted by the NHS Alliance and seen by the Guardian.Of respondents, 59% said they expect to freeze vacancies, with more than half (57%) likely to cut the number of clinical staff they employ this year.Earlier this week, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, announced plans to create a network of nearly 200 community mental health centres and mental health A&Es by 2029. Writingon LinkedIn, he said: “These services will make it much easier for people to get the right support, at the right time, in the right place.”View image in fullscreenThe UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, announced plans to launch additional community health centres this week.Photograph: Jack Taylor/Reuters Pool/APMental health charities welcomed the ambition but said if funding for staff and services was being cut, meaningful improvements to care would be “impossible”.One of the NHS mental health trusts affected, East London foundation trust, plans to cut a wide range of services and axe hundreds of jobs to close a £25m hole in its finances,the Guardian reportedon Monday.NHS mental health professionals at other trusts said similar plans were being drawn up where they work. They fear the cuts will strip back services so much that they will not be able to properly perform their duties or guarantee safe care in their areas.An NHS consultant psychiatrist, speaking on condition of anonymity, said: “This is not an isolated example in east London. Many mental health trusts are in a similar, if not worse, situation and are responding in similar ways through cutting jobs and compromising service delivery.”A mental health service manager at a third NHS mental health trust said: “Many mental health trusts are in a similar position. They have faced declining funding for the last couple of years alongside cost reduction targets.”Alex Stewart, assistant director of the NHS Alliance’s mental health network, said: “Mental health services are coming under extraordinary pressure as a result of rapidly rising demand for care and very tough financial conditions.“Despite this, we see many examples of innovation and great care which give real grounds for hope. But it’s increasingly evident that the trade-offs and difficult decisions over jobs and services which we warned about are making their mark.“Mental health leaders face particular pressures when finances are tight because a higher proportion of their expenditure goes on staff.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStudy finds three midlife health factors that could delay dementia for 13 yearsRead moreThe NHS Alliance survey, conducted in March before the new financial year, revealed widespread concerns about the need to make record efficiency savings in 2026-27.There were also concerns among the 37 NHS mental health providers responding to the poll that the focus on balancing the books would impede progress on providing more care outside hospital settings and increasing preventive mental health care.One NHS mental health trust leader told the survey there was “no investment for mental health community services” and their teams were “under resourced” to manage the rise in demand.Stewart said: “We welcome recent announcements on capital funding for community mental health centres and the confirmation of targets to improve access to mental health care. But in the face of rising demand, the share of national NHS spend on mental health is expected to reduce for the third year in a row.“It is essential that mental health investment is not allowed to fall behind, as the consequences of underfunding mental health for the wider NHS, the economy and public services will be significant.”Tom Pollard, the head of policy, public affairs and campaigns at Mind, said the results of the survey showed “the huge uphill battle we face” to save mental health services in England and ensure everyone could access high-quality care.He said: “The government set out a welcome ambition to move towards a more open access model of support through neighbourhood mental health centres. But if funding for staff and services is being cut, meaningful improvements to the mental health system will be impossible.”Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the trade union Unite, said: “We cannot balance the books on the backs of the most vulnerable in society and by underfunding mental health provision you simply kick the can down the road and it costs more in the long term.“Our members at health trusts across the country are outraged at attempts to cut jobs and services and will be fighting back with the full support of their union.”A Department ofHealthand Social Care spokesperson said: “As well as investing a record £16.1bn into mental health services this year, we have recruited more than 8,500 additional mental health workers since this government came into office, and only this week, we announced the rollout of 159 new NHS mental health facilities across England, backed by £343m in funding.“Later this year, our mental health strategy will outline how we plan to future-proof the mental health system, including responding earlier and reducing waiting times for support.”Explore more on these topicsMental healthHealthHealth policyNHSEnglandAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cambridge academics reject university’s attempt to end row over Jason Arday | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Group calls for ‘thorough and transparent investigation’ of hiring of professor who resigned after his claims came under scrutiny
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Group calls for ‘thorough and transparent investigation’ of hiring of professor who resigned after his claims came under scrutiny
Content: Jason Arday was selected as a torchbearer for the London 2012 Olympics.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAView image in fullscreenJason Arday was selected as a torchbearer for the London 2012 Olympics.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAJason ArdayCambridge academics reject university’s attempt to end row over Jason ArdayGroup calls for ‘thorough and transparent investigation’ of hiring of professor who resigned after his claims came under scrutinyRichard Adams, Education editorFri 7 Aug 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 17.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUniversity of Cambridgehas announced a review into the way it vets and hires senior academic staff in an effort to fend off external and internal criticism of its appointment of Jason Arday as a professor.But a group of Cambridge academics quickly rejected the university’s response, saying: “We strongly believe that a thorough and transparent investigation into the wider circumstances of this damaging episode is essential.”Ardayresigned earlier this weekafter mounting scepticism over his personal and professional claims, three-and-a-half years after he was acclaimed as Cambridge’s youngest black professor with a life story of educational disadvantage, including being unable to speak until the age of 11.Dons call for Cambridge leaders to take blame for Jason Arday appointmentRead moreCambridge sources said that university and college leaders had hoped Arday’s resignation would end the controversy. But internal anger has continued to grow over his appointment process and the threats to the university’s black staff from toxic media commentary.In a statementissued on Friday, Cambridge said: “Jason Arday has resigned from his post at the university with immediate effect. Regardless of this, and for clarification, the university will continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday’s appointment and tenure.“The findings will feed into a review of the process for the appointment of senior academic roles. In addition, and as previously stated, the university’s research policy committee will review the misconduct in research policy.”The Guardianrevealed on Thursdaythat Cambridge academics were demanding the university carry out a thorough investigation.The letter sent on Friday to Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, highlights the “toxic and frequently racist commentary” that has accompanied much of the online and media coverage, adding: “These manifestly false claims have the potential to set back the modest progress Cambridge has made in addressing historical underrepresentation, and to deter any Black academic from applying for or accepting a position at the university in the future.”Prentice became vice-chancellor of Cambridge in July 2023, after Arday’s appointment earlier that year.View image in fullscreenProf Deborah Prentice.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianThe letter states: “We therefore ask that you appoint an independent body comprising senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge to address these issues, with a clear timeline for completing its work and a commitment to share its findings with the university and the public.”The nearly 100 signatories are senior professors and Cambridge academics, including Suchitra Sebastian, a professor of physics, and Mónica Figueroa, a professor of sociology, as well as Timothy Gowers, a past winner of the Field medal for mathematics. Other prominent names include Nicholas Guyatt, a professor of North American history, Mary Laven, a professor of early modern history, Anuj Dawar, a professor of logic, and Clair Wills, the King Edward VII professor of English literature.The signatories want an independent investigation into the circumstances of Arday’s appointment, and any risk assessment made by the university’s management “when crafting a media narrative focusing on his youth, his race, and his transformative potential”.It also wants details of the university’s handling of allegations of academic misconduct against Arday, including whether the university was involved in efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations.The university has denied supporting Arday’s efforts to stop publication of critical coverage in the Times Higher magazine last year, or funding his use of lawyers.The signatories also call for an evaluation of the “enormous damage this episode has done to people of colour within and beyond the Cambridge academic community, and what can be done immediately to reassure them – and the wider public – that anti-racism and academic integrity at Cambridge are both essential and mutually reinforcing.”The rise and fall of Jason Arday: a full rundown of the questions being askedRead moreHowever, Cambridge’s Jesus College – where Arday was a fellow – has said it will drop its previously announced plans to carry out a parallel “process” to the university’s investigation first revealed on Wednesday evening.A message to staff from Sonita Alleyne, the college’s master, said: “Because Professor Arday’s college fellowship was contingent on his university appointment, his resignation brought his fellowship to an end. The college’s acceptance of his resignation concludes the process announced in last night’s statement.“This is a very difficult time for Professor Arday and his family. As he requested in his resignation letter, we hope that they are now afforded peace and privacy.”One Cambridge academic said the message showed that the university wanted to “draw a line” under the affair in the hope that it would subside.Arday’s resignation on Wednesday followed intense media scrutiny, beginning with accusations of plagiarism and followed by questions overa string of his claimsranging from endurance running and charity fundraising to confrontations with masked assailants.Cambridge initially defended Arday as “the victim of a vile campaign” before announcing that it would conduct an internal investigation of “new information” regarding Arday, who then resigned shortly after.On Friday night, the University of Glasgow said it would review its past appointment of Arday as a professor.A university spokesperson said: “Jason Arday was employed as professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow, from January 2022 to March 2023.“He left the university to take up his role as professorial chair at the University of Cambridge.“The principal has commissioned a review of the appointment with the aim of understanding all the facts and learning lessons for the future.”Explore more on these topicsJason ArdayUniversity of CambridgeHigher educationAcademicsUniversitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police investigating Ann Widdecombe murder reopen attempted burglary case from 2025 | Ann Widdecombe | The Guardian
description: Failure to pursue line of inquiry ‘which may have been relevant’ now being investigated by police watchdog
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Failure to pursue line of inquiry ‘which may have been relevant’ now being investigated by police watchdog
Content: Ann Widdecombe was found dead with serious injuries at her home in Devon on 9 July.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAnn Widdecombe was found dead with serious injuries at her home in Devon on 9 July.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianAnn WiddecombePolice investigating Ann Widdecombe murder reopen attempted burglary case from 2025Watchdog examines alleged failure to pursue a line of inquiry ‘which may have been relevant’Nadeem BadshahFri 7 Aug 2026 18.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCounter-terrorism police investigating the death ofAnn Widdecombesay they have reopened an old investigation into an attempted burglary last year.The incident at an address in Greater London was reported in April 2025.Since the case was reopened, CTP London said it had identified a line of inquiry “which may have been relevant” but was “not identified and pursued by [counter-terrorism police] at the time”.The police watchdog said it is now investigating the conduct of a CTP London staff member over allegations they “failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry” related to the attempted burglary.Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism policing, said: “As part of the ongoing investigation led by counter-terrorism policing south-east into the murder of Ann Widdecombe, officers have reopened an investigation into an incident reported to police last year.”CTP London made a “mandatory conduct referral” to the Independent Office forPoliceConduct (IOPC) on Friday.A spokesperson for the IOPC said: “We can confirm that the IOPC has decided to independently investigate the conduct of a counter-terrorism policing London staff member following a referral received earlier today.“The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025.“Counter-terrorism policing London has been notified of our decision, and no further information is available at this early stage.”Widdecombe, 78, a former Conservative minister, was found dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.Last month, a 28-year-old man was charged with the former MP’s murder.Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July.He was also arrested on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism but has not been charged with this offence.Devon and Cornwall police initially arrested a 26-year-old man from Newton Abbot in Devon, but later released him and said he was no longer part of the investigation.Widdecombe served as Conservative MP for Maidstone, Kent for 23 years. She subsequently represented south-west England as a member of the European parliament for the Brexit party and in 2023 joined Reform UK as a party spokesperson.Explore more on these topicsAnn WiddecombePoliceUK security and counter-terrorismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police and prosecution errors left proven sex offender free to murder two women in London | Crime | The Guardian
description: Delays to sexual assault charges and failures to report past convictions in court hearings gave Simon Levy chance to attack more women
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Delays to sexual assault charges and failures to report past convictions in court hearings gave Simon Levy chance to attack more women
Content: A screengrab from bodyworn video footage of Simon Levy being arrested in September 2025.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAA screengrab from bodyworn video footage of Simon Levy being arrested in September 2025.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PACrimePolice and prosecution errors left proven sex offender free to murder two women in LondonDelays to sexual assault charges and failures to report past convictions in court hearings gave Simon Levy chance to attack more womenViolence against women: has anything changed in policing since Sarah Everard’s killing?Vikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentFri 7 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTFirst published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 09.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCatastrophic errors left a persistent and proven sex offender free before he murdered two women in London, it can be revealed.On Friday, an Old Bailey jury found Simon Levy, 40, guilty of murdering Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo in March 2025 and Sheryl Wilkins five months later.Levy was on bail as a suspect for the first murder when he committed the second, after police said they lacked sufficient evidence to charge him.Months before the first killing, police arrested Levy for sexual assaults of women on trains but made errors that delayed charging him. While on bail, he carried out further attacks, taking the total to 10 across London. Although charged with most of the offences, Levy remained free and went on to commit his second murder.Prosecutors also admitted to bungling efforts to have Levy remanded in custody, by failing to provide three court hearings with key information demonstrating the full extent of the danger he posed to women.Simon Levy murders: has anything changed in policing since Sarah Everard’s killing?Read moreYet even before the attacks on women travelling by train, police and prosecutors knew Levy posed a serious risk.He was first jailed for a sexual offence in 2021. While in prison, he sexually assaulted a female prison officer.After his release, he carried out a series of sexual assaults on trains across London between 2023 and 2025. He was also the prime suspect in a rape investigation.In January, March and August 2025, Levy, from Tottenham in north London, savagely attacked three women who provided sexual services, killing two and leaving one seriously injured.The jury convicted him by an 11-1 majority of the murder of Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in a partly disused tower block on 17 March 2025. The scene was close to where Levy had lived after his release from prison following his first convictions for sexual offences.The jury was unanimous on all other verdicts and found him guilty of the murder of Wilkins, 39, in a Tottenham car park on 24 August 2025.View image in fullscreenSheryl Wilkins (left) and Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo.Photograph: Metropolitan policeHe was convicted of raping and attacking a third woman, 35, in January 2025, who survived. She was attacked in the same Tottenham car park, eight minutes’ walk from the home Levy shared with his mother and sister.Levy was impassive, wearing dark glasses because of an eye injury, as the jury delivered its verdicts, which condemned him to the mandatory life sentence for murder. He will be sentenced on Wednesday.The Crown Prosecution Service, the Metropolitan police and British Transport Police have admitted making errors.Kevin Southworth, a deputy assistant commissioner at the Met, which investigated the killings, described Levy as a “predatory monster”.
