He said Wilkins, the second woman murdered by Levy, would probably have been alive were it not for what he described as “collective system failures”.The litany of failings can only be reported now that Levy’s murder trial has ended, leading to the lifting of reporting restrictions on that and a trial earlier this year.A jury in February convicted him of 10 sexual assaults on trains, including one on a daughter travelling with her mother, as well as the attack on a female prison officer while he was in jail.View image in fullscreenScreengrab from CCTV footage showing Levy at Seven Sisters station in north London.Photograph: British Transport Police/PAPolice arrested Levy for a number of attacks on trains in November 2024, with CCTV tying him to the scene of the assaults. Six more occurred in the first five months of 2025. By May 2025, police wanted Levy remanded, fearing he posed a “high risk of reoffending” with his crimes “escalating”.The CPS admitted errors at three court hearings in May, June and August 2025, which ended in Levy remaining free. It would not specify publicly what those were, but a source authorised to speak for the organisation said they included failing to mention he had been arrested for Valencia-Trujillo’s murder, and that it could find no record or mention of Levy’s past sexual assault convictions, nor that he was a suspect in a 2024 rape.The CPS said: “We accept there was relevant information regarding bail that was not provided to the court when bail applications were being considered. Our actions fell short of the standards that victims, families and the public are entitled to expect … We could and should have taken a more robust approach to representations about bail.”Other errors and questionable decisions included:Levy failed to attend three crown court hearings for the train attacks, and the CPS accepts there is no evidence of a warrant being sought for his detention. For two he claimed illness, for the other that he had not been informed. His final non-appearance in crown court was on 11 August 2025. A fortnight later he murdered Wilkins. A CPS source said individuals involved in the Levy case had been disciplined.The assaults on the London tube network and trains were investigated by BTP. Officers arrested Levy, who was travelling on a stolen Oyster travel card, but handed it back to him, unaware it was stolen. With it he travelled to south London to commit his first murder, and carried out further sexual assaults on trains.BTP admitted the charging of Levy for his sexual assaults on trains in November 2024 was held up because of a delay in holding an identification parade after his arrest. His bail was extended, and during this delay he attacked and raped another woman and murdered Valencia-Trujillo. BTP said it had not referred its errors to the police watchdog. Instead it has moved one officer, who it says delayed the holding of the ID parade, out of investigations, and given a supervisor words of advice.BTP identified Levy as a suspect and charged him but never searched his home. Peter Fulton, BTP’s head of crime, said: “There’s a fine line between going fishing and breaching someone’s human rights.” He said that every woman who had reported Levy for attacking them on a train had seen him charged and convicted. When the Met, which investigated the murders, searched Levy’s home, evidence was found about his attack on the prison officer.The police watchdog has placed two Met officers under investigation over whether Levy was supervised correctly as a person on the sex offender register. A constable is under investigation for gross misconduct, meaning he could be dismissed. The other officer, under investigation for misconduct, is a detective sergeant.The Met downgraded his risk as a sex offender from high to medium in August 2024, in part because Levy was blind in one eye. The attack that damaged his eye occurred days after Levy is alleged to have raped a woman in May 2024 in north London, and detectives believe it was a reprisal for that.The failings come despite decades of promises from police chiefs, senior prosecutors, courts and government that the criminal justice system will better protect women from male violence after a series of scandals.View image in fullscreenLevy seen walking away from the car park at the back of a store in Tottenham, north London.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAHarriet Wistrich, of the Centre for Women’s Justice, said an independent inquiry was needed, while Andrea Simon, London’s victims’ commissioner, said: “There are striking parallels with other cases where escalating risk was not acted upon, with devastating and preventable consequences.“Critical opportunities to intervene were missed, despite him being a known violent offender.”The crime and policing minister, Sarah Jones, described Levy as a monster and said the failings that had allowed him to remain free were “deeply concerning”.Jones signalled the government would allow the relevant institutions and police watchdog to establish what went wrong. “The fact that Levy was able to inflict such devastating harm after being freed by police and the courts is deeply concerning,” she said. “It raises serious questions that require urgent answers.”Explore more on these topicsCrimeRape and sexual assaultViolence against women and girlsLondonEnglandMetropolitan policeCrown Prosecution ServicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Wasted medicine in England could fill 75 swimming pools a year, pharmacy group says | Pharmaceuticals industry | The Guardian
description: Industry body calls for greater scrutiny of patients with multiple repeat prescriptions to tackle ‘growing problem’
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Industry body calls for greater scrutiny of patients with multiple repeat prescriptions to tackle ‘growing problem’
Content: The National Pharmacy Association estimated that wasted medicine costs the NHS more than £480m annually.Photograph: Flavio Brancaleone/AAPView image in fullscreenThe National Pharmacy Association estimated that wasted medicine costs the NHS more than £480m annually.Photograph: Flavio Brancaleone/AAPPharmaceuticals industryWasted medicine in England could fill 75 swimming pools a year, pharmacy group saysIndustry body calls for more regular reviews of repeat prescriptions to tackle ‘growing problem’Nadeem BadshahFri 7 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe amount of wasted medicines thrown away inEnglandin one year could fill 75 swimming pools, according to a pharmacy group.The National Pharmacy Association (NPA) estimated that 3,400 tonnes of partly used medicines were disposed of in England in 2024-25.The organisation, which analysed data from regional health bodies, also estimated that the problem costs theNHSat least £480m annually.Olivier Picard, chair of the NPA, said: “Wasted medicines cost theNHSsignificant sums of money every year that could be invested in better services for patients.“More than this, wasting medicines can have environmental and health consequences, and we can do much more to tackle this growing problem.“As soon as a medicine leaves apharmacy, even if it is not used and is unopened, it must be disposed of, so it is important patients only get medicines they are sure they will use.”The NPA, which represents 6,000 independent community pharmacies in the UK, called for patients with several repeat prescriptions to have more reviews so that medicines that were no longer needed could be identified.It also urged the public not to “over order” medicine.Picard added: “We are urging patients only to request medicines if they really need them when ordering repeat prescriptions.A bitter pill: are you wasting your money on supplements?Read more“As well as this, patients who are prescribed multiple medicines should have these more regularly reviewed to ensure they are being fully utilised.“If a patient has any concerns about their medicines, they should speak to their pharmacist who can help them get the most out of their medicines.”Dr Rasha Abdelsalam Elshenawy, a senior lecturer at the University of Hertfordshire, said surplus medicines “aren’t only a financial and environmental problem – it’s a patient safety and resistance problem”.She added: “Leftover antibiotics kept at home are often taken later without medical advice, which fuels antimicrobial resistance, one of the biggest threats to modern medicine.“Regular medication reviews and only ordering what is needed protects patients, the NHS and the environment.”An NHS England spokesperson said it had taken action to ensure people could better manage their prescriptions on their mobile phones through the NHS app, including repeat prescriptions.“We know there is more to do, which is why several local NHS services are running campaigns to reduce medicines waste, alongside wider efforts to optimise medicines use that have also seen the total number of dependency-forming medications prescribed fall over the last decade,” they added.In June, health leaders warned that Britons were facing some of the“most severe” shortages of NHS medicines on record, including common painkillers, epilepsy drugs and HRT.The NPA and the Royal College of GPs highlighted long-lasting supply issues affecting Estradot, a hormone replacement therapy (HRT) medicine used by menopausal women, and Creon, a drug taken by people with pancreatic cancer and cystic fibrosis to help them digest food.Explore more on these topicsPharmaceuticals industryEnglandNHSHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Appeals court halts construction of Trump’s $400m White House ballroom | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Ruling put on hold for two weeks, allowing administration to appeal to US supreme court
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: Ruling put on hold for two weeks, allowing administration to appeal to US supreme court
Content: Donald Trump at the site of construction of the planned White House ballroom in Washington DC on 19 May 2026.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump at the site of construction of the planned White House ballroom in Washington DC on 19 May 2026.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersDonald TrumpAppeals court halts construction of Trump’s $400m White House ballroomRuling put on hold for two weeks, allowing administration to appeal to US supreme courtUS politics live – latest updatesRobert Taitin WashingtonFri 7 Aug 2026 13.41 EDTFirst published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA US federal appeals court has ordered the Trump administration to haltconstruction of the US president’s $400m White House ballroom, in a fresh blow to the controversial project.Trump administration quietly shifts $352m in federal funds for White House ballroomRead moreDonald Trump, whodemolished the historic East Wingof the White House last year to make way for planned ballroom, has repeatedly touted it as “a gift” to the US people.But in a major setback in a case testing ⁠his presidential authority, the Washington-based US ⁠court of ​appeals for the District of Columbia circuit upheld a preliminary injunction in a divided 2-1 order on Friday.The appeals court put ⁠its ruling on hold for two weeks, allowing the administration to appeal to the ​US supreme court. Writing on social media, Trump described the ruling as “totally wrong” and said an appeal would be filed.Explaining their majority decision, Judges Patricia Millet and Bradley Garcia wrote: “Each President is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House and its Executive Residence.”The judges also said it was for US Congress to determine whether the ballroom could ultimately be built. “Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help,” they wrote.“This holding has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy,” the judges added. “This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom.“What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court’s expeditious litigation without securing Congress’s authorization, as the constitution and laws require.”Trump criticized the decision, which he argued “severely jeopardizes the lives and welfare of the people who work, and will be working”, at the White House. “This unjust decision must be overturned by the Supreme Court in its entirety.”A third judge on the panel, Neomi Rao, who was appointed by Trump, dissented and sided with the president’s assertion that the ballroom project was within his authority. Her position earned praised from the president in his social media statement on Friday.The injunction was won by the National Trust for Historic ⁠Preservation, which sued last year after the Trump administration tore down the East Wing and began building a 90,000 sq ft (8,360 sq meter) ballroom without seeking authorization from Congress.The latest decision supports an earlier ruling issued by a US federal judge in April, which limited the construction project only to the undergound part of the project deemed necessary on national security grounds while blocking the hospitality facility envisioned by Trump for entertaining guests.At the time, Trump lambasted that decision, by Judge Richard Leon – appointed to the bench during George W Bush’s presidency – as the work of a “Trump Hating” judge who he alleged had “gone out of his way to undermine National Security, and to make sure that this Great Gift to America gets delayed, or doesn’t get built”.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpLaw (US)Washington DCnewsShareReuse this content

title: Black barrister was told ‘it’s not for defendants’ at London court car park | Law | The Guardian
description: Stephen Akinsanya says being mistaken for defendant shows lack of progress on racism within legal system
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Stephen Akinsanya says being mistaken for defendant shows lack of progress on racism within legal system
Content: Stephen Akinsanya: ‘There is still a perception that, if you’re black, you’re more likely not to be the lawyer, you’re more likely to be a defendant’.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenStephen Akinsanya: ‘There is still a perception that, if you’re black, you’re more likely not to be the lawyer, you’re more likely to be a defendant’.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianLawBlack barrister was told ‘it’s not for defendants’ at London court car parkStephen Akinsanya says being mistaken for defendant shows lack of progress on racism within legal systemHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentFri 7 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA black barrister has said a security guard told him he could not park in a court’s car park inLondonbecause “it’s not for defendants”.Stephen Akinsanya, who in June was awarded an OBE for raising awareness of youth knife crime and its prevention, said the incident, at an east London court about four weeks ago, illustrated the lack of progress on racism within the criminal justice system.He said: “It was a sort of reflection of what happened when I first qualified back in 1993, going into the same court, being asked by a security guard which case I was on trial in. And as a junior lawyer thinking: well, why does it have to be that I’m the one on trial? Why can it not be that I’m the lawyer?“And then 33 years later, pulling up in my car to park in the same court building, a security guard saying: ‘You can’t park here.’ And when I said why, he said: ‘Defendants can’t park in the car park.’”The barrister, who first mentioned the incident in a Criminal Bar Association podcast published this week, titled “Being Black in Criminal Justice – Is the Profession Racist?”, said he could not believe that “people are still prejudging an individual”. He said that, apart from the gown, he was wearing his barrister’s attire, which the security guard should have been familiar with. When he challenged the guard, “he was completely embarrassed” and raised the barrier to allow him to park, said Akinsanya.Keir Monteith KC told the podcast: “We’ve probably all experienced that situation early on and not so early on in our careers where we’ve been asked to go and sit in the dock.” He said others were still experiencing it but he personally was not, which he suggested was because he was a KC and known in a particular court.In 2020, the courts service apologised to two black barristers after one was mistaken for a defendantthree times in a dayand the othertwice in a day.Akinsanya said:“I’m privy to seeing how the bar has changed with a lot more people from diverse backgrounds entering the profession but there is still a perception that, if you’re black, you’re more likely not to be the lawyer, you’re more likely to be a defendant who’s attending court because you’re on trial.“I just think: why are we still in this position in the 21st century? Which makes one think about the wider conversation we were having [on the podcast] about the lack of black judges.”Judicial diversity statisticspublished last month showed that over the past 10 years the proportion of judges who are black has barely moved, creeping up from 1.4% to 1.6%, compared with 4% of the population in England and Wales. There are 79 black judges (43 in courts and the remainder in tribunals) out of 5,337 and just one senior black court judge, Mrs Justice Margaret Obi.Akinsanya said: “I could speak of colleagues of mine who are 40-plus years in [the profession] who are more than capable, more than able, [who] I know have applied and have been turned down.”He believes there should be targets to increase representation and a body that is held accountable if they are missed.Laurie Anne-Power KC told the podcast an oversight and scrutiny board was needed because “something’s going wrong”. She added: “The only way we can find out what is going wrong in that assessment phase of the process is to have a board that oversees every single aspect. Carry out comparisons. For example, look at the difference between applications for white applicants and black applicants – is there a difference? If there is not a difference, why is there a difference in outcome?”Monteith, who co-authored a 2022 report that saidthe judiciary was institutionally racist, criticised the “secret soundings” used to appoint judges, by which serving judges submit confidential assessments of a candidate’s suitability. “If we’re going to have a proper application of merit, then do it on what the individual brings to the interview room, not what people have in terms of chats that are never brought into the interview so the person can deal with it,” he said.Explore more on these topicsLawBarristersRaceLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Not afraid of controversy’: Edinburgh fringe rejects calls to cancel Amanda Knox comedy | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Festival organisers defend show after criticism from sister of Meredith Kercher, Knox’s murdered former flatmate
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Festival organisers defend show after criticism from sister of Meredith Kercher, Knox’s murdered former flatmate
Content: Amanda Knox said a petition against Cartwheel  contained ‘many false assumptions and completely mischaracterises the show’.Photograph: Matt Licari/APView image in fullscreenAmanda Knox said a petition against Cartwheel  contained ‘many false assumptions and completely mischaracterises the show’.Photograph: Matt Licari/APEdinburgh festival 2026‘Not afraid of controversy’: Edinburgh fringe rejects calls to cancel Amanda Knox comedyFestival organisers defend show after criticism from sister of Meredith Kercher, Knox’s murdered former flatmateCaroline DaviesandNadia KhomamiFri 7 Aug 2026 09.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Edinburgh festival fringe has said it is “not afraid of controversy” after it faced calls to cancel a sold-out show byAmanda Knox, who was wrongfully convicted for the 2007 murder of her flatmate Meredith Kercher in Italy.Knox’s comedy show, Cartwheel, has been condemned by Kercher’s family, with her sister, Stephanie, saying it “normalises and trivialises violence against women”. Apetitioncalling for it to be cancelled has been signed by more than 9,000 people.Knox, from Seattle in the US, and her then Italian boyfriend, Raffaele Sollecito, were convicted in 2009 for the murder and sexual assault of Kercher, a British foreign exchange student living in Perugia. They maintained their innocence and, after years of legal battles, were acquitted by Italy’s highest court in 2015.In a statement posted on Instagram, Knox, 39, said of the petition: “Cartwheel is a show about motherhood, raising a daughter in a world that is unfair and dangerous for women, and what it costs to be the kind of mother who tells her the truth about that. Neither the author of this petition nor anyone who signed it has seen Cartwheel.”View image in fullscreenA poster advertising Knox’s show in Edinburgh.Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty ImagesKnox, now a married mother of two, said the petition contained “many false assumptions and completely mischaracterises the show”. She added: “Cartwheel honours Meredith Kercher’s memory and calls out the violence that was done to her and to me.”Knox has previously said the show did not “joke about Meredith’s death”.Cartwheel is a reference to a story that alleged Knox did cartwheels in the police station after Kercher’s death.Tony Lankester, the director of theFringe Society, told BBC Radio Scotland: “We’re not afraid of controversy. The decision as to whether or not [the show] goes ahead lies with herself and it lies with the venue.”He added: “As sympathetic as we are to individual cases that crop up, and absolutely as a parent I can relate to the pain that they describe, but that can’t be a criteria, it can’t be one of the lenses that we look through.”Gilded Balloon Teviot, the show’s venue, said in a statement: “TheEdinburgh festivalfringe is an open-access festival. As a fringe venue, we provide a platform for a wide range of voices, in line with the fringe’s longstanding commitment to freedom of expression (within the confines of the law) and ensure our audiences can make informed choices.View image in fullscreenMeredith Kercher was murdered in 2007 in Perugia, Italy.Photograph: PA“Artists and companies choose to participate at our venue and take on the financial and creative responsibility for their work. Amanda’s show is a one-woman piece exploring themes of motherhood, presented independently by her.”Stephanie Kerchertold BBC Breakfastthat Knox was “naturally free to continue with her life as she wishes, but I think the problem with this particular project is that it is comedy”.“And whilst I appreciate comedy is there to push the boundaries … it very much normalises and trivialises violence against women and Meredith in particular.”Rudy Hermann Guede wasconvicted of Kercher’s murder in 2008. He was released from prison in 2021 after serving 13 years of a 16-year term.Claire Cochrane, a professor emeritus of theatre studies at the University of Worcester, said: “What happened to both Meredith Kercher andAmanda Knoxwas dreadful and of course I understand the Kercher family’s continuing grief.“However, vociferous campaigns mounted against artistic product based on unexamined assumptions about content and motivation undermines genuine attempts to deal with the personal legacies of violence and tragedy.“Comedy thoughtfully deployed can be both cathartic and therapeutic. I’m not going to be able to see Knox’s performance inEdinburgh. But I think it should go ahead and be properly and thoughtfully scrutinised.”Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Amanda KnoxMeredith KercherEdinburgh festivalFringe theatreFestivalsTheatrenewsShareReuse this content

title: Simon Levy murders: has anything changed in policing since Sarah Everard’s killing? | Crime | The Guardian
description: Experts say the attackers’ behaviour, and the handling of their cases, have striking similarities
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Experts say the attackers’ behaviour, and the handling of their cases, have striking similarities
Content: Sheryl Wilkins (left) was murdered by Simon Levy five months after he killed Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo.Photograph: Metropolitan PoliceView image in fullscreenSheryl Wilkins (left) was murdered by Simon Levy five months after he killed Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo.Photograph: Metropolitan PoliceCrimeSimon Levy murders: has anything changed in policing since Sarah Everard’s killing?Experts say the attackers’ behaviour, and the handling of their cases, have striking similaritiesSimon Levy convicted of double murder while free on bailVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentFri 7 Aug 2026 10.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 15.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbout 40 metres off Tottenham High Street, up a slip road for deliveries to a B&M homewares store, is a stretch of concrete paving behind a 2-metre wall topped with spikes.This is the patch of ground that Simon Levy tried to turn into his personal killing field.Twice he went with women, both of whom were sex workers, to the spot just eight minutes’ walk from the northLondonhome he shared with his mother and sister. The spot is out of sight of CCTV cameras dotted around the area, and in the shadow of the Tottenham Hotspur football stadium.One victim only just survived the sustained attack, including rape and strangulation, he inflicted on her in January 2025. Another, Sheryl Wilkins, paid with her life in August 2025.Between those attacks Levy had travelled to south London and, in March 2025, he murdered Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo.View image in fullscreenSimon Levy.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAHis double murder trial, whichended in convictions on Fridayheard from the survivor. Her testimony, the prosecutor Tom Little KC said during the trial, probably revealed what the other victims suffered.Little said the victims were vulnerable, and Levy believed that by targeting sex workers he was more likely to get away with his crimes.The survivor, who is 35 and has her anonymity protected by law, had been trafficked to Britain from eastern Europe.After they went behind the wall for sex, she asked Levy to pay. He jumped on her with such force he broke her clavicle. While raping her, he also started to strangle her.She told the Old Bailey jury he said: “Shut up. Be quiet. I have got you.”She added: “He was sticking his fingers in my throat so I could not make noise. I believe I’m going to die. I could not breathe … I was unconscious completely.”She awoke feeling “burning and pain”, and was bleeding from her genitals.View image in fullscreenScreengrab from CCTV showing Simon Levy walking away from the back of the B&M store in Tottenham on 24 August 2025.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PADays after the attack, the woman was arrested on another matter. She told officers of her ordeal and said she knew Levy by sight; she knew where he lived but did not know his name. She would later correctly pick Levy out of a police lineup.TheMetropolitan policesay she was unable to make a full statement for a further six months, despite their efforts to obtain one. The court heard that she was withdrawing from drug use.Levy, 40, was linked to the murders by DNA samples from the victims, travel card and phone data, and CCTV footage.After his arrest, he told police his eye injury, sustained during an assault in 2024, meant he rarely went out. He needed an appropriate adult present when detectives interviewed him and had dyslexia, autism and learning difficulties. He is believed to have been long-term unemployed.Neighbours knew little about him, and searches of his electronic devices showed some viewing of material about crime, violence and sex.The attacks on the women in 2025 were not Levy’s first.A history of sexual violenceLevy is suspected of a sexual assault as far back as 2017, which is still under investigation.View image in fullscreenA screengrab from mobile phone footage recorded by a victim of Simon Levy on the London Underground.Photograph: British Transport Police/PAHis first convictions came in 2021: one for assaulting a woman at a party in Camden in 2018, putting his hands into her underwear and touching her vagina; another for sexual assault by penetration of a woman on her way to the Notting Hill carnival, having penetrated her with his fingers.He was in prison firstfrom 2021-23 during which time he sexually assaulted a female prison officer at HMP Brixton.. Searches of his electronic devices showed him writing about his attraction to her.After his release, he carried out his first attack on a train in October 2023, for which he was only identified later.In 2024 he allegedly raped a woman in Tottenham. He was recalled to prison to complete the sentence he received in 2021, but not charged over the rape allegation, which is under renewed investigation.Released from prison later in 2024, he then intensified his attacks on London’s transport network, groping and sexually assaulting women on trains, often by trying to force his fingers into their vagina.In other offences, the court heard, Levy used “the hustle and bustle of busy, rush-hour trains as his cover”. He would get close to women and conceal his hand with a jumper or coat before attacking them.Peter Fulton, the head of crime for British TransportPolice(BTP), said Levy’s victims, who were mostly in their 20s, were attacked at random and on impulse.Levy crisscrossed London, armed with a stolen travel card, in one case boarding a train just minutes from his home, at White Hart Lane train station, to attack a woman.After women reported the offences to BTP, Levy was arrested, charged and bailed.Decades of failing womenThere were so many signs Levy was a danger, but how clear was it that his offending could turn murderous?After the first killing, in March 2025, Levy was arrested within days. The cause of death was inconclusive and he was bailed.Police feel aggrieved that attempts to have Levy remanded in jail in May and June 2025, after he had been charged with several train attacks and was a murder suspect, failed.View image in fullscreenA screengrab from CCTV showing Simon Levy at Stamford Hill station in north London.Photograph: British Transport Police/PAThe deputy assistant commissioner Kevin Southworth, head of public protection for the Metropolitan police, which investigated the killings, said: “I think on the basis that we put, and BTP put, this man before a court on two occasions and requested remand, I think the obvious conclusion is, had he been remanded at that time … he would have been in prison for sufficient period that he couldn’t have then gone on to commit a murder ….”Experts in tackling male sexual violence see similarities between Levy’s case and that of Wayne Couzens, the Met officer who kidnapped, raped and murderedSarah Everardin 2021. Previous, lower-level offending by Couzens, such as exposing himself to women,had been inadequately investigated by police.View image in fullscreenSarah Everard was kidnapped, raped and murdered by the police officer Wayne Couzens in 2021.Photograph: Family Handout/PAHarriet Wistrich, of the Centre for Women’s Justice, said the Levy case “shows a very clear pattern of escalating offending, from sexual assaults of women on public transport to rape and murder … perpetrators can become emboldened and move on to even more dangerous offending.”Wistrich added: “The failure of the criminal justice system to tackle his offending must have given him the message that it was easy to get away with it.”Southworth said he accepted crucial questions needed answering. “What did our officers know? And what should they have done, if they didn’t do it? I think one of the points of reflection … for the senior leadership of the Met is how do we, as a collective system, reflect on what went wrong here?”The Independent Office for Police Conduct is investigating the handling of the case.The revelations follow scandal after scandal over decades about how the criminal justice system fails women.Wistrich said: “The scale and variety of failings is shocking – in particular because had they been dealt with appropriately, two women need not have lost their lives.“It is particularly concerning that this has happened within five years of the horrendous revelations around Met police officersWayne CouzensandDavid Carrick, theBaroness Casey reportinto the Met [which found police to be institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic] …“This type of scandal tells us little, if anything, has improved in practice.”Explore more on these topicsCrimeMetropolitan policeRape and sexual assaultWomenSex workLondonPolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Thetford residents remain on edge after days of ‘mob rule’ over asylum plans | Norfolk | The Guardian
description: People voice frustration with officials’ failure to engage with community over placement of asylum seekers in area
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: People voice frustration with officials’ failure to engage with community over placement of asylum seekers in area
Content: Sue, 68, and her son Tommy, 32, with other protesters outside RAF Barnham, near Thetford, where the government is considering accommodating asylum seekers.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSue, 68, and her son Tommy, 32, with other protesters outside RAF Barnham, near Thetford, where the government is considering accommodating asylum seekers.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianNorfolkThetford residents remain on edge after days of ‘mob rule’ over asylum plansPeople voice frustration with officials’ failure to engage with community over placement of asylum seekers in areaBen QuinnPolitical correspondentFri 7 Aug 2026 15.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 15.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA smashed window pane and some broken eggshells on a footpath were some of the tell-tale signs of events that took place this week on a residential street at the edge of Thetford.On Friday afternoon it was not hard to find local people with a sense of foreboding after the latest disorder in theNorfolkmarket town which has seen crowds attempt to break into properties believed to be housing asylum seekers.“The main concern is safety, the proximity of children and that people just have not been consulted about this,” said Jenny Hollis, a former councillor, who indicated the proximity of a local school and nursery to a – now seemingly vacant – house on the targeted street in the north of the town.View image in fullscreenJenny Hollis: ‘Thetford is a small town.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian“Thetford is a small town where people know each other, but if you are putting young men who people know nothing about into an area, sometimes in the dark of night, then it will be a cause of concern,” she said in reference to asylum seekers.For three nights, Thetford was the scene of protests and disorder, with police officers being subjected to violence, windows smashed, fences broken and people attempting to break into a residential property, police said.However, after unrest which the local MP said had “put Thetford back decades”, there was also deep unease among residents and others about the prospect of racism poisoning local relations, fuelled by disinformation and the role of the far right in seeking to exploit tensions.“I have lived here for more than a decade and have come to call it home,” said a woman, originally from eastern Europe, around the corner from where the latest unrest took place. “The people are lovely, but last week was the first time that my partner was shouted at by someone who derided him as a ‘migrant’.”Amid chants of “We want them out” from a crowd of up to 200 people on the targeted street on Wednesday night, a male police officer was hit by a brick and a female colleague was seriously bitten, Norfolk constabulary said. The number of arrests in connection with disorder in different parts of the town had risen to six as of Friday.Asylum seekers had been removed from properties on Thursday for their safety, according to the police, and there was no answer at a number of homes believed to have been used for that purpose when the Guardian visited.“I have HMOs [houses of multiple occupancy] with asylum seekers in them on both sides of my house,” said one man. They had tended to keep to themselves, he said, but he had concerns about tensions in the area and what it would do to property prices.The three nights of disorder threaten to become the spark for the type of anti-immigration tensions that boiled over last year around a hotel outside the Essex town of Epping and spread elsewhere.If the unrest in Thetford is different, however, it is that it marks the first time HMOs in England have become the target of concerted and organised anger.Terry Jermy, the MP for South West Norfolk and a rare Labour presence in what has traditionally been a Conservative-leaning region, has criticised what he described as a lack of engagement by theHome Office, and given voice to people’s unease that cheaper, working-class areas have been chosen as the location for housing asylum seekers in HMOs.“The lack of engagement both with the community and elected officials has been a huge concern, along with the apparent lack of a strategy, in terms of a cohesive plan, but also to close down rumours and the spread of misinformation,” said Jermy.View image in fullscreenTerry Jermy: ‘What we have seen … is outright criminality, mob rule and vigilante-style antics.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian“I have been happy to acknowledge people’s concerns and support peaceful protest but what we have seen over the last few days is outright criminality, mob rule and vigilante-style antics which go way beyond the rule of law. These people – and in many cases I’m talking about those who have travelled to Thetford – claim to be proud to be British, but to be proud to be British is to support the rule of law.”Criticism has persisted over the use of HMOs and the choice of locations to house asylum seekers, with protesters in Thetford targeting a list of houses believed to be used by Serco, a company that has a multimillion pound contract with the Home Office.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSocial media accounts operated by prominent far-right activists, including Stephen Yaxley-Lennon – who calls himself Tommy Robinson – have disseminated footage from the protests. In one clip, a man can be seen directing crowds to an address where he said there were “invaders”, a term used by Robinson and others.View image in fullscreenDamage to the homes of people believed to be asylum seekers in Thetford.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianIn answer to the allegation it had mishandled its contract, a spokesperson for Serco said it worked under the direction of the Home Office, which tells it the number of people it expects to house in local authority areas based on overall national levels of demand.The Home Office has insisted the use of “large sites” is a key part of its strategy, and said the population of asylum seekers in hotels fell by 35% in the past year and by 63% from the peak of 56,000 in 2023.Figures from Reform UK have taken a prominent interest in the opposition to the use of HMOs.Scott Hussey, a member of the cabinet on Reform-controlled Norfolk county council, was at the scene on Friday, and said residents were frustrated at seeing their town being turned into “a dumping ground for illegal immigrants”.He said his understanding from meeting with the Home Office was that more HMOs were going to be sited in Thetford,and that this would add to tensions over proposals to use a nearby RAF base to house asylum seekers.Those who protested in Thetford this week included participants in a regular protest outside RAF Barnham, outside the town. Plans to house 3,750 migrants at the former base were revealed in June.Anna Turley, the minister for border security and asylum, said on GB News on Friday that people had a right to protest but that the disorder in Thetford had been “horrendous”.“What we’ve seen is spilling over into violence, which is just not acceptable,” she said. “Nobody should feel harassed, intimidated or threatened in their home, and certainly we shouldn’t see our emergency workers and our police attacked in the way that we have seen.”Explore more on these topicsNorfolkImmigration and asylumFar rightHome OfficeMigrationProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kemi Badenoch’s weird week: defence of ex-neo-Nazi raises questions over Tory direction | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Some in party are delighted by leader’s tack rightwards but opponents have savoured latest Conservative controversy
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Some in party are delighted by leader’s tack rightwards but opponents have savoured latest Conservative controversy
Content: Kemi Badenoch after accompanying police on a raid on a property in Surrey on Tuesday.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch after accompanying police on a raid on a property in Surrey on Tuesday.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAConservativesKemi Badenoch’s weird week: defence of ex-neo-Nazi raises questions over Tory directionSome in party are delighted by leader’s tack rightwards but opponents have savoured latest Conservative controversyAlexandra ToppingandJessica ElgotFri 7 Aug 2026 11.36 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was a moment in the middle of this week when a news alert raised eyebrows among the politically committed. It read: “Kemi Badenoch: Former neo-Nazi candidate would just be sorting out bins.” It was a collection of words that might prompt palpitations in the most sanguine of communications professionals, followed by panicked advice that retreat was necessary. But as a deeply weird week for the Conservative party came to a close on Friday, its leader appeared adamant she would hold the line.With Badenoch accused of aping Reform UK on policy and purging centrists from her party in recent weeks, her decision to stand by a man who was jailed after creating sexualised images of a Jewish MP and calling her a “rodent” has prompted concerns about the leader of the opposition’s political antennae and the Tories’ wider strategy.On Monday it emerged that Joshua Bonehill-Paine, a former neo-Nazi activist convicted of the sexist and antisemitic harassment of the Labour peer Luciana Berger, had beenselected as a Conservative candidatefor a local election in Somerset.A little over 48 hours later, Bonehill-Paine –creator of pro-right viral AI clipsthat often depict politicians on the left in an ugly light – withdrew his candidacy, saying Badenoch had instead asked him tobecome an adviserto the party’s culture and integration commission, focusing on how young men become radicalised.As pressure mounted, Badenoch said she was “sad” that Bonehill-Paine felt he “won’t be given the space to explain his position and represent his community”, chastising those who had called her judgment into question.“Piling on [people who have changed] and trying to get them cancelled may be sport for other parties,” she wrote on social media. “But this is a different Conservative party.”Her stance has left some in her party delighted by her persistent pugilism but others scratching their heads and looking to the door. For opponents, it has been a moment to savour, with Reform saying her support “beggars belief”, while locally focused Liberal Democrats delighted in criticising Badenoch’s insistence that as a councillor Bonehill-Paine would only have been “looking at parking, sorting out bins”.View image in fullscreenBadenoch asked Joshua Bonehill-Paine to become an adviser to the party’s culture and integration commission.Photograph: Channel 4 News/YouTubeThe embrace of Bonehill-Paine has come at a critical moment in Badenoch’s leadership. Last month she embarked on a purge of the Conservative parliamentary party,writing in the Telegraphthat it was “not a retirement home for failed politicians” and warning that anyone who supported net zero targets or Britain’s membership of the European convention on human rights (ECHR) would be blocked from standing as a candidate in the next election.The former ministerGavin Barwell lost the whip, and another former cabinet member,Grant Shapps, was blockedfrom standing again for the party. Sources said multiple Reform members had been blocked from joining the party. “To do that while welcoming this chap has definitely raised a few eyebrows,” one source said.The purge had left many young Tories and centrists politically homeless, said the former Tory activist Cody Butler, who resigned last weekend as chair of the One Nation Conservative Network and left the party. He said centrists, members worried about the climate crisis and conservation, and remainers – those whoMargaret Thatcher may have referred to as “Wets”– were “running out of road”.“We keep hearing the parliamentary party has never been more united,” Butler said. “But I think the real truth is the arsonists have taken control, and they’re trying to set the great oak tree of Toryism alight.”Badenoch also announced this week that a Conservative government wouldevict foreign nationals with leave to remain from social housing, prompting Reform’s Zia Yusuf to accuse her of trying to copy his party’s policy, and the homelessness charity Shelter to warn the policy would “drive up homelessness and put extreme pressure on councils”.Despite the private worries of some in the Tory party, delight in Badenoch’s unabashed tack rightwards is not difficult to find among the rank and file. “It’s going down really well,” said one MP. “The party thinks Kemi is doing brilliantly.”A senior Conservative adviser said the party was being clear on what it believed and why. “At the last election, voters would tell us they didn’t know what the party stood for. Kemi is changing that,” they said.View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch meeting police officers in Surrey on Tuesday.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PABut rightwingers are not the only ones enjoying the ride. Labour sources said they had been looking on and reaching for the popcorn this week. “Just as you think Kemi might finally be sorting out their tent, she spends a week focused on totally irrelevant nonsense,” said one. “Nothing trumps a person’s instincts and hers are just wrong.”In the yellow corner, gleeful Lib Dems point out that under Badenoch the Tories seem to be showing little interest in taking back any of the 60 seats they lost directly to their party in 2024 as part of a drubbing in which theConservativesshed a record 251 seats.Once the near unchallenged flagbearer of middle England, the Conservatives now have zero MPs in Oxfordshire, for the first time since 1777. A committed leftwing hiker could walk from Land’s End to London without passing through a Tory constituency. Despite Badenoch’s insistence that the May local elections showed“the Conservatives are coming back”, theparty lost about 500 councillors in Englandand ceded control of three local authorities. Even now, the Tories are skittering along at19% of the vote, compared with Reform on 24 and Labour on 23, according to Politico’s poll of polls.As a Tory, I say things are looking up. Farage is fading, and the looming threat to No 10 is called Kemi | Simon HartRead moreA senior Lib Dem source said: “It was widely expected that the Conservatives were at their lowest ebb in 2024 and would quickly start making progress. In fact, it’s us that have taken loads off them rather than the other way round.“Whether it is [on] fighting for more action on the climate or defending human rights, the Conservatives sound more like Nigel Farage than former leaders who were popular with middle England. It is genuinely giving us the biggest opportunity against them we have ever had.”Given current polling – and the results of the 2024 election in which the Conservatives lost about a third of their votes to Reform – attempting to woo those who voted for Farage was logical, said the pollster John Curtice. “The Tories are in a pretty dire state but not quite as dire as they were a few months ago,” he said. “By my calculation, they are now losing around 17% of those votes to Farage.”Polling indicates Badenoch’s personal approval rating is on the up: a YouGov poll last month put her net favourability at -11, the highest of any Conservative leader in more than five years.Curtice said the Tories were facing a dilemma: whether to try to build a more centrist coalition with the voters who had stuck with the party, or try to win back Reform voters. “But in [Reform] voters’ minds they are the party who failed to deliver Brexit properly and who created the Boris wave,” he said. “And the more fundamental problem is not to do with ideology, it’s to do with competence. Partygate trashed their ethical reputation, and [Liz] Truss trashed their reputation on the economy.”Robert Hayward, a Conservative peer and polling analyst, played down the theory that Badenoch was increasingly moving the Conservatives to the right but said she would have to adapt against a Labour party under Andy Burnham.Asked where it currently looked as if the Conservatives would gain seats on their current trajectory, Hayward was candid. “I don’t think that is very clear as yet, and that’s a major challenge to the party,” he said.“But it’s a problem for everyone. People’s allegiance to any political party is weaker now than at any moment during my lifetime. Who knows where we’ll be in December 2026, never mind on the eve of a general election.”Explore more on these topicsConservativesKemi BadenochnewsShareReuse this content

title: Monsters of God review – a messy feud between rival reptile smugglers gets the Tiger King treatment | Television | The Guardian
description: Director Eric Goode has found two enemies to rival Joe Exotic and Carole Baskin in his new documentary about the animal trade’s underworld
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Director Eric Goode has found two enemies to rival Joe Exotic and Carole Baskin in his new documentary about the animal trade’s underworld
Content: Er, isn’t this a series about snakes and stuff? … Monsters of God.Photograph: HBO MaxView image in fullscreenEr, isn’t this a series about snakes and stuff? … Monsters of God.Photograph: HBO MaxTV reviewTelevisionReviewMonsters of God review – a messy feud between rival reptile smugglers gets the Tiger King treatmentDirector Eric Goode has found two enemies to rival Joe Exotic and Carole Baskin in his new documentary about the animal trade’s underworldHannah J DaviesFri 7 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThrough the fear and general miasma of the Covid pandemic, TV brought people together like never before. Among the most-watched series of 2020 was of courseTiger King, Netflix’s hit about an improbably twisty feud between a gay, polyamorous big-cat breeder and convicted felon, and the conservationist rival whom he accused of murder (more specifically, of feeding her missing husband to the tigers in her sanctuary – which she denies). It was the perfect hit for quarantine: bold and ridiculous enough to get everyone talking, and with precisely no bearing on the grief and awfulness that was all around.Producer and co-director Eric Goode has made a smattering of Tiger King follow-ups since then, as well as another series, Chimp Crazy, about the self-described Dolly Parton of the primate world. His latest project – a co-production between his own outfit, Goode Films, HBO, and A24 – continues the theme, focusing this time on the reptile trade and taking its lead from the 2008 book The Lizard King by journalist Bryan Christy. It’s stuffed full of wild stories and even wilder characters: there are canny smugglers, underworld crime gangs, and even legitimate zoos that are said to have turned a blind eye to the provenance of their big, scaly friends. The series is centred on the US – although clearly the supply chain is global – and the two men who kickstarted the illegal trade: Hank Molt and copycat trader Tommy Crutchfield. Like Joe Exotic and Carole Baskin before them, there is no love lost between Crutchfield and Molt, and no odd biographical detail too trivial to skip over. Hank, says Tommy, “will turn anything good into bad”, while Hank reckons that Tommy is “one of the angriest and most bitter people I’ve ever met”. Along the way we learn that Hank used to be a mayonnaise salesman, and that Tommy worked at an extremely on-the-nose Florida establishment named Snake-a-Torium as a teenager, where he would later have his wedding reception.What follows is the story not only of their enduring beef and betrayals, but of other adjacent vendettas in the illicit reptilian market. Despite environmental concerns becoming increasingly en vogue in the late 60s, a “don’t ask, don’t tell” attitude still pervaded the world of wildlife trading, with many zoos happy to acquire what they needed from whoever happened to have it. There were, however, serious consequences for some of the creatures involved. With the police on his back, Molt once buried a stash of animals alive in New Jersey’s Pine Barrens, a location which would later become infamous via The Sopranos. When he was eventually arrested, Crutchfield would become the go-to guy. He supplied cobras to the makers of a Hollywood blockbuster, he says, and sold tortoises to Michael Jackson. He even bred distinctive white albino alligators, which he sold for £175,000 a pop.The gruesome, revenge-fuelled culmination of the men’s feud at the end of the first episode is the high point of Monsters of God, which then limps through four more instalments. The illegal animal trade gets entangled with the (less interesting) drug trade in the 80s, and – somewhere along the way – the story becomes less punchy and more of an attempt to shoehorn in every strange character and weird/shocking/grim (delete as appropriate) anecdote that the producers had access to. A tangent about a federal agent who wore a gorilla costume in a sting operation is rather funny but, er, isn’t this a series about snakes and stuff? It does feel like Monsters of God could have been a two-parter, but then maybe it’s simply too hard to kill your darlings when you have so many of them. The story of a German man who collaborated with Crutchfield (and who attempted to escape the feds by running across eight lanes of traffic, in handcuffs, and wearing Birkenstocks) is hardly essential. But it is clearly entertaining.Monsters of God may lack that tight narrative thread that makes you want to recreate lockdown and spend five hours parked in front of the TV. But Goode is a conservationist as well as a film-maker, and it’s clear that he is interested in what became of the species whose existence was endangered by men like these. Much of the final episode is dedicated to notorious dealer Anson Wong from Malaysia, and the smuggling that meant that the ploughshare tortoise became all-but extinct in the wild. There is one final bit of good news, though, and a sense that nature – perhaps – is healing. It might not be a conclusion ripped from the bizarre world of Joe Exotic, but it’s the perfect ending to a wildlife documentary.Monsters of God is on HBO MaxExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewTiger KingDocumentaryFactual TVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sky Country: Indigenous fashion weaves culture and climate together | Australian fashion | The Guardian
description: First Nations designers, models, artists and artisans gathered on Larrakia country this week for two major fashion events
Author: Ima Caldwell
Headline: First Nations designers, models, artists and artisans gathered on Larrakia country this week for two major fashion events
Content: Nelson Baker Bardi wearing Nagula Jarndu Designs.Photograph: (A)manda Parkinson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNelson Baker Bardi wearing Nagula Jarndu Designs.Photograph: (A)manda Parkinson/The GuardianAustralian fashionSky Country: Indigenous fashion weaves culture and climate togetherFirst Nations designers, models, artists and artisans from across Australia gathered on Larrakia Country in Darwin this week for the Country to Couture runway show and the National Indigenous Fashion awards. In between, Guardian Australia photographed several of the featured models and designersDelvene Cockatoo-Collins wins National Indigenous Fashion award for textiles harvested on CountryFirst Nations fashion celebrates weaving, wattle and waterways at Country to Couture 2026 – in picturesPhotography by (A)manda Parkinson with additional reporting byIma CaldwellFri 7 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTShareView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenModels CJ Rankin, a Kiyak woman, and Nelson Baker Bardi, a Nyikina man, wear Nagula Jarndu Designs.The art centre Nagula Jarndu (Saltwater Woman) began in Rubibi/Broome in 1987 as a place for Yawuru women to gather, preserve language, share knowledge and keep culture strong. Their hand-carved woodblock prints on cotton and silks, shown at Country to Couture, share stories of saltwater, plants, family and Country.View image in fullscreenCJ Rankin wears Corella & Crow.Shown at Country to Couture, the Madhan (Tree) collection by Corella & Crow uses upcycled materials including reclaimed curtains, alongside dyeing, printmaking, beading and embroidery, to celebrate the cultural and ecological significance of trees. Slow fashion processes are a way for the label to honour and care for materials, story and place.View image in fullscreenYvonne Rankin (left) and CJ Rankin wear designs by Yarrenyty Arltere Artists.Yarrenyty Arltere Artists’ collection Thepa Ilpalha is the work of Rhonda Sharpe, Dulcie Sharpe, Marlene Rubuntja, Louise Robertson and Sheree Inkamala, who bring their love of painted and soft sculpture birds to life in bold structured pieces on cotton.View image in fullscreenModel Jake Powers, a Yaruwu and Kija man, wears Lucas Schober.Model turned designer Lucas Schober showcased at Country to Couture for the first time. This ensemble, modelled by Jake Powers, is inspired by the gakinga (magpie goose), a migratory bird whose arrival to the Northern Territory symbolises the beginning of balnba (wet season). Here, Schober has taken feathers from the bird and hand-stitched them over a linen cape, which he has also printed with emblems of the bird.Powers was named this year’s Cecilia Cubillo Young Achiever at the National Indigenous Fashion awards. The 21-year-old Bardi, Yawuru and Kija man, who grew up watching international couture shows on YouTube from his home in Broome, also served as a stylist and production assistant at the ceremony.Powers told Guardian Australia he is working toward launching his own collection. “We’ve found a different ways to tell stories through garments, which is a whole other level of creativity and innovation that this industry needs,” he said.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: (A)manda Parkinson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFrom left: Jake Powers,Yvonne Rankin andNelson Baker Bardi, all wearing Lucas Schober.View image in fullscreenYvonne Rankin wears Bobbi Lockyer x Skye Lockyer x Mali Isabel.A three-way artist collaboration shown at Country to Couture, Bobbi and Skye Lockyer and Mali Isabel’s collection the Mermaid Collective is inspired by saltwater Country, mermaid mythology, cultural storytelling and activism. It blends streetwear with handcrafted details such as beadwork, weaving and embroidery. The “Save Lee Point” T-shirt refers to the ongoing campaignagainst defence housing expansion at Lee Point.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenCJ Rankin wears Bábbarra Women’s Centre (left) and Jaymee-Lee Chaquebor.The National Indigenous Fashion award’s Community Collaboration prize celebrated a cross-cultural printing partnership between Bábbarra Women’s Centre, based in the remote community of Maningrida, and Bengaluru’s Tharangini Studio. Bábbarra artists travelled to India to translate their ancestral lino-cut designs and cultural stories into woodblocks used for printing, while sharing techniques.Bardi artist Jaymee-Lee Chaquebor’s Jarrabinmy collection was shown at this year’s Country to Couture. The garments’ prints are deeply rooted in Bardi culture, storytelling and the relationship between land and sea.View image in fullscreenCJ Rankin wears MumRed.National Indigenous Fashion award finalist Samala Cronin is best known for her one-of-a-kind pieces. This year, she showcased her first ready-to-wear collection under her label MumRed at Country to Couture. The Flow State collection is designed to honour and celebrate every stage of the menstrual cycle.View image in fullscreenCJ Rankin wears Noongar Arts Fashion.Noongar Arts Fashion made their debut at this year’s Country to Couture with a collection titled Kambarang, a series of dresses celebrating the Noongar season of transformation and birth, when Wardandi Country comes alive with wildflowers – golden wattle blossoms, vibrant kangaroo paws, delicate orchids and everlastings.

title: It’s not just Homer: the new generation of poets enjoying epic success | Books | The Guardian
description: Christopher Nolan’s film has made the Odyssey a bestselling book again, but a slew of new poets are breaking sales records, and have more in common with the ancient Greek than you might expect
Author: Ella Risbridger
Headline: Christopher Nolan’s film has made the Odyssey a bestselling book again, but a slew of new poets are breaking sales records, and have more in common with the ancient Greek than you might expect
Content: Instagram heroine … Nikita Gill in 2021.Photograph: David M Benett/Dave Benett/Getty Images for The Happy Vagina & Atelier RomyView image in fullscreenInstagram heroine … Nikita Gill in 2021.Photograph: David M Benett/Dave Benett/Getty Images for The Happy Vagina & Atelier RomyBooksIt’s not just Homer: the new generation of poets enjoying epic successChristopher Nolan’s film has made the Odyssey a bestselling book again, but a slew of new poets are breaking sales records, and have more in common with the ancient Greek than you might expectElla RisbridgerFri 7 Aug 2026 11.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe death of poetry – much anticipated, much prematurely mourned – has been put off again, this time by the Odyssey. Thanks to Christopher Nolan’s film, sales of Homer’s epic rose 1,400% in the weeks around release – and it’s not alone.Poetrycollections are once again sailing up the charts: Lucas Jones, Donna Ashworth and Nikita Gill, among others, have all burst forth on to the bestseller lists.View image in fullscreen‘Life is the cloud’ … Lucas Jones.Photograph: Chad MooreThe word bestseller, it must be said, conjures up certain images: a TV tie-in cookbook; a sexy thriller. It does not, generally speaking, imply poetry. Poetry is a genre more often relegated to the adolescent, the academic, or the words inside sentimental birthday cards: either over-emotional or elitist, depending on which poet and which perspective. What it certainly is not is a money-spinner: nobody gets into poetry to make the big bucks. Nobody gets into poetry – not these days, anyway, not since Byron’s day – for the fame or the fortune.Poetry is the underdog of publishing and yet this year, according to a recent Guardian article, it is “expected to exceed £15m in annual sales for the first time since records began”; it might even, if the Greek epics continue to pull in readers (as they have for almost 3,000 years), climb to an astounding £17m. Even without the bolstering influence of Homer, poetry has been steadily climbing for the last three years, each one the best on record.In fact, reports of poetry’s surprising rise have been kicking around for more than a decade: Rupi Kaur’s million-dollar debut, Milk and Honey,set new records in 2014, and continues to sell. US magazine The New Republic named Kaur the “writer of the decade”. And yet she came to stand not so much for great art, as for a kind of synecdoche for what was wrong with art: Kaur became the mockable face of “the new poetry”, Instagrammable and Instagrammed, and accessed primarily – of course – by the young.A new audience is finding poetry, particularly (though not exclusively) through social media: a new generation of poets, particularly but not exclusively performance poets, have come to prominence through Instagram, TikTok, and other short-form video formats. These writers, while we can quote them on the page, lose something by being written down.“At my funeral I’d like there to be sunflowers, a truly inconvenient amount / For I too will have spent a lifetime searching for the light,” runs a couplet from Harry Baker’s Sunflowers, but the poet’s charismatic presence somehow conveys something more of the full power of his meaning.View image in fullscreenSailing into the charts … Donna Ashworth.Photograph: Copyright Susie Lowe and Donna AshworthMany of these poems, beginning on social media and ending in huge sold-out tours, rely on a connection between speaker and listener: a pause, a stillness, a sustained thread in the chaos of the internet, of singular attention to one poem through to the end.This is poetry for the social media age, for sure. But then, what is the Odyssey except social media?The Odysseyis meant to be read out loud; to be told; to be spread; to be shared. What we know as a single written text is, in fact, only the most static, frozen form of the original viral myth.It is tempting to think of these bestsellers as a new kind of poetry, but it is in fact a very old one. It is unafraid of emotion, of sentimentality, of faith and love; it is concerned less with the establishment of a brand new voice than with the need to give voice to a collective thought. It is not about originality. (Hence, perhaps, the accusations of self-help; banality; and even plagiarism that have been flung at some of these newly popular poets.) These are poems designed to resonate rather than to disturb. In times of division, these poems are made to connect.All writing is about connection, even when it’s not. But the immediacy of the connection between author and reader is somehow easiest in poetry: when it works, there’s a direct shot to the heart, a human-to-human hot-wiring together that compresses time and space to get to the point.What social media offers these poets is a new way to gather people round the fire – and, for some, a way to get to be the one speaking at last. If poets can reach their audiences directly, then different poets may be, perhaps, given a chance not just to speak but to be heard: working-class poets, queer poets, poets who don’t fit the “male, pale and stale” classical canon.This is how poetry thrives. Poetry needs the new so that it can keep on telling the oldest stories we have: love, despair, grief, hope, joy, community, companionship. Long may it live – as thrilling as every other bestseller on the charts.Five bestselling poets you should know aboutLucas Jones: actor, TikTok star, bestselling poetWrites about: masculinity, faith, life, death and loveFrom I Saw God on the Train, from the new collection I Still Believe In Miracles:You want white clouds and endless skies? Err, yeah. Look around. You don’t have to die […]I know it probably brings you some painto think of the dead as just dust in a grave […] Life is the cloud, and death is the rain.Hollie McNish: winner of the Ted Hughes prize, author of Slug, Lobster, Virgin, Plum and Nobody Told MeWrites about: sex, motherhood, longing, politics, power and loveFrom call me:call meeven if you’re in the wrong place at the wrong timewith a full moon and a lone wolf whimpering bloody-pawed from your insides[...]i do not care what you have done … i am no god i am no judgei am your mother – call me and i will comeNikita Gill: permanently on the bestseller chart, 850,000 Instagram followersWrites about: feminist-flavoured myths, magic, legends and love93% Stardust:We have calcium in our bones,iron in our veins,carbon in our souls,and nitrogen in our brains.93 percent stardust,with souls made of flames,we are all just starsthat have people names.Lemn Sissay: Sunday Times bestseller, OBE, books include Let the Light Pour InWrites about: family, adoption, the fabric of society, race, home, hope, and loveFrom Let the Light Pour In:If the phone won’t ring make the callIf the mountain won’t move shift itIf the birds won’t sing, sing to them all,And if the sun won’t rise, lift itLen Pennie:British book award winner, Scots language poet also writing in EnglishWrites about: language, linguistics, shame, stigma, suffering, surviving, the patriarchy, overthrowing the patriarchy and loveFrom The Vow, from Poyums Annaw:To be loved through each compromise, question or qualmTo be sheltered from storm andenshrined in the calmTo be held, not like glass, but the end of a deal …Explore more on these topicsBooksPoetryThe OdysseyHollie McNishRupi KaurfeaturesShareReuse this content
