title: It must be tricky for Farage to remember what’s what. It’s so hideously complicated | John Crace | The Guardian
description: I can’t pass up the moment the Reform leader celebrates his byelection victory against ‘the establishment’ – a man with a dustbin on his head
Author: John Crace
Headline: I can’t pass up the moment the Reform leader celebrates his byelection victory against ‘the establishment’ – a man with a dustbin on his head
Content: Nigel Farage: ‘Come on. Who doesn’t forget a few million pounds?’Photograph: Peter Nicholls/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNigel Farage: ‘Come on. Who doesn’t forget a few million pounds?’Photograph: Peter Nicholls/Getty ImagesDigested weekPoliticsIt must be tricky for Farage to remember what’s what. It’s so hideously complicatedJohn CraceI can’t pass up the moment the Reform leader celebrates his byelection victory against ‘the establishment’ – a man with a dustbin on his headFri 7 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareMondayYou would have thought that after 35 years of writing for the Guardian I would have mastered some of the basics of holiday protocol by now. Apparently not. While I had remembered to let the newsdesk know I wouldn’t be writing the political sketch for two weeks, it had completely slipped my mind to inform the Saturday editor. So rather than leave her with the headache of an empty page, you’re getting an extra dose of me this week. And, in truth, I don’t mind because, for what is a usually empty August, there’s an awful lot still going on. I’ve even told the newsdesk that I’d like to write next Friday as I can’t pass up the momentNigel Faragecelebrates his byelection victory against the “establishment”, AKA a comedian with a dustbin on his head. This summer has been quite the reckoning for Reform. First some excellent investigative reporting from the Guardian and the Sunday Times, followed by even some of the party’s most loyal followers in the Spectator and the Telegraph beginning to turn. We will know the game is up when GB News begins to have doubts about Nige. It can only be a matter of time.This time last year, Reform was dominating the polls and setting the news agenda with weekly press conferences. Now it’s as if Nige has placed himself in a witness protection programme as he tries to avoid anyone asking about his financial arrangements. There again, it must be tricky for Nige to remember what’s what as it all seems so hideously complicated. There’s the £5m from Thai crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne that was first a gift to spend on Ferraris, then to pay for his security and now could bea downpayment on the £1m per year Nige said he would need to make it worth his while to return to full-time politics. Then there are funds travelling from various offshore bank accounts from George Cottrell – the boy who liked to call Nige “Daddy” – to his mum, Fiona, and then on to Dicky Tice. Some of which – no one is quite sure which – seemed to end up in Reform’s bank accounts. Nor can Nige even quite remember when he did decide he was politically active despite owning a majority share in Reform. Confusion doesn’t seem to begin to cover this. Nige still has a week to get his story straight for the Clacton voters.TuesdayWhat with one thing and another – first Jill’s cancer and then breaking her shoulder – it’s looking unlikely we will be making it to Minneapolis to see our daughter, Anna, and her husband, Robert, for a second year. . Instead they have come to visit us for a week, so we have been trying to plan fun things to do in London. Today, given Robert is American, we thought we should all go to see the exhibition to mark the 250th anniversary of American independence at the British Museum.Truly, five minutes that none of us will get back. I’m trying to be generous to the museum here. Perhaps the trustees and curators have become so obsessed with not tearing the Bayeux Tapestry to shreds that they completely took their eye off the ball. Because this exhibition was an embarrassment. A darkened room with just four items on display. A peace medal made by Paul Revere. A tomahawk that doubled as a peace pipe and had been given to a British general. A wampum belt that had been made by Native Americans. All of which looked like they had been dug out of the museum’s storage department as an afterthought.Then the piece de resistance: a facsimile of a declaration of independence, complete with a notice saying that the original, which is kept in Chichester, would be on display in September. Thanks for nothing.What was the British Museum thinking? You’d have been disappointed if any of that had been on display at your local library. I guarantee that anyone coming to my house to see the ceramics I have collected over the years would have had a better time.WednesdayView image in fullscreenChris Hoy: ‘Why is the Prince of Wales poking me in the ear?’Photograph: Matthew Childs/ReutersNo one wants to kick a man when he’s down, but I can’t help thinking that Jason Arday – the professor of sociologywho has just resigned from the University of Cambridge– has been badly let down by his former employer. Surely someone must have thought of putting his PhD thesis through a plagiarism detector before offering him a job? The most alarming thing about Arday is that he seems clearly unwell. A fantasist who makes it hard to take almost anything he says as the truth. The list is seemingly endless: his claim to be a world-class athlete who once ran 600 miles in six days, or saying he had been part of the epic TV documentary series Seven Up. A programme that has been watched by millions of people over the years.Somehow, though, Cambridge managed to overlook all this and more. The greater the fable, the more the university defended him. And in the process it has done far more damage to him than if it had quietly and systematically gone through the evidence and declined to offer him a professorship. Thanks for applying, but no thanks.Worse still, Cambridge has done a huge disservice to other academics of colour because it has opened the gateway to rightwing critics who will now claim that many other professors at other universities got their jobs on a nod and a wink. Jasonhas a book coming out later this month. If Simon & Schuster has any thought for its own credibility and Arday’s wellbeing it will quietly announce the book has been delayed “indefinitely”.ThursdayMaybe there’s something in theair, butKemi Badenochseems to be having a bit of a moment. Having appeared on the Political Currency podcast this week to accuse Reform of “woke” politics and to rubbish Andy Burnham for having done nothing of any value – er, it’s only been two weeks and he’s already promised to solve social care. I guess there’s no pleasing some people.Badenoch has now nailed herself to the cross of defending the former neo-nazi Joshua Bonehill-Paine, who was jailed for harassing the Jewish Labour MP Luciana Berger. In Badenoch’s view, Bonehill-Paine is a reformed man and deserved a second chance to serve as a Tory councillor because all he would be doing was sorting out the “bin collections”. Bonehill-Paine clearly had second thoughts when some of his CV turned out to be nearly as creative as Jason Arday’s and he withdrew as a Conservative candidate. Only for Kemi to appoint him as a Tory special adviser.Now I’m all for second chances. But Badenoch didn’t seem to think the Labour cabinet minister Lou Haigh deserved rehabilitation to atone for her phone fraud: a conviction that predated Joshua’s by many years. As far as Badenoch was concerned, Haigh still had to repay her debt to society. It’s also curious to know what is and isn’t acceptable in today’s Tory party. A bit of previous for antisemitism and Hitler loving? Just fine. Believing in net zero and the European convention on human rights, not so much. Grant Shapps has been banned from standing as a Tory MP because he happens to believe in the climate crisis. There again, maybe Kemi understands her party better than most. The columnist Tim Stanley caused huge waves in the Telegraph by writing that maybe climate change was true after all, and got 9,000 comments of complaint. All for saying what 99.9% of the rest of us know to be true.View image in fullscreenAnna Wintour and Elephant: Both to each other: ‘You look absolutely fabulous.’Photograph: Dustin Satloff/Getty ImagesFridayIt’s been hard to keep up with the excesses and moral corruption of the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino. As I write, various football bodies and national organisations have expressed their lack of confidence in him but for the time being he appears to be just about hanging on to his job. Maybe he will even ride this one out. But it has struck me that one person has remained silent throughout the scandal:David Beckham. For the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, Beckham was paid millions to be a Fifa ambassador. His one contribution was to say he hadn’t spotted any gay people being persecuted. Top detective work from DB. This time round in the US, David seemed content being an unofficial ambassador, there to be filmed sitting in the VIP seats wearing a suit and looking miserable most of the time as he notched up another £24m that he doesn’t need in advert endorsements. He seemed to be Infantino’s mute puppet. He said nothing when Gianni devalued Fifa by awarding Donald Trump a peace prize. He said nothing when Gianni introduced hydration breaks and extended the half-time interval during the final. He said nothing when Gianni bowed to Trump’s demand to overturn Folarin Balogun’s red card. And he has said nothing while Gianni has tried to sell off stakes and reinvent the competition as an even fatter cash cow. It all feels so sad. A mini tragedy. David used to be almost a national treasure. Someone who appeared to have both a sense of what is right and wrong and also a good sense of humour. Now he just appears to be obsessed with wealth and status. Over the last few months, he could have been a voice for the country, speaking up against the commercialisation and obvious corruption of Infantino’s regime. We would all have loved him for it. Instead he has trashed his brand by being complicit. The only obvious reason for his silence is that either he doesn’t think Infantino has done anything wrong, or he just isn’t bothered as long as the cash keeps coming. It would be nice to be proved wrong. We want our Becks back.Explore more on these topicsPoliticsDigested weekNigel FarageDavid BeckhamReform UKKemi BadenochUniversity of CambridgecommentShareReuse this content

title: How divided is the UK really? Here’s a way to find out | Brendan Cox | The Guardian
description: Social media-fuelled riots and a fractured political system make us feel more divided than ever, but is that so? Our study hopes to reveal what bring us together – and pushes us apart, says Brendan Cox, co-founder of the Together Coalition
Author: Brendan Cox
Headline: Social media-fuelled riots and a fractured political system make us feel more divided than ever, but is that so? Our study hopes to reveal what bring us together – and pushes us apart, says Brendan Cox, co-founder of the Together Coalition
Content: Jo Cox is remembered at an event during Glastonbury festival in 2016.Photograph: Ian Gavan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJo Cox is remembered at an event during Glastonbury festival in 2016.Photograph: Ian Gavan/Getty ImagesOpinionPoliticsHow divided is the UK really? Here’s a way to find outBrendan CoxSocial media-fuelled riots and fractured politics make us feel more divided than ever, but is that so? Our study hopes to reveal what bring us together – and pushes us apartTake part in the National ConversationBrendan Cox is co-founder of the Together Coalition, which acts as the secretariat for the Independent Commission on Community and CohesionFri 7 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.13 EDTShareWhen my late wife Jo Cox was killed by a far-right extremist 10 years ago, the phrase “more in common”,taken from her maiden speech in parliament, became a rallying cry against extremism and division.The phrase succinctly articulated that, no matter our differences, we have more in common than that which divides us.In the decade since, that solidarity has faded. But it hasn’t just faded as time has elapsed: it has been replaced by a cynicism and a polarisation that it’s hard to overstate.In an era of hostile states, algorithmsdesigned to incite rageand collapsing community institutions, repeating the mantra that we have “more in common” is no longer enough. It’s time we mapped out that common ground.Because what we have in common matters. It’s the strength of our connections that defines what we are willing to commit to each other. It determines the strength of our democracy and is the basis of social solidarity. It defines everything from our commitment to the welfare state to our ability to fight wars and defend ourselves.So it’s pretty remarkable that we haven’t mapped the strength and nature of those connections. I guess we have taken them for granted in the past. Yet with a digital environment that now actively seeks to escalate, exacerbate and exaggerate our divisions, that complacency is no longer an option.That’s where the Independent Commission on Community and Cohesion comes in, a cross-party group co-chaired by former Conservative chancellor Sajid Javid and former Labour MP Jon Cruddas. Central to the commission’s work is theNational Conversation, a project with Oxford University to build the best picture we have ever had of what we have in common, what connects us, what divides us, and the kind of country we want to build together.In any other era, that kind of national research exercise would have been prohibitively expensive. You would have needed thousands of researchers interviewing members of the public, classifying and coding responses, before trying to summarise the millions of data points.National Conversation project launches as Britain risks ‘being torn apart by differences’Read moreAI makes this kind of exercise possible at scale for the first time. It means as part of the survey you can leave a 60-second voice note on your vision for the country. It means you can identify places on a map that bring you together or write open text. Our ability to gather all this information means the national conversation will provide the richest ever snapshot of what future we want to build together.Our hope is that the results will help provide us all with a common understanding of our connections, perhaps some reassurance and a chance to play back to our country what vision connects us still.But its insights will only be a strong as its inputs. Which is why I’m asking you to take just a few minutes to share your vision of the country you want to see. We’ll be publishing the results in a few months. Thousands of others have already joined the conversation but every voice that takes part deepens the insights and adds richness to our understanding of the nature of our connections.In future, we hope the National Conversation will become an institution like the census – not answering who we are and where we live, but the country talking about what unites us. We’d like you to be part of the start of this journey byadding your voice today. Because in a world that is trying to tear us apart, the least we can all do is speak up for the future we want to see.Brendan Cox is co-founder of the Together Coalition, which acts as the secretariat for the Independent Commission on Community and CohesionDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsPoliticsOpinionCommunitiesSocial mediaJo CoxDigital mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: Why are ultra-processed food firms panicking and suing? Because they know time is running out | Felicity Lawrence | The Guardian
description: As the harm caused by their products becomes more evident, manufacturers are resorting to denial and lawsuits to keep regulation at bay, says former Guardian special correspondent Felicity Lawrence
Author: Felicity Lawrence
Headline: As the harm caused by their products becomes more evident, manufacturers are resorting to denial and lawsuits to keep regulation at bay, says former Guardian special correspondent Felicity Lawrence
Content: Illustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianOpinionUltra-processed foodsWhy are ultra-processed food firms panicking and suing? Because they know time is running outFelicity LawrenceAs the harm caused by their products becomes more evident, manufacturers are resorting to denial and lawsuits to keep regulation at bayFri 7 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 04.11 EDTShareIt is rare for people to drop dead holding the incriminating packaging, but there is no longer any serious doubt that consuming a diet of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) risksa catalogue of life-shortening illnessesfrom heart disease and stroke to diabetes and cancer. Because these diseases are degenerative over time, the food and drink industry has been able to argue for decades that its UPFs are fine in moderation. It would have us believe that there is no such thing as a “junk” individual food, only poor diets overall, and that its products therefore should not be subject to any restrictions.Just as with climate breakdown and smoking, the science on harm caused by foods high in fat, salt and sugar is now settled, but the industry continues to deny and distract to delay action. Two weeks ago,a new report highlightedthe lengths to which big food has gone to stop governments implementing policies that would tackle the global crisis of diet-related disease.Since 2010, it and its lobby groups have brought 235 lawsuits against governments. More than a third of cases where the plaintiff was identifiable were filed by top global brands, led by Coca-Cola, PepsiCo and Mondelēz. The cases add up to595 years of litigation, according to the investigative group Lighthouse Reports, which has been monitoring the trend around the globe alongside academics, the Guardian and other media outlets.The litigation strategy is cynical but effective and Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of theWorld Health Organization, is damning. “Litigation has been used to oppose or weaken public health measures on obesity and unhealthy diets,” he said. “These delays cost countries billions in healthcare and legal expenses and create a regulatory chill that deters governments from adopting vital protections.”Protections are much needed. Around the world more than1 billion people live with obesityand a further 2 billion are overweight. In many countries, including the UK, US and Australia, UPFs have become staples, and make up half the average diet.​Hence the industry manoevres. Faced with mounting ​worldwide concern, ​it can no longer hold back the tide of evidence any more than fossil fuel or tobacco companies can, but like those sectors, it hopes to tie governments up for a few years more while it protects its profits, even if that takes us to a tipping point at which state health services are overwhelmed.As with fossil fuels and tobacco, the problem is existential for the food industry. Although manufacturers say they are making their food and drinks healthier, the bald truth is that the economic structure of the agrifood system means that is not possible in any real sense. Manufacturers of UPFs take cheap commodity crops, most often corn, soya and sugar cane and sugar beet, and break them down into their constituent parts. These crops are cheap because governments, especially in the US and EU, have long subsidised farmers, who are a powerful voting lobby, to produce surpluses of them. Farm subsidies and exports of food surplus have been a plank in US geopolitical strategy since the end of the second world war. Donald Trump in factincreasedsupport to farmers in the US in his One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025.Separated into processed parts – bulk oils, proteins, sugars, and starches – these cheap commodity crops are stripped of the fibre and many of the vitamins, minerals and other micronutrients we need for health. But they can be reconstituted as “added value” processed foods, with the help of flavouring, colouring and texturising additives to replace what has been lost, or sold as high-value animal feed for the world’s ever-growing intensive livestock industry. Unlike minimally processed foods such as perishable fruits and vegetables, they don’t go off and have the advantage of a long shelf life.My general rule of thumb however, is that added shareholder value is in inverse proportion to human nutritional value. The arrival of anti-obesity drugs has seen the industry tacitly admit it. As people taking GLP-1 weight-loss drugs find their appetites shrinking, they are buying fewer UPFs. Retailers have developed “nutrient-dense” but calorie light meals in response, for a premium, as if meals should be anything but nutrient dense as a matter of course.The fact is we need to stop eating UPFs in any significant amount, just as we need to leave oil in the ground and give up smoking. The more the public realises that, the greater the industry’s need to keep marketing to us and block any government attempts to help us make better choices. It is no coincidence that the majority of lawsuits brought or threatened by the top food and drink companies occur in countries that have been in the vanguard of identifying the harm from UPFs, such as Brazil, or in restricting them, such as Mexico with itssugary drink taxes.In the UK it was Kellogg’s that sued the secretary of state for health in 2021 over plans to control promotions on foods high in fat, salt or sugar (HFSS), including many of its breakfast cereals. Its UK marketing company argued in the high court that the health secretary was acting beyond his powers and that such controls breached its rights under the Human Rights Act (by assault on its right to freedom of commercial expression and on its companies’ “goodwill” monetary value). Tellingly, its lawyers cited case law involving British American Tobacco. They also pleaded that, although more than half of its breakfast cereals fell foul of the HFSS limits thanks to their ingredients, if you took into account the milk people ate with its products, they looked much healthier. Kellogg’slost its case, with Mr Justice Linden, the trial judge, noting that mixing a high-sugar breakfast cereal with milk does not “alter the fact that it is high in sugar”. But in losing, Kellogg’s tied up considerable government time and resource.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt would be transformative if governments across the world switched distorting agricultural subsidies away from corn, soya and sugar, crops which are also associated with ecological destruction. They could support greater local production of healthy fruit and vegetables instead. Negotiating global agreement seems overwhelmingly daunting, with individual states having few levers to pull.But there is also a lesson here and it is that, as with so much policy, small battles patiently won do make a difference. Curbs on promotion – clearer labelling, no two-for-one offers, no end-of-aisle positioning – may seem small fry, but the fact that the industry and its lobbying groups choose to fight costly delaying litigation shows these incremental changes do have an effect. Manufacturers are right to see government action as a threat. It needs to be.Felicity Lawrence is a former Guardian special correspondent, and is author of Not on the Label: What Really Goes Into theFoodon Your PlateExplore more on these topicsUltra-processed foodsOpinionFood & drink industryFoodHealthObesityWorld Health OrganizationcommentShareReuse this content

title: I stand to defend vertical drinking. Is a pub that doesn’t allow it a real pub at all? | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: The time-honoured tradition of standing up with a drink, gossiping and putting the world to rights is under threat. If councillors ban it, we’ll all lose out, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: The time-honoured tradition of standing up with a drink, gossiping and putting the world to rights is under threat. If councillors ban it, we’ll all lose out, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: Monmouth Street in Covent Garden, London.Photograph: Jonathan Wilson/AlamyView image in fullscreenMonmouth Street in Covent Garden, London.Photograph: Jonathan Wilson/AlamyOpinionPubsI stand to defend vertical drinking. Is a pub that doesn’t allow it a real pub at all?Simon JenkinsThe time-honoured tradition of standing up with a drink, gossiping and putting the world to rights is under threat. If councillors ban it, we’ll all lose outFri 7 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 04.53 EDTShareIt is unbelievable: unconscionable. Westminster Council is moving against“vertical drinking” in pubs, starting with Soho. It claims drinking standing up is noisy and disruptive. It makes pubs, the council says, boisterous places where customers crowd round bars, get drunk and become pains in the neck in the street outside.Westminster’s new draft licences would require pubs to be only for seating, to have “table service in place of open bar space”. Pub users should, presumably, sit down, shut up and wait to be served, like decent Westminster people who use wine bars.The councilbalks at claims it seeks a ban, but here’s the thing: the reason the council apparently dislikes vertical drinking is the reason Britons have done it for ever. It is liquid sociability. It suits all sorts and ages. It encourages people to chat with strangers, pick arguments, spill beer down jackets and reduce traffic outside to a crawl. No one has to book tables or be turned them away when it is “full”. They can come and go, or stay all day.British pubsare now closing fast. In the past 10 years roughly one has closed every day,to an all-time low of 39,000. Numbers have taken two big hits. The first was the loosening of planning laws that have allowed the change of useof licenced premises into housing.The other hit was the Starmer government’s stinging increase in business rates and jobs taxes, with its stamping out of casual youth employment. Some pubs faced bankruptcy overnight.I have a pub a few yards from my front door. Most evenings the place is “vertically” packed, as is the forecourt and the street outside. The noise is a nuisance to some but it ends at 10pm. More to the point, the pub is a beacon for the surrounding neighbourhood. Old and young, elegant and shabby, British and foreign, all sit chatting inside and out. Argument and laughter echo down the street. They bring it to life.In the years I have lived in this street, shops, offices and cafes have opened and closed. The pub, a free house, has survived them all. It is a point of reference, a place to meet, a refuge for stray dogs and sometimes stray people. The forecourt offers a gallery to watch the world go by.When I briefly studied town planning, I now realise we were never taught a breath of sociology. Planning was like architecture. It was about buildings unrelated to the people who might use them. Humans rarely appear in pictures in architecture magazines. It is as if they spoil the show. Hence today, seeing the pub as a community institution does not register in the planner’s rulebook.If anything is vexing social intercourse at present, particularly among the young, it is the decline in human interaction. The villain of the piece is the mobile phone and social media. My statistic of the year is Atlantic magazine’s report thatthe number of words people speak every day, from 16,632 in 2005 to 11,900 in 2019. We have turned to silence. Online has replaced conversation.Experts are rightly calling the alarm. Talk matters to our brains. And that means talk in company. Nor is it just conversation that is important. It is casual conversation with people we do not know that needs mental effort. When Jane Jacobs, the urban theorist and author ofThe Death and Life of Great American Cities,studied the American street, she noted its role in making people adjust their relations with each other. A chat with an old friend is easy, but with a stranger it is an exercise in community. That is the value of the pub exchange, of vertical drinking.Some pubs are simply very crowded. Long may they be so. But some are where older people go daily just to be in company. They were well satirised in Wodehouse’s classicMulliner Nights, where characters named after their favourite drinks swapped anecdotes at all hours, led by “hot scotch and lemon”. These places are in effect A&E departments for the relief of loneliness, the endemic disease of our age.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs “village” institutions continue to decline, in town as well as country, the church, the old people’s club, the sports centre, the corner shop are all disappearing as places of daily resort. We are retreating into ourselves. That the pub should go too, at the very moment of become the community’s last defining institution, is a tragedy.Westminster may have problems with what it calls its West End “cumulative impact zone” – what we call crowds – but it should not take it out on the public house. As one pub after another closes at the bidding of the property market, these places should be fostered. They are more than fun. They are the last whirlpools of social connection before we all vanish online.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsPubsOpinionSocial etiquetteHealth & wellbeingLondonSocial mediaSmartphonescommentShareReuse this content

title: When it comes to marriage and divorce, is gen Z the sensible generation? | Van Badham | The Guardian
description: This happily married gen Xer celebrates the fact marriage rates are down. It shows Australians have the freedom and opportunity to make the best decisions for them
Author: Van Badham
Headline: This happily married gen Xer celebrates the fact marriage rates are down. It shows Australians have the freedom and opportunity to make the best decisions for them
Content: ‘Even better than having the ability to more easily leave an unhappy marriage is not getting into one in the first place.’Photograph: Brus_Rus/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Even better than having the ability to more easily leave an unhappy marriage is not getting into one in the first place.’Photograph: Brus_Rus/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionMarriageWhen it comes to marriage and divorce, is gen Z the sensible generation?Van BadhamThis happily married gen Xer celebrates the fact marriage rates are down. It shows Australians have the freedom and opportunity to make the best decisions for themFri 7 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 20.12 EDTShareThe Australian Bureau of Statistics reported last month that the marriage rate is declining. As someone who champions marriage, is married and thinks a wedding is lovely, I think it’s great news.According to the data, the crude rate of registered marriages per 1,000 residents aged 16 and over fell from 5.5 in 2024 to 5.3 in 2025, with the largest falls occurring among the 25-29s and 30-34s.Why do I celebrate? Because these figures remind us that Australia is a sensible, progressive nation whose liberal social institutions have given individuals the freedom and opportunity to make the best decisions for our own lives.This includes exercising our right to divorce, an event also represented in the ABS statistics. Divorces granted rose by 4.1%, the crude divorce rate up from 2.1 to 2.2.The process of relationship breakdown is always painful, the circumstances causing marriages to fail are often sad, and legal separation is usually a practical nightmare. Yet it was within my own lifetime that Australian law once compelled people in relationships that were unbalanced, dysfunctional, mistrustful, unhappy or loveless to stay married if they couldn’t meet narrow legal criteria to make a case for their divorce before the courts.What makes a good wedding these days? I say flirting and chaos, but not three days in a French castle | Rachel ConnollyRead moreAs populist right political movements all over the globe push nostalgia politics andregressive social policiesalong with them, it’s worth remembering that the “good ol’ days” of divorce law in Australia once meant that even couples seeking amicable divorces could be obliged into deceit to obtain them. Before the present “no-fault” divorce framework arrived in 1975, practices like “staged adultery” involved recruiting hotel rooms, photographers and private detectives to meet evidence thresholds for divorce proceedings.But even better than having the ability to more easily leave an unhappy marriage is not getting into one in the first place – which is why I’m excited about the decrease in the marriage rate, especially as it pertains to age cohorts.Reporting on the ABS data, The Australianquoteda demographer claiming that “the expensive property market keeps the divorce rate unnaturally low, because it’s just too expensive to split up”. While that may be true, we should resist the temptation to interpret trends in Australia’s divorce and marriage rates within an exclusively material frame. Yes, Deloitte’sglobal surveyof gen Z and millennials found these cohorts are delaying “life decisions” due to financial concerns, but Nick Tebbey from Relationships Australia made a pertinent observation: “people are more aware going into long-term relationships these days of who they are and what they expect out of it, so they are only making a commitment to marriage when they feel genuinely ready.”Gen Z are a favourite target of chastising concern from elder generations, claiming the kids arelazy,entitled, undisciplined and unemployable; “snowflakes” who are too fragile to cope with adult life;blank, vapidandaddicted to phones;lonely and anxiouswithpoor mental health; andsexless.Yet looking at the ABS data, I wonder if we may have stumbled on to the reality of the “sensible generation”, given gen Z’s habit of delaying marriage exists alongside theirlower teen birthratesandlower rates of alcohol use.As for their recorded anxiety, loneliness and existential tensions, just maybe these are problems you can admit and address when your mid-to-late 20s aren’t otherwise dominated by jobs that exploit you, kids you’re not equipped to parent, relationships you don’t know how to get out of and the consequences of staggeringly stupid decisions made while drunk.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI am gen X; covered in the scar tissue of a far less sensible youth. I’ve been a longtime, pub-rantingadvocate of banning marriage for everyone on the less-wrinkled side of 30. To make an emotional commitment to another person so serious and so total it bears the imprimatur of the state is a tough ask for a rookie player. The complex interchange of shared responsibility threatens to overwhelm me almost daily and I (a) didn’t get married until the age of 47 and (b) genuinely like the guy.The gen X prophet Hal Hartley suggested in his 1990 film Trust: “A family’s like a gun – you point it in the wrong direction, you’re gonna kill somebody.” I suspect he witnessed the dysfunction of married-too-young family setups just as the rest of my generation did. By themid-70s, the median age for a first marriage was just 23-24 for men and 21-22 for women, which are the ages of kids I’d still expect to stand up for me on the bus. Note: marriage ages began their climb to present medians of 31 and 30 after 1976, when Australia’s “no fault divorce” legislation came into effect. That year, divorce rates peaked – more than double the number of today’s. It was a backlog effect for a generation of couples finally able to do-over some youthful mistakes.Of course, very young adults can and do make serious relationships work, but liberalisation of the marriage institution and the attitudes around it mean they can do so through marriage or unmarried cohabitation orliving apart together, or they can enjoy asituationship, hooking-up, or any lifestyle variation from no partners to every available partner within walking distance – not from social expectation or cultural pressure but because they know themselves.Gen Z should celebrate their good judgment and marriage advocates our progress.Marriagehas not been rejected. It has been chosen.Van Badham is a Guardian Australia columnistExplore more on these topicsMarriageOpinioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Le Corbusier’s social housing was meant to be the dream. In a summer of extreme heat, it is a nightmare | Anna Richards | The Guardian
description: When temperatures get to 40C inside, and French building regulations won’t even allow shutters, these tenants’ listed homes are simply unlivable, says Anna Richards, a journalist based in Lyon
Author: Anna Richards
Headline: When temperatures get to 40C inside, and French building regulations won’t even allow shutters, these tenants’ listed homes are simply unlivable, says Anna Richards, a journalist based in Lyon
Content: Corbusier’s final project: the Unité d'Habitation de Firminy-Vert, south-east France.Photograph: Guido Paradisi/AlamyView image in fullscreenCorbusier’s final project: the Unité d'Habitation de Firminy-Vert, south-east France.Photograph: Guido Paradisi/AlamyOpinionExtreme heatLe Corbusier’s social housing was meant to be the dream. In a summer of extreme heat, it is a nightmareAnna RichardsWhen temperatures get to 40C inside, and French building regulations won’t even allow shutters, these tenants’ listed homes are simply unlivableFri 7 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 11.31 EDTShareThe population of Firminy, south-eastFrance, has been dwindling for decades. Its recent history is one of factory closures in a region built by steel, and locals tell me that many people leave for better opportunities in neighbouring Saint-Étienne, or to live in the Haute-Loire’s countryside.On the top of a hill, however, stands Firminy’s pride:l’Unité d’Habitation, an imposing tower of concrete designed by Le Corbusier. The architect’s final project is an oddity – a building for people, where two-thirds of the apartments are dedicated tohabitations à loyer modéré(or HLM – social housing); but also a piece of history, whose facade and roof were listed asmonuments historiquesin 1993.It was also designed for a 1960s climate, not thesweltering temperatureswe have experienced for much of the summer. For its residents, the tower feels increasingly like an unlivable furnace – and because of its protected status, that is unlikely to change soon.We are on the brink of the fourth heatwave of the year when I meet a group of residents at the bottom of l’Unité d’Habitation. They have had enough. Inside their flats, during a heatwave, the temperatures regularly reach 35C, and can rise to 40C.“I slept on the floor because it was the only place I could stay cool,” says Aurélie Mohamed, who has lived in l’Unité d’Habitation for five years.“I slept on the balcony,” says Nathalie Rouchouse, who moved in 15 years ago.“My godmother was one of the original residents ofLe Corbusier, and I can remember coming here aged nine,” Chantal Hospital tells me. “We marvelled at the building; we were so proud of it in Firminy. It’s been 26 years since I moved in, and now I’m doing my best to move out. I never want to live in a historic monument again.”L’Unité d’Habitation has no shutters, but adding them would not be a straightforward task. Any change to the facade of a historic monument is subject to a long list of rules, and can’t currently be done without the authorisation of the architectes des bâtiments de France (ABF). For now, residents resort to DIY methods, hanging blankets or panels made from tinfoil across the windows, but it’s no substitute.When a person owns a part of a historic monument, as is the case with the third of apartments in private ownership in l’Unité d’Habitation in Firminy, there are certain benefits to its listed status. They are entitled to a grant of 40% of the cost of the work when they carry out renovations, and they are able to claim some tax reductions.View image in fullscreenThe lack of exterior protection from heat and sunlight at Firminy Vert.Photograph: Hemis/AlamyBut social renters are caught in the middle of the rules imposed on all historic monuments in the country, and the actions and investment ofHabitat et Métropole, the social landlord that manages the HLM part of the building. Habitat et Métropole didn’t answer any of my questions regarding the Firminy site.The relentless heatwaves have highlighted a class divide in France. The residents of l’Unité d’Habitation are far from the only ones living in HLMs tocomplain of 40Cinside their homes, and in some respects they are better off than those in poorly designed buildings elsewhere. Le Corbusier’s famouspilotisallow for better airflow underneath the tower.This class element is even more apparent in Firminy, where the Le Corbusier site, including parts of l’Unité d’Habitation, is also a tourist attraction. About 20,000 visitors a year come to see l’Unité d’Habitation, its showroom apartment and the kindergarten, which is no longer used as a nursery. Aurélie Mohamed, Nathalie Rouchouse and Chantal Hospital’s home is a living museum, but although tourists pay to visit their building, none of the money from ticket sales is injected back into the site. It is run as a separate operation and Géraldine Dabrigeon, the chief curator ofSite Le Corbusier, says that the revenue from ticket sales only covers guides, advertising and insurance. Even though the part open to tourists is run separately, it strikes me as rather zoo-like to have people paying to visit somewhere while the residents swelter behind blankets hung to compensate for the lack of shutters.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCharles-edouard Jeanneret, better known as Le Corbusier in his atelier in 1955Photograph: Imagno/Getty ImagesLe Corbusier’s vertical towns were built at a time when social initiatives were booming, and they were designed to support those on lower incomes. Now, the very people these buildings are designed for are being penalised for living in a keepsake of France’s social history.Under anew proposal,brought forward by the French government on 7 July in response to the heatwaves, local councils could gain greater power to modify historic buildings. Rather than the ABF having the definitive say on any modifications, its opinion would be regarded as merely advisory. Critics in the conservative newspaper Le Figaro say that such a move would lead to a “concrete and soulless France”. But the residents of l’Unité d’Habitation already live in a concrete block – one without shutters.“At some point, a choice will need to be made,” says Chantal Hospital. “Does the building stay residential, as Corbusier intended, or does it become a museum?”The problem isn’t necessarily that l’Unité d’Habitation is a historic monument, but rather that HLMs across France leave the poorest and most vulnerable suffering the worst of the heatwaves. To be both a historic monument and an HLM, however, means to have all the disadvantages of an underfunded HLM while also being subject to the list of strict rules imposed on historic monuments. It makes the prestige of their “monument historique” plaque rather hollow for the renters – especially when their makeshift provisions for the heat can be gawked at by visiting tourists. At what point do we respect architecture and history over people’s living conditions?Speaking under the tower, residents told me they had been raising these issues for years. But the Fondation Le Corbusier only discussed the increasing impact of heatwaves on the various Le Corbusier sites this year, one board member said. It plans to look through his old architectural plans to see if it would be possible to install shutters that fit with the listed facade. If the foundation fights sufficiently for its residents, particularly those in HLMs, perhaps the renters will finally reap the rewards of living in a listed building. The fact that this is only just being discussed, however, makes me feel this may be too little, too late.There is also a significant risk that the HLM renters of l’Unité d’Habitation will fall foul of the famous complexities of French bureaucracy, in a case of too many cooks. In that instance, the whole complex affair could drag on for so long that these homes become uninhabitable.The number of heatwaves isexpected to increase fivefoldin France by 2050. While the rich are largely responsible for the climate crisis, those living in social housing, without air conditioning or shutters, will be the first to suffer the consequences.Anna Richards is a journalist and travel writer based in LyonExplore more on these topicsExtreme heatOpinionArchitectureFranceLe CorbusierEuropeClimate crisiscommentShareReuse this content

title: With their assault on science, Trumpists aren’t just harming America – they’re harming themselves | Jan-Werner Müller | The Guardian
description: The administration is subjugating science to political imperatives, a major blow to US soft power and technological progress
Author: Jan-Werner Müller
Headline: The administration is subjugating science to political imperatives, a major blow to US soft power and technological progress
Content: ‘The ideological assault on universities continues.’Photograph: Tierney L Cross/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The ideological assault on universities continues.’Photograph: Tierney L Cross/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesOpinionTrump administrationWith their assault on science, Trumpists aren’t just harming America – they’re harming themselvesJan-Werner MüllerThe administration is subjugating science to political imperatives, a major blow to US soft power and technological progressFri 7 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 12.10 EDTShareTheTrump administrationis waging an unprecedented war on institutions devoted to research and higher learning. While plenty of countries have harmed universities by imposing neoliberal logics on academia – creating artificial markets in the name of spurring professors to be more productive – the Trumpist subjugation of all science to political imperatives has no equivalent in a democracy; if anything, it is reminiscent of Stalin’s Soviet Union. The assault now also targets foreign students and any kind of international collaboration – a major blow to US soft power. Why are Trumpists engaging in what can only be described as an act of wanton self-injury?Project 2025’sRussell Vought, the director of the office of management and budget,initiated the rule changethat would make any federal grantsubject to review by political appointees– including funds for science that so far have been allocated through judgment by first-rate fellow scientists. This measure would furnish Trumpists with a new weapon to threaten universities along the lines of: “Nice medical school you have there – pity if something were to happen to it because your administration had failed to come into alignment with the president’s priorities.”Then there isthe strategyrecently presented by Trump’s science adviser, a former employee of Peter Thiel, with the unique distinction of havingno relevant experience in researchwhatsoever. Michael Kratsios wants to shift decision-making from experts in universities to private corporations, which, helped by AI, are supposedly better positioned to spot potential breakthroughs. This constitutes a major break with the enormously successful approach the US took after the second world war: pour taxpayer money into basic, open-ended science which no private company would risk sponsoring – but with both citizens and American capital eventually benefiting from the inventions that came out of fundamental research. Kratsios wishes the government to adopt “the intentionality of a serious investor” in order to usher in a new “golden age of science” (declaring something “golden” seems enough to succeed in Trump-world). De facto, as critics haverightly pointed out, this seems a strategy to take money from what Trumpists perceive as their political enemies – universities – and shovel it to their allies in tech.Meanwhile, the more directly ideological assault on universities continues. Having failed to tempt select institutions of higher learning with a “compact” to receive preferential federal treatment last year, Linda McMahon, the fake-wrestling-executive-turned-anti-education secretary, isnow asking university presidentsto pledge allegiance to the administration through statements on their websites: among other things, they are supposed to explain how they will increase “intellectual pluralism” (read: affirmative action for conservatives); deal with campus protest (read: police student speech the Trump administration does not like); and make education more provincial (serving America first) and instrumental (only immediate employability andvocational credentialismcount) – and less critical of “our civilizational inheritance”.In the spirit of Stephen Miller-type nativism, international donors are targeted no less than international collaboration in general; visas for PhD students are nowlimited to four years(an unrealistic time frame for many academic subjects), with possible extensions if students spend time and money on appealing to the Department of Homeland security (instead of doing actual research). The fact that many researchers in the past have stayed in the US after obtaining their doctorates, contributing to national wealth (just like America Firsters would presumably want) or went back to their countries with good feelings to the US – all that counts for nothing.Is the US trying to make scientists’ work so difficult that they simply give up? | Daniel MalinskyRead moreWhat explains such self-harm? Rightwing hostility to higher education is nothing new: from intellectuals supposedly being communist eggheads in the 1950s, to moral panics about “political correctness” in the 1990s and “wokeness” in recent years, there is the basic stance made explicit by JD Vance in 2021: “Universities are the enemy.” But Trump’s rule has brought together a novel coalition, one divided by many issues but united in their desire to destroy universities as we know them. Among them: the Maga hardcore with its traditional anti-intellectualism and nativism; the Silicon Valley oligarchs who imagine their companies replacing (and monetizing) university functions; and conservatives in name, but radicals in practice who want to take over higher education, but, failing that,would like to burn the whole system down.Also novel, in the wake of Covid, is the commitment of so many on the right to the idea that, somehow, science and freedom are opposites, that not having ever to listen to people who know something better than you do is the essence of personal liberation. If that emotional fuel for the new anti-intellectualism were not powerful enough, there is a highly flammable desire for revenge – amply on display in theendless attacks on Anthony Fauci.To be sure, Congresshas not gone alongwith some of the major funding cuts for science Trump keeps requesting; even Republican politicians quietly resist when monies would stop flowing to their districts. And the new OMB rule, it seems, isbeing blockedin a funding deal reached in the Senate this week. But one cannot rely on such occasional pushback by one Republican or another, because none of them has offered a principled defense of the postwar model (in fact, given the conduct of the likes of the senatorsThom Tillis and John Cornynthis week, it seems fair to say that “principled Republican” is fast becoming a contradiction in terms).University leaders and prominent scientists have to hold the line in opposing possible “deals” with the Trump administration; everyone could have learned by now that Trumpists will not stick to their end of the bargain. More importantly, those seeing things wrong with peer review, for instance, or too much administrative busywork for researchers – and some of these problems are real – have to realize that Trumpists are the last who can be trusted to solve them.Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton UniversityExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionDonald TrumpUS educationUS politicsUS universitiescommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Jason Arday: diversity advocates must stand firm | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Serious failings by one academic, and his bosses at the University of Cambridge, should not be allowed to undermine wider progressive goals
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Serious failings by one academic, and his bosses at the University of Cambridge, should not be allowed to undermine wider progressive goals
Content: ‘With hindsight, it seems extraordinary that details of Jason Arday’s remarkable life story were not examined sooner.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘With hindsight, it seems extraordinary that details of Jason Arday’s remarkable life story were not examined sooner.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianOpinionUniversity of CambridgeThe Guardian view on Jason Arday: diversity advocates must stand firmEditorialSerious failings by one academic, and his bosses at the University of Cambridge, should not be allowed to undermine wider progressive goalsFri 7 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 15.08 EDTShareJason Arday’sresignationfrom the University of Cambridge on Wednesday marked a full stop of sorts, but not an end to the furore surrounding his promotion to a professorship at the age of 37.Academic colleagueshave demanded, with justification, that an investigation into his appointment to the faculty of education in 2023, and the subsequent fallout, should include people from outside the university. Allegations of plagiarism and claims made by Mr Arday about his background, career and charity fundraising remain under scrutiny. The memoir for which he said he had received ahuge advance, billed as atriumph over adversityincluding an early autism diagnosis, is scheduled to appear later this month. His publisher, Simon & Schuster, ought to pause while inquiries run their course.But several things are already clear. By failing to do due diligence on Mr Arday before launching him, with fanfare, as Cambridge’s youngest-ever black professor, and through its inadequate response to later challenges, the university has done aserious disserviceto black and neurodivergent scholars more widely. It has also set back the efforts of all the people and groups who have worked in good faith, over many years, to boost the presence of underrepresented groups in influential positions.Such imbalances, which remain pronounced in many areas of public life, including academia, are the consequence of prejudices and discrimination, as well as unequal access to resources and opportunities. Thegleewith which some rightwingers have pounced on Mr Arday’s fall from grace is not solely due to relish in his exposure – or the angst among liberals that this provokes. It is because they want to stoke a sense of grievance among white supporters, and to pour scorn on diversity initiatives across the board.Such efforts to discredit policies aimed at supporting autistic people, and those from ethnic minorities, to achieve their full potential must be strenuously resisted. With hindsight, it seems extraordinary that details of Mr Arday’s remarkable life story were not examined sooner. He was wrong to report a Times Higher Education journalist,Jack Grove, to the police, on the basis of a series of emailed queries. But Mr Arday is an individual. While there are lessons to be learned from his over-hasty ascent, the answer is not to give up on equity as a goal.The scandal comes at a bad time in more ways than one. Rightwing parties continue to makehostility to migrantspart of their core offer to voters, and will seek to capitalise on what will be presented as “Black Lives Matter gone mad”. But consequences within the academy must be taken seriously too. Universities areunder massive strainowing to funding shortfalls, which have been worsened by new limits and levies on international students. Some are at risk of going bust, and the reputational blow to the sector inflicted by this scandal can only make the situation worse.The discipline of sociology, already a target of intellectual conservatives who dislike its radical roots, may also see adverse effects, as its standards are questioned. Needless to say, Cambridge colleges will be relatively insulated from such collateral damage, which is likely to be most severe at less wealthy universities with less privileged intakes. This is a grim irony, and one that should prompt serious self-reflection by an elite institution that should have known better than to be so careless.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Gianni Infantino: in the interests of the game he professes to love, he should go | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The Fifa president’s attempt to brazen out the storm, after attempting to sell a stake in the World Cup to private equity, adds insult to injury
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The Fifa president’s attempt to brazen out the storm, after attempting to sell a stake in the World Cup to private equity, adds insult to injury
Content: Gianni Infantino (centre) leaves after attending a football match in Rabat, Morocco, on Wednesday.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino (centre) leaves after attending a football match in Rabat, Morocco, on Wednesday.Photograph: APOpinionGianni InfantinoThe Guardian view on Gianni Infantino: in the interests of the game he professes to love, he should goEditorialThe Fifa president’s attempt to brazen out the storm, after attempting to sell a stake in the World Cup to private equity, adds insult to injuryFri 7 Aug 2026 12.57 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 15.08 EDTShare“How did you go bankrupt?” a character isaskedin Ernest Hemingway’s novel The Sun Also Rises. “Gradually, then suddenly” comes the reply. Right now, Fifa’s justly besieged president, Gianni Infantino, is experiencing something similar in relation to the loss  of his own authority.Since taking over the running of world football’s governing body in 2016, Mr Infantino has survived regular criticism of amonetisingapproach which has often come at a sporting cost. But since egregious plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law wereleakedto the media, his credibility has been draining away at speed.After crisis talks this week at Fifa’s lavish new African headquarters in Rabat, Mr Infantino authorised a half-hearted and incompleteapology, acknowledging that the now aborted project “could have been handled differently”. But it is very hard to imagine how a sell-off to private equity that would have imperilled the governance of the world’s most popular sport (and possibly led to Mr Infantino’s personal enrichment) could have been handled well. This was, simply, a betrayal of the game’s interests by the president of an organisation that already sits on billions of pounds worth of reserves.View image in fullscreenArsene Wenger.Photograph: Amanda Perobelli/ReutersMr Infantino should resign. But despite crushing condemnation of his actions from senior Fifa figures, and football greats such asArsène WengerandLuís Figo, he appears determined to brazen out the storm. As a result, what happens now looks like becoming increasingly messy. Over the course of 10 years, Fifa’s president has carefully cultivated allies in the global south. Breaking ranks with their regional federation, Mexico and Argentina on FridayjoinedAfrican nations in expressing support for his continued leadership.Much will therefore depend on European football’s governing body, Uefa. On Thursday itrespondedwitheringly to Mr Infantino’s attempt to draw a line, and restated a loss of confidence in his presidency. On Friday, Norway became the first federation to calldirectlyfor Fifa’s president to stand down. The next step will be to follow through on a threat to boycott Fifa-run competitions, starting with the Under-20 Women’s World Cup due to be held in Poland next month.That, clearly, would be a very serious move. But it was a serious abuse of power to negotiate a deal mortgaging the World Cup’s future to speculators seeking to extract even more wealth from it. From the dubiousawardof the 2022 World Cup to Qatar, to Fifa’ssuspensionof inconvenient red cards, Mr Infantino is used to provoking and ignoring controversies. This one must come with consequences.With haughty presumption, the statement from Mr Infantino’s Rabat bunker said the organisation “will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process”. The chutzpah is almost impressive. But really, dream on. Unless Fifa’s president resigns, is forced out, or is ousted via an election next March, the global game is in danger of descending into an ugly civil war – all because of one man’s attempt to sell off the family silver in unprecedented fashion. Mr Infantino was much mocked for his “Today I feel gay … today I feel [like] a migrant worker”responseto critics prior to the Qatar World Cup. It would be greatly to the benefit of the sport he professes to love if he could show some self-awareness now.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Jason Arday affair has much to say about the current state of academia | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Letters: Guardian readers reflect on the university system’s approach to Black academics and how it deals with job applications and promotions
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Guardian readers reflect on the university system’s approach to Black academics and how it deals with job applications and promotions
Content: ‘Within higher education, Jason Arday is well known for the kindness he promotes.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Within higher education, Jason Arday is well known for the kindness he promotes.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianJason ArdayLettersThe Jason Arday affair has much to say about the current state of academiaGuardian readers reflect on the university system’s approach to Black academics and how it deals with job applications and promotionsFri 7 Aug 2026 12.57 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.40 EDTShareYes, the recent Jason Arday scandal should be a wake-up call to the left, as Jason Okundaye suggests (The takedown of Jason Arday has overjoyed the right, and must be a wake-up call for the left, 6 August), but it should also be a wake-up call to anyone who cares about university systems and protocols around appointment and promotion.What I have seen at UK universities suggests that Arday was not simply an individual who slipped through the net, but that university systems often fail to detect or challenge exaggerated claims. If anything, those with greater institutional privilege are more likely to get away with exaggerations, embellishments and even falsehoods on their CVs and promotion applications.I have witnessed and reported on what appeared to be falsehoods in promotion applications with no repercussions; in fact, in both cases the applicants were promoted (and both were white). In one case, an applicant claimed to have given several keynote addresses, while conference websites indicated that he had been only an ordinary conference speaker. In another, an applicant claimed to be a co-author of a book when she was listed as a “data collection contributor”.Why, after I highlighted inaccurate claims, were these people still promoted? I cannot say. But from speaking with colleagues at other universities, this is far from unusual. Those willing to stretch the truth can rely on overworked colleagues with little time to factcheck and a system depending heavily on applicants’ honesty.This lack of accountability is grossly unfair on the many academics who report honestly on their accomplishments and do excellent work without resorting to such tactics. Perhaps the pressure to meet increasingly demanding and sometimes unattainable standards is driving this behaviour.The number of permanent academic jobs has not kept pace with the number of PhD graduates, and competition for academic posts has intensified. Nevertheless, we need more checks and verifiable criteria to help prevent future scandals and to restore confidence in academic integrity.Name and address suppliedThe case of ProfJason Ardayis an important insight into the academic world. Public expectation of academia and its most prestigious institutions is that these are purely meritocratic. In my experience this is not the case. One of the questions we should be asking is why an academic would be moved to fabricate a CV? Academic pressures can be intense, as evidenced by the needless suicide of Prof Stefan Grimm in 2014.Furthermore, low-level racism is common in the university setting, in which there is a “chumocratic” culture that promotes similar or like-minded individuals. Ethnic minorities, or those who question the establishment, may be excluded from reaping the full benefits of their academic endeavours in an environment in which career-defining decisions such as promotion, publication and grant success are subjective.At present, pending full investigation, it may be unclear if Jason Arday is perpetrator or victim, but the academic environment in which he has operated is unlikely to be completely blameless.Salim KhakooProfessor of hepatology, University of SouthamptonJason Arday’s story has divided opinion among my friends and associates, and Okundaye’s piece articulates why. Whether the accusations of plagiarism or lying hold up, only time will tell. But in the meantime, a man and his family are in an intolerable position.What troubles me equally is the frame surrounding Arday before any of this surfaced: the youngest Black professor in Cambridge’s history, a story of triumph over adversity. That framing is seductive – it’s the stuff that films are made of – but it sets a trap. It suggests Black excellence is only coherent when it becomes a redemption story. But that isn’t equal opportunity; equality doesn’t require anyone to be a miracle.I don’t know if Arday lied. I’m not signing petitions declaring the allegations “entirely false”. But I will still buy his book, because I think he has been let down by more than himself.Memuna FornaLondonHere’s what I think Jason Arday represents: an obsession among liberal Britain with Black people’s “inspiring stories”; a man for whom making things up became a sad habit, and what happens when you become trapped in it; a reminder that, depressingly, the path to flourishing while Black is to be better than perfect, and some people will never believe you’re there by merit; and how a victim of a coordinated campaign can be taken down. All these points are true. It’s a sad story.Colton RichardsLondonI really appreciated the down-to-earth sanity of Jason Okundaye’s piece on the case of Jason Arday. So much hype, so much spiteful sniping, seldom thoughtful or without an agenda. Underneath it all, I can’t help feeling that Cambridge University did little to cover themselves in glory.However, I suspect that few have thought about Jason Arday, the person, and what he might be going through. I feel a sense of admiration for him, without being in a position to judge any of the allegations made against him. Some compassion would go a long way.Linda RheadHampton, LondonIt is a deeply concerning to hear of theresignation of Prof Jason Arday, a huge loss. Your report (5 August) refers to the Guardian’s own investigation, with revelations that this professor may have inflated his running achievements and overstated threats to his personal safety. On the former, instances of much more egregious displays of ego in academia are far from rare, without any apparent damage to the standing or careers of many professors.On the latter, one has to ask what it takes for an institution to act to protect Black staff and students. Experiences of racism are far from unusual, and the psychological toll they take is well documented. Rather than undermine those who seek help in the face of abuse, the Guardian might wonder: what does it take to make us listen and understand?Dr Isabel ShutesLondon School of Economics and Political ScienceWithin higher education, Jason Arday is well known for the kindness he promotes; many thousands of the students and staff he has encountered over the years will attest to this. In today’s world – particularly within the context of recent coverage surrounding Arday – the significance of this should not be underestimated.The accusations against Arday raise many polarising and contentious issues, and debates will no doubt continue for some time. In all of this, I urge commentators and commenters to remember the principles of respect and humanity, not to mention kindness.Name and address suppliedHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Let’s all get on board with travel etiquette | Social etiquette | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers add to a guide for handling tricky situations on public transport
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers add to a guide for handling tricky situations on public transport
Content: ‘Women could be menstruating, in the first trimester of pregnancy (the most exhausting time) or have endometriosis.’Photograph: Getty/Posed by modelView image in fullscreen‘Women could be menstruating, in the first trimester of pregnancy (the most exhausting time) or have endometriosis.’Photograph: Getty/Posed by modelSocial etiquetteLettersLet’s all get on board with travel etiquetteReaders add to a guide for handling tricky situations on public transportFri 7 Aug 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTShareRe your article on travel etiquette (The ultimate guide to travel etiquette: how to handle 36 tricky situations, from manspreaders to smelly armpits, 4 August), it’s totally wrong to advise people not to give up seats for a woman any more. Women could be menstruating, in the first trimester of pregnancy (the most exhausting time, and not one you advertise with badges saying “Baby on board”), perimenopausal, menopausal or have endometriosis (excruciating pain). Women live with a level of pain and discomfort as routine, for much of their lives. Yes, of course men can be suffering with specific ailments at specific times, but it is not part and parcel of being a man. Gentlemen, please just do it.Helen WalkerLondonTo your list of dubious travel behaviours, I’d like to add constant sniffing and its more guttural and nauseating relation, snorting. It seems that handkerchiefs, tissues and even the concept of blowing your nose have gone out of fashion. I am frequently nauseated by this on planes and trains, and if I don’t have headphones with me I have to resort to blocking my ears. I have not yet had the courage to speak to a culprit (although I have often been tempted to pass them a tissue).Judith MilburnHartlepool, County DurhamI enjoyed your guide to travel etiquette. It was very sensible and reflective of our modern society. I had to smile at the guidance for offering your seat to elderly people – as a man in my mid-50s who is (happily) fit and healthy, I always have to remind myself that people offering me a seat aren’t commenting on my physical state, they are just being kind to a stranger.Given the increasing incidence of harassment on public transport, particularly of women, it might be helpful to give some guidance as to what to do if you see someone being harassed – that’s a tricky balance of ensuring the safety of yourself and those around you, but it is (sadly) a reflection of the times.However, you didn’t go into enough detail about one of my biggest bugbears – people who insist on keeping their backpacks on on crowded buses and tubes where standing space is at a premium. It’s frustrating, and occasionally very problematic, when people aren’t aware that the space they’re taking up by keeping the backpack on is much larger than their unencumbered body. As they move or turn they bump into whatever you’re holding, and it reduces the opportunity for others to join the service.It’s a simple rule: take the backpack off and have it at your feet – always – to avoid encroaching on other people’s personal space and to free up space for others. Or maybe my middle-aged grumpiness is just getting the better of me on this one.Peter AntolikLondonRecently, after a three day-visit to London, I returned home to Devon and jokingly complained that Londoners constantly made me feel old. Every journey I made on public transport, someone offered me a seat. On two occasions a woman offered me a helping hand as I descended the stairs on a bus. I am a six-foot, healthy 80-year-old and can easily manage to stand for a short journey but, as my wife pointed out, it is much nicer to smile and accept the offers. On another bus, a woman offered to move so that my wife and I could sit together. In conclusion, I felt I should point out that Londoners, in my experience, do not really need much of your advice. They already have an embarrassment of politeness riches and made me feel much happier about the human race.Paul WesleyTotnes, DevonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
