title: China’s AI ecosystem is not as open as it claims. Nor is any other country’s | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Letters: Responding to an article by China’s ambassador to the UK, Prof Paul H Cleverley advocates shared openness standards, while Dr Claire Jenkins says British AI can offer a distinctive path
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Responding to an article by China’s ambassador to the UK, Prof Paul H Cleverley advocates shared openness standards, while Dr Claire Jenkins says British AI can offer a distinctive path
Content: A display by Chinese AI company Minimax during the World AI Conference in Shanghai on 17 July 2026.Photograph: Ng Han Guan/APView image in fullscreenA display by Chinese AI company Minimax during the World AI Conference in Shanghai on 17 July 2026.Photograph: Ng Han Guan/APAI (artificial intelligence)LettersChina’s AI ecosystem is not as open as it claims. Nor is any other country’sResponding to an article by China’s ambassador to the UK,Prof Paul H Cleverleyadvocates shared openness standards, whileDr Claire Jenkinssays British AI can offer a distinctive pathFri 7 Aug 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 12.58 EDTShareAmbassador Zheng Zeguang rightly celebrates openly released AI models, and the Chinese labs behind Qwen, DeepSeek and Kimi have led the way – competition that benefits everyone, especially where models can run on modest hardware in the developing world (The future of AI hinges on openness and cooperation. China and Britain can gain much by working together, 30 July).But his claim that openness is a defining feature of China’s AI development deserves scrutiny. TakeGeoGPT, the geoscience system from Zhejiang Lab showcased at last month’s World AI Conference as a model of jointly governed open science. It is promoted to countries as open, yet under the model openness framework – endorsed in arecent UN report– it would not qualify as open at all. It releases model weights (built mainly on Alibaba Qwen, whose licences are not Open Systems Interconnection-compliant),no training data or application source code is released, and its governance committee answers to Zhejiang Lab itself.Domain rivals show what fuller openness looks like. The European Space Agency’sEarth Virtual Expert(EVE), also built for the Earth sciences, releases its training and evaluation tooling, while the US non-profitAi2’s OLMogoes further still, publishing everything needed for reproducibility.The distinction matters. A free hosted service is not an open one: GeoGPT’s usersroute their datathrough China’s legal jurisdiction, creating real dependency and sovereignty risks.None of this is unique toChina. The US private-enterprise model raises much the same concerns. That is really the ambassador’s own point extended: no country’s ecosystem is quite as open as its diplomacy suggests. If the UK is to gain from the cooperation he proposes, it should press for shared openness standards like the UN-recommended model openness framework as the basis for any joint work. Honest measurement, not just the language of openness, is where real partnership begins.Prof Paul H CleverleyRobert Gordon University, AberdeenYour article rightly argues that Britain cannot afford to be a passive consumer of AI while the US and China shape the technologies that will define the future. Yet the debate should not be reduced to a geopolitical race.The real question is what kind of AI Britain wishes to build. Our greatest strength is not simply our research universities or life-sciences sector, but the NHS, our public institutions and a long tradition of ethical inquiry. These provide an opportunity to develop AI that is trustworthy, transparent and directed towards the public good rather than solely commercial advantage.Healthcare illustrates both the promise and the risk. AI can reduce administrative burdens, improve diagnosis and widen access to care. However, public confidence depends on strong governance, meaningful human oversight and assurance that patient data serves citizens rather than corporate or geopolitical interests. Recent work by the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency’snational commissioninto the regulation of AI in healthcare has highlighted exactly these concerns.Britain should resist the temptation to imitate either Silicon Valley’s market dominance or China’s state-led model. Instead, it could offer a distinctive path: AI that combines innovation with democratic accountability, scientific excellence and social justice. That would be a form of leadership worthy of Britain’s traditions – and one that others might choose to follow.Dr Claire JenkinsWollaton, NottinghamshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: I love football, so I support lots of clubs | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Letters: Millwall remain my main club, but others have turned my head, writes Michael Opitz. Also letters from Neil Bage and Ariel J Friedlander
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Millwall remain my main club, but others have turned my head, writes Michael Opitz. Also letters from Neil Bage and Ariel J Friedlander
Content: ‘Tottenham- and Arsenal-supporting friends will never understand my soft spot for both clubs.’Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Tottenham- and Arsenal-supporting friends will never understand my soft spot for both clubs.’Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianSoccerLettersI love football, so I support lots of clubsMillwall remain my main club, but others have turned my head, writesMichael Opitz.Also letters fromNeil BageandAriel J FriedlanderFri 7 Aug 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTShareI read Luke McLaughlin’s article with a great deal of empathy, yet still with some uneasiness about the taboo of having more than one club (Have you ever switched allegiance as a football fan? You are not alone, 1 August). A world I inhabit.I too was at theMillwallv Forest game marred by crowd trouble. It was my first! My family are mostly Millwall, who remain my club, but having seen them drop down the divisions and play in the third tier, my head was turned by better technique and Tottenham- and Arsenal-supporting friends. They will never understand my soft spot for both clubs.Not to mention family in Germany giving me a Freiburg shirt, making them my German team. Then the gift of a Champions League ticket at Celtic Park put another team in the mix, so I’m checking a lot of scores. Now in the Borders, I am agitating to see Gala Fairydean Rovers this season. They will be yet another team for me to keep an eye on.To this day, when people ask me which team I support, I pause sheepishly and say, “Millwall but…”. I suppose I just love football!Michael OpitzKelso, RoxburghshireOver the course of his life, a man could well change his wife owing to personal choice or events outside his control. It is quite likely that his political views will sway depending on the ineptitude of governing parties or his own finances. His religious persuasion may be amended or completely turned off. But he must never, ever, change his football allegiance, particularly for the heinous crime of glory-hunting, else he shall always be known as a plastic fan.Neil BageBourne, LincolnshireIf Luke McLaughlin wants to change teams, good for him. I often wish that I could. However, similar to the last words of Queen Mary I, when I am dead and opened you shall find my blue and white hooped heart. It’s not just that QPR was our local team. It’s not just that going to matches with my father wasourtime, unbreached by family or his congregation.Despite its rather rocky record over the last 50 years, I’ve stuck with the club. Chairmen, managers and players come and go. There are promotions and relegations (we don’t do cups). The fans remain. And the longer we stay (and the longer we suffer), we begin to understand how our commitment to the cause is at the root of the club’s identity. We hold its memories, and create new ones. We give it life. And it gives us hope. I understand that Luke feels this is too much for him. I’ll give him a wave at the Millwall game next week.Ariel J FriedlanderModena, ItalyHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Infantino’s World Cup sell-off debacle has rocked football but Fifa’s crisis has deep and rotten roots | Fifa | The Guardian
description: It has been a remarkable few days for an institution that may be irredeemable but this is a story that stretches back to a decision in 2010
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: It has been a remarkable few days for an institution that may be irredeemable but this is a story that stretches back to a decision in 2010
Content: Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell the World Cup led to a backlash which leaves him scrabbling to save his presidency.Composite: Getty, Alamy, Reuters, ShutterstockView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino’s plan to sell the World Cup led to a backlash which leaves him scrabbling to save his presidency.Composite: Getty, Alamy, Reuters, ShutterstockFifaInfantino’s World Cup sell-off debacle has rocked football but Fifa’s crisis has deep and rotten rootsIt has been a remarkable few days for an institution that may be irredeemable but this is a story that stretches back to a decision in 2010Jonathan WilsonFri 7 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are decades in which nothing happens, and weeks in which decades happen, and those weeks tend to result in leaders being toppled. Not even a fortnight ago, Gianni Infantino wastaking his victory lapon Instagram, attacking “those behind their pens and papers, behind their screens spreading hate and false rumours” who had dared to question elements of his World Cup, which had generated a record $15bn in revenues. But the next day came the revelation of his plan to sell the World Cup to outside investors and a backlash that has him scrabbling to save his presidency.It has been a remarkable few days, but this is a story whose roots stretch way back, to the decision in Zurich in 2010 to award the 2022 World Cup not to the USbut to Qatar, to a furious Bill Clinton hurling an ashtray across the room and demanding action, to an FBI inquiry into corruption, and to the flipping of the larger-than-lifeConcacaf general secretary Chuck Blazer, who had two apartments in Trump Tower, one for himself and one for his cats.Mexico and Argentina line up behind Infantino to deepen football’s civil warRead moreBlazer now appears as the cheery, bearded, acceptable face of Fifa corruption. He drove about on a mobility scooter with his parrot, Max, on his shoulder and once high-fived Vladimir Putin after the Russian president suggested he looked like Karl Marx. But it was Blazer’s evidence that led to the arrests at Zurich’s Baur au Lac hotel in 2015 andthe resignation of Sepp Blattersix days later.The overwhelming favourite to replace Blatter was the president of Uefa, Michel Platini. He, though, was unacceptable to the US, because it was his decision to switch his vote to Qatar, following – although he maintains not as a result of – a meeting at the Élysée Palace with the then French president Nicolas Sarkozy and the crown prince and prime minister of Qatar.Conveniently, evidence was found of a payment he had received fromFifain 2011 leading to his suspension. The Berne federal prosecutor, Michael Lauber, broke protocol to name Platini as something “between a witness and a suspect”. It was enough: Platini stepped aside and Infantino stepped in as Uefa’s candidate. Lauber subsequently became attorney general of Switzerland only to resign after secretly meeting Infantino while investigating Fifa. Platini was subsequently cleared and is suing both Fifa and Infantino.View image in fullscreenChuck Blazer’s evidence led to the resignation of Sepp Blatter (left) in 2015.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesAt the time, Infantino was the secretary general of Uefa, notable largely for his comical earnestness while conducting Champions League draws. He was elected Fifa president in February 2016, defeating the Bahraini Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, the president of the Asian Football Confederation, an avid hunter of wild boar who denied allegations of complicity in the torture of pro-democracy campaigners. Key had been a late change of mind by the Caribbean bloc: Sunil Gulati, the president of the US Soccer Federation, took credit for his persuasiveness.With an ally elected, the US, Mexico and Canada won the right to host the 2026 World Cup. “You wanted to have it there and I wanted to have it there, and we really did it before we came to office,” Donald Trump, performing his classic trick of supervillain exposition, told Infantino at a dinner in Davos in 2020. The order of events is worth reiterating: Infantino was elected in February 2016, Trump was inaugurated in January 2017, the World Cup hosting decision was taken in May 2018.The US has been a constant in Infantino’s presidency. He took power at a time when the US attorney general, Loretta Lynch, was promising to swill corruption out of Fifa but in terms of decisive action that has amounted to little more than a handful of cases involving dodgy South American broadcast rights deals. In May 2019 Fifa appointed as legal representatives the US law firm Paul Weiss. A few weeks earlier Paul Weiss had named a new senior partner: the former US attorney general Lynch. The following year,she praised Fifa’s newfound “transparency and ethical behaviour”.Few would agree with her. Infantino arrived promising reform, yet within a year he was removing two leaders of Fifa’s ethics commission. The same weekend that Trump sacked James Comey as head of the FBI, in part for investigating Russian interference in US politics,Infantino fired Miguel Maduro, the chair of the governance and review committee, for blocking the re-election as a Fifa vice-president of the head of the Russian Football Union Vitaly Mutko on the grounds that as Russia’s sports minister he breached guidelines on political involvement.View image in fullscreenLoretta Lynch promised to swill out corruption from Fifa during her time as US attorney general but there was minimal decisive action.Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesInfantino repeatedly bypassed the Fifa council, ducked the scrutiny of press conferences and came increasingly to rule by fiat. Theplan to sell off a chunk of the World Cupis just the most egregious example. Why would he keep a plan of such revolutionary significance from his senior staff? Why would he give his members 53 days to consider such a plan, offering them a cash bonus to acquiesce? Why would he undermine his own tournament with hydration breaks and a half-time show in the final? Why override disciplinary protocols so the right players will be on the field, seemingly to highlight the tournament’s commercial appeal to potential investors?The people who were in on the deal were connected to the Trump family,specifically Joshua Kushner, the brother of the president’s son-in-law. Again, questions immediately arise. Why would you sell off 21% of all future revenues for only 28% of what this World Cup made? Infantino’s relationship with Trump – awarding him the inaugural Fifa Peace Prize, appearing with him at world events, giving him a Club World Cup trophy, renting an office for Fifa in Trump Tower that is seemingly barely used – had already brought criticism.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUefa’s robust and united response, thethreat to boycott Fifa tournaments, was evidently not anticipated. The plan is dead, at least for now. Infantino, damaged, clings on, having rallied at least some senior Fifa staff atan emergency meeting in Rabatthis week. The chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, one of the two members of the five-man inner council who voted against the plan when informed about it the day before the World Cup final, was, notably, not there. Plans toexpand the World Cup to 64 teams, rallying Infantino’s base, have been accelerated.View image in fullscreenGianni Infantino’s relationship with Donald Trump has attracted plenty of criticism.Photograph: Image Photo Agency/Getty ImagesLetters of support that had looked as if they would ensure Infantino a further term unopposed are being withdrawn. On Friday, perhaps impressed by the promise of the 2030 World Cup final being in Casablanca, the Confederation of African Football pledged its support,joining Mexico, Argentina, Qatar, the UAE, Lebanon, Kuwait, Bhutan and Sri Lanka in backing Infantino.Perhaps there will be an election, as scheduled, next March. Perhaps Infantino can muster a majority among Fifa’s 211 members. But Uefa has vowed to “paralyse” Fifa until he is gone. The first tournament that might be boycotted is the Under- 20 Women’s World Cup, which begins in Poland on 5 September. Poland has made significant investment in infrastructure and is keen for the tournament to go ahead as scheduled but its football federation would be unlikely to step outside the Uefa bloc.Infantino is getting his karmic kicking, but why did football take so long to rebel against Fifa? | Jonathan LiewRead moreThe politicking goes on although already the discussion seems more about who might challenge or defeat Infantino than about how to change Fifa, where clientelism has reigned since João Havelange won the 1974 presidential election. The institution itself is rotten; it may be that it is irredeemable.It’s very hard to know how genuine Infantino’s attempt to reform Fifa was, but it quickly foundered. And so Fifa’s attempt to move on from the crisis caused by the executive who rented an apartment for his cats in Trump Tower has wound up back in Trump Tower, with a president who rents an office there.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Niewiadoma crushes Tour de France Femmes rivals on Mont Ventoux and takes overall lead  | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Kasia Niewiadoma took a spectacular solo victory on the legendary Mont Ventoux, securing a slim overall lead in the Tour de France Femmes after stage seven
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Kasia Niewiadoma took a spectacular solo victory on the legendary Mont Ventoux, securing a slim overall lead in the Tour de France Femmes after stage seven
Content: Kasia Niewiadoma on the podium after a devastating display of climbing on Mont Ventoux.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKasia Niewiadoma on the podium after a devastating display of climbing on Mont Ventoux.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesTour de France FemmesNiewiadoma crushes Tour de France Femmes rivals on Mont Ventoux and takes overall leadPole leaves fellow contenders behind on iconic climbDemi Vollering trails by 15sec, Marlen Reusser by 39secJeremy Whittleat Mont VentouxFri 7 Aug 2026 13.43 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 19.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKasia Niewiadoma took a spectacular solo victory on the legendary Mont Ventoux, securing a slim overall lead in theTour de France Femmesafter leaving behind her fellow race favourites Marlen Reusser and Demi Vollering.“It’s hard to describe my feelings because I’m still blown away by what just happened,” Niewiadoma,who won the yellow jersey in 2024, said of the first Tour stage victory of her career.Tour de France Femmes 2026: Kasia Niewiadoma wins on Mont Ventoux and takes yellow – liveRead moreIn one of the most memorable climbing performances on the fearsome Giant of Provence, the 31-year-old Polish rider took back the best part of two minutes on Reusser, who had led the race sinceTuesday’s individual time trial. With two stages remaining Niewiadoma leads overall by 15sec from Vollering, the 2023 champion. Reusser trails by 39sec in third after stage seven.Vollering’s initial attack, which came on one of the climb’s few hairpins, the Virage du Bois, was promptly closed down by Reusser and Niewiadoma, who, just as they had atMont Brouilly on stage five, stuck doggedly to the Dutch rider’s wheel. Their collective effort was enough to force the issue, and the trio rode ahead to contest the stage.Niewiadoma’s decisive acceleration came just under 10km from the summit, after she, Reusser and Vollering had moved ahead of the front group. Vollering and Reusser seemed more focused on each other, hesitating as Niewiadoma went clear. That sealed their fate. Since its rebirth in 2022, Niewiadoma has always finished on the podium of the Tour, and her epic duel with Vollering on Alpe d’Huez in 2024 may yet be replayed in this weekend’s racing in the hills around Nice.“It means the world to me to get the yellow jersey by winning on the Ventoux,” she said. “A lot of work went into it. Each year you have to come to the Tour even stronger than the year before because the level is going up so much.”View image in fullscreenMarlen Reusser (in yellow) and Demi Vollering pursue Kasia Niewiadoma on Mont Ventoux.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesNiewiadoma’s pace took her clear on the approach to Chalet Reynard, while Reusser and Vollering appeared to be riding through treacle. In fact, it was more of a tactical stalemate that was finally broken when Vollering attacked Reusser in the final kilometre to finish second on the stage. Reusser crossed the line in a weary fourth place but there was plenty of suffering elsewhere on a stage in which a number of big names fell by the wayside.Among those to leave even before the stage started was Anna van der Breggen of SD Worx-Protime, who dropped out on Friday morning. The 36-year-old Dutch rider, who finished second overall in the Vuelta and third in the Giro earlier this year, was described as “not feeling at her best”. “We kept hoping she would start to feel better as the race progressed, but unfortunately that improvement never came. We decided not to take any unnecessary risks and to give her the rest she needs,” said the sports director Danny Stam.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEven on the less arduous slopes, before the notoriously steep bend at Saint-Estève that signals the start of the official climb, the peloton was dramatically reduced. Multiple riders fell away as the gradient increased. Early casualties of the pacesetting included the defending champion, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, and Kim Le Court,winner of stage six, both of whom definitively waved goodbye to any lingering thoughts of a high overall finish. Ferrand-Prévot’s Visma Lease-a-Bike teammate Femke de Vries was another who suffered as the Ventoux’s gradients bit into tired legs and the pair joined forces in a bid to limit their losses.At the front, Reusser’s Movistar team sought to control any attacks, but Vollering’s FDJ United-Suez proved equally as resilient. Noemi Rüegg made a huge effort to set the pace for the EF Education-Oatly team leader, Cédrine Kerbaol, but was eventually swept away by Vollering’s accelerations. Niewiadoma spent time training on the Ventoux in June with her husband, the former professional Taylor Phinney, saying she sold the idea to him as a “romantic getaway”.There may be little love lost, however, between Niewiadoma and her old rival Vollering in the Tour’s final 48 hours. “We have a strong team,” Niewiadoma said, “but I’m expecting a massive fight for everything – points, bonus seconds, everything – because the gap is so small.”Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jay-Z’s Roc Nation Sports making waves in European football transfer market | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Vinícius Júnior and Yan Diomande are among more than 100 players at an agency owned by the hip-hop legend
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Vinícius Júnior and Yan Diomande are among more than 100 players at an agency owned by the hip-hop legend
Content: Roc Nation Sports have had to deal with two separate legal challenges over their handling of Yan Diomande, who has joined Real Madrid.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRoc Nation Sports have had to deal with two separate legal challenges over their handling of Yan Diomande, who has joined Real Madrid.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesTransfer windowJay-Z’s Roc Nation Sports making waves in European football transfer marketVinícius Júnior and Yan Diomande are among more than 100 players at an agency owned by the hip-hop legendEd AaronsFri 7 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the end there was a clear winner. And Jay-Z’s latest victory came only 24 hours after the first record featuring him actually rapping for four years had been released by his wife, Beyoncé, on an extended remix pack of Morning Dew (Donk).These days, the man who remains one of the most influential artists in hip-hop has his fingers in many pies, from thestreaming service Tidaland his own streetwear brand, to champagne and cognac. But it is Roc Nation Sports – an offshoot of his entertainment company of the same name founded in 2008 – making headlines in the summer transfer window.Arsenal hopes dashed after Vinícius Júnior extends Real Madrid contract to 2032Read moreEstablished five years later in partnership with Creative Artists Agency, it began mainly representing players from the NBA, NFL and MLB, including Kevin Durant. Bayern Munich’s Jérôme Boateng was the first football client, in 2015, before Roc Nation Sports International (RNSI) was established four years later with a focus on stars at big European clubs.Based in London, it now has more than 100 players on its books, includingVinícius Júnior– the Brazil forward who signed a lucrative new contract with Real Madrid this week believed to be worth around €25m. That came after Arsenal had been linked with a blockbuster move for the 26-year-old.In July 2023 RNSI took over the successful Brazilian agents TFM – who already represented Vinícius, Gabriel Martinelli, and Endrick – and renamed it Roc Nation Sports Brazil.In negotiations that have lasted two years, it had hoped to persuade Real to increase their star asset’s salary to €30m a year to match Kylian Mbappé, and allowed his contract to enter its final 12 months in an effort to drum up interest elsewhere. WhileArsenal– now exploring other attacking options including Everton’s Iliman Ndiaye – are believed to have been willing to pay a big fee for Vinícius, it is understood that they thought signing him on a free transfer next season was more likely.Nonetheless, Real upped their offer and Vinícius stayed. It is a decision that looks likely to cost them the chance to sign Rodri from Manchester City afterBarcelona stole a marchon their great rivals.View image in fullscreenA phonecall from Vinícius Júnior reportedly led to Yan Diomande signing with Roc Nation Sports.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APOn the same day as the new six-year contract for Vinícius was announced, Yan Diomande flew to the Spanish capital to complete hisrecord £115m transfer from RB Leipzig. The 19-year-old – who has made only 46 appearances at senior level for the German club and for Leganés in the Spanish second division but is already the most expensive African player in history –was picturedwith his agents, Nathan Campbell and Kareem Gbaja on a private jet. RNSI has been reported to have been paid up to £17m in commission and fees.A long-running saga that began whenLiverpoolhad a £70m bid rejected by Leipzig in June ended with Diomande signing a seven-year deal at the Bernabéu on Thursday. It has provided a telling insight into the mechanisms of a modern transfer, with every week bringing a fresh twist. Having been told they must pay in excess of £100m to sign Diomande, Paris Saint-Germain withdrew from the race at the end of July after releasing a statement that said the European champions “will not engage in the inflationary and manipulative games of certain player agents”.RNSI has also had to fend off two legal challenges, including one from the former Bournemouth winger Max Gradel who claims that his agency, Maxidel Management, had an existing agreement with Diomande. Gradel has filed a complaint with Fifa, although world football’s governing body did not block the player’s move to Real. Dez Bamba – who is president of Diomande’s first club, AFI Sud Comoé in Côte d’Ivoire – has said that the winger was persuaded to join RNSI after receiving a call from Vinícius. RNSI has not commented on the case.Meanwhile, the Rainbow World Groupinstigated proceedingsat the high court in London and the British Virgin Islands against Diomande in mid-June “to enforce binding image rights and intellectual property agreements tied to his early career development”. It is claimed Rainbow invested significant resources in the winger, including taking him for trials at Chelsea, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace and Newcastle before he was signed by Leganés. RNSI has not commented on the case.Given Diomande’s meteoric rise, perhaps it is no surprise that clubs are flocking to invest in African academies.Jeff Luhnow – the former general manager of the Astros and St Louis Cardinals who won three World Series baseball titles and owns Leganés as part of his Blue Crow network of clubs –told the Guardian last yearDiomande was expected to be the first of many after they set up recruitment and development programmes in several African countries, including Ghana and Zambia, in the past several years. “We’ve got more players like that in our pipeline,” said Luhnow.RNSI announced in November that it has signed eight young African stars, including the Ghana Under-17 midfielder Joseph Narbi and Francis Gomez, a Gambian winger currently at AC Horsens in Denmark. “We believe Africa is a hotbed of untapped footballing potential, and our expansion here is a natural progression of our global vision,” said Campbell.In the dog-eat-dog world of football agents Jay Z’s new kids on the block are certainly making their presence felt.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowReal MadridJay-ZArsenalLiverpoolfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Will Lankshear starts off in style to see Middlesbrough past Wrexham | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: The £10m summer signing from Spurs scored a fine volley on his debut for Boro, who by advancing to the second round have improved on last year already
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The £10m summer signing from Spurs scored a fine volley on his debut for Boro, who by advancing to the second round have improved on last year already
Content: Will Lankshear (centre, wearing No 7) instantly endeared himself to the Riverside faithful.Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWill Lankshear (centre, wearing No 7) instantly endeared himself to the Riverside faithful.Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesCarabao CupWill Lankshear starts off in style to see Middlesbrough past WrexhamPA MediaFri 7 Aug 2026 17.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 19.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWill Lankshear’s debut strike ensuredMiddlesbroughmade a winning start to the season as they beat Wrexham 1-0 in the Carabao Cup first round. Lankshear, a £10m summer signing from Tottenham, scored the only goal of the game in the 61st minute as he hooked home an excellent first-time volley.Middlesbrough almost claimed a seventh-minute opener but when Adilson Malanda prodded Sebastian Berhalter’s cross goalwards from close range, Danny Ward kept the ball out with a superb point-blank save.Middlesbrough 1-0 Wrexham: Carabao Cup first round – liveRead moreDanny Imray wasted a decent chance forWrexhamwhen he failed to make a proper connection from Callum Doyle’s cross and the visitors went close again six minutes before the break when Sam Smith fired a low shot into the legs of Sol Brynn after he was rolled into space by Nathan Broadhead.Lankshear came close with an effort that was curled just over the bar at the start of the second half, but the 21-year-old did not have to wait too much longer for his first goal in a Boro shirt. Leo Castledine headed Jeremy Sarmiento’s cross into Lankshear’s path, and the striker swivelled neatly before hooking a superb first-time volley into the far corner.Boro almost doubled their lead with three minutes remaining but Morgan Whittaker’s low strike rebounded off the post.After the match the Middlesbrough manager, Kim Hellberg, expressed his delight with the instant impact Will Lankshear has made since joining the club. “He was very impressive and the most impressive thing has been seeing how well he has worked on the training ground,” Hellberg said. “How hard he works on the training ground and how much he wants to learn.“It’s a joy to watch and when you add the person he is to the quality he has as a footballer on the pitch, you have a very good striker. I’m happy to have him here.”Wrexham’s manager, Phil Parkinson, felt his side had given a decent account of themselves just four days after returning from a pre-season tour of the US. Parkinson said: “I thought we had enough half-chances, particularly in the first half, to have progressed in the competition. The game really separated from one quality finish from their lad. We had some good build-up play, but just didn’t quite have that clinical edge.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It was a big ask in terms of coming back from America on Monday and you’ve got to give the lads credit for going close. There were a lot of positives in the performance.”Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupMiddlesbroughWrexhammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Leeds extend lead at top of Super League after thrilling late win at Wakefield | Super League | The Guardian
description: Chris Hankinson’s late try helped Leeds hit back from 16-0 down to beat second-placed Wakefield 24-22 in a Super League classic
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Chris Hankinson’s late try helped Leeds hit back from 16-0 down to beat second-placed Wakefield 24-22 in a Super League classic
Content: Chris Hankinson touches down three minutes from time to complete Leeds’ comeback.Photograph: Alex Whitehead/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenChris Hankinson touches down three minutes from time to complete Leeds’ comeback.Photograph: Alex Whitehead/SWpix.com/ShutterstockSuper LeagueLeeds extend lead at top of Super League after thrilling late win at WakefieldWakefield 22-24 LeedsHankinson’s try seals victory after 16-point deficitAaron Bowerat DIY Kitchens StadiumFri 7 Aug 2026 17.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 19.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhisper it but perhaps that was the performance of a champion side. All week the talk had been aboutWakefield Trinityand whether this could be the night they declared themselves as a Super League force in front of a sell-out crowd against Leeds Rhinos.In the end, they probably did that, despite the result. These two West Yorkshire rivals served up a classic under the Belle Vue lights but in the end, despite never leading until the 77th minute, Leeds mustered up all their strength and championship credentials to complete a comeback which began when they trailed by 16 points with half an hour left.Super League closes in on gamechanging investment from Australia’s NRLRead moreAt that stage it felt inevitable that Wakefield would be going joint-top of the table with Leeds. Trinity, a Championship side two years ago, looked as though they were about to deliver their biggest statement yet that they could be about to end their 60-year wait for a major trophy. However, the Rhinos dug deep and found a way.James McDonnell’s try gave them hope before three minutes later Cameron Smith, the game’s outstanding player who will play for Wakefield in 2027, scored to mean a 22-6 lead for Wakefield had suddenly been reduced to 22-18. As it entered the championship rounds, it was Trinity who blinked, as Chris Hankinson seized on a Jake Connor kick, with Connor converting to win it.This was a result and a performance born out of Leeds and Brad Arthur’s darkest moment together. Last year they were beaten in the final seconds by St Helens in the playoffs and the Rhinos spent all pre-season warning there would be no repeat. This felt like living proof of that; Leeds showing they can go to the well in the toughest of times to secure a huge win.“That’s the evidence of us learning from it,” Arthur said. “We’ve done the work. Under a bit of pressure we kept our composure, our key players kept composure. I challenged them at half-time to go right to the 80th minute … boy, they did it.” Leeds were outplayed for large stretches here, with Wakefield good value for their 16-6 half-time lead.Tries from Isaiah Vagana, Caleb Hamlin-Uele and Jayden Myers put Trinity in control, and had the majority of this sell-out crowd dreaming of going joint-top. Brodie Croft’s try just before the break gave Leeds hope but when Jack Sinfield scored against his former club to make it 22-6, it looked as though the momentum was back with Wakefield.The Rhinos were on the ropes. But this group are built differently in 2026, with McDonnell’s try starting the comeback and Hankinson’s finishing it – with Leeds surviving a frantic final few moments to go four points clear with five games left. With this win Leeds are now heavy favourites to finish top, which would result in their first piece of silverware in six years.As for Wakefield, they will be bruised by this. Having lost by four to Wigan in the cup quarter-finals and now by two here to the league leaders, this was perhaps a subtle lesson again about the final step they still have to take. They should, however, take great pride from this – and great heart from what they did for the most part if they meet Leeds again in the playoffs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The story this year is not over,” Wakefield’s coach, Daryl Powell, said. “Leeds might have got off tonight but I’m pretty comfortable going against them again in a playoff game. They’re a great side but I watched us thinking if we play how we did in the first half we’re a fair team to defend against and play against.”One thing is for certain: if these two meet again under the lights at Old Trafford in eight weeks and serve up a repeat of this classic, nobody will be complaining.Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueWakefield TrinityLeeds RhinosRugby leaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Andrew Flintoff makes surprise exit as England Lions head coach after two years | Andrew Flintoff | The Guardian
description: Andrew Flintoff has stepped down as head coach of England Lions, saying he has taken great pride in seeing ‘the best young cricketers in the country’ develop
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: Andrew Flintoff has stepped down as head coach of England Lions, saying he has taken great pride in seeing ‘the best young cricketers in the country’ develop
Content: Andrew Flintoff has been head coach of the England Lions since September 2024.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndrew Flintoff has been head coach of the England Lions since September 2024.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesAndrew FlintoffAndrew Flintoff makes surprise exit as England Lions head coach after two yearsOther demands meant he was unable to commit fullyMike Yardy will step in for upcoming Pakistan fixtureAli MartinFri 7 Aug 2026 14.15 EDTFirst published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndrew Flintoff has decided to step down as the head coach of England Lions with immediate effect before his winter spell working in Australia’s Big Bash League (BBL).The former all-rounder, 48, has been in charge of England’s second string since September 2024 and had been given the all-clear to leave this winter’s Lions tour of South Africa early to take up his new role at BBL side Sydney Thunder.But the England and WalesCricketBoard announced on Friday evening that Flintoff has left the role. He is said to have decided the BBL job – plus TV work and family commitments – means he cannot commit fully to the Lions.Dazn buys Australia series rights as platforms jostle over England white-ball tourRead moreIn an ECB statement, Flintoff said: “Unfortunately I’ve made the decision to step away from my role with the Lions. Not only have I enjoyed my time having the opportunity to work with the best young cricketers in the country, but have taken great pride in seeing them develop.”Flintoff’s departure is somewhat abrupt, with Rob Key, the England men’s team director, having moved to defend his former teammate and close friend last week amid recent criticism of his role with the Lions team.“We’ve been incredibly fortunate to have him do it,” said Key. “I thought it was disrespectful for people to say that he shouldn’t have been doing it. He’s been outstanding in that job, and we’ve been incredibly fortunate to have him.”Flintoff had recently been negotiating with the counties over player availability for the quasi-Lions XI that will serve as warm-up opposition for Pakistan’s Test squad in a four-day match at Beckenham starting on Wednesday.Mike Yardy, the head coach of England Under-19s, will now run that team – officially the Professional County Club Select XI – using young players not currently in the Hundred or not required by their counties in the Metro Bank One-Day Cup.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile, England’s senior squad to face Pakistan in the first Test at Headingley, which starts on 19 August, has suffered an injury doubt, with the opener Emilio Gay having retired hurt while batting for Durham an apparent shoulder problem. Ollie Pope, a middle order player, is currently the reserve batter in the squad and so a full-time opener may have to be called up if Gay’s injury proves significant.Explore more on these topicsAndrew FlintoffEngland cricket teamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Georgia Hunter Bell: ‘Getting the tube to work I was like … oh my God, I’ve kind of messed up my life’ | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Georgia Hunter Bell tells Sean Ingle about making the most of a second chance after quitting at 23, learning from Keely Hodgkinson and eyeing an LA 2028 double
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Georgia Hunter Bell tells Sean Ingle about making the most of a second chance after quitting at 23, learning from Keely Hodgkinson and eyeing an LA 2028 double
Content: Georgia Hunter Bell is enjoying a comeback straight out of a Hollywood feelgood movie.Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGeorgia Hunter Bell is enjoying a comeback straight out of a Hollywood feelgood movie.Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty ImagesAthleticsInterviewGeorgia Hunter Bell: ‘Getting the tube to work I was like … oh my God, I’ve kind of messed up my life’Sean IngleThe favourite for 1500m gold at the European Championships on her second chance after quitting at 23, learning from Keely Hodgkinson and eyeing an LA 2028 doubleFri 7 Aug 2026 09.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Igrew up and was always just good at running,” says Georgia Hunter Bell, as she remembers the moment she felt her career was over at 23. “I always thought that I would be a professional athlete, go to the Olympics, all of that. So it was quite brutal when I had to make peace with the fact that it was not going to happen.”At that stage Hunter Bell’s body was broken. Her teenage promise – she was the UK’s top 15-year-old having run a 2min 8sec 800m – worn away by injuries aggravated by overtraining in the US collegiate system. She retired; found a job in tech; didn’t run on the track for five years. And then came a comeback straight out of a Hollywood feel-good movie.London to face Rome, Munich and Nairobi after confirming 2029 World Athletics bidRead moreOver the past two years, the 32-year-old has won six major medals – including an Olympic 1500m bronze, world 800m silver and world 800m indoorand Commonwealth golds. And this week she arrives at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham as Britain’s hottest favourite for gold in the 1500m.But to understand Hunter Bell’s immense drive and fortitude – and what has made her the athlete she is today – you have to go back to the dark days, when her youthful dreams were struck down by life’s harsh realities.“Actually the first year that I quit, I was like: ‘Thank God, I’m done,’” she says. “Because it had got quite sour towards the end. I was resenting it. I was racing badly. I was injured. I was completely falling out of love with it.“But a year or two later, when I was back in London and getting the tube to work, I was just kind of being like: ‘Oh my God, I am an adult now. This is it. And I have kind of messed up my life’.“I knew that the potential was there and it was never fulfilled, and I really struggled to deal with that,” she adds. “And there were a few bad years where I wasn’t very excited for life.”She admits that the 23-year-old Georgia was a little lost. “When I look back, I feel really bad for her,” she says. “But that is now part of my strength. Because I’ve been through all of that, I have that perspective, and it makes me a way better athlete.”The second-chance journey of a lifetime began with a March 2022 parkrun for fun ina not-too-shabby 5km time of 16min 14sec. Then, in November 2022, she reunited with her old coach Trevor Painter and his wife, Jenny Meadows, who guidedKeely Hodgkinson to Olympic goldin Paris.View image in fullscreenGeorgia Hunter Bell arrives in Birmingham as the hot favourite after her Commonwealth Games victory.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThe world duathlon title followed in 2023 along with a 1500m in 4:06, just four seconds off the Olympic qualifying time. That winter she also went on her first altitude camp, when Painter and Meadows realised they had an unpolished diamond on their hands.“They really made me believe,” Hunter Bell says. “They were looking at me keeping up with everyone. After one hill session, Jen pulled me in and was like: ‘You can run the Olympic qualifying time’ and that’s when I was like, ‘OK, I am going do this’. Then it went from ‘You can run the time’ to ‘You can make the team’ to ‘You can actually get a medal.’”Meadows’s prophecy turned into reality. Days before her 30th birthday, Hunter Bell was able to quit her job to become a professional athlete. “Obviously they were a bit sad to see me go,” she says. “But they were like: ‘You’re living your dream. And to get another shot is so exciting’.”And even at 32, Hunter Bell is still getting better.This year, she is the second- fastest woman in the world over 1500m and the fifth-fastest over 800m. “It’s difficult deciding which to do because I feel like I’m actually pretty equal in both,” she says.Her coaches can’t decide either. “Jen thinks there’s a lot more potential in the 800m, and then Trev thinks I have a better aerobic base, which is maybe suited for the 1500m a bit more,” she says, smiling.What is clear is that she can beat anyone at either distance – as she proved by thrashing the 800m world champion Lilian Odira at the Commonwealth Games in a tactical masterclass.For the first part of the race she went to the front and kept it steady. But with Odira out of position on the back straight of the second lap she struck for home, blitzing the last 200m in 27 seconds. “Jen and I watched the rounds,” Hunter Bell explains. “And we anticipated what we thought she might do.”Beating Odira proved something else too: she could handle the pressure of expectancy. “I used to relish being the underdog in 2024,” she says. “But I found it quite a hard adjustment to be favourite. Last year I was like: ‘Oh, I don’t love this: people are asking me to do press conferences, people are asking me how I’m going to win.’ And I made some mistakes in 2025, which were really important to learn from.”Gold medals over 1500mat the world indoors in Torunand the 800m at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow showed Hunter Bell is a fast learner. And, unsurprisingly, she goes into the Europeans as a hot favourite to win the 1500m, with only the French athlete Agathe Guillemot, the sixth fastest in the world this year, looking a danger.View image in fullscreenGeorgia Hunter Bell has learned to relax more while working with Keely Hodgkinson.Photograph: Hannah Peters/Getty ImagesSo what has allowed her to keep improving? Hunter Bell is full of praise for Painter and Meadows, whose coaching focuses on high-speed efforts on the track – with little time for slow running. On weekends, for instance, she rides her bike for hours rather than doing a long run.She also emphasises the importance of recovery. “You have to be quite disciplined with what you do in your spare time,” she says. “You’re almost trying to be horizontal for as much as you can during the day. When you’re not training or racing, you’re chilling out and letting your body recover.”Training with Hodgkinson certainly doesn’t hurt either. So what has she learned most from the 800m Olympic champion?“We’re at different phases in our life, but we get on really well,” she says. “She’s very chilled, which I’ve really learned from.“At college, I would be very regimented. If something went wrong, I felt that everything had gone wrong. Whereas she’s very like: ‘Oh, I forgot my spikes. I’ll get some others.’ She goes with the flow and is very composed when she gets on the start line. She also really relaxes me, and she’s quite playful and fun.”And what has she learned from you? “I would be interested to hear what she would say,” Hunter Bell laughs. “Maybe because I have achieved something that on paper you wouldn’t think is possible, that’s helped her see that you can actually do anything. And maybe I’ve helped her be on time more. I’m always like: you need to go!”For now, Birmingham is foremost on her mind. But Hunter Bell admits that shewants to emulate Kelly Holmesby going for an 800m/1500m double at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.She even talked with Holmes about attempting it last year at the world championships in Tokyo, before deciding against it. However, she believes it is a harder feat to achieve in the modern era – because there are so few slow races in the heats.View image in fullscreenGeorgia Hunter Bell is still getting better at the age of 32 after returning to the sport.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images“The idea of me winning a gold in the 800 and 1500 in LA is kind of unthinkable because the races are so quick, and what they demand from your body is so much,” she says. “They are almost flat out sprints always, whereas they used to be a bit more tactical.“That’s why I really enjoyed running a tactical 800m at the Commonwealth Games. Because, last year in Tokyo, it was balls to the wall from the gun.”But given what she has achieved so far, would you dare bet against Hunter Bell defying sporting gravity again? Especially as she believes there is plenty left in her tank.“I think my training age is a lot younger than 32, just because I didn’t have all those years of racing and being on the circuit,” she says. “Remember Kelly did her double Olympic gold at 34. Look at Messi at 39. What’s previously been seen as old has pushed way back.“So everything is leading towards LA – that’s the north star.” And, like Hunter Bell, it is shining brighter than ever.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Spain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy | Spain | The Guardian
description: Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to Ceuta
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to Ceuta
Content: The checks, which come ‘amid the persistent irregular migration pressure’ facing Italy, will starts at midnight on Saturday.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/APView image in fullscreenThe checks, which come ‘amid the persistent irregular migration pressure’ facing Italy, will starts at midnight on Saturday.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/APSpainSpain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from ItalyMove comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to CeutaAgence France-PresseFri 7 Aug 2026 17.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 17.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpain has announced it will introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass rush of people fromMoroccointo Ceuta.The checks, which come “amid the persistent irregular migration pressure” facingItaly, will start at midnight on Saturday and last until 7 September, Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement.Hours earlier,Spainthreatened Italy with countermeasures if it did not swiftly lift its own border checks, drawing a rebuff from Rome.The rare spat between the EU and Nato allies came after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco to Spain’s north African territory on 30-31 July in an unprecedented, deadly rush.The scenes infuriated EU members that back a hard line on irregular immigration, including Italy, which imposed border checks on people arriving from Spain for one month.Russia-linked accounts spread far-right narrative online during Ceuta migration crisis, analysis findsRead moreThe Spanish government criticised the measure on Friday as “unfair, contrary to the EU’s interests and discriminatory for the Spanish population”.Foreign minister José Manuel Albares described it as “a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity”.“We urge the government of Italy to rectify, put an end to the checks and treat Spaniards like other European citizens,” he added.He threatened “proportional measures” in response by Sunday if Italy failed to comply.Within hours, the government of Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it “had no intention of revising the decision” before 15 August, when it said Spanish authorities “expected a new wave of migration” to hit Ceuta.Meloni’s office said in a statement: “Italy does not accept ultimatums or impositions from abroad regarding national security and border control.“Only when there is certainty that there are no security or terrorism risks to Italy, that no new wave is occurring, and that no irregular migrants are heading toward European territory, will the decision be reconsidered.”Spain’s interior ministry announced the reciprocal measures within hours.Spanish police have been monitoring online rumours and social media about possible fresh arrivals in Ceuta in mid-August, according to local media. But authorities have not expressly said they expect a repeat of last week’s rush.Border authorities would in the meantime “do their utmost to ensure maximum ease of movement for Spanish and European citizens” who are not affected by border checks, the Italian statement added.Italy, which does not share a land border with Spain, introduced border controls at maritime and air entry points for third-country nationals arriving from Spain.The move, announced on 31 July, was an “extraordinary measure” intended to “safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation”, Meloni said at the time.She was among several EU leaders who called for Spain to be suspended from the visa-free Schengen travel zone after the Ceuta incident, despite such a move being legally impossible.Italy’s coalition government has sought to stop the tens of thousands of people who land in small boats on the country’s shores each year.The Spanish government warned against “creating rifts and sterile conflicts driven by internal electoral motives” and said “we trust that pro-European sentiment, common sense and good faith prevail”.‘Morocco feels emboldened’: Trump’s influence in spotlight after Ceuta disasterRead moreOf the 72,000 people who entered Ceuta, 70,000 have returned to Morocco, according to official Spanish figures.Spanish authorities said 80 people died in the crossings.Moroccan rights groups, however, estimate the figure to be higher. The Moroccan Association for Human Rights and the European Coordination for Human Rights in Morocco on Friday said at least 141 deaths were recorded and that the toll was likely to rise.Morocco’s interior ministry has said 11 people died on its side of the border, all but one by drowning.Those who remain in Ceuta – including hundreds of unaccompanied children – face dire living conditions with little access to food, water and shelter.Explore more on these topicsSpainItalyMoroccoMigrationAfricaEuropeMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Thailand school shooting: eight killed including suspected attacker, police say | Thailand | The Guardian
description: Teenager killed his grandparents ⁠before opening fire at school near Bangkok, where more than 30 were wounded
Author: Natasha May
Headline: Teenager killed his grandparents ⁠before opening fire at school near Bangkok, where more than 30 were wounded
Content: Schoolgirls being carried away from the scene of the shooting in Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi province.Photograph: Wason Wanichakorn/APView image in fullscreenSchoolgirls being carried away from the scene of the shooting in Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi province.Photograph: Wason Wanichakorn/APThailandThailand school shooting: eight killed including suspected attacker, police sayTeenager killed his grandparents ⁠before opening fire at school near Bangkok, where more than 30 were woundedNatasha Mayin BangkokFri 7 Aug 2026 10.16 EDTFirst published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 00.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Thai teenager killed his grandparents before opening fire at his school, where he shot five people dead and took his own life, police have said, in an attack that has shaken a country struggling to deal with gun violence.The 14-year-old wounded more than 30 people in the ⁠shooting at the prestigious Debsirin Nonthaburi school northwest of Bangkok. Nine people were in a critical condition, the Thai health department said.For Prompong Namwong, an English teacher at the school, it was a normal morning until a panicked student from another class flung open the door, trying to find somewhere to hide. In the corridor, Prompong heard other teachers shouting that there had been a mass shooting downstairs.View image in fullscreenPrompong Namwong.Photograph: Natasha MayWhen Prompong recounted the ordeal to the Guardian, he hesitated between calling the 14-year-old, whom he saw run in front of his classroom, “killer” or “student”.At that moment, “I thought I was going to die, for sure,” he said.The suspected attacker fired at least 26 bullets with a gun belonging to his grandfather, and was found with 34 additional ammunition rounds.1:06Students seek safety during Thai school shooting – videoThe suspected shooter remained inside the school after reports of the attack emerged, Arsit Sampantharat, the permanent secretary of the interior ministry, told PPTV.A lockdown at the school was declared over in about half an hour. Prompong said that when he heard a knock, he thought it was the end of his life, but instead it was the police coming to their rescue.Images from the scene showed students running with only socks on their feet as they were evacuated from the school.Locator mapThe children, as is customary across Asia, had taken their shoes off outside their classrooms, but in the panic to escape the grounds, the shoes were left strewn around lunch tables and the stairs outside classrooms.By the afternoon, the sports area where the students would usually have been playing was filled with officials and the media, as the country’s leader vowed to implement new gun laws.The prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, told reporters the new law would allow only government officials on duty to carry guns, but did not provide any ⁠specifics, including whether the legislation would tighten gun ownership requirements.Thailand has thehighest rate of civilian gun ownership in south-east Asia, and in 2017 the Switzerland-based Small Arms Survey placed the country 13th worldwide for small-gun possession.A number of mass shootings have occurred in recent years in Thailand, including incidents at schools and a large Bangkok mall, and a 2022 attack in the country’s north-east that ‌killed 37 people including 22 children.The country’s licensing regime still lacks mental health screening for people applying to have a ⁠gun and does not require periodic reassessments ​for licence holders, according to Piyaporn Tunneekul, an ​associate professor at Nakhon Pathom Rajabhat University in Thailand.View image in fullscreenPolice at the scene in Bang Kruai district.Photograph: Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP/Getty ImagesPichanan Thiengtham was in the teachers’ lounge when she heard the shots at about 10am. But she said she could not believe at first that it was a gun: “There were so many shots and they lasted for a long time without stopping.”It was only when the art teacher saw one of the injured students that she realised what was happening. “I took the injured student to get first aid and then transferred them to the hospital [in the school] building.”Kiatikhun Verapongpradith, an emergency worker, described arriving as the shooting was taking place. He said his team had treated students with injuries to the back, chest and arms.They found a male teacher lying dead on an upper floor of the school, and in another room they found a female teacher with wounds to her chest and arm, Kiatikhun said.View image in fullscreenAn injured teacher receiving medical attention at the scene on the outskirts of Bangkok.Photograph: Chalinee Thirasupa/ReutersThe school is part of the Debsirin network, founded by the Thai royal family. Its alumni include prime ministers, scholars and writers.Prompong found out in the school’s group chat that some of his friends had not survived. “They’re all good teachers. I don’t know what to say.”He said: “My life has to go on, but right now … it’s a very great shock. I never thought to myself that it would happen – really happen – in my school.”Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsThailandGun crimeAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: French officers halted small boats at sea 10 times since spring | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Disclosure challenges Conservative and Reform claims that police are refusing to intervene
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Disclosure challenges Conservative and Reform claims that police are refusing to intervene
Content: A French warship and navy rib alongside an inflatable ‘small boat’ carrying migrants across the Channel after leaving northern France.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA French warship and navy rib alongside an inflatable ‘small boat’ carrying migrants across the Channel after leaving northern France.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesImmigration and asylumFrench officers halted small boats at sea 10 times since springDisclosure challenges Conservative and Reform claims that police are refusing to interveneRajeev SyalHome affairs editorFri 7 Aug 2026 13.46 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 14.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe French authorities have halted small boats at sea in the Channel on 10 occasions since the spring, officials said on Friday.Despite claims from the Conservatives and Reform that the French were refusing to intervene in small boat crossings, maritime prefect officers were using “intervention tactics” to board or control vessels at sea and take asylum seekers back toFrance.The disclosure comes as political parties are once again attempting to seize the initiative over small boats over the summer.Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, last week confronted French police on a beach near Boulogne and uploaded footage to X of an officer saying: “Our order is to let them go. We just have to say to them, ‘Don’t do that. It’s dangerous.’”Earlier this week, Reform MP Lee Anderson visited Calais and said the French police were “literally waving these people on to boats”.In an unusual intervention, the director of maritime and small boats at Border Security Command, Charlie Eastaugh, said: “The incidents we have seen in the Channel over the last few weeks are a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting people for profit. It is easy to look at out-of-context images and think little is happening to stop these crossings – this is simply not true.Has the UK government’s strategy on small boat crossings been effective?Read more“I know personally how tirelessly French officers have been working to disrupt launches before they reach UK shores. Their efforts include facing violent people with weapons, dispersing huge crowds, arresting smugglers, seizing equipment and collating vital evidence to help our prosecutions.”Every confrontation with asylum seekers was assessed by commanders as well as individual police officers and gendarmes, who were expected to balance the safety of their officers with that of the public, including large groups of often agitated people and gang members, officials said.On Sunday, when Andy Burnham visited HM Coastguard in Dover, Border Force officers had been warned that it was a “red day”, when conditions were calm enough for several small boat crossings.Two small boats attempted to launch from France, but one was intercepted at sea, while the other was halted on land.Small boats crossing the Channel were down by 43% compared with January to mid-July 2025 – from 21,690 people who crossed last year to 12,469 over the same period this year.The drop has come despite hot and dry conditions, which are usually associated with an increase in crossings.UK officials believe that government initiatives to “stop the boats” by financing the French authorities with another £660m in April have disrupted the business model of people smugglers in northern France and reduced the number crossing to the UK.Gangs are adapting their tactics. Boat launches have spread further along the coast, with some leaving from Belgium and others from as far south as Dieppe, a journey of 70 miles (113km) to the UK, compared with the Calais to Dover route of 27 miles.Officials are concerned the trend towards “mega-dinghies” – larger motorised boats – is putting more people at risk. More than 170 migrants were rescued on Tuesday after the boat they were using to cross the Channel caught fire.The sustained drop in crossings was a welcome development for Burnham, allowing him to focus his early weeks in government on setting out his policy agenda.Shabana Mahmood, who Burnham has kept in post as home secretary, has been reluctant to celebrate the recent drop because she is conscious the trend could change if there is an increase in arrivals in the late summer and autumn months.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeFranceChris PhilpMigrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: US police officer accused of killing three people in Mexico arrested at border | Texas | The Guardian
description: Chad Eberle of Texas charged over deadly shooting in Saltillo that officials say stemmed from custody dispute
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Chad Eberle of Texas charged over deadly shooting in Saltillo that officials say stemmed from custody dispute
Content: Members of the Mexican army at the border in Piedras Negras, Coahuila state.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMembers of the Mexican army at the border in Piedras Negras, Coahuila state.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesTexasUS police officer accused of killing three people in Mexico arrested at borderChad Eberle of Texas charged over deadly shooting in Saltillo that officials say stemmed from custody disputeMarina DunbarFri 7 Aug 2026 16.49 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 16.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleATexaspolice officer has been arrested inMexicoafter authorities there accused him of killing three people and critically injuring the mother of his child in what investigators say stemmed from a dispute over the custody of the minor.The Coahuila attorney general’s office said 35-year-old Chad Eberle was arrested on Wednesday at the border on a warrant accusing him of femicide and qualified homicide, according toLa Razonde Mexico, a newspaper based in Mexico City. Under Mexican law, femicide refers to the intentional killing of a woman or girl because of her gender.According to La Razon, the deadly shooting happened in July in Saltillo,Mexico, after an argument over Eberle allegedly not having permission to take his three-year-old son. Two women and one man were killed in the attack.The victims were identified by La Razon with the first names and ages of Ana Laura, 44; Laura Jaquelín, 22; and Emanuel, 44. The child’s 26-year-old mother was also shot in the head and remained in critical condition, officials said.Investigators said Eberle was arrested while attempting to cross from Mexico into Texas through the international bridge at Piedras Negras, across from Eagle Pass,KTXSreported. Eberle had left the residence with his son in a gray Chevrolet Silverado, prompting investigators to launch a manhunt as they tracked the vehicle toward the Texas border, theUS Sunreported.He was then intercepted before he could re-enter the US with the child. The three-year-old was unharmed and was later placed in the care of Coahuila’s child welfare agency.TheSan Antonio Expressidentified Eberle as a police officer in the central Texas town of Santa Anna. Before that, he worked as a deputy constable with Bexar county – which includes San Antonio – and also served as a police officer for the Northside independent school district.The Express reported that Eberle also held law enforcement positions in theTexascommunities of Somerset, Marble Falls, Gregory, near Corpus Christi, Lockney in the state’s panhandle, and Bangs in the west. According to the newspaper, a 2022 Facebook post from the Lockney police department described Eberle as an army veteran.In a social mediaposton Thursday, Coahuila attorney general Federico Fernández said: “It is reported that at [9.59p] Chad ‘N’ has been admitted to the Saltillo men’s penitentiary in compliance with [an] arrest warrant, where he has been placed at the disposal of the competent judicial authority, in accordance with the corresponding procedure.”He added: “Likewise, the minor is already in the city of Saltillo, under the custody and care of the prosecutor’s office for boys, girls and the family (Pronnif), in order to guarantee the comprehensive protection of his rights.”Texas news outletColeman Todayobtained a statement from Santa Anna city officials which described Eberle as “one of our reserve officers … [who] was on a personal leave of absence until December.“The Santa Anna police department has been in contact with the US consulate in Mexico and [the Texas commission on law enforcement].”That statement also said Eberle was “an unpaid reserve police officer hired in November 2025 and worked one weekend per month.“Due to the ongoing investigation, no other public comment will be made.”Explore more on these topicsTexasUS crimeMexicoUS policingAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: William Orbit, pop producer for Madonna, All Saints and more, dies aged 69 | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Musician’s projects included Madonna’s Ray of Light, Blur’s 13 and All Saints’ chart-topping singles Pure Shores and Black Coffee
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Musician’s projects included Madonna’s Ray of Light, Blur’s 13 and All Saints’ chart-topping singles Pure Shores and Black Coffee
Content: Ray of light … William Orbit in 2022.Photograph: Eva PentelView image in fullscreenRay of light … William Orbit in 2022.Photograph: Eva PentelPop and rockWilliam Orbit, pop producer for Madonna, All Saints and more, dies aged 69Musician’s projects included Madonna’s Ray of Light, Blur’s 13 and All Saints’ chart-topping singles Pure Shores and Black CoffeeBen Beaumont-ThomasFri 7 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWilliam Orbit, the British music producer whose dreamy yet propulsive style invigorated work by Madonna, Blur,All Saints, U2 and more, has died aged 69.A statement on his social media, attributed to family and friends, said he died at home on 23 July. “He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness,” the statement read. No cause of death was given.Orbit was most famous for his collaboration withMadonnaon her 1998 album Ray of Light: his strikingly original backings, rooted in trip-hop, jungle and techno, marked a new chapter for one of pop’s greatest stars, resulting in hits such as Frozen, The Power of Goodbye and the giddy title track. It had multi-platinum sales across the world, won Madonna three of the five Grammy awards she was nominated for in 1999, and has become seen by many as Madonna’s single greatest studio album.But his work stretched far beyond one client, spanning Blur’s exploratory, emotionally scarred album 13, All Saints’ UK No 1 Pure Shores, Pink’s UK No 3 new wave hit Feel Good Time and more. He was credited as a guest artist on the latter, and released a raft of albums and singles under his own name: his electronic twist on Samuel Barber’s Adagio for Strings, aided by a trance remix by Ferry Corsten, reached the UK Top 5 in 1999.Success came relatively late for Orbit – at least in pop music terms. He was born William Wainwright in 1956 and raised in north London, the son of two teachers he described as “decidedly working class and poor … they’d struggled to become middle class”. He left school at 16 and became what he described as a “post-hippie”, living in a squat, doing occasional low-paid labour and, by his recollection, consuming “a Mars bar and an acid tab a day”.In 1980 he formed the electronic/ambient trio Torch Song with Laurie Mayer and Grant Gilbert, and were signed to the label IRS, releasing three albums between 1984 and 1987. Well versed in electronic music production after gradually assembling a studio full of digital and analogue gear, he was hired to create the soundtrack to the Rob Lowe and Patrick Swayze film Youngblood, and remixes for pop artists – including Madonna. Wielding hip-house breakbeats and puckish instrumentation, he gave a chirpier cast to her prowling, sexually infatuated early 90s singles Justify My Love and Erotica.He was now on Madonna’s radar, but it would be later in the decade they would work together on original tracks. In the interim, Torch Song released another album in 1995 and he had another successful project, Bassomatic, whose psychedelic baggy epic Fascinating Rhythm hit the UK Top 10. He’d released his solo debut album in 1987, and found acclaim in the 90s with a series of albums with the title Strange Cargo. 1993’s Strange Cargo III featured a young Beth Orton on a track; Orbit produced her debut album Superpinkymandy the same year, and went on to remix her single Central Reservation.Meanwhile, Madonna was struggling to make a new album and redefine herself: she had scrapped sessions with R&B producer Babyface in favour of a search for a new collaborator, and only had a small handful of songs for a new album. Orbit’s pedigree meant he was invited by her manager to submit tracks and was hired: “Just hang in there, work on your stuff, get your chops together and eventually you get a stroke of luck,” he later reflected. He and Madonna worked up much of the album together in studios in New York and Los Angeles.“William is a complete madman genius,” Madonna said of the Ray of Light sessions. “I’d come to him with an idea of where I wanted to go musically, hum melodies or read lyrics, and then leave him alone in the laboratory. Sometimes he’d go in the direction I wanted and sometimes he’d swerve off somewhere else entirely. We’d end up with trance tracks that were eight minutes long and then keep adding and subtracting until we had real verses and choruses. We really put our noses to the grindstone.”View image in fullscreenOrbit with Madonna at the 1999 Grammys, accepting the best pop album award for Ray of Light.Photograph: YouTube/GrammyOrbit’s astonishing range of sound – heavy breakbeats, acoustic guitars, trance synths and more – was put to use on everything from sweeping ballads to the pell-mell acid house of the title track, re-establishing Madonna’s credentials as a vanguard pop star and earning her first non-video Grammy award wins.Eager not to repeat herself, she switched her core producer up again for her next album Music, to Mirwais, though Orbit was retained for three of its tracks. He also produced two successful standalone Madonna singles which appeared on soundtracks: 1999’s Beautiful Stranger, from Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me, and her 2000 cover of Don McLean’s American Pie, from The Next Best Thing (which she also starred in). Orbit returned for her 2012 album MDNA, co-producing six of its songs. Earlier this year, Orbit said: “I will always love that woman. For real. She made my career.”The late 1990s were a hugely industrious period for Orbit. In 1999, he released Pieces in a Modern Style, an album of classical reworkings including his successful take on Samuel Barber (an earlier 1995 version had been deleted from sale after an objection from composer Arvo Pärt).1999 also saw the release of Blur’s album 13: similarly to Madonna, Blur wanted to reinvent themselves after five albums with producer Stephen Street, and had been impressed by Orbit’s earlier remixes of their work (collected on the album Bustin’ and Dronin’). 13 charted Damon Albarn’s breakup from musician Justine Frischmann, and the frontman later described Orbit’s role on the album as “a psychiatrist”. Like Ray of Light, 13 is regarded as one of the most singular and brilliantly realised albums in Blur’s catalogue, with Orbit crafting experimental yet commercial material with the group, including hit singles Tender and Coffee and TV.Ray of Light’s success meant that he was also courted by a range of pop artists in the years that followed, including Britney Spears, Melanie C, Robbie Williams, Chris Brown, Pink, No Doubt and ex-Girls Aloud singer Nadine Coyle.
