He collaborated with co-writer Beck on Pink’s Feel Good Time – another film soundtrack hit, for 2003’s Charlie’s Angels: Full Throttle.He brought the psychedelic Ray of Light palette of guitars, bleeps and breakbeats to two superb singles by British girl group All Saints: Black Coffee and Pure Shores, both UK chart-toppers. Regarded by pop fans as some of Orbit’s masterpieces,he told the Guardian in 2021he initially thought the latter song was “pure shite” because it had taken so long to make: “When you really slave over something, it takes years until you can really listen to it with pleasure.” He worked with All Saints again on two tracks from 2018 album Testament.Orbit produced two new songs forU2which appeared on their compilation The Best of 1990-2000: Electrical Storm, which reached No 5 in the UK, and The Hands That Built America, which was used as the theme for Martin Scorsese’s 2002 film Gangs of New York.View image in fullscreenWilliam Orbit pictured in 2015.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianOrbit’s only other full-album project for a pop artist was Katie Melua’s fourth album The House, released in 2010. His work rate slowed thereafter, though he did bring a long-lost pop curio to fruition: There Must Be More to Life Than This, a Freddie Mercury and Michael Jackson duet, originally recorded in the early 1980s but eventually produced by Orbit and released in 2014.Orbit also continued to release solo albums, adding six more after Pieces in a Modern Style, including a 2010 sequel to that release. His most recent album is 2022’s The Painter.Madonna, drugs and helicopter-trained dogs: the dark, starry life of William OrbitRead moreIn March this year, he scotched rumours of a possible new project with Madonna. “Let’s put this Madonna ROL [Ray of Light] 2.0 thing to rest here and now folks. Can get exhausting. Is not going to happen … I have an album ready that imho is indeed the successor to ROL. Everything about how it was made and how it sounds yells that from the first few bars. And I reached out. And there has been heard. Nil response.”He told the Guardian in 2021 that he struggled with substance use four years before. As well as heavy marijuana use, he was taking “LSD, mushrooms, MDMA, coke, some hormones that everybody was experimenting with. Codeine. I wasn’t aware of what I was doing and I ended up having a psychotic episode.” He was sectioned. “Fortunately, once the drugs were out of my system, I finally got back to being normal – and out I was,” he said.Melanie C was one of those paying tribute, writing: “Such an honour to have worked with this great man.”Music industry mogul Merck Mercuriadis called him “a genius … arguably the most important producer of the 90s and noughties and his influence will forever be felt”.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockMadonnaAll SaintsU2BlurnewsShareReuse this content

title: At least one person dead in California wildfire allegedly sparked by chainsaw | California wildfires | The Guardian
description: Police arrested Herbert Wayne Smith, 65, in connection with the Gann fire, which has burned more than 15 sq miles in Calaveras county
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Police arrested Herbert Wayne Smith, 65, in connection with the Gann fire, which has burned more than 15 sq miles in Calaveras county
Content: Flames consume vegetation near Copperopolis on Tuesday in Calaveras county, California.Photograph: Noah Berger/APView image in fullscreenFlames consume vegetation near Copperopolis on Tuesday in Calaveras county, California.Photograph: Noah Berger/APCalifornia wildfiresAt least one person dead in California wildfire allegedly sparked by chainsawPolice arrested Herbert Wayne Smith, 65, in connection with the Gann fire, which has burned more than 15 sq miles in Calaveras countyDani AnguianoFri 7 Aug 2026 15.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 15.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least one person has died in a wildfire burning in the foothills of California’s Sierra Nevada mountain range that officials believed was sparked by a man using a chainsaw.Police arrested Herbert Wayne Smith, 65, in connection with the Gann fire, which has destroyed seven buildings, scorched more than 15 sq miles in Calaveras county and killed a well-known dog breeder in the town of Angels Camp.In an interview withKCRA, Smith told reporters he did not mean to spark the fire. Monday was his birthday, he said, and he had been using machinery to cut scraps in order collect money for a celebratory meal with his wife.“I’m so sorry for everything that’s happened,” Smith told the news station. “This is going to destroy my life, one way or another.”1:28Night footage shows wildfires burning across California hills – videoOfficials allege that Smith is responsible for “recklessly causing” the blaze on Monday while “operating equipment capable of producing sparks” without clearing flammable vegetation as required, according to the California department of forestry and fire protection. Prosecutors will determine whether to file criminal charges.In 2018, Smith was charged with igniting another fire,KCRA reported, and was accused of “willfully and unlawfully [setting] fire to any forest, brush, or other flammable material which is on any land that is not his own, or under his legal control, without the permission of the owner, lessee, or agent of the owner or lessee of the land”. He pleaded no contest and received a sentence of 36 months’ probation.As of Friday morning, the Gann fire had burned more than 10,000 acres and was about 40% contained.Investigators will determine whether the fire contributed to the death of the person found in a burned home near the town of Angels Camp, the Calaveras county sheriff’s office said. Friends have identified the victim as Susan Solari and a neighbor toldCBS Sacramentothat she refused to leave her dogs.“I told them she was there, that her dogs were there and she couldn’t get her dogs out,” Joan Wilson told the outlet. “She wasn’t going to leave them.”The Gann fire comes amid a grueling fire season in the American west.Three major fireshave continued to burn around the city of Spokane in north-eastern Washington and have destroyed at least 800 buildings. A 37-year-old man has been arrested for allegedly sparking one of the fires, and court documents accuse him of studying how tomaximizethe blaze’s destruction.No deaths have been reported in Washington. Officials reported on Thursday that cooler temperatures and calmer winds have allowed firefighters to make progress.Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsCalifornia wildfiresWest CoastCaliforniaWildfiresnewsShareReuse this content

title: Could England and Wales ever run out of water? | Water | The Guardian
description: Last month in England was the driest July since records began almost two centuries ago. How concerned should we be?
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Last month in England was the driest July since records began almost two centuries ago. How concerned should we be?
Content: The Swithland Reservoir in Leicestershire which is currently at less than 44% capacity. Pictured in July 2026.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenThe Swithland Reservoir in Leicestershire which is currently at less than 44% capacity. Pictured in July 2026.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.WaterAnalysisCould England and Wales ever run out of water?Pippa Neilland Safeerah AhmedLast month in England was the driest July since records began almost two centuries ago. How concerned should we be?Fri 7 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 10.24 EDTShareHalf ofEnglandand all of Wales are officially in drought. But what does this mean and could taps eventually run dry?What does it mean to be in drought?There is no single definition of drought and every drought is different. But they are all characterised by a prolonged period of low rainfall creating a shortage of water.Some droughts are short and intense, like the recent “flash drought” declared across half of England, which developed quickly because of unusually low rainfall and high temperatures. Others can take a long time to develop over multiple seasons due to prolonged low rainfall.What are the drought conditions like this summer?Helen Wakeham, the chair of the National Drought Group, said this year’s drought was “exceptionally serious” and would have long-lasting impacts on the environment and the economy. In July, England received 7% of the long-term average rainfall, making it thedriest Julysince records began almost two centuries ago.View image in fullscreenA dried-up pond in Falmer, East Sussex.Photograph: Glyn Kirk/AFP/Getty ImagesThere was also a record-breaking drought in 2022, which affected large parts of the country and was the worst in some areas since theinfamous drought of 1976.But isn’t the UK famously rainy?Yes, the UK does have a global reputation for its wet weather and we did seeparticularly heavy rainin the first half of the year.While winter rainfall can help to replenish reservoirs and groundwater, summers are becoming exceptionally hot and dry. Combined with climate-induced heatwaves, we are using water faster than nature can replenish it.Drought is only over when river, groundwater and reservoir levels are back to normal, and this can take time.A key issue is also storing water during times of plenty. There has not been a new reservoir built anywhere in the UK since 1992. The National Farmers’ Union is calling on the government to streamline the planning system to make it quicker and easier for farmers to build on-farm water storage systems.Additionally,researchby Greenpeace UK found that 2.87bn litres of water a day is wasted by water companies through leaky pipes in England and Wales – enough to fill 1,150 Olympic-sized swimming pools and amounting to a fifth of all water pumped through the network.Where do water companies get the water?Most of the water comes from lakes, reservoirs, rivers and groundwater. This is then pumped to water treatment plants before being directed to homes. The amount of water that companies can take is controlled by environmental regulators.During times of drought, water companies can use drought permits and drought orders to take more water. Last yearSouthern Waterapplied for a drought order that allowed it to draw water from an internationally prized chalk stream and rare salmon habitat.Do only water companies take water from the environment?No, water companies are not the only ones taking water from the environment. Agriculture, power generation, manufacturing, fish farms and golf courses are all big users of water.View image in fullscreenMaize is watered in a field in Shropshire on 5 August 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesAnalysis by theEnds Reportrevealed 47bn kilolitres (kl) of water was extracted from the environment in England in 2023. Electricity generation took 26bn kl, public water supply took 9.2bn kl and agriculture took 2bn kl.Why are England and Wales running out of water?The Environment Agency has estimated England’s public water supply could be short by 5bn litres a day by 2055 without urgent action to future-proof resources.Water demand is going up as the population grows and new industrial demands from datacentres and energy infrastructure require more water. Plus, the water available to supply those needs is going down as the effects of the climate crisis kick in, and we have greater variability and unpredictability of rainfall and greater water demand during hotter, drier summers. There has also been a lack of investment over several decades in fixing leaks and building new reservoirs.Isn’t there also a water quality crisis?Yes, there is a serious problem with water pollution. Recentgovernment datarevealed that every single English water body is polluted with toxic chemicals, while just 14.3% of surface waters achieved good ecological status.Do people in England and Wales use more water than elsewhere?The Consumer Council for Water has estimated the average person in England and Wales uses 139 litres of water a day. In Europe, this figure tends to be lower, for example in Germany individuals use about 120 litres per day. In the US, the average American is estimated to use 310 litres per day.View image in fullscreenThe average person in England and Wales uses 139 litres of water a day.Photograph: David Calvert/AlamyHow can individuals reduce water wastage?Smart metering programmes can help households look at their water consumption. The Environment Agency has suggested opting for a low-flow shower head, which uses about half the amount of water per minute compared with a standard shower head. You can also request a cistern displacement device from your water company, which can reduce each toilet flush by at least one litre.However, one of the biggest ways you can reduce your water consumption is through your diet. Someestimatessuggest a vegetarian diet could reduce your water consumption by 27% to 41%.How can drought resilience be improved as climate breakdown accelerates?There have been three droughts in the past five years so becoming more resilient is essential. While we can all take steps to reduce our water use, investment is key.The Environment Agency expects 60% of the predicted 2050 water deficit to be addressed by water companies managing demand and dramatically reducing leaks. The remaining 40% would come from boosting supply, including the building of new reservoirs and water transfer schemes.Can water companies go further than a hosepipe ban?About 40% of the population of England is under a hosepipe ban – officially called a temporary use ban – which is a legal restriction imposed by water companies to conserve water during times of low supply and high demand. Breaching the ban is a criminal offence and can lead to a fine of up to £1,000.Water companies are all required to have drought management plans setting out what they would do in an “emergency drought” scenario. This could see rota cuts introduced where water is limited to a few hours each day.Water companies can apply to the government for a drought order, which allows them to change someone else’s licence to take water from the environment. They can also prohibit or limit non-domestic customer uses of water under non-essential use bans, and can manage the water pressure in drought-affected areas.As well as investment in fixing leaks and building new reservoirs, nature-based solutions can play an important role to help mitigate the impacts of dry weather.If nothing changes, could we actually run out?Yes, without investment and reductions in our water use, we are facing a serious problem.In some areas, the impact is already being felt. For example Sussex, Cambridgeshire, Suffolk and Norfolk have all seen housing and business development delayed due to water supply availability and ageing or inadequate water infrastructure.View image in fullscreenA man drinks from a fountain at a park in London.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPASouth East Water said this week supplies in its area were “critically low” and warned customers they may lose supply unless demand for water in the area dropped.In areportwritten in the aftermath of the 2025 drought, which resulted in the driest spring in 132 years, MPs warned that without action to reduce water use and build new supply infrastructure, England’s taps could run dry.In the infamous drought of 1976, several water companies closed off supplies, with the public having to use standpipes in the street.Dr Anna Murgatroyd, a lecturer in hydrology at Newcastle University, said the current conditions were equivalent to, if not worse than, 1976 and so “we could end up seeing similar shortages”. But she said it was hard to say at this stage whether that was likely given the uncertainty of the weather. She added that water companies had more efficient systems today than they did in 1976.What does this mean for the future?Water companies are channelling record investment into fixing leaks and while it has been more than three decades since a major new reservoir was built in England and Wales, several are in the planning stage.But as the climate crisis intensifies, the risk worsens, and even if England and Wales manage their domestic resources efficiently, it will still face the knock-on effects as countries across the globe grapple with their own water shortages.The headline of this article was amended on 7 August 2026 to refer to England and Wales, rather than the UK. Also, the average usage of 139 litres of water a day is for people in England and Wales, not in the UK as stated in an earlier version; and the 47bn kilolitres of water extracted from the environment in 2023 was in England only. Groundwater was added to the list of main sources of water.Explore more on these topicsWaterWater industryEnglandanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Extreme heat breaks temperature records in central and eastern Europe | Extreme weather | The Guardian
description: Slovakia reaches new high of 42C as authorities in Poland forced to shut down Kozienice and Połaniec power plants
Author: Matthew Taylor
Headline: Slovakia reaches new high of 42C as authorities in Poland forced to shut down Kozienice and Połaniec power plants
Content: Shrivelled sunflowers near the village of Kovilj, Serbia.Photograph: Andrej Isaković/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShrivelled sunflowers near the village of Kovilj, Serbia.Photograph: Andrej Isaković/AFP/Getty ImagesExtreme weatherExtreme heat breaks temperature records in central and eastern EuropeSlovakia reaches new high of 42C as authorities in Poland forced to shut down Kozienice and Połaniec power plantsEurope’s dry riverbeds and scorched earth – in picturesMatthew TaylorandAjit NiranjanFri 7 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 03.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTemperature records have been broken in several countries across central and easternEuropeas the extreme weather that has caused wildfires and droughts across the continent continues.Countries includingSlovakia, Austria and Hungary registered record temperatures. On Thursday, the Slovakian hydrometeorological agency said a new high of 42C (108F) had been reached in Dolné Plachtince.Authorities inPolandwere forced to shut down the Kozienice and Połaniec coal-fired power plants after critically low water levels in the Vistula River limited cooling water supplies. The disruption removed about 1.3GW of capacity from Poland’s power system.On Wednesday, the Polishprime minister, Donald Tusk, had urgedemployers to look after their staff and provide air conditioning and cold water.View image in fullscreenLow water levels in Poland’s Vistula River on Thursday.Photograph: Wojtek Jargiło/EPAInGermany, climate activists demanding an end to the use of fossil fuels demonstrated outside the chancellery against the lack of government action to keep people safe from extreme heat. An estimated 11,900 people across the country have died from heat this summer, according to new estimates from the Robert Koch Institute.“This extreme heat and its consequences are the result of a fossil fuel policy that is completely irresponsible and extremely dangerous,” said Annkatrin Schwirten, from Fridays for Future Berlin. “We must not become accustomed to thousands of heat-related deaths every summer.”The Hungarian prime minister, Péter Magyar,wrote on X on Thursdaythat the nuclear power station which had been temporarily powered down would be going back online.“Good news: we are already nine centimeters above the Danube’s Sunday low point, and rain is expected in the Austrian catchment areas,” he wrote. “One of the turbines at the Paks nuclear power plant is operating. Regardless of this, on today’s hot day there will still be a strong need for voluntary reductions in electricity consumption.”The brutal heat and continuing drought conditions arebeing supercharged by the escalating climate crisis, and experts warn these are putting huge pressure on local populations, critical infrastructure and wildlife across the region.Paweł Pomian, from EKO-UNIA, a Polish environmental organisation, said “power plants driving climate change were increasingly becoming its victims”, adding that the impact of this summer’s extreme conditions, fuelled by the burning of fossil fuels, should be a “wake-up call not only for Poland, but for the whole of Europe”.“The faster we develop wind and solar power – technologies that require the least water to generate electricity – the better we can protect both energy security and our rivers,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenEnvironmental experts examine part of the Danube riverbed in Budapest on Thursday.Photograph: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP/Getty ImagesThe scorching heatwaveshave also deprived vegetation of moisture and primed much of the continent for wildfires. About half a million hectares have burned across the EU since the start of the year, mostly in Spain and France, according to data published by the European Forest Fire Information System on Thursday. A further 292,000 hectares (721,000 acres) have burned in Ukraine.We launched a war on nature. Now we are in a climate warzone | Rebecca SolnitRead moreThe severity of fire weather – the hot, dry and windy conditions that make it harder to battle blazes when they break out – has set new records for the time of year, by alarming margins in some countries.In Austria, which had a record high temperature of 41.2C on Wednesday, cumulative fire weather is more than twice as severe as the previous record for this time of year.InCzechia, which registered a new national temperature record earlier in the summer, fire weather by early August was more than 50% worse than the previous record, and in Slovakia it was 32% worse.Last week, arapid analysis by the World Weather Attribution consortiumfound that global heating had made last month’s hot, dry and windy weather at least 20 times more likely in Spain and twice as likely in France.Explore more on these topicsExtreme weatherClimate crisisDroughtEuropeSlovakiaAustriaHungarynewsShareReuse this content

title: Weather tracker: central and western Europe brace for more sweltering heat  | Extreme weather | The Guardian
description: High 30s celsius forecast for France, Spain and Italy next week, before affecting Germany, Poland and Czechia
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: High 30s celsius forecast for France, Spain and Italy next week, before affecting Germany, Poland and Czechia
Content: Low water levels in the Rhine River caused by hot weather and prolonged drought in Düsseldorf, Germany.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APView image in fullscreenLow water levels in the Rhine River caused by hot weather and prolonged drought in Düsseldorf, Germany.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APExtreme weatherAnalysisWeather tracker: central and western Europe brace for more sweltering heatEd WaltonHigh 30s celsius forecast for France, Spain and Italy next week, before affecting Germany, Poland and CzechiaFri 7 Aug 2026 07.59 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 12.14 EDTShareAnother pulse of heat is expected to affect central and westernEuropenext week. The latest forecast models show daily maximum temperatures well into the high 30s celsius widely across France, Spain and Italy during the first half of the week, while Germany, Poland and Czechiawill experience the highest temperatures towards the end of the week. The shift in the focus of the heat as the week progresses can be attributed to the movement of high pressure. At the start of the week, low pressure centred in the Atlantic and high pressure centred over the low countries will draw warm air from southern Europe northwards into parts of France. During the working week, the high pressure will slip a little farther south and east, enabling the warm air once situated over western Europe to make inroads into parts of Germany and central Europe.The heat in central and western Europe this summer has been unrelenting. Last week’sweather trackerhighlighted record-breaking temperatures for the month of July in Austria. However, only a few days later, on 4 August, the all-time record was shattered with 41.0C achieved in Stammersdorf, north-east of the capital, Vienna. This comfortably broke the previous all-time record set in August 2003 by 0.7C. Unbelievably, that record was broken again the following day when 41.2C was recorded in Deutsch-Altenburg. Slovakia also set an all-time record on the same day, of 41.4C. The continuing European heatwave, associated with a vertically extensive anticyclone, raised the freezing level above 4,000 metres across much of the Alpine region. This represents a level in the atmosphere well above many Alpine glaciers, accelerating the seasonal melting process. On the opposite side of the Atlantic, 51.8C was recorded in Badwater, California, the highest temperature in the US for 2026 so far.Although south-eastern parts of Europe have eluded the worst of the summer heat, wildfires have ignited in recent days. Extremely strong northerly wind gusts in excess of 70mph ripped through the Greek Islands on 29 July, causing medium-voltage power lines to sway and produce sparks that set fire to vegetation below. Part of the palm forest at Preveli beach, Crete, was damaged by a wildfire but the centre of the forest was spared from the worst of the destruction.Explore more on these topicsExtreme weatherEuropeanalysisShareReuse this content

title: England striker Ivan Toney charged with assault after Soho nightclub incident | UK news | The Guardian
description: Met police say charge relates to alleged assault that reportedly took place in December at venue in London
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Met police say charge relates to alleged assault that reportedly took place in December at venue in London
Content: Ivan Toney will appear at Westminster magistrates court next month.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenIvan Toney will appear at Westminster magistrates court next month.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAUK newsEngland striker Ivan Toney charged with assault after Soho nightclub incidentMet police say charge relates to alleged assault that reportedly took place in December at venue in LondonKevin RawlinsonFri 7 Aug 2026 07.03 EDTFirst published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 05.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault after an incident at a nightclub in Soho in December last year.Scotland Yard said the striker had been charged on 31 July with assault causing actual bodily harm. Toney, who plays for the Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, is due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on 24 September.The Sun newspaper reported in December that Toney had been arrested after an alleged head-butt. It claimed a fan recognised the footballer and grabbed at him while seeking a photograph with him before the incident.On Friday the Metropolitan police said the charges related to an incident on 6 December at a nightclub on Wardour Street in central London, reportedly the now-closed 100 Wardour Street.A spokesperson for Toney said: “Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court.”Toney was at the centre of one of the most curious transfers on deadline day in August 2024 when he completed a late move from Brentford to Al-Ahli worth a reported £40m. He has also played for Newcastle United and his home town club Northampton Town, as well as several others on loan as he looked to establish himself.Seen as a late bloomer in football terms, he had made only two Premier League appearances before his 25th birthday, but went on to score 67 goals in 128 appearances over the next three seasons at the top level.He has played 10 times for England, scoring once in a friendly match against Belgium in 2024, and was part of the 2026 World Cup squad, making appearances against Argentina in the semi-final and in the win over France as England finished third.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tory plan to ban foreign nationals from social housing condemned as ‘divisive’  | Social housing | The Guardian
description: Housing charity says move would drive up homelessness, while Labour dismisses proposal as ‘unserious’
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Housing charity says move would drive up homelessness, while Labour dismisses proposal as ‘unserious’
Content: The Conservatives party said about 230,000 homes would become available if foreign nationals were barred from accessing social housing.Photograph: Commission Air/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Conservatives party said about 230,000 homes would become available if foreign nationals were barred from accessing social housing.Photograph: Commission Air/AlamySocial housingTory plan to ban foreign nationals from social housing condemned as ‘divisive’Housing charity says move would drive up homelessness, while Labour dismisses proposal as ‘unserious’Caroline DaviesFri 7 Aug 2026 03.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 15.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlans to ban foreign nationals from social housing under a Conservative government have been condemned as “divisive”.Under proposals revealed on Friday, the party said about 230,000 homes would become available if foreign nationals were prevented fromaccessing social housing.Ending new tenancies for all foreign nationals, as well as current tenancies for couples where neither person is a UK, Irish or EU citizen with settled status, would free up an estimated 228,144 homes for British families, the party said.Under the plans, tenants inEnglandwho do not qualify for the housing would be expected to move out of their homes within six months.A council housebuilding boom is central to Burnham’s vision. Can it be done?Read moreForeign nationals with settled status, refugee status or specific humanitarian protections currently qualify for social housing. Asylum seekers are not eligible for social housing, unless in exceptional circumstances such as domestic abuse cases.Labour described the plans as “an unserious, unworkable proposal, copied from Reform, that does nothing to tackle the housing crisis the Tories themselves created”.Sarah Elliott, the chief executive of housing charity Shelter, said: “These divisive plans would brutally kick people out of their homes, including thousands of families and pensioners who have lived in them for decades. And let’s not forget that social tenants pay rent, which goes back to the public purse and into society.“It is completely senseless to ruin people’s lives, drive up homelessness and put extreme pressure on councils. This policy does nothing to deliver new social homes, which is what we desperately need.”The Royal College of Nursing said: “The worst thing in the world would be to cause serious housing worry for a workforce that keeps our services running, posing serious risk to patient care. Those advocating for them need to offer reassurances – and quickly – or explain why it is just that some of our most brilliant nursing staff may face housing insecurity.”Under the plans, any single person currently living in social housing who is not a UK, Irish or EU citizen would lose their social housing. This includes those with children. Anyone with EU settled status would not be evicted.For future tenancies, UK nationals and those with EU settled status would be eligible, however, any new EU citizens without settled status would not be. Couples, where neither of them is a UK or EU citizen and they do not have EU settled status, will lose their entitlement.Le Corbusier’s social housing was meant to be the dream. In a summer of extreme heat, it is a nightmare | Anna RichardsRead moreHelen Whately, the Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary, said: “Making Britain your home should be earned by working, paying tax and integrating. It should not come with a free ride on the benefits system. Britain cannot be a cash machine for the world.“Labour has lost control of immigration and lost control of the welfare bill, and it is British families picking up the bill and sitting on waiting lists. The next Conservative government will make foreign nationals ineligible for social housing. Nearly 230,000 homes could go to British families.”In 2024-25, 88.5% of main householders – the person in whose name the social home is rented – were UK or Irish nationals and 11.5% were non-UK/Irish nationals, according to the EnglishHousingSurvey.There are an estimated 470,000 non-UK and non-Irish citizens living in social housing.Explore more on these topicsSocial housingConservativesEnglandCommunitiesHousingImmigration and asylumShareReuse this content

title: Primary schools to be told to identify children at risk of future unemployment | Youth unemployment | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Neet crisis review to call for teachers to be asked to spot those at risk of leaving education jobless at 16
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Exclusive: Neet crisis review to call for teachers to be asked to spot those at risk of leaving education jobless at 16
Content: Alan Milburn said ministers needed to ‘make somebody responsible’ for identifying and supporting the children who risked becoming unemployed.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAlan Milburn said ministers needed to ‘make somebody responsible’ for identifying and supporting the children who risked becoming unemployed.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianYouth unemploymentPrimary schools to be told to identify children at risk of future unemploymentExclusive:Neet crisis review to call for teachers to be asked to spot those at risk of leaving education jobless at 16What can Dublin teach us? Milburn goes on quest to learnRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentFri 7 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePrimary schools in England should be required to identify children at risk of leaving education at 16 without finding a job, a government review is to recommend.Alan Milburn, who is leading areview into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness, said he would call for sweeping changes in education policy alongside a shake-up of the benefits system to address the problem.Speaking to the Guardian, he said ministers needed to “make somebody responsible” for identifying and supporting the children who risked becoming Neet (not in employment, education or training) after their GCSE year up to the age of 24.“The warning signs are there from a very early, early age. You know, frankly from preschool,” he said.“So, definitely primary schools should be identifying children who are at risk of being Neet. And secondary schools and other services should be intercepting, intervening, supporting and helping those young people to get on a different path.”View image in fullscreenAlan Milburn bakes with local children at a regional youth resource centre in Dublin.Photograph: Patrick Bolger/The GuardianIn an interview during a visit to Dublin this week, the former Labour health secretary said the recommendation would form part of his final report into Britain’s youth worklessness crisis, which is expected this autumn.Britain’s young adults are bearing the brunt of a rise in unemployment, with the number of 16 to 24-year-olds who are Neetsurpassing a million earlier this yearfor the first time in more than a decade.Representing as many as one in eight young people, the rate has swelled at a significantly faster rate than in other countries amid a sharp rise in mental ill-health and a tough jobs market.Milburn’s review comes as Andy Burnham puts tackling the crisis in youth employment at the top of his agenda for government, including changes in his first weeks as prime minister toretool technical education and apprenticeships.Labour is also gearing up for a fresh tilt at welfare reform amid concerns over a spiralling benefits bill and the hit to the economy and people’s lives from a prolonged period out of work.chart showing The UK has one of the worst Neet rates in EuropeMilburn said welfare reform would form a critical plank of his final report, but cautioned that any steps to restrict benefit payments for young people would need to be accompanied by higher levels of education, health and job support.He said that by the time a young person reached the benefit system it represented an “upstream failure” in education, skills and health policy because a functioning system could have helped them to find a job.“I think we’ve got to turbocharge that education; that support. We’ve got to turbocharge opportunities for young people; we’ve got to make it easier for young people to get a job,” he said.“And alongside opportunities, of course, there has got to be some obligations. Of course.”Burnham has said he is determined to reform the welfare system as part of his efforts to fix Britain’s dismal track record on youth employment, but would also provide more support for young people.Speaking on a fact-finding mission to the Republic of Ireland, which has recorded the fastest fall in Neet rates in the EU over the past decade, Milburn said that far too often youth disengagement began long before the age of 16.Suggesting that it can start before a child even reaches the school gates, he highlighted a study in Bradford that found children who were not school-ready at the age of 4 to 5 were almost three times as likely to become Neet by the time they reached the age of 16 to 17.Graph comparing UK and Ireland youth unemployment“We know what the correlated factors are [for a child at risk of becoming Neet] – whether that is poverty; mental health, or being in care. What we don’t do is take that knowledge and turn it into action.”Under the proposal to be outlined in his final report, schools inEnglandwould be expected to flag a child’s risk of becoming Neet from the end of primary school, including by drawing on attendance records.The Department for Education would also be asked to refresh its pupil premium guidance to emphasise that the extra money schools in England receive for supporting the most disadvantaged children could be used for tutoring and mentoring schemes for those at risk of becoming Neet.Official figures show rates of school absence have ballooned since the Covid pandemic, with the number of pupils persistently absent – missing at least a 10th of school time – almost doubling to 1.3 million pupils in 2024 and 2025. Rates of severe absence – missing half of class time – and persistent absenteeism have also dramatically increased.Milburn’s interim report in May warned that persistent absenteeism was associated with a 3.9 times greater risk of a young person being Neet by the time they reached the age of 16 to 18, and a 6.3 times greater risk of a young person being locked out of earning or learning for a sustained period.While some schools have strategies using so-called “Roni” (risk of Neet indicator) tools, the practice is not widespread or mandated.“We’ve got to get upstream because what we’re doing is we’re paying – this country, and young people – are paying the price of failure,” said Milburn.Explore more on these topicsYouth unemploymentYoung peoplePrimary schoolsSchoolsUnemploymentEducation policySocial exclusionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Meet the offenders cleaning canals in the West Midlands as an alternative to prison | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: With the debate over prison overcrowding and what to do about it raging, one initiative offers an alternative solution
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: With the debate over prison overcrowding and what to do about it raging, one initiative offers an alternative solution
Content: Steve Warmer rests after collecting litter from alongside the canal.Photograph: Tom Pilston/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSteve Warmer rests after collecting litter from alongside the canal.Photograph: Tom Pilston/The GuardianPrisons and probationMeet the offenders cleaning canals in the West Midlands as an alternative to prisonWith the debate over prison overcrowding and what to do about it raging, one initiative offers an alternative solutionTom Pilston andHaroon SiddiqueFri 7 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the prison overcrowding crisis shows no sign of abating and the debate rages overearly releases, an initiative in the West Midlands offers an alternative to custodial sentences.The Guardian was offered rare access to the project, under which, instead of being sent to prison, convicted offenders work on the improvement of waterways and green spaces around Smethwick. It is a small part of the community payback scheme, which in total clocked up an estimated 5m hours across England and Wales in the last year.Community payback is not suitable for everyone but covers a wide range of adult offending and can be included as part of suspended sentences. The Sentencing Act, which received royal assent in January, introduces a presumption for courts to suspend short custodial sentences of 12 months, which will mean more offenders carrying out community-based punishments.On the day the Guardian visited the Smethwick project last month, the temperature was already in the high 20s by 9.30am when the participants arrived at the canal for a day of strimming and cutting back overgrown vegetation, and clearing beer cans, plastic bags, bottles and condoms from the towpath and the canal itself.View image in fullscreenSteve Warmer: ‘Me and my wife now litter pick in our own street.’Photograph: Tom Pilston/The GuardianAmong them was Steve Warmer, a 54-year-old with a painful hip, dressed in a grey tracksuit, who was recently convicted of an offence that can attract a fine, a driving ban and up to six months in prison. As two of his fellow participants were given nets to trawl the canal for rubbish and thick, green duckweed, Warmer was handed a picker and the first of many black rubbish bags.Warmer, a factory worker from Dudley, said he was “the last one standing [alive]” out of his group of friends. “I actually enjoy this work,” he said. “It gives me knowledge of life and other people.”The aim of community payback is to combine punishment with rehabilitation, and Warmer added: “Me and my wife now litter pick in our own street.”View image in fullscreenParticipants were given nets to trawl the canal for rubbish and thick, green duckweed.Photograph: Tom Pilston/The GuardianNot everyone working at the canal was as positive as Warmer, who had completed 126 of 250 hours of a community payback sentence. In the hot weather, the work was particularly demanding, with plenty of water breaks needed as the temperature rose further in the afternoon.Courts can order between 40 and 300 hours of community payback, to be completed within a specific timeframe. Offenders must work up to 28 hours each week over three or four days if they are unemployed. If they are employed, it will be organised around their working hours. Failure to comply without reasonable excuse can result in enforcement action and a return to court.The supervisor at the Smethwick project on the day Warmer was there was Mo Ghafoor, who spent 10 years as a corporate banker and whose responsibilities now included driving the van that transported the offenders and equipment to the site.View image in fullscreenMo Ghafoor helps out a first-time member.Photograph: Tom Pilston/The Guardian“This is 100% more fulfilling’ he said. “I used to help businesses with profit but I was just a voice on the phone. Here I make a difference in the heart of my own community. I help my own mental health and that of others, the community and individuals.”Other forms of community payback, formerly known as community sentences, include removing graffiti, decorating public places and buildings such as community centres, and planting trees. Anyone cannominate a project for the scheme, provided it benefits the local community, does not take paid work away from others, and doesn’t make a profit for anyone.Among the offenders who will spend less time in prison and more time in the community as a result of the Sentencing Act are burglars, shoplifters and criminals convicted of assault.The latest statistics, from July to September 2024, show that adults released from custody with sentences of less than 12 monthshad a reoffending rate of 68.2%, compared with 22.9% for sentences of 12 months or more.While critics might see community payback as a soft sentencing option, it is not a view shared by Ghafoor. “We look at the individual to whom it gives a structure to their life,” he said. “It often breaks a negative cycle and changes their mindset, and therefore brings reoffending down.”This article was amended on 7 August 2026 to correct the spelling of Mo Ghafoor’s surname.Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceCommunitiesWest MidlandsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Businessman was ‘preparing champagne’ to celebrate Caruana Galizia murder, court hears | Daphne Caruana Galizia | The Guardian
description: Taxi driver says he acted as middleman between Yorgen Fenech and three men already convicted of €150,000 contract killing
Author: Juliette Garside
Headline: Taxi driver says he acted as middleman between Yorgen Fenech and three men already convicted of €150,000 contract killing
Content: Melvin Theuma, centre, pictured in 2019, says he acted as a middleman in a plot to murder of journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.Photograph: Vincent Kessler/ReutersView image in fullscreenMelvin Theuma, centre, pictured in 2019, says he acted as a middleman in a plot to murder of journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.Photograph: Vincent Kessler/ReutersDaphne Caruana GaliziaBusinessman was ‘preparing champagne’ to celebrate Caruana Galizia murder, court hearsTaxi driver says he acted as middleman between Yorgen Fenech and three men already convicted of €150,000 contract killingJuliette GarsideFri 7 Aug 2026 13.40 EDTFirst published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe businessman accused of paying for hitmen to murder the journalistDaphne Caruana Galiziawas impatient for the killing to take place, and once texted from his boat to say he was “preparing champagne” to celebrate, a jury inMaltahas heard.Yorgen Fenech, the 44-year-old heir to a property empire that includes several Hilton hotels, is on trial in Malta for complicity in the murder of Caruana Galizia. She died in a car bombing in October 2017 after publishing a series of revelations about senior politicians that were so damaging they triggered a snap general election.The key witness in the case, a taxi driver who says he acted as middleman between Fenech and three men already convicted of accepting €150,000 (£128,000) to carry out the killing, took the stand on Friday to begin his testimony.Melvin Theuma, who has been living under witness protection since agreeing to testify in return for a pardon, said Fenech had told him to contact a known criminal and set up the killing because he wanted to protect his uncle Raymond Fenech, the head of the family business.View image in fullscreenFlowers placed in front of a portrait of murdered journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia during a vigil outside the law courts in Valletta, Malta.Photograph: Jonathan Borg/AP“Bring him here, I need him to kill Daphne because she’s going to publish information about Uncle Ray,” Theuma claimed Fenech had told him.Theuma has previously testified that over time the explanation changed, and the hit was designed to stop revelations about Yorgen himself.The conversation took place in April 2017. The two men were friends, having known each other for years, although Theuma told the jury it was not an equal relationship.“He’s a lion and I’m a mosquito,” Theuma said of the accused.The taxi driver, who had cultivated a friendship with Fenech over a shared interest in horseracing and betting, is regarded by the prosecution as key to securing a conviction. He has given police multiple recordings of conversations he had with Fenech after the murder.Before taking the stand, Theuma had to be certified as fit to give evidence, having previously tried to take his own life. In 2020, having already secured a pardon, he swallowed acid and slit his own throat. He will be allowed to give evidence seated, with his back to Fenech and his lawyers, having previously complained of intimidation.He began his testimony by apologising to the victim’s family, saying: “My cross was too much to bear; I can’t imagine what theirs was like.”After receiving the order from Fenech, Theuma said he went to the docks in Marsa, where the hitmen, brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio and their associate Vincent Muscat, used a warehouse known as the potato shed as a base.“Alfred got into my taxi and I told him ‘I have someone who wants to kill Daphne Caruana Galizia’.“He asked if the person could pay, and I said yes, of course.”View image in fullscreenYorgen Fenech pictured in 2019. He is on trial in Malta for complicity in the murder of Caruana Galizia.Photograph: Yara Nardi/ReutersTheuma said he never told the hitmen who had sent him. He told the court Fenech had agreed to the price, but then asked him to call off the attack after Malta’s then prime minister, Joseph Muscat, called a snap general election. Instead, he asked Theuma to place a €150,000 bet for him on Muscat securing a second term.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen Muscat was returned to power with a landslide victory in June 2017, Theuma said Fenech rang him that night. “He sounded tipsy. He told me to go ahead with the Daphne job. I didn’t do anything, he sounded drunk.”A few days later, he gave Fenech his winnings from the bet – €300,000, minus a commission. Nothing more was said about Caruana Galizia. But a few days later, Fenech summoned him and gave him an envelope stuffed with cash. “I asked him, ‘What’s this?’ He said: ‘It’s the €150,000 to have Daphne killed.’”The hitmen were given a €30,000 deposit and began scoping the journalist’s movements. Theuma was given a burner phone to contact them with. The witness said he took the phone with him to Disneyland for a family holiday, and that Fenech wanted reassurance he had not left Malta without it. The businessman became impatient as time passed.“Yorgen would ask me every few days: ‘When will they kill her?’ Once, he was on his boat and texted me to say he was preparing champagne in case it happened.”Theuma said Fenech helped to plot Caruana Galizia’s routine, identifying a cafe and restaurant that she frequented.Maltese politicians ‘involved’ in plot to kill Daphne Caruana Galizia, court hearsRead moreThe witness broke down as he described the moment he learned of the death from the television news. Wiping his eyes, he said: “I was living a normal life, I didn’t want for anything. Then I turned on the TV and saw that Daphne was dead. My life ended. When she was killed, my life was blown up.”He also revealed he had been in regular contact by text message with Caruana Galizia’s sons, Matthew and Paul. He said: “I was involved in their mother’s murder, and they speak to me. They tell me I will feel better after the trial. But I know I won’t. The remorse is too great.”Fenech, who is on trial for complicity in the voluntary homicide of Caruana Galizia, denies the charges. The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsDaphne Caruana GaliziaMaltaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Argentina’s government posts ICE-style video of immigration operation | Argentina | The Guardian
description: Social media video shows 60-year-old woman being led away in handcuffs, but she was released minutes later
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Social media video shows 60-year-old woman being led away in handcuffs, but she was released minutes later
Content: Javier Milei in Buenos Aires in July.Photograph: Luis Robayo/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJavier Milei in Buenos Aires in July.Photograph: Luis Robayo/AFP/Getty ImagesArgentinaArgentina’s government posts ICE-style video of immigration operationSocial media video shows 60-year-old woman being led away in handcuffs, but she was released minutes laterTiago RogeroSouth America correspondentFri 7 Aug 2026 14.40 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Argentinian government posted a video on social media showing a 60-year-old woman being led away in handcuffs by two federal police officers during an immigration operation in Buenos Aires.The woman’s face is shown unblurred in the video, which has nearly 1m views and depicts one of hundreds of such operations carried out by the administration of the far-right president, Javier Milei, directly inspired by Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown in the US.Visibly distressed, appearing to be in pain and with one hand bandaged, the woman is shown against a heavy metal soundtrack as the words “Illegal foreigner or criminal record? Out!” flash across the screen.In another video, she is described as “a Peruvian national subject to an arrest warrant for fraud and robbery”.But there was no arrest warrant for her.The woman, who asked to be identified only by her initials, PLS, said she was released just minutes after being paraded in handcuffs before photographers and television crews covering the operation, which took place last February.“They just drove me around the block and said: ‘Get out. You’re free.’ I asked: ‘Why did you put me through all this?’” she said.“My face was everywhere on social media. I started getting calls from relatives living abroad – back in Peru, in Spain, the US and Germany – asking me: ‘What happened? What did you do?’” she added.According to her lawyer, PLS is a legal permanent resident and was subject only to a “whereabouts inquiry” – requiring her to be notified about a separate case – which, under Argentinian law, does not entail arrest or any other form of coercion.“Her detention was unlawful, and the authorities used it as propaganda for their operations against immigrants,” said Lucía Galoppo, a lawyer at the NGO Centro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS), which is representing PLS.CELS sees her case as a striking example of how Milei isreshapingthe country’s immigration laws to bring them closer to those of Trump – whom the Argentinian presidentopenly admires– including by creating anArgentinian versionof the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).Checks on people’s immigration status existed before, but they have becomefar more frequent, large-scale operations involving not only immigration agents but federal police.Much like Trump, Milei has turned raids in poorer, traditionally immigrant neighbourhoods into a “public spectacle”, said Galoppo.Since taking office in December 2023, the self-styled libertarian has introduced a series of changes to immigration law by decree, bypassing congress.The latest came in late July, when Milei invoked his claim that there had been an “anti-Argentina” wave since the World Cup tojustify a decreeallowing the deportation of foreigners who promote “messages of hate” against the country or any Argentinian citizen.Critics pointed to theironythat, had countries Milei recently visited adopted the same rule, the president himself could have been expelled afterinsultingBrazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva,and Spain’sprime minister, Pedro Sánchez.Other decrees include ending the automatic right to permanent residency for foreigners who have a child born in the country or marry an Argentinian citizen, and requiring immigrants to prove they have sufficient financial means to support themselves – in a country where more than 40% of workers areinformally employed.While making it harder to obtain documentation, Milei has also restricted free access to public hospitals, previously available to everyone but now limited to permanent residents, except in emergencies.“The state is manufacturing a problem to manufacture a security-based response,” said Galoppo. “Argentina doesn’t have an immigration problem,” she added. In the 2022 census, immigrants made up 4.2%, the lowest proportion since records began in 1869.Galoppo believes Milei is targeting immigrants as part of a strategy to create an “internal enemy” that distracts from domestic problems – alongsidecorruption scandals, his “chainsaw” austerity policies have brought inflation under control, butunemploymentandpovertyhave risen.Milei did not respond to requests for comment.CELS filed freedom of information requests with the government about its immigration operations. There were 851 between 1 January and 26 June. The government provided further details on only 590 of them, in which just 2.2% of the foreigners stopped were found to have irregular immigration status.“These operations are highly theatrical, deploying hundreds of police officers in an attempt to imitate raids in the US, but the tiny number of people found to have irregular status shows they are not justified,” said Galoppo.In the lawsuit filed against the state on behalf of PLS, CELS alleges that she was subjected to unlawful deprivation of liberty, degrading treatment, public humiliation and abuse of authority. PLS has lived in Argentina since 2006.The “whereabouts inquiry” involving her relates to a 2021 case. In it, a person whose phone was stolen alleged that money had been transferred from their account to one in PLS’s name and then to a third account. PLS denies any involvement, saying her own phone had been stolen months earlier and may have been used to create an account in her name.Her lawyer said being sought for notification did not justify her detention.The security ministry also did not respond to requests for comment.PLS said she felt ashamed and afraid to leave home after the operation, costing her her livelihood as a street food vendor. “If I saw a police officer, I was frightened thinking they might arrest me,” she said.But she added that she had no intention of leaving: “I’ve done nothing wrong. I’m not a criminal. I’m someone who works. I liked Argentina, and I want to stay here.”Explore more on these topicsArgentinaJavier MileiICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Donald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel indicts settler over death of Palestinian activist who worked on No Other Land | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Yinon Levy charged with manslaughter in first exception this decade to culture of impunity for Israelis who kill Palestinians in the occupied West Bank
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Yinon Levy charged with manslaughter in first exception this decade to culture of impunity for Israelis who kill Palestinians in the occupied West Bank
Content: A demonstrator holds a photo of Awdah Hathaleen during an August 2025 protest in Tel Aviv over his death.Photograph: Tamir Kalifa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA demonstrator holds a photo of Awdah Hathaleen during an August 2025 protest in Tel Aviv over his death.Photograph: Tamir Kalifa/Getty ImagesWest BankIsrael indicts settler over death of Palestinian activist who worked on No Other LandYinon Levy charged with manslaughter in first exception this decade to culture of impunity for Israelis who kill Palestinians in the occupied West BankEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemFri 7 Aug 2026 09.49 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 10.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProsecutors in Israel have indicted an extremist settler for shooting a Palestinian activist last July, the first attempt this decade to hold an Israeli responsible for killing a Palestinian in the occupiedWest Bank.Yinon Levy, who was under western sanctions, is charged with manslaughter over the death of Awdeh Hathaleen, an English teacher and peace activist. In his last moments, Hathaleenfilmedthe settler drawing his weapon and opening fire towards him.Hathaleen’s family said Levy should have been charged with first-degree murder over the well-documented attack in the village of Umm al-Khair.Reckless manslaughter carries a maximum prison sentence of 12 years, far less then murder.“This was not an accident,” said his cousin Tarek Hathaleen. “Yinon Levy must be held fully accountable for Awdeh’s killing.”The charges nevertheless represented a “significant development”, Hathaleen added, after years of near-total impunity for Israelis who attack Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.0:53Palestinian activist recorded moment he was killed by settler in West Bank – videoMy sweet friend Awdah Hathaleen was murdered by a West Bank settler. May his memory be a revolution | Emily GlickRead moreIsraeli settlers and soldiers have killed more than 1,500 Palestinians this decade, according torights group B’tselem. Levy is the first person indicted over any of those deaths.Military prosecutors last brought charges over a 2019 shooting of a young man who stopped to help victims of a traffic accidentThe last time civilian prosecutors brought charges was in 2018 over the killing of a mother of eight, hit by a rock as she was driving.Settler violence and ethnic cleansing has surged in the occupied West Bank over the past three years, supported by far-right Israeli cabinet ministers who hold security, defence and finance portfolios.Levy’s indictment over one of the highest-profile killings in that period does not represent a policy shift for Israel, rights groups said.Hathaleen had worked onNo Other Land, the Oscar-winning documentary about his community’s decades-long struggle against the Israeli state and settlers, to stay in their homes and lands in the south Hebron hills.“It’s important to see this killing as part of an ongoing and systematic situation in the West Bank,” said Ziv Stahl, executive director of Yesh Din, an Israeli rights and advocacy organisation.“I don’t think these charges are an indication of increased law enforcement or accountability. It is more likely due to the fact that [Awdeh Hathaleen] was a well-known activist and the case got a lot of media exposure and public critique. It’s more about an appearance of law enforcement, rather than actual law enforcement.”Levy, who was under sanctions for violence against Palestinians by the UK, EU, Canada and Australia at the time of the attack, was briefly detained last year but policereleasedhim after three days under house arrest.He spent the last year free and continued establishing illegal outposts in the occupied West Bank, said Yair Dvir, spokesperson for B’tselem.“The decision to indict Yinon Levy is the exception that proves the rule,” Dvir said. “The impunity Israel grants to soldiers and settlers who harm Palestinians is not a failure of the system – it is a central component of a policy designed to allow the violence to continue and escalate.”The culture of impunity spurred the former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert tocallfor the International Criminal Court to bring charges against “Jewish terrorists”, saying intervention was needed to halt the violence.Levy is also charged with armed trespassing and malicious property damage in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair.Before Hathaleen was shot, another settler drove a bulldozer through Palestinian land, destroying trees and property. When a resident approached and asked him to stop, the driver knocked the man down with the bulldozer blade.Even if the case goes to trial, any verdict could be many years away, and Israeli judges have a record of lenient treatment of Israelis who attack Palestinians.The Israeli soldier who shot 23-year-old Ahmad Manasrah dead in 2019pleaded guiltyto the equivalent of negligent homicide and was sentenced to three months community service for the killing. He has not been publicly named.Eight years after a 2018 attack that killed 47 year-old Aisha Rabi, an Israeli courtruledthat a settler had thrown the stone that killed her.Judges did not hand down a conviction or sentence, instead ordering a review because the man, who was not named, was 16 at the time of the attack. No further details have been made public.Hathaleen’s family say they will continue to fight for Levy to face full trial. “Justice requires more than simply bringing a charge,” said Tarek Hathaleen. “Awdeh was not only my cousin. He was my childhood friend and someone very dear to me. His absence has left a pain that will never go away.”Sufian Taha contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineIsraelMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Scramble to house hundreds camping in Rome heatwave after squat eviction | Italy | The Guardian
description: Officials try to find homes for residents as talks to save social assistance hub collapse amid government crackdown
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Officials try to find homes for residents as talks to save social assistance hub collapse amid government crackdown
Content: While some people were accommodated by friends and family, more than 200 have been sleeping in tents outside the building.Photograph: Claudia DeganuttiView image in fullscreenWhile some people were accommodated by friends and family, more than 200 have been sleeping in tents outside the building.Photograph: Claudia DeganuttiItalyScramble to house hundreds camping in Rome heatwave after squat evictionOfficials try to find homes for residents as talks to save social assistance hub  collapse amid government crackdownAngela Giuffridain RomeFri 7 Aug 2026 08.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRome authorities are scrambling to find homes for hundreds of peoplesleeping in tents in extreme heatafter talks aimed at saving Italy’s most high-profile centre for housing and social assistance collapsed amid a crackdown by Giorgia Meloni’s government on squatted buildings.The approximately 400 evicted residents of Spin Time Labs, located in a 10-floor building in Rome’s Esquilino district occupied by grassroots groups since 2013, will not be allowed to move back in after its private owner refused Rome council’s offer to buy the property. The residents were forced out at the end of last month.A spokesperson for Italy’s interior ministry, which had set its sights on shutting down Spin Time, confirmed that the owner had taken repossession of the building “in accordance with the law”.View image in fullscreenFormer residents of the Spin Time Labs building are sleeping in tents in extreme heat.Photograph: Claudia DeganuttiThe move has reignited political debate over occupied or squatted buildings, which Meloni’s government regard as dens for criminality – including those supported by leftwing associations. Critics have questioned why Meloni and her coalition allies have long been so decisively against Spin Time while the neofascist CasaPound has occupied a state-owned building in the same neighbourhood for more than 20 years, using the premises as its headquarters.People of all nationalities, about a quarter of them children, were forced to evacuate Spin Time on 29 July after a minor fire, which was quickly extinguished by a group of residents before it could spread.The building was locked up by police during safety checks, before being placed under two judicial seizure orders – one linked to the owner’s long-running legal battle to regain possession and the other to the fire.While some people were accommodated by friends and family, more than 200, including elderly people and those with ill health, have been sleeping in tents outside the building. One child was hospitalised this week after suffering breathing difficulties.View image in fullscreenThe Spin Time building was locked up by police amid safety checks before being placed under two judicial seizure orders.Photograph: Claudia DeganuttiRome’s leftwing council, supported by the Catholic church-run charity Caritas, is now seeking alternative solutions.In an interview on In Onda, a talkshow broadcast on the TV channel LA7, the mayor of Rome, Roberto Gualtieri, said the response to the council’s offer had been an “irrevocable no” and that despite presenting what he believed was the best possible deal he “had the impression that the decision had already been taken”.The owner had cited unspecified legal weaknesses in the proposal, Gualtieri said, adding that he felt “irritated” about the situation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenRome’s leftwing council is seeking alternative solutions for the former residents.Photograph: Claudia DeganuttiHe described Spin Time, which over the past decade has transformed into a space offering various social and cultural services, including a food bank, a restaurant and co-working, as “the mirror of a failure of Italy’s Second Republic, which stripped away a pillar of welfare”. The Second Republic is a political term for the era of government that began in the early 1990s.The initiative has provided a lifeline for hundreds of people, including Marco Perilli, an Italian construction worker who was one of the community’s first residents. He became homeless after a divorce.As of Friday, people were still camped outside. Perilli said they would continue to do so until a real solution was found. “We are trying to understand how things will proceed but we resist and will continue to resist. The owner refusing the offer means Spin Time is over, but for us it’s not over – we will find another space.”Explore more on these topicsItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Boeing 737 Max operators told to check fuselages for cracks | Boeing | The Guardian
description: Inspections ordered by US regulator will affect about 470 aircraft, after reported problems in earlier models
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Inspections ordered by US regulator will affect about 470 aircraft, after reported problems in earlier models
Content: The Federal Aviation Administration issued the airworthiness directive on Thursday.Photograph: Elaine Thompson/APView image in fullscreenThe Federal Aviation Administration issued the airworthiness directive on Thursday.Photograph: Elaine Thompson/APBoeingBoeing 737 Max operators told to check fuselages for cracksInspections ordered by US regulator will affect about 470 aircraft, after reported problems in earlier modelsBusiness live – latest updatesGwyn TophamTransport correspondentFri 7 Aug 2026 06.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 06.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US aviation regulator has ordered inspections of the fuselages ofBoeing737 Max planes for possible cracks in a component.The Federal Aviation Administration airworthiness directive will affect an estimated 471 aircraft and follows reports of cracks in earlier Boeing models.The inspections, which will start from September, follow a similar FAA regime for previous Boeing 737 Next Generation models dating back to 2021.Cracks were found in a component called the bear strap – sheets supporting the fuselage around the exit doors – on the older planes. The FAA said on Thursday that no such cracks have yet been found in 737 Max craft but that the similar design and build process makes the model susceptible to developing them.It added that without action it could “lead to the inability of a principal structural element to sustain limit loads and adversely affect the structural integrity of the airplane”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUS air force names eight killed in Boeing B-52 test flight crash in CaliforniaRead moreA Boeing spokesperson said that it had been working with airlines operating 737s for several years, after first identifying and notifying them of the issue in 2019.“The FAA airworthiness directive published today mandates the inspections, as it did for the 737 Next Generation,” they said on Thursday. “We support both directives and continue to support our airline customers.”Boeing added that the inspections would provide multiple opportunities to identify and correct problems before any cracks exceed critical length, and it was working through engineering changes to tackle the cause.Attention on engineering problems on Boeing planes has intensified since the disastrous entry into service of the 737 Max model, whose flaws led to the deaths of hundreds of passengers intwo crashesin 2018 and 2019 before it was grounded worldwide.In 2024a panel blew outof a 737 Max in mid-flight for Alaska Airlines, and concerns about production problems led to Ryanair, its biggest customer for the model, sending engineers to Boeing’s US factories to help to oversee the delivery of the planes it had ordered.Explore more on these topicsBoeingAirline industryAerospace industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: The White House’s plan to vet potentially dangerous AI is cloaked in secrecy | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: A Trump administration framework on AI testing leaves a lack of transparency – and plenty of open questions
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: A Trump administration framework on AI testing leaves a lack of transparency – and plenty of open questions
Content: Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersView image in fullscreenSam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)AnalysisThe White House’s plan to vet potentially dangerous AI is cloaked in secrecyNick Robins-EarlyA Trump administration framework on AI testing leaves a lack of transparency – and plenty of open questionsFri 7 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 11.20 EDTShareAfter months of talking with tech industry leaders, theTrump administrationfinalized a framework this week for how it will test new artificial intelligence models for safety and cybersecurity risks. So far, the White House is keeping details of the framework private, in a blow to transparency and potential boon for secretive AI companies.On Tuesday, staff from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, Nvidia and Microsoftattended a private meetingwith White House officials to review the AI framework. Multiple outletshave sincereportedthat although the volunteer vetting process for new AI models has been settled, the White House does not plan to release its policy publicly and will only share testing criteria with a select few tech companies.The Trump administration and tech industry’s opaque process for how they will check if new AI models threaten global cybersecurity has left numerous questions about how the framework will operate. It remains unclear what level of scrutiny models will face and what safety benchmarks they must meet, leaving businesses, foreign governments and the public in the dark.The White House, OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.Discussions over creating an AI cybersecurity framework began earlier this year after the release ofAnthropic’s Mythos model, which the company withheld from public release in April over concerns that it could be used to hack into IT and financial systems. The model’s capabilities sparked a small geopolitical crisis over cybersecurity, as well as spurred the Trump administration toreconsider its hands-off approachto AI regulation in favor of slightly more oversight.In June, the White Houseissued an executive orderthat called for AI companies to voluntarily submit their new models for government review up to 30 days before release. The order was a watered-down version of initial notions to make some parts of the vetting process mandatory. Tech moguls including Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerbergreportedlypersonally lobbied Trump against the mandate. The order also left an August deadline for determining the framework, which the White House and AI companies now appear intent on keeping to themselves.The murky nature of the framework increases uncertainty for businesses reliant on AI models, as well as on foreign governments increasingly worried that frontier AI models can pose unexpected security risks. It also means that outside researchers and cybersecurity experts have little visibility into how the government is assessing new AI models, with only companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic privy to the process.It is also unclear which companies’ models will be subject to government review, since the executive order does not define what qualifies as the advanced AI it targets. Open source models, which are free to download and use, for instance, will be excluded from the framework,according to Axios.The framework comes amid persistent security concerns surrounding new AI models. Over the past month OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta havedisclosedthat their new modelshacked into outside organizationsduring what were intended to be isolated security tests. OpenAI and Anthropic also agreed to delay the release of new AI products over cybersecurity concerns and fear that their models could be used to hack into financial systems or otherwise create harm.Earlier this year, the Trump administration ordered the Center for AI Standards and Innovation tostop issuing public reportson AI model assessments while it worked out a framework. It is unclear whether those reports will resume now that the framework is finalized.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Trump administrationUS politicsComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: New Mexico court orders Meta to pay $567m over harms to children’s mental health | Meta | The Guardian
description: Ruling comes as part of second phase of landmark trial that found social media company enabled harm against users
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Ruling comes as part of second phase of landmark trial that found social media company enabled harm against users
Content: Mark Zuckerberg, the Meta chief executive, outside court in Los Angeles in February.Photograph: Jill Connelly/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg, the Meta chief executive, outside court in Los Angeles in February.Photograph: Jill Connelly/Getty ImagesMetaNew Mexico court orders Meta to pay $567m over harms to children’s mental healthRuling comes as part of second phase of landmark trial that found social media company enabled harm against usersUwa Ede-Osifoand agenciesThu 6 Aug 2026 22.24 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 20.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleANew Mexicocourt has ordered Meta, the parent company of Facebook, to pay $567m into a fund aimed at redressing adverse mental health impacts from the social media giant’s platforms.The Thursday ruling comes as a part of the second phase of a landmark trial the social media giant lost in March.
