At the time, a jury found that the company knowingly harmed children’s mental health and concealed what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms, andimposed the maximum penalty: a $375m fine.The ruling on Thursday is an addition to that fine, bringing the total amountMetais responsible for to $942m.Judge Bryan Biedscheid said the bulk of the money – $420m – would be used for treatment services for young people in New Mexico. The rest will go toward awareness and prevention, screening services and other costs over the next five years.The March trialwas the first to findMeta liable for acts committed on its platform, and followed a 2023 Guardian investigation that revealed how Facebook and Instagram had become marketplaces for child sex trafficking.Several former Meta moderators told the Guardian there were instances where they flagged harmful content related to child grooming, but the cases were not escalated.Inthe second phaseof the trial, which began in May, prosecutors had asked the judge to impose fundamental changes at Meta aimed at reining in addictive features, improving age verification, and preventing child sexual exploitation through default privacy settings and closer oversight.The judge has also ordered other changes, including that Facebook andInstagrambuild banner and informational screens to clearly explain its protection features, best practices, and tools to address inappropriate comment.Those changes, and an educational campaign in New Mexico, would be subject to review by the state.The court said federal children’s privacy laws prevent Meta from applying age-verification tools to children under 13. The court also noted that ordering verification of children’s ages only for Meta and not other social media companies would be “inequitable and unduly injurious” to the company.Instead, the court ordered Meta to continue to improve its age-assurance tools in New Mexico, which include using artificial intelligence to determine people’s age based on signals such as who their friends are and what types of content they post and consume. Meta must also attempt to develop a dedicated “under-13-years-of-age prediction model” in the next two years.Additionally, Meta should also request proof of age for Instagram andFacebookusers in New Mexico it estimates to be under 13. If it determines a user to be under 13, or under 18 but without being able to estimate a specific age, Meta must treat the user as under 13 or under 18 until the user verifies their age.The company must also partner with schools or a child safety organization to create a reporting portal where school staff can flag users who may be under 13. And it must delete personal information it has collected on users under 13. The court also ordered Meta to report on its progress twice a year on how it is complying with the abatement measures.New Mexico’s attorney general, Raúl Torrez, hailed the judgment.“This case has always been about protecting children, standing up for families, and making sure that one of the world’s largest technology companies cannot profit from practices that endanger young people without consequence,” Torrez said in a statement.“Today’s decision is a victory for every parent who has worried about what social media is doing to their child and every child who deserves to grow up safer online.”A Meta spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian on Thursday that the company “disagrees with the ruling” and planned to appeal.“We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content. We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts,” the statement continued.The total amount Meta is responsible for is a small fraction of its annual profit, which was about $60bn in 2025. Still, it represents another setback for Meta as it faces a wave of accusations from families of children harmed by social media.The company is embroiled in a slew of lawsuits in other US states over its alleged harms to young people. In a trial in Tennessee thatbegan last month, the state has accused the company of disregarding internal warnings about teenagers’ compulsive use of Instagram, which has been linked to eating disorders and depression, among other adverse effects. Meta is also gearing up for a trial later this month in federal court in Oakland, California.What comes out of New Mexico is the first of many dominoes that could fall for Meta, said Laura Edelson, an assistant professor at Northeastern University focusing on social media and cybersecurity.“America is not going to pass a law that bans social media,” Edelson said. “But if companies like Meta know they’re causing harm to users by product design, the states are finally finding a way to rein this in.”Explore more on these topicsMetaInstagramNew MexicoMark ZuckerbergFacebookSocial networkingnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK house prices flat in July, says Lloyds, as buyers struggle with affordability | Housing market | The Guardian
description: Property prices in ‘suspended animation’ owing to higher mortgage rates and uncertainty in Middle East
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Property prices in ‘suspended animation’ owing to higher mortgage rates and uncertainty in Middle East
Content: House prices in Greater London were down 1.3% year on year to an average of £533,930.Photograph: Karl Hendon/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHouse prices in Greater London were down 1.3% year on year to an average of £533,930.Photograph: Karl Hendon/Getty ImagesHousing marketUK house prices flat in July, says Lloyds, as buyers struggle with affordabilityProperty prices in ‘suspended animation’ owing to higher mortgage rates and uncertainty in Middle EastBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaFri 7 Aug 2026 05.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUK house prices were broadly stagnant in July as prospective buyers were squeezed by higher mortgage rates, uncertainty around the Middle East and stretched affordability, according to the lender Lloyds.The averagepropertycost £299,253 in July, down by £143 compared with June, the bank’s monthly index found.Prices are only 0.1% higher compared with a year ago, the weakest rate of annual growth since November 2023, Lloyds said.Amanda Bryden, the head of mortgages at the lender, said many would-be buyers were struggling with affordability, especially as recent events in theMiddle Eastprompted a rise in mortgage rates.“While housing demand remains broadly steady, activity continues to respond quickly to changes in mortgage rates,” she said. “Looking ahead, we expect market activity and house prices to remain relatively stable over the remainder of the year. Developments will be shaped by both how mortgage rates respond to the outlook for inflation and wider household confidence.”Rising tensions in the Middle East have stoked fears around inflation, feedingexpectations of interest rate risesthis year. The average rate for a two-year fixed residential mortgage rate stood at 5.63% on Friday, according to the market tracker Moneyfacts, while the average five-year deal was 5.67%. Both were below 5% at the start of the year.Anthony Codling, an analyst at the broker RBC Capital Markets, said the Lloyds research showed a narrative of “suspended animation”.“Prices are neither falling sharply nor rising with any conviction, trapped in a narrow two-year range by the twin vices of stretched affordability and mortgage rates that refuse to fall far enough for long enough,” he said. “The market is not in crisis, but the green shoots that flickered briefly in early 2026 have wilted.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK house prices up just 0.1% in July as buyers remain cautious on interest ratesRead moreNorthern Ireland remained the best performer across the UK, Lloyds found.House pricesgrew by 7.4% compared with last year, with the average hitting £231,131.Prices in Scotland rose by 3.6% to an average of £223,246, while in Wales annual growth stood at 1.6%, with the average property value at £231,458.In England, price growth was strongest in the north, with the north-east reporting annual growth of 2.8%, taking the average to £182,488, while prices in the north-west rose 2.1% to £247,836.The weakest areas were in the south-east, where prices fell 2% to an average of £381,146, and Greater London, which recorded a 1.3% decline to £533,930.Nicholas Finn, a managing director at the London estate agent GarringtonPropertyFinders, said England’s north-south property divide was “becoming more entrenched”.“In southern areas, a glut of supply is attracting too few serious buyers, and this is steadily dragging down prices,” he said. “In northern England, the forces of supply and demand are more balanced. The buzz surroundingNo 10 North, and the prospect of job creation and government investment in northern areas, are boosting sentiment and supporting the upward trajectory in prices.”Explore more on these topicsHousing marketHouse pricesPropertyLloyds Banking GroupConsumer affairsUK cost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Out of the blue: James Cameron’s surprise departure would be good for Avatar | James Cameron | The Guardian
description: The director has yet again hinted that he may step away – but if he does actually relinquish control, it would likely benefit the franchise
Author: Ben Child
Headline: The director has yet again hinted that he may step away – but if he does actually relinquish control, it would likely benefit the franchise
Content: Everyone’s favourite multibillion-dollar bioluminescent space jungle … the original Avatar, from 2009.Photograph: WETA/APView image in fullscreenEveryone’s favourite multibillion-dollar bioluminescent space jungle … the original Avatar, from 2009.Photograph: WETA/APWeek in geekJames CameronOut of the blue: James Cameron’s surprise departure would be good for AvatarBen ChildThe director has yet again hinted that he may step away – but if he does actually relinquish control, it would likely benefit the franchiseFri 7 Aug 2026 08.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 11.49 EDTShareAfter directing the highest-grossing film trilogy of all time, and having spent more than two decades bending technology, studio executives and several hundred million dollars’ worth of underwater motion capture to his will,James Cameronthis week signalled that he may be ready to hand the future of the Avatar franchise to another director. Indeed, he bent Hollywood to his will so completely that it became almost impossible in the early 2010s to watch a blockbuster without uncomfortable plastic glasses, and without objects on the screen being hurled pointlessly towards the audience. Still, the Canadian film-maker now appears to be seriously considering handing over everyone’s favourite multibillion-dollar bioluminescent space jungle to someone else.“There’s been momentum in the Avatar universe for 21 years at this point because we started in 2005,” Cameron told Denise Donlonin an interviewfor Canada’s governor general’s performing arts awards. “It’s been kind of an unbroken continuum. So this is the point where I’m looking at the landscape and asking, ‘What are the other stories I want to tell? How many of them do I need to direct myself versus writing and/or producing with other film-makers?’”He added: “I haven’t made any decisions yet. I’m still in this liminal state of mapping out, you know, kind of the last act. And I don’t know if that last act will last a year or 20 years.”This is not the first time Cameron has threatened to abandon his plans for Avatar. When he floated the possibility in 2022,I noted in this columnthat, at the rate the sequels were then progressing, he would be 106 by the time Avatar 5 reached cinemas and might require his own consciousness to be uploaded into a Na’vi. Yet only two years later, he insisted that anyone hoping to prise the next two films from his hands would have to run him over with a bus. It is therefore something of a surprise to find him once again contemplating life beyond Pandora.View image in fullscreenDisappeared into the cultural undergrowth … 2025’s Avatar: Fire and Ash.Photograph: 20th Century Studios/PAPart of the problem is that Cameron’s record of handing cherished projects to other directors (while remaining aboard as producer) is decidedly mixed. Kathryn Bigelow’s Strange Days (1995), which Cameron conceived, co-wrote and produced, became a cult classic rather than a hit. Steven Soderbergh’s Solaris (2002), produced by Cameron, turned cosmic mystery into two hours of George Clooney staring mournfully at a space station. Robert Rodriguez’s Alita: Battle Angel (2019), developed for years as a potential project for Cameron to direct, made respectable money but failed to turn enormous eyes and cyborg rollerball into the beginning of a global religion.Then came Terminator: Dark Fate (2019), on which Cameron served as producer and story godfather while Tim Miller directed, only for the franchise to discover that resurrecting Linda Hamilton, Arnold Schwarzenegger and most of the plot of the original Terminator was not enough to persuade audiences that a sixth attempt to keep humanity out of the clutches of killer robots from the future was required. Cameron later described the edit as a “bloodbath” of creative battles, while Miller, the director ofDeadpool, said the experience had left him with no desire ever to work with his famously exacting producer again.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow far can James Cameron’s Avatar saga go after its billion-dollar box office triumph?Read moreYet there is an argument that Avatar may benefit from a new guiding hand. Last year’sAvatar: Fire and Ashrecycled enough of its predecessors’ story beats to suggest that Pandora’s supply of unexplored territory may be running low. It still made almost $1.5bn worldwide, but disappeared into the cultural undergrowth with all the stealth of a 9ft fluorescent cat person. There was a distinct sense that this once most innovative of film franchises had become the cinematic equivalent of Oasis circa Be Here Now. Here was a product still vast, lavish and unmistakably itself, but now expending previously unimaginable quantities of money and effort to sell the memory of a past revolution rather than start a new one.Cameron may not exactly have run out of ideas, but there’s only so far one man can travel when his entire dramatic toolkit consists of 9ft blue cat aliens riding space dragons and discussing the spiritual properties of trees. Tolkien himself might have struggled when faced with the prospect of Quaritch returning from the dead for the umpteenth time, and the Sully family discovering yet another previously unmentioned branch of Na’vi society with its own accent, ceremonial headwear and highly specialised mode of transport.Perhaps we should simply let Cameron get on with something else for a change. After everything he has done for genre film-making over almost half a century, he has surely earned the right to make at least one film without Sigourney Weaver returning as the teenage daughter of her own dead mum, or without anybody having to learn how to hold their breath for seven minutes. At some point, even Pandora may need somebody new to decide what all its phosphorescent magnificence is actually for.Explore more on these topicsJames CameronWeek in geekAvatarScience fiction and fantasy filmscommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s a Pan-African story’: the artists telling the amazing true tale of Zambia’s mission to reach space  | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The nation’s audacious 1960s rocket programme was met with ridicule. Now, more than 60 years on, this curious episode is inspiring film-makers, playwrights and a circus show at the fringe
Author: JN Benjamin
Headline: The nation’s audacious 1960s rocket programme was met with ridicule. Now, more than 60 years on, this curious episode is inspiring film-makers, playwrights and a circus show at the fringe
Content: Moonage daydream … the cast of Astronauts.Photograph: Circus Zambia & Wake The BeastView image in fullscreenMoonage daydream … the cast of Astronauts.Photograph: Circus Zambia & Wake The BeastEdinburgh festival 2026‘It’s a Pan-African story’: the artists telling the amazing true tale of Zambia’s mission to reach spaceThe nation’s audacious 1960s rocket programme was met with ridicule. Now, more than 60 years on, this curious episode is inspiring film-makers, playwrights and a circus show at the fringeExplore the rest of our Edinburgh festival 2026 coverageJN BenjaminFri 7 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn February 1960, Harold Macmillan, the UK’s Conservative prime minister, gave his seminal “wind of change” address to the Parliament of South Africa in Cape Town, announcing the end of the age of colonial rule on the African continent. He had given the same speech in Ghana a month earlier but the South Africa speech received significantly more press attention because of its perceived confrontation with the apartheid regime. The speech began a chain reaction: four years later, the British Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland was dissolved, establishing a newly independentZambia.Amid the hopeful energy of the nation’s birth emerged Edward Mukuka Nkoloso, the father of the Zambia National Academy of Science, Space Research and Philosophy, with an announcement that the young country would officially join the space race.Many thought this was a bizarre move – the competition for space primacy was originally part of a rivalry between the cold war superpowers. But now Zambia, in its infancy and without a fully functioning government, was not only set to join them; Nkoloso vowed to beat them into space and on to the moon. He was roundly ridiculed from all angles. Western media commentary took a particularly savage tone, calling the group “a bunch of crackpots”.View image in fullscreenLift off … A scene from Circus Zambia and Wake the Beast’s Afronauts.Photograph: Meshach/Circus Zambia & Wake the BeastIn his 1965 book, The New Unhappy Lords, the far-right British journalist AK Chesterton used the Zambian space programme as “proof of the absurdity in the idea that Africans should be ready for self-rule”.But Nkoloso was undeterred. He wrote an op-ed titled We’re Going to Mars! With a Spacegirl, Two Cats and a Missionary, asked Unesco for a £7m grant, and continued work on his mission with 12 young men and women handpicked for his training programme. The curriculum was mostly delivered on a remote farm a few miles outside the capital city, Lusaka. It included swinging the “Afronauts”, as they were so named, on ropes that were then cut as they reached their height, dunking them in rivers, and rolling them down hills in barrels.double quotation markNkoloso’s space project is a vehicle to imagine beyond traditionally western conceptions of what the future could look likeThere were at least some scientific principles behind the exercises: the rolling barrels had an effect similar to being in a centrifuge; the rope cutting was a crash course in freefalling, and the river dunks simulated a splashdown. “Some people think I’m crazy, but I’ll be laughing the day I plant Zambia’s flag on the moon,” Nkoloso told reporters.The space programme never did take off. Nkoloso’s application for funding from Unesco was unsuccessful and further requests for money from countries including Israel, the Soviet Union, the United States and the (then called) United Arab Republic went unanswered. Without financial resources, the idea was unsustainable. The negative press attention also affected morale – it was reported at the time that some of the trainees went on a drinking spree and never returned; 17-year-old Matha Mwambwa – Nkoloso’s most promising recruit – became pregnant and returned home to raise the baby. The Zambian government formally distanced itself from the mission and the programme was eventually quietly abandoned, with Nkoloso pivoting to a career in politics.View image in fullscreenAstro-futurism … Circus Zambia and Wake the Beast’s Afronauts.Photograph: Circus Zambia & Wake The BeastIn the years since, there has been some debate about whether or not the Zambian space mission was a genuine endeavour. In an interview with the Zambian-American writer and academic Namwali Serpell, Kenneth Kaunda – the first Zambian president and a close friend of Nkoloso – laughed when he was asked about the space mission. “It wasn’t a real thing! He wasn’t a scientist … it was more for fun than anything else,” he told her. A common theory is that Nkoloso was satirising the absurdity of the United States and Soviet Union spending billions of dollars to go to space when the money could have been better used to solve problems on Earth. He probably knew he couldn’t compete and his aim was actually to get the world talking about Zambia.Whatever the truth, it is clear that Nkoloso’s endeavours have made a significant impact on Zambia’s space exploration ambitions. Last year, the African Union formed the African Space Agency, with Zambia part of the group representing the south. And in 2024, the country completed a significant milestone in its journey to space by installing its first ground-receiving station. Nkoloso died in 1989, but the country is on its way to achieving his dream.Despite its downfall, the Zambian space programme continues to influence artists the world over, particularly in the past decade or so. One of the most well-known interpretations of the Afronauts story is the science fiction short film of that name by Ghanaian film-maker Nuotama Frances Bodomo, which premiered at the Sundance film festival in 2014. “I feel very connected to it as a Ghanaian,” says Bodomo. “Edward Nkoloso’s story is a Ghanaian one too. He’s of the generation of soldiers who went abroad to fight in the second world war for the British army, being promised land back, and when he returned he didn’t get those things – that’s also my grandfather’s story. It’s a Pan-African story of that time.”View image in fullscreenUp in the air … Circus Zambia and Wake the Beast’s Afronauts.Photograph: Meshach/Circus Zambia & Wake the BeastMore recently, Company Christoph Winkler, a Germany-based dance theatre ensemble, produced a two-part short film series, respectively titled We’re Going to Mars and We’ll Unite the Galaxies. Filmed in Uganda and the US in 2021, part one celebrates the spirit of optimism that fuelled the space programme, while the follow-up imagines blackness unbound from a single planet, let alone a single continent, through a fever dream of space travel.The fascination with the mission continues later this year as writer Ryan Calais Cameron teams up with director Monique Touko to deliver a “true-ish” take on the nation’s defiant dream. Their production,The Afronauts, has its UK premiere at west London’s Royal Court in November.double quotation markI was excited to find a story that is Zambian. It felt just like raw materialAll these works use Nkoloso’s vision of space exploration as a way to imagine beyond traditional western conceptions of what the future could look like, repositioning black Africans as leaders and trailblazers. In many ways, Nkoloso was an early – though perhaps largely forgotten – pioneer of Afrofuturism, a term coined in the 90s by cultural critic Mark Dery.While there has been considerable attention from outside the country, it’s clear that these historic events mean a great deal to Zambians too. This month, Circus Zambia, a Lusaka-based social enterprise that offers circus- and life-skills training to young people from marginalised backgrounds, brings its showAfronautsto the Underbelly at Edinburgh festival fringe. The production is a collaboration with UK-based theatre company Wake the Beast, co-founded by the Irish theatre-maker Adam McGuigan, and combines aerials, juggling and partner acrobatics to share this epic piece of African history.View image in fullscreenParallel universe … Circus Zambia and Wake the Beast’s Afronauts.Photograph: Circus Zambia & Wake the BeastThe partnership between the two companies goes back many years. McGuigan – who previously lived in Zambia for a decade and still regularly works within the country’s theatre industry – also co-founded BarefeetTheatre, a cultural movement that seeks to empower vulnerable children living on the streets of Lusaka through theatre workshops. It was through this programme that he met a young Gift Chansa, who would go from service user to facilitator at Barefeet, and eventually go on to co-create Circus Zambia. The two of them co-direct the Underbelly production, which also appeared at the UK’s Wilderness and Latitude festivals in July.“We started working on the show in 2019 and were planning to bring it to Edinburgh that year, then Covid came,” Chansa tells me over Zoom during a break from rehearsals last month. Before that, most of its shows were adaptations of well-known western works such as West Side Story and The Emperor’s New Clothes. “I was excited I found something that is Zambian,” he says. “It felt just like raw material, nobody had done a theatre production of it at that time. We are Zambians who are pushing the Zambian narrative with something that feels authentically Zambian – made for Zambia, by Zambia. We call that Zambia Ku Chalo.” A saying that literally translates as “Zambia to the world”.Circus Zambia performsAfronautsat the Underbelly, Edinburgh, to31 August;touring the UK and Ireland, 4 to 12 September,with the support of the Irish embassy, Lusaka, Zambia;tour starts Liverpool.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalPerformance artZambiafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cats review – it’s a jellicle jumble as Andrew Lloyd Webber’s moggies get the zoomies | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Macavity and co are back, with the balance in Drew McOnie’s stylish revival tipped in favour of dance and acrobatics over storytelling
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Macavity and co are back, with the balance in Drew McOnie’s stylish revival tipped in favour of dance and acrobatics over storytelling
Content: Glimmering and glittering … Melanie La Barrie and the cast of Cats.Photograph: Mark SeniorView image in fullscreenGlimmering and glittering … Melanie La Barrie and the cast of Cats.Photograph: Mark SeniorTheatreReviewCats review – it’s a jellicle jumble as Andrew Lloyd Webber’s moggies get the zoomiesRegent’s Park Open Air theatre, LondonMacavity and co are back, with the balance in Drew McOnie’s stylish revival tipped in favour of dance and acrobatics over storytellingArifa AkbarFri 7 Aug 2026 10.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndrew Lloyd Webber’s cats are back and they could not inhabit a more feline-friendly space than this lush green corner of Regent’s Park. The trees swish around their nocturnal prowls and the brilliant moon on the steel crescent set shines down on their song and dance. The big cats up the road in London Zoo would surely approve?Up to a point. These animals, directed and newly choreographed by Drew McOnie, are more balletic and graceful than those in the 1981 original and the production definitely reclaims the musical’s reputation fromTom Hooper’s filmwhich many found to be a dog’s dinner (although some of us really didn’t mind it). Sami Fendall’s set glimmers and glitters while her costumes rise from earthy colours to flamboyant leotard and catsuit get-ups.This perky crew don’t just sit and sit like the Old Gumbie Cat, they dance and dance and dance through the flimsy and patchwork story of “Jellicle cats” convening for an annual ball in which one will be reborn for another chance at life. Using TS Eliot’s playful 1939 collection Old Possum’s Book of Practical Cats as its lyrical basis, Lloyd Webber’s musical is only slightly less strange in concept than his singing train carriagesin Starlight Express, also recently revived. As with the poems, the musical is constructed as an introduction to each cat contender in a series of vignettes, which here resemble an elegant feline variety show at times, an old-school film fantasia at others.View image in fullscreenAn elegant feline variety show … The cast of Cats.Photograph: Mark SeniorThat is partly the problem: it is a hodgepodge in style, although always very stylish. The musical’s sung-through nature does not lend itself to cohesive storytelling and the balance here is tipped too much in one direction so it seems like Cats: TheDance, with extended choreographed sequences and circus-like acrobatics. It results in some lovely expressive scenes but makes the structure even more disjointed, with less of a story to bind it.Some of the cats are more characterful than others: Old Deuteronomy (Melanie La Barrie) plods around a little generically, Macavity (Dianté Lodge) is sufficiently mysterious, the criminal duo Mungojerrie (Danny Nattrass) and Rumpleteazer (Briana Craig) come as a classic variety hall double act. The highlight, without doubt, is Rum Tum Tugger with his eponymous song, which Jaydon Vijn sings with the hip-thrusting swagger of a young Mick Jagger, David Bowie and an alley cat on heat, rolled into one. Vijn brings such a lot of (c)attitude and personality that you wish the others could all be a little more Rum Tum.View image in fullscreenUnused comic chops … Gary Wilmot as Gus.Photograph: Mark SeniorGumbie Cat (Charlotte Riby) is endearing when her eponymous number comes up but Gary Wilmot’s comic chops seem redundant for his turn as the old, nostalgic theatrical cat, Gus (why not cast him in a more playful role?). Mr Mistoffelees (Jet Yau) also comes on to showcase some street dance, spinning on his head.Taziva-Faye Katsande, an understudy stepping in as Grizabella, builds to a storming final rendition of Memory, the signature song of the show. Her vocal abilities are faultless but her characterisation is less polished and you are left wondering who Grizabella is, exactly, and what has got her back up.They fall out of character and become a preening, prowling chorus, too much of an ensemble. Some of the movement between cats has a slow, ritualistic quality which verges on corny and slows the pace considerably. By the end, you well and truly know how to address these cats but you would also quite like them to curl up and take a nap now.AtRegent’s Park Open Air theatre, London, until 19 September. Thentouring the UK and Irelanduntil 19 June 2027.Explore more on these topicsTheatreAndrew Lloyd WebberMusicalsDanceTS EliotCatsAnimalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Alley Cats review – the genital jokes in Ricky Gervais’s sweary cartoon are just exhausting | Television | The Guardian
description: There are glimmers of potential in this comedy about a potty-mouthed feline gang. But not even the great voice cast or a cute kitten can save it from being lazy, crude and boring
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: There are glimmers of potential in this comedy about a potty-mouthed feline gang. But not even the great voice cast or a cute kitten can save it from being lazy, crude and boring
Content: Animal edgelord … David Earl as Puke in Alley Cats. Cr. Courtesy of Netflix © 2026Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenAnimal edgelord … David Earl as Puke in Alley Cats. Cr. Courtesy of Netflix © 2026Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewAlley Cats review – the genital jokes in Ricky Gervais’s sweary cartoon are just exhaustingThere are glimmers of potential in this comedy about a potty-mouthed feline gang. But not even the great voice cast or a cute kitten can save it from being  lazy, crude and boringLucy ManganFri 7 Aug 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsuppose the question is really: what do you do after redefining comedy for your era? After The Office, that exquisitely observed, agonising, heartbreaking, hilarious examination of the human condition co-created with Stephen Merchant,Ricky Gervaismanaged Extras – off-peak but still great – and then continued a downward trajectory that his latest offering, Alley Cats, does nothing to arrest.You can see what the six-episode animated series about a gang of homeless cats wants to be. It wants to be an exquisitely observed, agonising, heartbreaking, hilarious examination of the human condition. But it can’t be bothered. Easier by far, especially as it’s on Netflix and unshackled from mainstream broadcasters’ rules about swearing, to call everyone a C-word and sigh at the inevitability/sweet release of death every five minutes. Nihilism – gotcha! So dark, man, so edgy!Gervais plays Gus, the corpulent, complacent (“I’m probably the best cat in the neighbourhood”) misanthropy-maxxing leader of the ragtag group. His right-hand man, Fang (Andrew Brooke) is the gang’s bruiser and not much beyond that and Puke (David Earl) is the disgusting one, providing the lads with all the material they require about anal sex, fingering and the varying states in which genitals can be found. A regular visitor to their squat is the cat they call “Ponce” (Tom Basden) – real name Rupert (of course) – who is a pedigree, lives with a family, enjoys regular meals, brushing and puddings (“You fucking ponce!”). He has also, of course, been neutered, which fills in the joke-gaps left when the anal sex/fingering/genitals stuff runs out. Ponce himself remains unbothered by his testicular lack. “They cloud the judgment,” he explains serenely, in one of the handful of lines that could raise a smile rather than a weary checking of how long is left.But, for now, we’re in the dark alley with these cats, plus the girl who lives upstairs – Olive (Diane Morgan), who is, Gus notes with glee, really thick. In a further sign of the laziness of the whole endeavour, though, she’s not. After a few token tries to establish her as such, she simply becomes a perfectly ordinary cat (it would also, it seems, have been too much effort even to make her a smart cat they only think is stupid), with a bit of a thing for Ponce until she finds out he doesn’t have the urge or the equipment to provide her with the kittens she wants.Into the mix is brought a lost kitten, Kitten (Jo Hartley), who – I am sorry to tell you – awakens fatherly instincts in Gus and begins to teach him and the rest of the gang about love and what it means to be a family. Gervais the sentimentalist is always a far more unnerving proposition than Gervais the misanthrope, so you are best advised to approach Kitten’s scenes with the utmost caution. There are several in which Gus has to comfort Kitten, who has not yet mastered the cool nihilism thing, about the fact of death. “I don’t want to not exist. I want to live for ever!”, says Kitten. Gus replies – and I think here we are aiming for “tenderly and awkwardly” – that although a cat may no longer be around physically, he “lives on in the memories of friends and family”. Kitten brightens. “So you’ll live on through all the things you’ve taught me!” And lo, Gus himself is comforted. The viewer – for whom this is an entirely unearned attempt at an emotional beat because Gus has not yet taught Kitten a single, solitary thing – is not.On we go, through an equally unmoving death of Gus’s mother, innumerable diatribes about obvious targets like spiders (“Maybe it’s the eight fucking legs and10 fucking eyes the cunts have got!” “Fucking shit creatures, mate!”), lengthy descriptions of Puke’s baroque proclivities that are usually a way of Gervais trying to engineer some kind of controversy (one involves Aids monkey rape that I’m honestly too tired to detail further).There are a handful of moments in which you can see, maybe, what might have been. Gus in front of his love interest Lara (Kerry Godliman) has echoes of David Brent’s eternal vulnerability and evokes memories of Gervais’s talent for a kind of compassionate skewering of male frailties. Ponce provides some moments of relative subtlety (“And where is that in the league tables?” he enquires politely after Gus and Fang’s lauding of the university of life. “Quite low, I’d imagine”) and some shelter from the hail of uninventive swears and pointless rants. But otherwise Alley Cats feels like a creative cul de sac, leaving you not consumed by laughter but the wish that Gervais could stop indulging himself in lesser projects, go away, rest up and let his genius ferment once more, however long it takes. title: Hamnet to On Falling: the seven best films to watch on TV this week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The gut-wrenching performance that won Jessie Buckley an Oscar. Plus, a powerful critique of the gig economy by debut director Laura Carreira
Author: Simon Wardell
Headline: The gut-wrenching performance that won Jessie Buckley an Oscar. Plus, a powerful critique of the gig economy by debut director Laura Carreira
Content: Overlooked … Jessie Buckley stars as Agnes Shakespeare in Hamnet.Photograph: Agata Grzybowska/APView image in fullscreenOverlooked … Jessie Buckley stars as Agnes Shakespeare in Hamnet.Photograph: Agata Grzybowska/APThe seven best films to watch on TV this weekTelevision & radioHamnet to On Falling: the seven best films to watch on TV this weekThe gut-wrenching performance that won Jessie Buckley an Oscar. Plus, a powerful critique of the gig economy by debut director Laura CarreiraSimon WardellFri 7 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekHamnetFrom a Roman muscle man to William Shakespeare, Paul Mescal is showing his range right now. But in Chloé Zhao’s version of Maggie O’Farrell superb novel, he has to play second fiddle to Jessie Buckley. It’s her Oscar-winning turn as Agnes – the Bard’s unsung wife – that gives the drama its gut-wrenching power. Agnes is the heart to Will’s brain, more attuned to the mysteries of the natural world, and aware that his genius will take him away from her. But their differing reactions to a family tragedy push them further apart … Hamnet is a difficult book to adapt, its potency coming from its unarticulated emotions, but Zhao has pulled it off brilliantly.Friday 14 August, 8.10am, 8pm, Sky Cinema PremiereParallel MothersView image in fullscreenIdentity crisis … Janis (Penélope Cruz) and Ana (Milena Smit) star as mothers whose babies are swapped at birth.Photograph: Sony/AllstarJust before his latest twisty film, Bitter Christmas, hits cinemas, here’s another chance to see Pedro Almodóvar’s equally knotty 2021 drama, which explores family secrets in the domestic and national spheres. It features a standout performance from Penélope Cruz as photographer Janis, who gets pregnant by a forensic anthropologist investigating the forgotten civil war victims of Franco – including her ancestors. When her newborn gets swapped with that of the young Ana (Milena Smit), fate intertwines their lives. A forceful experience.Saturday 8 August, 11.10pm, BBC FourSpeedView image in fullscreenWheel deal … Keanu Reeves and Sandra Bullock star in Speed.Photograph: United Archives GmbH/AlamyIf Jan de Bont’s 1994 action thriller didn’t propel Keanu Reeves to stardom (Point Break arguably did that in 1991), it was his biggest box-office hit to date – and it was most definitely a breakthrough moment for Sandra Bullock. She is her co-star’s equal as a passenger who has to take the steering wheel of an LA bus primed to explode if it goes under 50mph. Reeves has the more superficially heroic role as a police bomb disposal officer, but both have their moments in a terrifically tense series of freeway set-pieces, while Dennis Hopper is reliably unhinged as their foe.Sunday 9 August, 9pm, Film4MissingView image in fullscreenSearching … June (Storm Reid) tries to track down her mother in Missing.Photograph: Screen GemsA thematic sequel to the 2018 film Searching, Nick Johnson and Will Merrick’s 2023 thriller continues its conceit of restricting what we see to computer screens and smartphones. So after Storm Reid’s June discovers her mother, Grace (Nia Long), has vanished while on holiday in Colombia with new boyfriend Kevin (Ken Leung), she uses the panoply of digital resources – voicemails, FaceTime, doorcams, even tourist webcams – to investigate remotely. It’s all inherently claustrophobic, which helps generate a sustained level of unease and, soon enough, peril.Tuesday 11 August, 9pm, Film4Gladiator IIView image in fullscreenFighting for freedom … Paul Mescal is Lucius in Gladiator II.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyIt has taken 24 years for Ridley Scott to get back to the Colosseum. But there’s still a lot of familiarity in his ancient Roman sequel – from returning characters to elaborate fight scenes and animal antics. Paul Mescal stars as Lucius, the son of Russell Crowe’s Maximus, who is living a quiet life in north Africa until an invading Roman army take him into slavery. From there, it’s a short hop to becoming a rebellious gladiator, under the gimlet gaze of his owner Macrinus (a lip-smacking Denzel Washington).Wednesday 12 August, NetflixA Child of My OwnView image in fullscreenFake news … Ana Celeste Montalvo as Alejandra in A Child of My Own.Photograph: Courtesy of Netflix/2026Maite Alberdi’s documentary starts as a straightforward ripped-from-the-headlines dramatisation of a secret adoption, shot in the vibrant palette of a telenovela. Mexican hospital worker Alejandra has just had her third miscarriage when she meets Mayra, who doesn’t want the baby she will give birth to. Mayra agrees to hand her newborn over to Alejandra, who meanwhile will pretend to be going through her own pregnancy. It’s when their plan goes wrong that the film pulls the rug out from under the viewer. As other voices enter the frame, is the narrative we have been consuming true at all?Thursday 13 August, NetflixOn FallingView image in fullscreenLack of fulfilment … Joana Santos stars as Aurora in On Falling.Photograph: Sixteen FilmsPortuguese immigrant Aurora (Joana Santos) works as a “picker” in an Amazon-style warehouse in Scotland. It’s a monotonous but time-sensitive job that has reduced her to a zombie-like state; she’s too tired and/or poor to enjoy her free time and struggles to connect with her mostly foreign colleagues and flatmates. And when her phone needs a costly repair, that’s all it takes to tip her over the edge. Laura Carreira’s debut feature is heart-breaking social realism with a Ken Loach feel, but where he rails at capitalism’s evils, Carreira sees bureaucratic indifference.Friday 14 August, 11.05pm, BBC TwoExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioThe seven best films to watch on TV this weekfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘There is an alternative to capitalism’: after addiction and losing a home to LA wildfires, indie rockers Diiv start again | Music | The Guardian
description: No stranger to rebuilding after disaster, the US band’s frontman Zachary Cole Smith now sees the entire capitalist project as ripe for reinvention, on a surprisingly upbeat new AG Cook-produced album
Author: Jazz Monroe
Headline: No stranger to rebuilding after disaster, the US band’s frontman Zachary Cole Smith now sees the entire capitalist project as ripe for reinvention, on a surprisingly upbeat new AG Cook-produced album
Content: Diiv, from left: Zachary Cole Smith, Colin Caulfield, Ben Newman and Andrew Bailey.Photograph: Louie KovatchView image in fullscreenDiiv, from left: Zachary Cole Smith, Colin Caulfield, Ben Newman and Andrew Bailey.Photograph: Louie KovatchMusicInterview‘There is an alternative to capitalism’: after addiction and losing a home to LA wildfires, indie rockers Diiv start againJazz MonroeNo stranger to rebuilding after disaster, the US band’s frontman Zachary Cole Smith now sees the entire capitalist project as ripe for reinvention, on a surprisingly upbeat new AG Cook-produced albumFri 7 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZachary Cole Smith used to be a miserable interviewee. He had plenty to say – always generous, always voluble – but spoke with grim introspection, chastising himself and cataloguing his misdeeds with a fervour that engulfed him like his oversized T-shirts. A decade later, the Diiv frontman who materialises on my screen seems well rid of that old self. Suspiciously well rid of it, perhaps. He looks as if he has stepped out of a middle management meeting.“Precisely!” Smith concurs cheerfully, speaking via video call from a back garden in La Cañada, California. “We’re trying to have a visual language, which is fun. We’ve never done that with what we wear.” The singer-guitarist, 41, wears thick-rimmed square glasses, slicked-back black hair and a pinstripe shirt, its neck clasped by a tie printed with stock market emblems. He has an earnest but pranksterish energy. He uses the word “fun” so many times – more than a dozen within 10 minutes – that I suspect he is testing some sort of subliminal PR strategy.The Diiv album he is promoting is called Zirp! (meaning “zero interest-rate policy”) and produced by Alex “AG” Cook, the bubbly, neon pop accelerationist and co-conspirator of Charli xcx. Cook is by no means a natural fit for Diiv, who are one of the least garish bands around. Their buzzy early albums set 80s goth to a motorik pulse, with dream-pop riffs refracted like sunlight into a cobwebbed drawing room. Though they have likely benefited from the TikTok-aided shoegaze revival, their fourth album, 2024’s Frog in Boiling Water, waded into the swamp of anti-capitalist ennui. Cook has helped airlift them out: on Zirp!, for the first time in years, Diiv sound like they are finally having – hang on a minute …Diiv: The Fountain – video“It’s fun to do something fun,” proclaims Smith, smoking the first of several cigarettes. Today’s costume, accordingly, is based on a darkly comic figure: “the recession-era, stock market crash guy”. Smith strikes a pose like Rodin’s Thinker if he had just cost his hedge fund a billion dollars. “This kind of vibe, with the dishevelled suit.”To go with the look, the band coined a tongue-in-cheek genre dubbed the New Alternative. It reminds Smith of both the loathed Thatcherite slogan “there is no alternative” and the influential Mark Fisher book Capitalist Realism: Is There No Alternative? “I really want to reclaim that word,” Smith says. “Thereisan alternative to capitalism.”For starters, he dreams of a publicly owned streaming library that could operate as an alternative to the current ecosystem, particularly Spotify. “I do feel that that company absolutely should not exist and should be dismantled,” he says. “For Spotify, [music] is just fodder in their ecosystem. They’re selling tech. Apple is a company that’s selling phones. And music is this resource that they can pillage and plunder.”View image in fullscreenZachary Cole Smith at FYF Fest 2016 in Los Angeles.Photograph: Kevin Winter/Getty ImagesNew songs Evangelizer and The Crash are similarly forthright: the former, a wraithlike monologue, depicts “BlackRock master keys” and “Palantir-Pfizer collab pills” in what Smith calls a “post-capitalist hellscape”; the latter is a wonky, end-of-days art-pop screed by a narrator determined to “throw the billionaires screaming in an alligator pit”. As to what a New Alternative might be, he concedes that the term, for now, describes nothing beyond a break from “some kind of norm”. He shrugs helplessly, then seems to remember he is wearing a tie. “Alternative stocks are up!” he declares.One afternoon in January 2025, Smith invited his bandmates to his home in Altadena to demo My Star, a thrashing alt-rock love song to his one-year-old son. As they left, a windstorm was brewing. When nearby Eaton Canyon went up in flames in the wildfires, Smith and his wife, who was seven months pregnant, decided to gather their son’s belongings. “We gotta do bedtime,” he remembers thinking. “Let’s just pack up his little crib and his little jammies and get a hotel room, and then the power won’t go out.”By 3am, their hotel secured, Altadena was ablaze. “Our neighbours were describing the scene: it’s raining orange, it’s snowing orange.” Three hours later, “everything was gone. Then at 6.30am, our son woke up and was just like, ‘What are we doing today!’” As their adrenaline ebbed, the gravity of the loss struck. “All of a sudden, we had nothing. But once he woke up, we just had to make everything be normal.”Their home was now a pile of rubble beside the burnt-out carcass of a car. Finding a new place was hard “because so many people were displaced”, says Smith. A series of temporary lodgings led the family – now including their second child – to the La Cañada house where they have lived for the past six months, awaiting a distant peaceful life. “Where we’re at now feels like where we’ll be until we rebuild our house, which is a slow process,” he says. “But one that, I think, at some point, will become fun.”View image in fullscreenDiiv in 2016, from left: Devin Ruben Perez, Zachary Cole Smith, Ben Newman, Andrew Bailey and Colin Caulfield.Photograph: David A Smith/Getty ImagesWork on Zirp! swiftly resumed. Inspired by a 2023 arena tour supporting Depeche Mode – and a dip into the band’s 1980s catalogue – Smith had already decided to “surrender perfectionism, work quickly and not be precious”. Having run into Cook at a party, he cemented the partnership after hearing the grunge anthem Bewitched from the producer’s triple album Britpop. Cook renders Diiv’s shoegaze textures as if in arcade mode: portentous riffs wriggle like pop-punk earworms; feedback harbours micro melodies like radio jingles. “Knowing the songs were gonna wind up in front of Alex made it so much more fun to take risks,” says Smith.There were other benefits to recruiting an auteur producer. Though Smith single-handedly produced and masterminded the first two Diiv albums, the band gradually became more collaborative as he treated, and finally cut out, his drug use. “Addiction is all about control,” he says. “You want to block out what anybody else is saying, so it lends itself really well to dictatorship.”His addiction had become a minor scandalin 2013, when Smith and then-girlfriend Sky Ferreira were arrested for possession of heroin and ecstasy (he took full responsibility). He went to rehab, left and relapsed. He spent four years talking up Diiv’s second album and playinglacklustre showsin a period of heightened scrutiny: drummer Colby Hewitt was dealing with his own substance use and bassist Devin Ruben Perez had been exposed for bigoted messageboard posts. (Both left the band.) As Diiv threatened to slip through his fingers, Smith became preoccupied with collecting rare coral reefs in a 50-gallon saltwater tank at his Brooklyn apartment.View image in fullscreenChannelling a ‘spirit of fun and playfulness and risk and experimentation’.Photograph: Louie KovatchWith the help of his girlfriend (whom he married in 2020) and mother-in-law, Smith kicked drugs in 2017. The “ego destruction” of sobering up prompted him to democratise the band. “I’ve worked to repair the trust with my bandmates and whoever I damaged during my active addiction,” he says. “I just want to utilise that to get us to where we want to be,” moving forward in a “spirit of fun and playfulness and risk and experimentation”.Indie music has been invaded by fake fans and cynical viral campaigns​. Here’s how deep it all goesRead moreSmith has spoken relentlessly about all those he has let down and lied to. After all that, I ask, how did it feel to receive $100,000 in crowdfunded wildfire aid for his family, from a community that trusts and supports him? “I want to cry just thinking about it,” he says, choking up. “It taught me something, you know? It was profound. I’ve never experienced love like that. And it did feel like …” He sighs. “I felt like I deserved it.” As part of his recovery, Smith has helped others living with addiction and maintained a network of the similarly afflicted. “I feel like we earned it through being good to our friends, family and communities,” he says, “being available to people or letting a band borrow the van. I don’t know how I would have learned that lesson any other way. But it was probably the most meaningful thing that’s ever happened to me, on an interpersonal level.”The rebuilding of Smith’s family home remains clogged up in various city-planning departments. “But the Altadena community is stronger than it’s ever been,” he says, lighting another cigarette. “The relationships we have with other families that lived on our street is remarkable. Even the crowdfunding – the silver lining is how it showed this sense of community, lifting each other up.” For a little while, it seemed as if the fire would consume their whole world. “It could have felt really alienating, but luckily, we had each other.”Zirp! is released via Fantasy Recordings on 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMusicDrugsPsychedeliaIndiePop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the anxiety-ridden sugar rush of Tiffany Day and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Day’s latest album Halo is all high-energy exhaustion, injected with a crushing electroclash chaos that illuminates her insecurities in bright neon
Author: David Renshaw
Headline: Day’s latest album Halo is all high-energy exhaustion, injected with a crushing electroclash chaos that illuminates her insecurities in bright neon
Content: Breakthrough and burnout … Tiffany Day.Photograph: Ally WeiView image in fullscreenBreakthrough and burnout … Tiffany Day.Photograph: Ally WeiAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the anxiety-ridden sugar rush of Tiffany Day and the week’s best new tracksDay’s latest album Halo is all high-energy exhaustion, injected with a crushing electroclash chaos that illuminates her insecurities in bright neonDavid Renshaw,Ben Beaumont-ThomasandLaura SnapesFri 7 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromLos AngelesRecommendedif you likeSlayyyter, Charli xcx, UnderscoresUp nextHaloout now. UK and Ireland tour starts in DecemberRight now popstar breakthrough and burnout are a hair’s breadth from one another. Enter Tiffany Day, a Wichita-raised artist who first went viral in 2017 when a video of her singing Hallelujah on a school trip blew up online. She spent the subsequent years unsuccessfully chipping away at building on that virality, cycling through acoustic guitar covers and bedroom R&B. Only by channeling her frustrations into this year’s anxiety-ridden sugar rush Halo did Day finally regain her early momentum.Day’s music stands out for its robust balance of giddy hyperpop and frank vulnerability: think of it as the tears-on-the-dancefloor dynamic for the infinite scroll era. Halo opens with Everything I’ve Ever Wanted, a plainspoken ode to the coveted come-up and the dreaded fall-off, in which Day panics about success. “When something good comes crashing into me, it’s like I can’t breathe,” she frets through a smear of Auto-Tune.Halo is high energy but came from a place of exhaustion, with Day concluding that this album would be her last. Past caring about others’ opinions, she injected it with a crushing electroclash chaos that illuminates her insecurities in a bright neon hue. On songs like DoIt4me and Pretty4u she alternates between freaking out in front of the mirror and hiding in the corner at parties, exposing herself further from behind walls of yo-yo synths and hacksaw bass lines. It’s enough to make youthful insecurity feel manageable, or to make you thank god those days are a thing of the past.David RenshawThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenPitying … Coco and Clair Clair.Photograph: Coco & Clair ClairCoco and Clair Clair – One OneIf you loved squirming underSmerz’s withering gaze last year, let your skin prickle to this Atlanta, Georgia duo’s addictive, pitying dismissal of an ungrateful ex, as menace encroaches on their minimalist, stumbling percussion.LSHelen – Dead Shark IIEleven years after Helen’s debut, Liz Harris (AKA Grouper) unexpectedly reforms her dream-pop band. Full of silt, stardust and rumble, Dead Shark II is as good as the genre gets.LSLancer – 2LateAfter his ultra-emotional, 80s-sampling rap tracks Cry and Southpaw this year, the UK vocalist switches up to singing for his synthwave-ballad debut for XL, restless and upset in the choppy wake of a breakup.BBTBlack Bananas – Eddie’s AlbumThe side project from Royal Trux’s raw-voiced vocalist, Jennifer Herrema, is back and on supremely fun form, flexing taut disco-funk behind a beaded curtain of murky lo-fi chillwave production.BBTEden Aurelius – Entre NousThe NYC producer’s beautiful new album of ambient compositions and featherlight dub techno has a milky-sun blend of warm and cool, though its title track adds a touch more heat with a very subtle dancehall pulse.BBTHana Stretton – FromThe lo-fi, blanketed intimacy and the British-Australian songwriter’s heavy, layered vocals suggest peeping under the bed and finding a tiny choir laying in wait, from a new release on Phil Elverum’s label.LSNew Radicals – One Night Only (Break Loose Break Free!)The film it soundtracks, of the same name, looks weird (The Purge … for pre-marital sex?) but the first NR song since 1999 is cause for celebration, with Gregg Alexander’s knack for secular affirmations designed to lure hangdogs out of their holes.LSSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistElectronic musicPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Grieg Lyric Pieces album review – Feltsman brings a probing flexibility that transforms this music | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Feltsman’s comprehensive survey of the Lyric Pieces is revelatory and authoritative
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Feltsman’s comprehensive survey of the Lyric Pieces is revelatory and authoritative
Content: Vladimir Feltsman performing at Carnegie Hall in New York in 2009.Photograph: Hiroyuki Ito/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVladimir Feltsman performing at Carnegie Hall in New York in 2009.Photograph: Hiroyuki Ito/Getty ImagesClassical musicReviewGrieg Lyric Pieces album review – Feltsman brings a probing flexibility that transforms this musicVladimir Feltsman(Nimbus)Feltsman’s comprehensive survey of the Lyric Pieces is revelatory and authoritativeClive PagetFri 7 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussian-American pianist Vladimir Feltsman’s love of Grieg’s Lyric Pieces dates back to his childhood in Moscow and his first piano teacher, EM Timakin, who introduced him to the works. Part homage, then, this comprehensive survey draws on the accumulated wisdom of over 60 years in a set that abounds with interpretative imagination.View image in fullscreenVladimir Feltsman: Grieg – Lyric PiecesFeltsman approaches Grieg as if it were Schumann, bringing a probing flexibility that transforms this music into more than just occasional salon pieces. Book I’s famous Arietta, for example, responds eagerly to his supple sense of rubato. He also points up the composer’s cosmopolitan influences, with a Nocturne that could almost be Chopin, a Scherzo redolent of Saint-Saëns and a Nordic Valse-Impromptu that could only be by Grieg.Up-tempo showpieces are dispatched with theatrical flair. Book II’s Leaping Dance cuts a hoppity-skippity caper while his Hallings, those fast-paced Norwegian folk dances, are full of pungent harmonies and earthy rhythms. Feltsman’s March of the Trolls, steadier than most, builds a menacing head of steam to equal a Mussorgsky picture. However, it’s in the quieter pieces – jewels such as Melancholy, Homesickness or the late Summer Evening – where lightness of touch and pristine articulation pay dividends.For authority and inspiration, Feltsman can stand alongside Gilels and Andsnes, although he makes entirely individual choices. Brightly recorded and played almost without breaks, these consistently surprising accounts make you fall in love with Grieg’s endearing miniatures all over again.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: Flo: Therapy at the Club review – skirting the dancefloor and overly sweating the small stuff | Music | The Guardian
description: The British R&B girl group’s follow up to 2024’s Access All Areas is lyrically spicy and musically diverse but somewhat slow paced and lacking the euphoria and hedonism the title suggests
Author: Kate Solomon
Headline: The British R&B girl group’s follow up to 2024’s Access All Areas is lyrically spicy and musically diverse but somewhat slow paced and lacking the euphoria and hedonism the title suggests
Content: Unhurried … (from left) Renée Downer, Stella Quaresma and Jorja Douglas AKA Flo.Photograph: Alex J PiperView image in fullscreenUnhurried … (from left) Renée Downer, Stella Quaresma and Jorja Douglas AKA Flo.Photograph: Alex J PiperMusicReviewFlo: Therapy at the Club review – skirting the dancefloor and overly sweating the small stuff(EMI)The British R&B girl group’s follow up to 2024’s Access All Areas is lyrically spicy and musically diverse but lacks the hedonism the title suggestsKate SolomonFri 7 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Flo burst out in 2022, the trio were hailed as the second coming of the R&B girl group, and even paid homage to their harmonising forebears Destiny’s Child, Sugababes and SWV in the intro to debut albumAccess All Areas. They didn’t quite hit as expected – only one single scraped the Top 40 – but they sound undeterred on a vibey second album that adds lyrical spice and musical left turns.View image in fullscreenFlo: Therapy at the Club.Therapy at the Club follows the flow of a night out, but one rooted in the slight mania of romantic disappointment rather than euphoric release. Pose is a pared-back interpolation of Pump Up the Jam, skittering hi-hat hits echoing the clicks of confidence-boosting burst-mode selfies. On Remedied, Flo are distracted by the admin of getting a cab as big-band horns blast behind an anxious beat; with its 3/4 time signature, piano and dreamy melismatic vocals, the title track sounds more like sashaying through the park than the soundtrack to copping off with strangers.Like any self-respecting girl group, Flo have their balladry down: Floating is a belter, showcasing their chemistry as the three vocal lines soar around each other. But at 16 often mid-paced tracks, the album drags. Miss U Missing Me meanders through a ghosting situation that ends up feeling kind of justified. The overall disconnect between theme and energy is distracting: there’s self-assurance to Therapy at the Club’s unhurried pace, though more time sweating it out on the dancefloor would make it a more satisfying listen.Explore more on these topicsMusicR&Balbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: The best recent science fiction, fantasy and horror – review roundup | Science fiction books | The Guardian
description: The Salt Kingby Natasha Pulley; A Trade of Blood by Robert Jackson Bennett; Netherwood by Jake Arnott; Fawn by CN Vair
Author: Lisa Tuttle
Headline: The Salt Kingby Natasha Pulley; A Trade of Blood by Robert Jackson Bennett; Netherwood by Jake Arnott; Fawn by CN Vair
Content: Visions of saltwater in Natasha Pulley’s The Salt King.Photograph: Jose A Bernat Bacete/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVisions of saltwater in Natasha Pulley’s The Salt King.Photograph: Jose A Bernat Bacete/Getty ImagesScience fiction booksThe best recent science fiction, fantasy and horror – review roundupThe Salt King by Natasha Pulley; A Trade of Blood by Robert Jackson Bennett; Netherwood by Jake Arnott; Fawn by CN VairLisa TuttleFri 7 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenThe Salt King byby Natasha Pulley (Gollancz, £22)The latest from the author of The Watchmaker of Filigree Street blends an apocalyptic end-of-the-world tale with folk horror and two slowly developing love stories. Avelyn Brocken is a trainee priest at the Vatican, sent to check out a possible miracle in the fens of East Anglia. His only qualification for the job is that he was born and raised in Hreodwater, a strange community based around a salt mine with its own language, religion and rituals. But what begins in Hreodwater, involving the mysterious salt light and a sleeping king deep in the mine, threatens civilisations. An original, rich and gripping tale that’s also an interesting exploration of the power of faith.View image in fullscreenA Trade of Bloodby Robert Jackson Bennett (Hodderscape, £25)A new case for Ana and Din, the crime-solving team introduced in the Hugo and World Fantasy award-winning novel The Tainted Cup, focuses on a murder among the cattle-ranching gentry of the Empire of Khanum. The murderer has been caught red-handed, unable to remember what happened. The victim was his lover, and their families were enemies; he is the last of his line, and fears his family is cursed. The detectives suspect a more material and dangerous adversary behind the scenes, with access to a terrifying weapon. This is the sort of other-world fantasy with close ties to speculative fiction, based on natural laws and science rather than any magical system, and some of the issues it raises are of immediate concern in today’s world of shrinking resources. Great world-building and a masterfully conceived mystery make for a compelling cross-genre blend.View image in fullscreenNetherwoodby Jake Arnott(Titan, £18.99)London is too expensive, so artist Adam and his partner Justine buy a house in Hastings. The room at the top will make the perfect studio for Adam, whose career has stalled after drink, drugs and quarrels. They’re intrigued by the property’s “special feature” – a cave hidden behind a locked door in the back wall. After they move in they discover a Latin phrase carved into the wall, layers of candle wax, a mysterious sealed bottle: evidence of occult rituals? It turns out the previous owner was a devotee of chaos magic, inspired by the notorious Aleister Crowley, who died in a Hastings boarding house called Netherwood. Justine fears they could be in danger, sensing the ghostly presence of a frightened girl, but at the same time, their new home is inspiring Adam to create his most powerful paintings, winning back the support of his agent and the promise of big money. A wonderfully unnerving, evocative horror in which Hastings looms large as the most uncanny place in England.Fawnby CN Vair (3AM, £20)This debut begins with deceptive gentleness, introducing the reader to Tess, a witch in present-day America who sold her soul to the devil in 1935, the price for surviving a murderous attack. She hardly seems to have aged, but is careful to keep the locals from noticing, using spells to turn unwanted attention away and keep herself and her animal sanctuary safe. Things start to go wrong when she rescues a fawn, born at the wrong time of year with teeth and a thirst for blood. She ignores advice to put it down, but when the local cop insists it must be destroyed, and a new preacher arrives in town, seeming to turn her friends against her, she struggles to maintain control. Just when she needs them most, the old spells are failing her. Like a newborn fawn, she’s doomed to be seen as prey. Tess refuses to accept defeat, on any level; she will do whatever it takes to survive in this disturbing, seductively written fiction about power and female rage.Explore more on these topicsScience fiction booksFantasy booksFictionHorror booksShareReuse this content

title: What Happened to Liberal Democracy? by Daron Acemoglu review – how to fix the system | Politics books | The Guardian
description: The Nobel-winning economist takes aim at elites for no longer meeting the needs of the masses
Author: Steven Poole
Headline: The Nobel-winning economist takes aim at elites for no longer meeting the needs of the masses
Content: Trump supporters storm the Capitol building in Washington on 6 January 2021.Photograph: Anadolu/Anadolu Agency/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump supporters storm the Capitol building in Washington on 6 January 2021.Photograph: Anadolu/Anadolu Agency/Getty ImagesBook of the dayPolitics booksReviewWhat Happened to Liberal Democracy? by Daron Acemoglu review – how to fix the systemThe Nobel-winning economist takes aim at elites for no longer meeting the needs of the massesSteven PooleFri 7 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 12.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2009, the tech billionaire Peter Thiel published an essay with the portentous title The Education of a Libertarian, in which he announced: “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” Since the 1920s, he wrote, “the vast increase in welfare beneficiaries and the extension of the franchise to women” had rendered the notion of “capitalist democracy” an oxymoron. To be fair, Thiel still seems happy to exercise his freedom to extract money from democracies, via his co-founding ofPalantir, which was lately given lots of money by the NHS.Thiel calls himself, as many such do, a “classical liberal”, but Daron Acemoglu argues that his ilk still has much in common with left-liberals. All of them, he writes, agree on “the desirability of basic individual rights and freedoms (including the right not to be coerced and the freedoms of expression, religion, association, and choice); constraints on power, especially political power; and broad protections for equality before the law”. On his telling, by the mid-20th century democracy with liberal characteristics had amply proved its worth: blue-collar labour was generously rewarded, and there was a sense of “shared prosperity”.But now, he argues, liberal democracy is in a crisis, largely owing to the abandonment of the working class by liberalism’s “progressive” wing. In post-industrial Europe and the US, the left ceased to speak of economic class and spoke instead of identity. It is a similar diagnosis to that offered by the French sociologist Didier Eribon in his Retour à Reims, and indeed by Bernie Sanders, who has spoken of “a Democratic party which has abandoned working-class people”, but Acemoglu is happier to wield culture-war rhetoric even as he deplores the culture wars. He accuses the left, for example, of being obsessed with both “social engineering” (via diversity initiatives) and “thought policing”, which is impossible (he means speech policing).His solution is a new contract of “working-class liberal democracy”, which concentrates on improving the standard of living of the least educated or skilled. This is to be done by focusing on economic growth (reducing, for example, the regulatory hoops one must apparently jump through to become a hairdresser or a masseur), encouraging more community decision-making (possibly imitating the citizens’ assemblies used in the Republic of Ireland), and making social media companies responsible, as publishers, for the messages they promote to users (good luck!). He suggests legislating in favour of “worker AI”, by which employees could use expert systems based on machine-learning to help them be more productive, so that nurses, for instance, could take more medical decisions. (He doesn’t report having consulted doctors on this idea.)Acemoglu is a smooth and intelligent writer, and there is much in here to fascinate, particularly when he is on home turf: there is a brilliant explanation of why the American tax code perversely incentivises automation and job destruction, and how the enviable happiness of Norway and Sweden, far from being a result of some innate Nordic wisdom, followed deliberate economic reforms enacted as recently as the 1930s. He is also laudably ready to admit when there is no “ready-made answer” to liberalism’s tensions – between, say, a value of community cohesion and a value of welcoming others who are different.But his expansive rhetoric does lead to some internal inconsistencies. Acemoglu denounces throughout the progressive-liberal elites in exactly the same way as modern populists do (Farage-like, he even says liberalism’s troubles have reached “boiling point”). Yet, having eased the reader through a potted history of the ideas of Rousseau, Hobbes, Locke, Mill, Kant, Voltaire et al, he concedes that liberalism itself was the invention of a small bunch of clever people: “an ideology created by a highly learned group of philosophers”. So maybe elites are good, sometimes? And Acemoglu can hardly escape the charge that his own book – one written by a Nobel-winning economist, no less – is itself an example of the kind of top-down “elite debates” he claims to think are sterile. Nor should he try to, because the charge would be stupid; indeed, the kind of thing that an elite billionaire like Peter Thiel would say.What Happened to Liberal Democracy?: Remaking a Politics of Shared Prosperity by Daron Acemoglu (£25).
