title: EA Sports FC 27: what does the next instalment of the world’s biggest football game have in store? | Games | The Guardian
description: The all-conquering franchise’s revamps are technically impressive, its transfers more true to life – and its new grassroots social hub is surprising fun
Author: Steve Boxer
Headline: The all-conquering franchise’s revamps are technically impressive, its transfers more true to life – and its new grassroots social hub is surprising fun
Content: Something fresh … EA Sports FC 27.Illustration: Electronic ArtsView image in fullscreenSomething fresh … EA Sports FC 27.Illustration: Electronic ArtsGamesEA Sports FC 27: what does the next instalment of the world’s biggest football game have in store?The all-conquering franchise’s revamps are technically impressive, its transfers more true to life – and its new grassroots social hub is surprising funSteve BoxerFri 7 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs if the world wasn’t sufficiently football-obsessed, it’s time to prepare for the arrival of its biggest football video game. EA Sports FC 27 (the franchise that used to be Fifa – what better time to no longer be Fifa-branded?) is due to be released on 25 September. I just spent two intense days in Vancouver, where the EA FC games are made, playing FC 27 and talking to its developers.With an annual franchise such as EA FC, it helps to have something fresh to entice regular fans, and FC 27 has a whole new element, entitled the Grounds. It’s a physical hub-type area, similar to the City as seen in 2K’s recent NBA 2K basketball games, but much more pleasant to frequent, split as it is into areas inspired by British, French and Argentinian street-football culture.The Grounds provides a new physical home for an existing element of EA FC: Clubs, its casual online mode in which you control a single player and play matches closer to kickabouts than real-world football, but beyond that, it has plenty of other activities and distractions.Visitingthe GroundsI spent about an hour in the Grounds, and found it more enjoyable than expected. Among its buildings are playing areas, whose entrances act as lobbies where you can choose to play against random people or to set up a custom game with your FC 27-owning friends. Each playing area hosts a specific type of game, and the Grounds has a map that you can teleport around.It rewards exploration: I encountered targets that could be smashed by spawning a football and drop-kicking it, some of which were clumped into mini-games. Its games offered clever twists on the Clubs blueprint. In one 3v3 game, target areas appeared for short periods, and if I scored from one, I got a bonus goal for my side. And one game based on dodgeball gave its players three lives, which they would lose if others successfully kicked a ball at them.The Grounds should prove popular: it has been tastefully and cleverly constructed and will no doubt expand as new game-types are added. You could also envisage it, in future years, hosting a narrative mode along the line of the Journey from Fifa 17 to 19.Gameplay revamps galoreFC 26 marked a mission by EA Sports to improve the franchise’s responsiveness by enactinga surprising number of changes to its fundamental gameplay, and that process continues apace in FC 27.Although anyone who played FC 26 will testify that those efforts actually caused some new problems, such as an annoying tendency for defensive interceptions to bounce back weirdly into the path of forwards. EA Sports, according to gameplay design director Kantcho Doskov, took radical action to eliminate such aberrations: “We had to completely strip out the existing system for interceptions and build a new one from scratch. We spent six months doing that.”View image in fullscreenLess AI … EA Sports FC 27.Illustration: Jamie Wrench/Electronic ArtsVia a build that let me play Champions League games between a limited number of teams, I found that to be a worthwhile exercise: those defensive bounce-backs were blissfully absent. But an awful lot more was also in evidence in FC 27 on the gameplay revamp front.Much of this – perhaps counterintuitively at a time when AI is worming its way ever deeper into all our lives – involved paring back the in-game AI. That’s certainly the case for the defensive AI: whereas previously, defenders would rush towards the ball, getting pulled out of position and opening up annoying gaps, FC 27 now gives much more manual control over defensive jockeying, movement and tackles.Crossing, previously AI-assisted, has been revamped in FC 27, leaving it up to me to get the direction and weight of cross right, then giving me more of a chance to position my centre-forward correctly. The AI controlling forward players, meanwhile, has been improved, so that off-the-ball players now move much more helpfully, allowing pass-and-move sequences, and they are much better at staying onside.I was also impressed by revamped two-stage corner and free-kick systems. But FC 27, gameplay-wise, achieves what FC 26 set out to, this time with no evident anomalies, and feels more responsive to your inputs than any of its predecessors.Making transfers more true-to-lifeFC 27’s Career Mode, in which you get to play out your fantasies of managing your favourite team, has also been extensively revamped – primarily with a view towards making its transfer system more like the one that operates in the real world, and to force you to do more actual management.The headline means of doing the latter is called Dynamic OVR. OVR is simply jargon for any player’s all-important overall rating; where previously OVRs remained constant, in FC 27’s Career Mode they will go up and down depending on form, fitness and general happiness. Thus, you will have to rest your best players over the course of a long season, but you may also be able to buy players cheaply with artificially low OVRs if, say, they are coming back from injury.View image in fullscreen‘It was about extracting the fun bits of the jobs’ … EA Sports FC 27.Illustration: Electronic ArtsPete O’Donnell, FC 27’s Career Mode game director, explains how the game’s transfer system has been modernised: “Previously, you could do things instantly, which was good for a game but was not very realistic. We looked at how clubs interact with each other, how they do the deals themselves, and we spoke to scouts and directors of football. Then it was about extracting the fun bits of those jobs.”The new system will back you up with more data; now each player will have an xTV (Expected Transfer Value) rating, which should speed negotiations. FC 27 will also reflect clubs’ real-life transfer policies, according to O’Donnell, with clubs’ boards requesting that you sign certain players. Press conferences in FC 27 will force you to make decisions that will please some players and annoy others, and 20 Unexpected Events have been added to Career Mode.Ultimate Transfer: a new showcaseFC 27’s Ultimate Transfer (FUT) mode, the hardcore card-based system that provides a home for most of FC’s loot box action, will have a new headline feature in the form of a Gallery, which will showcase all the players and card-sets collected, rather than just first 11s.View image in fullscreenA new headline feature … EA Sports FC 27’s FUT Gallery.Illustration: Electronic ArtsEA Sports says it has also “streamlined” FUT’s previously impenetrable Squad-Based Challenges (SBC) system, and has made a tweak designed to avert stalemates, which affected the latter stages in FUT in FC 26, by restricting plus-level FUT players to three, rather than five, play-styles. But the nature of FUT – which develops over a long period post-launch – means that it will take a while to ascertain whether those changes prove effective.Now rated 16There will be another major change to FC 27 that has nothing to do with how it plays: because it contains microtransactions, it will now be rated 16+ rather than the previous 3+, after a policy change at age-rating organisation Pegi. Given the game’s enthusiastic young and teenage audience, we asked EA Sports’ top brass to comment, but they blandly responded: “While the game functionally remains the same, this has resulted in a new Pegi age rating. It marks a change in the way we are giving the information to players and parents.”Beyond Pegi’s European jurisdiction, the game will be rated E for Everybody. But in the UK, parents should think hard about letting youngsters play a 16-rated game. If they are worried about their offspring racking up huge bills for FUT transactions, the good news is that a new Ultimate Plus Edition of the game, which includes loads of stuff that would previously have cost in-game currency, will go on sale. But the bad news is it costs £139.99 and will only be available as a pre-order before 31 August.EA Sports FC 27 is out on 25 September on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, and PC. It will also launch on PS4, Xbox One, and Switch, but without some features, such as the new Grounds mode.Explore more on these topicsGamesPlayStation 5Xbox series S/XNintendo Switch 2featuresShareReuse this content

title: Pony Island 2 Panda Circus: gallop out of hell in this phantasmagorical follow-up to 2016’s indie hit | Games | The Guardian
description: Daniel Mullins explains how he plans to follow up his quirky classic without losing what made it stand out in the first place
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Daniel Mullins explains how he plans to follow up his quirky classic without losing what made it stand out in the first place
Content: Bamboozling … Pony Island 2: Panda Circus.Illustration: Daniel Mullins GamesView image in fullscreenBamboozling … Pony Island 2: Panda Circus.Illustration: Daniel Mullins GamesSummer games previewsGamesPony Island 2 Panda Circus: gallop out of hell in this phantasmagorical follow-up to 2016’s indie hitDaniel Mullins explains how he plans to follow up his quirky classic without losing what made it stand out in the first placeIgnas VieversysFri 7 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGlitchy aesthetics. Literally collapsing menu boxes. The game taunting you by “possessing” your Steam friends. Technical tricks of this nature may sound gimmicky in 2026, but they felt excitingly unorthodox a decade ago, when Pony Island came out to critical acclaim.Fans of Daniel Mullins, the celebrated indie developer of Inscryption, will be forgiven for forgetting that Pony Island 2: Panda Circus is in active development. After all, it’s been almost three years since the announcement – and a full decade since it was first teased as an Easter egg in Pony Island’s ARG (Alternate Reality Game) – with only a single trailer and a bunch of tunes from the soundtrack released to the public.View image in fullscreenItching to glitch … Pony Island 2: Panda Circus.Illustration: Daniel Mullins GamesWhile the announcement trailer teases the return of endless-runner sequences and glitchy menus, Panda Circus is seemingly a far bigger and more complicated project than its predecessor; hence the 3D landscapes, pixel art JRPG sequences and even apparent nods to games such asThe Case of the Golden Idol. Which is why Mullins claims that, at least in terms of gameplay variety, Panda Circus is closer to The Hex and Inscryption than the original game.“[Pony Island 2] is multifaceted in its gameplay and wide-ranging in its influences. But this time the disparate game systems are united by more common elements,” he says, referencing the drag-and-drop “hacking” puzzle. “That simple premise was extended into an endless amount of blocks and holes of various descriptions.”The plot sees a historical warrior who was slain on his crusade and was damned to hell, where he’s tormented by a video games-making Lucifer. This comically morbid tale “is the strongest link to its predecessor” from a narrative standpoint – although, we’re told, this warrior won’t be Theodore (Pony Island’s protagonist), but a different ancient crusader.In the gameplay that we do get to glimpse in the trailer, the player and his furry companion are traversing through the top-down map, visiting villages and places of interest. It plays like “Oregon Trail through medieval China”, Mullins says after I mention noticing hunger and thirst bars. All this is happening while you’re being tormented by lordly King Yan, the Chinese god of death, played by voice actor SungWon Cho in lavish full-motion interludes.View image in fullscreenBack in the ring … Pony Island 2: Panda Circus.Illustration: Daniel Mullins GamesOther sections promise different mythological themes and menacing deities – an overarching structure that will be familiar to those who played Inscryption. Then there is the Earth Prison, a three-dimensional hub that our hell-bound protagonist can explore, accessing different chapters by using what seems to be a mythical USB stick.If the devil is truly in the details, Mullins gives him plenty of places to hide: Panda Circus seems to be brimming with them. “There is an almost unmanageable number of bespoke, one-off game systems,” he says. “It’s too big to fit in my mind now and that is a new challenge.”The indie dev admits he would have “been troubled” if he knew just how long it would take to make Panda Circus – even with a handpicked team of collaborators. “I’m very lucky because it was a total chance that we started working together,” Mullins says about composer Jonah Senzel, whom he has worked with ever since the original Pony Island. “He turned out to be a genius.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile Mullins shies away from showing any new piece of gameplay, Panda Circus, now in its “final stretch” phase of development, is undergoing private beta. As for the release date: “it may become public knowledge soon,” he hints coyly.Bombastic boss battles, an ARG that will see fans dissecting previous games with archaeological zeal (“I bet they’ll crack it in a couple weeks,” Mullins quips), and meta moments that wink at you cheekily are all to be expected from the developer’s most ambitious project to date.“All the time has gone into making a big game that’s just downright turgid with secrets. There are worlds within worlds and layers upon layers.” Another classic Mullins joint, then, and we couldn’t be more ready.Pony Island 2: Panda Circus is in development forPCwith plans for Linux/Mac “not long after”.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: In the Black review – rewarding drama about the Faustian pact of big business | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Quaz Degraft draws on his knowledge of high finance for these misadventures in a material, misogynist world
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Quaz Degraft draws on his knowledge of high finance for these misadventures in a material, misogynist world
Content: Sweetly told … Quaz Degraft in his play In the Black.Photograph: Matt Dale/Fern PhotographyView image in fullscreenSweetly told … Quaz Degraft in his play In the Black.Photograph: Matt Dale/Fern PhotographyEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewIn the Black review – rewarding drama about the Faustian pact of big businessUnderbelly, Bristo Square, EdinburghQuaz Degraft draws on his knowledge of high finance for these misadventures in a material, misogynist worldMark FisherFri 7 Aug 2026 12.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou don’t hear much about the American dream these days, but for Kofi Grady, a first generation Ghanaian American, the opportunity for betterment in the land of the free is real. Brought up by a disciplinarian father whose definition of success is not just money but job security, he is a young graduate who puts his mathematical skills to work in a trillion-dollar financial company.Driving him is the sense of comfort and control he experienced as a teenage joyrider in a high-performance car. What he never had he craves the most.Actor and writer Quaz Degraft knows the world he describes. Like Kofi, he worked in high finance, but rather than end up in an orange jumpsuit helping fellow prisoners with their sums, as his character does, he jumped ship and reinvented himself as a performer. His solo show – back on the Edinburgh fringe after a well-received run last year – paints an insider picture of a corporate culture in which profit and personal success override all other considerations.Target Audience review – zingy satire puts media types in an apocalyptic pickleRead moreIn a sweetly told piece of storytelling, featuring a rollcall of colleagues, friends and double dates, Degraft describes the implicit Faustian pact of big business: put in the hours, say the right things, keep quiet about the abuses and wait for the bonuses to roll in.Above all, this is a #MeToo play told from the male perspective. Kofi is not directly connected to the assault of a female worker but is complicit in its cover-up, much as anyone would be who chooses silence over confrontation, private gain over honourable whistleblowing.That Degraft makes it seem like an everyday tale of a young man innocently trying to settle into a new job belies his deeper purpose: to reveal the insidious nature of male power. The insight is not new but, in Abigail Onwunali’s stripped-down production, it is subtly done.AtUnderbelly, Bristo Square, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Oberon review – part panto, part grand opera, Weber’s final work has charm but doesn’t quite convince | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: There’s a new narration delivered by Tamsin Greig and the crack forces of the Monteverdi Choir, the ORR and world-class singers, all led by Mark Elder, but the 200-year-old piece remains a strange hybrid
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: There’s a new narration delivered by Tamsin Greig and the crack forces of the Monteverdi Choir, the ORR and world-class singers, all led by Mark Elder, but the 200-year-old piece remains a strange hybrid
Content: Indefatigable … John Findon and the Monteverdi Choir in the semi-staging of Weber’s Oberon at the Proms.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenIndefatigable … John Findon and the Monteverdi Choir in the semi-staging of Weber’s Oberon at the Proms.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouProms 2026ReviewOberon review – part panto, part grand opera, Weber’s final work has charm but doesn’t quite convinceRoyal Albert Hall, LondonThere’s  a new narration delivered by Tamsin Greig and the crack forces of the Monteverdi Choir, the ORR and world-class singers, all led by Mark Elder, but the 200-year-old piece remains a strange hybridAlexandra CoghlanFri 7 Aug 2026 08.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 08.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePirates! Princesses! Mermaids! Fairies! A magic horn! You name it and Carl Maria von Weber chucked it at Oberon – his fantastical, nonsensical, often farcical romp of a final opera, which sees a French knight and his Arabian beloved subjected to magical trials and hardships so that fairy king Oberon can win an argument with queen Titania.You can see how it happened. The opera’s English libretto (the work was premiered at Covent Garden in 1826) is based on a German poem, itself adapting a French chivalric romance, is a patchwork whose lumpen dialogue (and, latterly, unpalatable attitudes) have rendered it all but unstageable in living memory. Enter Mark Elder, the Orchestre Revolutionnaire et Romantique and Monteverdi Choir to giveOberon a Proms premiere 200 yearsin the making.Tackling the problem head-on, this semi-staging binned the dialogue, replacing it with author Timothy Knapman’s new narration, which wrestles an impossible plot (a “franchise spin-off” from A Midsummer Night’s Dream, as he puts it) into arch rhyming couplets and knowing pop-culture references. It’s often funny, but there’s an awful lot of it, even when delivered by the ever-watchable Tamsin Greig.View image in fullscreenEver watchable… Tamsin Grieg narrates Timothy Knapman’s new text to Weber’s Oberon at the Proms.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouThis is a passion project for Elder. You could hear it in the crisp attack and deliberate shading he demanded of the orchestra – by turns Mozartian or Mendelssohnian in their silver-footed fairy-music, Wagner-broad in brass sallies and pageantry. It’s unfashionable to suggest it, but in a venue of this size (and fluctuating temperature), with anachronism already in the drama, might a contemporary symphony orchestra have given us greater punch and brilliance than a period band? For all the score’s charm and vivacity it’s also dangerously close to Gilbert and Sullivan at times, even before tuning sours in the heat. No wandering minstrels in the Monteverdi Choir however, who dispatched their choruses with subtlety and style, all while acting up a storm under Emma Doherty’s light-touch direction.John Findon’s indefatigable Sir Huon was a musical chameleon in a role that demands a Mozart tenor, a Bellini tenor and occasionally even a Wagner tenor, with soprano Jennifer Davis, a luxurious, expansive Reiza. Listen out for young American mezzo Rachael Wilson, a knockout as maid Fatima, all gilded legato and smooth-polished tone, handsomely matched by Yannick Debus’s Sherasmin. Presiding over all was Nicky Spence, hamming it up deliciously (in a foretaste of the Last Night of the Proms) as Oberon.Weber died just months after Oberon’s premiere – from tuberculosis, rather than complications from the libretto. It’s a peculiar epitaph: part panto, partgrandopera. Will Oberon’s Proms premiere also be its final festival outing? Even with the help of a whole section of magic horns, it’s hard to imagine otherwise.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026OperaClassical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Target Audience review – zingy satire puts media types in an apocalyptic pickle | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: With characteristic wit, Dan Bishop’s comedy develops from a jolly send-up of the vacuous TV industry into a politically astute play about power
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: With characteristic wit, Dan Bishop’s comedy develops from a jolly send-up of the vacuous TV industry into a politically astute play about power
Content: An industry beholden to charismatic bullshitters … from left: James Coward, Molly Windust, Henry Calcutt and RhéAna Kamalu in Target Audience.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn industry beholden to charismatic bullshitters … from left: James Coward, Molly Windust, Henry Calcutt and RhéAna Kamalu in Target Audience.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewTarget Audience review – zingy satire puts media types in an apocalyptic picklePleasance Courtyard, EdinburghWith characteristic wit, Dan Bishop’s comedy develops from a jolly send-up of the vacuous TV industry into a politically astute play about powerMark FisherFri 7 Aug 2026 06.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 15.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘I’ve never read anything Greek, but I bet if feels exactly like this,” says Isabelle (RhéAna Kamalu) at the apocalyptic height of this zingy comedy. She is a gen Z intern whose end-of-times neuroses have suddenly become justified after she receives a government alert to stay indoors. Maybe she did not want to die young, after all.The line has the characteristic wit of playwright Dan Bishop, author of last year’sBrainsluts, but the scene itself is unexpected. Wind back to the start of Target Audience and you will find something much more ephemeral.It begins as a jolly send-up of a vacuous screen industry, one beholden to charismatic bullshitters such as Angie – short for Angus (James Coward) – and the tyranny of audience data. We could be watching the BBC satireW1Aor David Mamet’s Speed-the-Plow as a production company brings in Tobias (Henry Calcutt), a politically sensitive writer, to see if he can add an edge to their scripts in development.Edinburgh festival 2026: 10 terrific shows we’ve already reviewedRead moreOne of these is called Citizen 54, the other Thorns. If it were not for the poster for Horizon (tagline: “The future is round”), you could believe they had never made a film, preferring endless days of platitudes and statistics. With his sidekick Bruiser (Molly Windust, also starring inRockpoolsat the fringe), Angie flatters Tobias as quickly as he undermines him. He is not an artist but a cog in the wheel.If the material is familiar, the actors make it seem fresh in Bishop’s entertaining production. If he got rid of the scene changes, it would be more pacy still. But the playwright is playing the long game and what emerges from the airhead character comedy is a satire about moral compromises that affect not just the telly we watch but the late-capitalist power structures we inhabit. Funny, yes, but also politically astute.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Silence of the Lambs review – Hannibal Lecter’s daring stage outing is a shock to the system | Theatre | The Guardian
description: There are electrifying – and also queasy – moments in this version of the classic 90s horror about the interrogation of a psychotic psychiatrist by an FBI rookie
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: There are electrifying – and also queasy – moments in this version of the classic 90s horror about the interrogation of a psychotic psychiatrist by an FBI rookie
Content: Avoiding the hissy lip-sipping … John Partridge as Hannibal Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenAvoiding the hissy lip-sipping … John Partridge as Hannibal Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs.Photograph: Marc BrennerTheatreReviewThe Silence of the Lambs review – Hannibal Lecter’s daring stage outing is a shock to the systemCurve, LeicesterThere are electrifying – and also queasy – moments in this version of the classic 90s horror about the interrogation of a psychotic psychiatrist by an FBI rookieMark LawsonFri 7 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSoon after the hostile reception of thetheatrical version of Trainspotting, another landmark 1990s movie, The Silence of the Lambs, attempts a similar manoeuvre. In this case, director Nikolai Foster is surely sensible not to turn this source material into a musical. And adapter Gina Gionfriddo is working not from Jonathan Demme’s film but Thomas Harris’s 1988 novel about the dangerous interrogation of psychotic psychiatrist Dr Hannibal Lecter by FBI rookie Clarice Starling for his insight into serial killer Buffalo Bill.The biggest risk of theatricalised movies is that the acting becomes a form of karaoke. Mollie Gallagher, making a confident stage debut in effectively the lead role, echoes Jodie Foster’s Virginia accent and ramps up the pugnacious posture and walk. John Partridge’s Lecter, who is more sonically American than Hopkins’ variation on his Welsh register (the character is actually Lithuanian), avoids the hissy lip-sipping and also injects less charm and culture.Another jeopardy of staged films is that much of a cinema director’s job is moving the camera in, out and around while the frame of a stage is essentially a default wide shot. Nikolai Foster, however, impressively varies the perspective. He creates a sort of split-screen by bracketing the main scene with a silent tableaux of other characters.View image in fullscreenOliver Farnworth (Jack Crawford), Mollie Gallagher (Clarice Starling), Andrew Joshi (Lamar) and Sam Jackson (Buffalo Bill) in The Silence of the Lambs.Photograph: Marc BrennerIn the Lecter-Starling scenes, Howard Hudson’s lighting subtly directs our gaze, encouraging a sort of tight focus. Careful placing of characters also allows a clever approximation of a two character shot.Another moment interrogates the relationship between audiences and the horror stories. The genre-standard autopsy scene feels rawly appalling when played downstage without the protection of a multiplex screen or the camera cutting away from views. The brief touch between the two main characters also electrifies live.But, for all Foster’s imaginative presentation of the action, the content can feel queasy. The Buffalo Bill strand, sometimes more a main than subplot, means that much of the evening consists of watching women stalked and tortured.Gionfriddo is a front-rank dramatist – twice a Pulitzer prize finalist, including for Becky Shaw, a London success – and intelligently addresses this problem. Stressing the pervasive sexism of the 1983 setting, she also, reflecting changes in attitudes across the four decades since novel and film, gives the female victims – neatly differentiated by Lottie Amor – more plot-time and agency. A shocking new line (spoken twice) reflects the devastating calculations a victim may make with the aim of survival.Most daringly, while all versions of the Lecter-Starling narrative have seen it as a sort of love story, the stage version maximises the romantic context, albeit on a scale from warped to desperate. Buffalo Bill targets single women on the dating scene. The status of FBI boss Jack Crawford (Oliver Farnworth) as a recent widower is emphasised and haunts his mentorship of Starling.A risk of such crossovers is that they will encourage streamer searches for the film instead, but it’s a show worth seeing.AtCurve, Leicester, until 15 August. title: Sam Neill filmed role in Legend of Zelda film adaptation before his death  | Movies | The Guardian
description: The New Zealand actor, who died last month aged 78, will appear in live-action movie of popular video game, which is set for release next year
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: The New Zealand actor, who died last month aged 78, will appear in live-action movie of popular video game, which is set for release next year
Content: The King of Hyrule? Sam Neill pictured in 2016.Photograph: Variety/Penske Media/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe King of Hyrule? Sam Neill pictured in 2016.Photograph: Variety/Penske Media/Getty ImagesMoviesSam Neill filmed role in Legend of Zelda film adaptation before his deathThe New Zealand actor, who died last month aged 78, will appear in live-action movie of popular video game, which is set for release next yearLaurence PhelanFri 7 Aug 2026 09.57 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe New Zealand actor Sam Neill completed filming of a role in the forthcoming adaptation ofThe Legend of Zeldavideo game before he died, which will be one of his final screen appearances.According toa report in Deadline, Neill, whodied of pneumonia last month aged 78, will appear in the live-action movie, which finished filming in April this year and is set for release next May. Which role Neill plays has not been announced, but fans of the games have suggested that he would be a good casting choice for the King of Hyrule, the fictional fantasy realm in which the Zelda games are primarily set.Neill had also filmed parts in Godzilla x Kong: Supernova, which is scheduled for release in next March, and The Last Resort, a romcom in which he plays the father of the female lead, Daisy Ridley, also scheduled for release next year.Sam Neill obituaryRead moreSince the original Legend of Zelda game was published by Nintendo in 1986,more than 20 titlesin the main series have been released, along with various spin-offs and remakes. An estimated 170-190m copies have been sold, making it Nintendo’s most popular franchise after the Super Mario Brothers and Pokémon series. There have already been manga adaptations and an animated TV show based on Zelda, but the forthcoming production will be the first film adaptation.Two English actors, Benjamin Evan Ainsworth and Bo Bragason, play the lead roles of Link and Princess Zelda. The film is directed by Wes Ball, who is also responsible for the YA Maze Runner trilogy and, most recently, Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes.Neill had an extensive and varied career in film and television spanning five decades, but was especially loved for his work in horror and fantasy cinema, including Possession, Omen III, In the Mouth of Madness and three Jurassic Park films.Explore more on these topicsFilmSam NeillScience fiction and fantasy filmsThe Legend of ZeldaNintendoGamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘These cooks ripped each other apart’: Dominic Sessa on playing Anthony Bourdain, kitchen bullies and the joys of being a 70s barfly | Movies | The Guardian
description: After his breakthrough in The Holdovers in 2023, Sessa has gone back to the 70s again for Tony, the biopic of bad-boy chef and Kitchen Confidential author Bourdain. And, he says, a big part of him would like to stay there
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: After his breakthrough in The Holdovers in 2023, Sessa has gone back to the 70s again for Tony, the biopic of bad-boy chef and Kitchen Confidential author Bourdain. And, he says, a big part of him would like to stay there
Content: ‘Sometimes when you’re young, it’s to your detriment that you don’t allow yourself to fail in a productive way’ … Sessa.Photograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Sometimes when you’re young, it’s to your detriment that you don’t allow yourself to fail in a productive way’ … Sessa.Photograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianMoviesInterview‘These cooks ripped each other apart’: Dominic Sessa on playing Anthony Bourdain, kitchen bullies and the joys of being a 70s barflyRyan GilbeyAfter his breakthrough in The Holdovers in 2023, Sessa has gone back to the 70s again for Tony, the biopic of bad-boy chef and Kitchen Confidential author Bourdain. And, he says, a big part of him would like to stay thereFri 7 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDespite being just 23, Dominic Sessa is perhaps as intimately acquainted with the 1970s as those who grew up then. Although the New Jersey-born actor has only starred in five films, two of them are marinated in the fashions, sounds and mores of the decade. In his new movie,Tony, he plays the 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain, future bad-boy celebrity chef, bestselling author of Kitchen Confidential and host of its hit TV spin-off. Tony restricts itself to one summer in 1975, when Bourdain bummed around the coastal resort of Provincetown, Massachusetts, falling in love, scrubbing pans in a seafood joint and catching the cooking bug. “For a rootless young man with sensualist inclinations,” he wrote, “it was the perfect getaway.”A 70s retro vibe also hung over Sessa’s debut film. In Alexander Payne’s Oscar-winning 2023 comedy-dramaThe Holdovers, he played Angus Tully, a surly student forced to board at school over Christmas with only his classics teacher and the cook for company. That picture wasn’t merely set in 1970; it seemed, with its faded palette and fake crackles on the print, to have beenmadethen.The most convincing period touch in each film, however, is Sessa himself. He has been described as having a “1970s face”, a euphemism for “unconventional”. His crown of dark, jumbled curls looks as if it was scribbled in crayon by a hyperactive child, while his wide, narrowed eyes are set high and far apart in his upside down triangular face. He projects inner conflict: when Tony and Angus behave arrogantly and disagreeably, even aggressively, Sessa’s features suggest a wounded quality that hints at future self-disgust for any misdeeds.Sessa was barely aware of Bourdain before making Tony. “I knew of him but he didn’t have any significant meaning for me,” he shrugs, speaking over video call from a Manhattan hotel room. A gangly six-footer, Sessa is all elbows, collar-bones and sharp edges as he stares down the webcam in a brown-and-white checked shirt. “I think the only way to do the film honestly and without hesitation was to not have a strong opinion about him.”Now that he has been immersed in Bourdain’s history, he has clearer ideas about the pioneering chef’s appeal. “I think he made people feel an overwhelming sense of potential in themselves,” he says. “He inspired this movement where there’s hundreds, probably thousands, of YouTube channels by people who dedicate their lives to showcasing what’s being eaten in different parts of the world. He was a rebellious person, someone who acted with integrity.”Tony’s director Matt Johnson, who brought such vitality to the tech origin storyBlackberryand the recent time-travel comedyNirvanna the Band the Show the Movie, pointed Sessa towards two chapters fromKitchen Confidential, the memoir written in gunslinger prose and billed as a story of “sex, drugs, bad behaviour and haute cuisine”. There, the actor found the characters who inspired the film’s triumvirate of Provincetown kitchen mentors, the men Bourdain likens to “gods” and “pirates”: the wise head chef (Antonio Banderas), the coke-snorting Jack-the-lad (Leo Woodall) and the taunting, vulgar mischief-maker (Stavros Halkias).View image in fullscreenSessa as Anthony Bourdain in Tony.Photograph: Seacia Pavao“The restaurant we were filming in had only closed a couple of days earlier, so we were in a fully operating kitchen,” he explains. “Stavros learned how to make lobster rolls, Leo learned to shuck oysters. Matt was, like: ‘Dom, you go in and wash the dishes, and Stavros and Leo are gonna make fun of you.’ They made it all real for me. I felt genuinely intimidated by them. They’re so nice but I think they enjoyed the chance to bully me.”Dramatising Bourdain’s youthful exploits put Sessa in mind of his own misspent summers growing up on the Jersey Shore. He was raised in Ocean City, which was tranquil throughout the year then bustling with tourists during the holidays. His mother is a teacher; his father, who he has described as “a payroll guy”, died when Sessa was 14. He tells me he got his “opinionated” side from his mum, his sense of humour from his dad. “Jackass was one of the first movies he showed me,” he says fondly.After his father’s death, Sessa won a sports scholarship to attend Deerfield Academy, a boarding school in Massachusetts. “The only time I’d be home was in the summer breaks when it would basically be like a party. I worked in a bakery where I had early starts, and I’d be getting drunk on the beach before going to work; I was a mess. At that age, you felt you were invincible, you couldn’t get in trouble. We felt like we owned the place. We’d throw beach parties, then cops would chase us off the beach. You’d go to whoever’s house and their parents were gone so you’d destroy the place. We were menaces. Reading about the way Tony described his time in Provincetown, I was like: ‘Yeah, I get that. I understand.’”Partying wasn’t the only element in the film that chimed with him. “Playing Tony, I felt as if I was playing an unlikable side of myself,” he says, his tone no longer flippant. “He’s insecure and defensive at the start of the movie. I think a lot of young men have a very defensive way. You want people to respect you and treat you like an adult. But you feel as if you’re pretending. Deep down, there’s something underdeveloped that is hard for us to admit to. We’re always trying to hide that. I’m constantly going through that in my life.”View image in fullscreen‘I want to escape the modern era’ … Sessa.Photograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianHe sits back in his seat as if surveying the scene before him. “Like, doing this interview, I’m pretending to be an adult, you know? Sometimes when you’re young, it’s to your detriment that you don’t allow yourself to fail in a productive way because you’re constantly trying to protect your ego.”What would his remedy be for young men like him? “Wilful hardships,” he says. “Deciding to go through hard things. Comfort is attractive. And we’ve built a culture around the comforts of the world. Where you really develop and learn the most about yourself is in doing something genuinely difficult. That’s what Tony does in this film.”The picture opens with a quote from Kitchen Confidential in which Bourdain describes his younger self as being “badly in need of a good ass-kicking”. Sessa sings from the same hymn sheet. “These cooks verbally abused each other, ripped each other apart. It’s an initiation process in a way, a rite of passage. There’s love on the other side of it.”If the actor’s view of kitchen life is impossibly romantic, very far from the widespread toxic culture that only this year led to the resignation from Noma of René Redzepiafter accusations of workplace abuse, then that is fully in keeping with the tone of Tony. This is a movie so reluctant to spoil the audience’s buzz that it doesn’t even reveal in the end titles that Bourdain is dead, let alone that hetook his own lifein 2018.Any toughness or complexity in the film comes from Sessa, whose performance ratifies his standing as both a 21st-century star-to-be and a 1970s pin-upmanqué. How does he explain the period fixation? “Maybe it says something about me. Like I want to escape the modern era.” Does he? “Yeah, I think so. I love being in the bars, the smell of cigarettes. It’s like stepping into a time machine.” No mobile phones, no social media. “Everybody’s looking up, talking to one another.”Eye contact isn’t the only behavioural difference he has noticed. “The impression I get is that young people back then were more confident in speaking, and perhaps more mature in interactions with adults. Nowadays it takes longer. I have friends in college who still can’t handle a social environment because of the way we’ve grown up. Especially after Covid. My generation gotscrewed.”Sessa was at Deerfield when the pandemic struck. “They designed a way to keep us on campus and in a bubble. The kids who got sick were sent to the old abandoned health centre.” His low rumble of a voice is interrupted by his sudden, honking laugh, as if acknowledging that this all sounds suspiciously like an episode of Scooby-Doo.View image in fullscreenCabin fever … Sessa with Da’Vine Joy Randolph in The Holdovers.Photograph: Seacia PavaoThat cabin-fever scenario was almost a rehearsal for playing Angus. “This was right before The Holdovers, so I guess I got used to feeling trapped,” he says. In 2022, the film-makers were visiting local schools to scout potential locations, no more expecting to find their Angus than Sessa was anticipating being cast as one of the leads in a Hollywood movie.As a financial aid student, he had felt out of place initially at Deerfield, where he had gone to pursue his dream of becoming a hockey player. When a broken femur in his freshman year put him out of action before the season had even started, theatre became his backup option.“I wasn’t being myself when I first got to school,” he says. “I was acting in a way that wasn’t genuine to who I was. I saw these kids, the way they dressed and carried themselves, and I didn’t feel I belonged in that environment so I had to role-play how these people were. I didn’t think they would accept me otherwise. But once I started doing theatre, I made so many more friends. People wanted to get to know me because I was putting myself out there.”Tony review – knives out in tasty reheat of Anthony Bourdain’s memoirRead moreHockey lost its appeal. “I saw it ending and it not being a part of my life much longer. I was never gonna be the best player in school. I would probably be one of the worst.” There is no need to remark on his chances of being one of the best actors instead. The acclaim he received for The Holdovers – 21 nominations from awards bodies and critics’ circles in the US and UK, including eight wins and a Bafta nod – tells its own story.In between The Holdovers and Tony, he turned down lead roles and studied drama for a year and a half at Carnegie Mellon University, taking supporting parts to keep his hand in. He played Michelle Pfeiffer’s sullen son, recently dumped and strumming an emo version of The 12 Days of Christmas, in the comedy Oh. What. Fun. In Tow, he was a non-profit lawyer whose client (Rose Byrne) tells him: “My car is older than you.” Multiplex-goers saw him as an upstart magician with Robin Hood ethics, stealing from crypto bros and diamond magnates, in the threequel Now You See Me: Now You Don’t.It is Tony, though, that he credits for the second turning point in his brief career. If The Holdovers set him on his current path, Tony has helped him decide on the kind of actor – and person – he wants to be. Since making the film, he has been heeding the advice of Bourdain, who wrote: “Good food and good eating are all about risk.”“I’ve been open to eating in a lot more B- and C-health-rated places,” Sessa says. But it’s not only about what’s on his plate. “In life generally, I feel more motivated now to follow my gut and take risks and live in the moment.” He mentions Shades of Paradise, a “crazy Euro-crime film” that he recently made in Barcelona, as an example: it gives him his first bona fide baddie to play after a string of messed-up but essentially decent guys. “I thought: ‘This is something really fun that I want to do.’” That’s his motto for today. “I’m doing what feels right.”Tony is in cinemas from 14 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmBiopicsAnthony BourdainfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sir Christopher Ondaatje obituary | Philanthropy | The Guardian
description: Businessman and philanthropist who helped fund a new wing for the National Portrait Gallery
Author: Charles Saumarez Smith
Headline: Businessman and philanthropist who helped fund a new wing for the National Portrait Gallery
Content: Christopher Ondaatje at Glenthorne, his house in Devon, 1998.Photograph: Marc Hill/AlamyView image in fullscreenChristopher Ondaatje at Glenthorne, his house in Devon, 1998.Photograph: Marc Hill/AlamyPhilanthropyObituarySir Christopher Ondaatje obituaryBusinessman and philanthropist who helped fund a new wing for the National Portrait GalleryCharles Saumarez SmithFri 7 Aug 2026 05.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 05.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy 1988, the businessman Christopher Ondaatje had made a great deal of money as a publisher and stockbroker on the Canadian stock exchange. As he later described it to Sue Lawley onRadio 4’s Desert Island Discsin 2002, while on holiday in Tanzania he decided to give up his business interests and devote himself to “having fun” – travelling, writing, spending time with his family, and giving large chunks of his wealth away.He had already invested in a home for himself, Glenthorne, a rambling 19th-century house in a remote place next to the sea north of Exmoor, allowing him to turn his attention to British institutions, including the National Portrait Gallery, the Royal Geographical Society, the Royal Society of Literature and the Labour party. He approached philanthropy in the same way as his business transactions, doing research on how the money could transform institutions.I first met Ondaatje in September 1996, when I was director of the National Portrait Gallery. We were in the early stage of raising money for a new wing, actually a back-of-house extension, designed byJeremy Dixon and Edward Jones. We had been promised funds by what was then the Heritage Lottery Fund on condition that we raised £4m. I intuited, as it turned out correctly, that this was a project which Ondaatje might be willing to help fund.He did so with extraordinary generosity, providing the great bulk of the matching funding required for a building project that opened in May 2000 as theOndaatje Wing. Although the project is now nearly invisible underits recent make-over, it transformed the way the public used the gallery and its visitor numbers. At a time when public institutions were being required to seek private support, Ondaatje demonstrated how venture philanthropy could be used to good effect.Ondaatje had been born in Kandy in what was then Ceylon (now Sri Lanka) to a prosperous tea-planting family of part-Dutch, part-Sinhalese descent, one of the four children of Mervyn Ondaatje and Doris (nee Gratiaen). But, as his younger brother, the writerMichael Ondaatje, terrifyingly describes in his 1982 memoir Running in the Family, their father took to the bottle and his parents divorced after Christopher had been sent away to boarding school in the UK. It was a humiliation that gave him his drive and determination, and the ambiguity of his relationship to the British.View image in fullscreenThe entrance to the Ondaatje wing at the National Portrait Gallery, London, 2015.Photograph: Graham Turner/The GuardianEducated at Blundell’s school in Devon, Ondaatje excelled at sport, but had to leave a year early when the money for his education ran out. In 1951, his mother moved to England, to Notting Hill Gate, in London, where she ran a boarding house. Christopher went to work for National and Grindlays Bank in the City, but realised that the prospects for someone part-Sinhalese were not good, so, in 1955, aged 22, with 13 Canadian dollars in his pocket, he emigrated to Canada.In Toronto he joined a brokerage firm, Burns Bros & Denton, for a year before moving first, into selling advertising and copyrighting for magazines in Montreal and then into financial journalism back in Toronto. In 1959 he married Valda Bulins, a Latvian-born, tennis-playing science graduate.Ondaatje discovered he had a great gift for making money, became a founding partner in 1970 of the stockbrokers Loewen Ondaatje McCutcheon, established a publishing firm, Pagurian Press, in 1967 and used it as a vehicle for wider-ranging investments. His wealth made it possible to buy Meisner’s Island off the coast of Nova Scotia and persuade his brother Michael to study at Toronto University.In 1983, Ondaatje was visiting Blundell’s when he discovered that Glenthorne, which he had visited as a schoolboy, was for sale. He bought it, renovated it, and filled it with his library and collection of Victorian furniture, portraits and Sinhalese antiquities. He began to spend an increasing amount of time in England, for which he had a strongly romantic, partly nostalgic and imperial fondness, in spite of the fact that he sometimes felt cold-shouldered by the British establishment.Meanwhile, Ondaatje was establishing himself as a writer. It was always assumed that this was in competition with his younger brother, Michael, who was so colossally successful – best known for his Booker prize-winning novel The English Patient – but I never saw evidence of this. It was more a way of pursuing his interests in travel and exploration.His first book, co-written with Gordon Currie, was Olympic Victory: The Story Behind the Canadian Bob-Sled Club’s Incredible Victory at the 1964 Winter Olympic Games (1967), describing his involvement as a member of the second bobsleigh team. This was followed the same year by The Prime Ministers of Canada, 1867-1967.In 1992, he published The Man-Eater of Punanai: A Journey of Discovery to the Jungles of Old Ceylon. Sindh Revisited: A Journey in the Footsteps of Captain Sir Richard Burton appeared in 1996, and a second book following the routes of the Victorian explorer, Journey to the Source of the Nile, was published in 1998; he was passionately interested in the life of Burton.These led him to support the Royal Geographical Society, where he funded its handsome new lecture theatre and helped the digitisation of its collections. He also supportedan annual prize for the Royal Society of Literature“for a distinguished work of fiction, nonfiction or poetry, evoking the spirit of a place”, and was, for a time, joint owner of theLiterary Review.It was perhaps more surprising, since his politics were not obviously of the left, that he became a donor to Tony Blair’s Labour party, but he regarded Blair as nearly as rightwing asMargaret Thatcher. He got on well withTessa Jowelland enjoyed playing tennis with the Labour peer and party fundraiser Michael Levy. He was made CBE in 2000 and knighted in 2003.Ondaatje is survived by Valda, his three children, David, Sarah and Jans, his brother, Michael, and sister Gillian (his sister Janet predeceased him), and 18 grandchildren and great-grandchildren.Philip Christopher Ondaatje, financier, philanthropist and writer, born 22 February 1933; died 20 July 2026Explore more on these topicsPhilanthropyBankingHistory booksBiography booksobituariesShareReuse this content

title: New faces, fresh memories and a grand day out with Aardman – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Arresting portraits from Catherine Opie, exploring the past with paint and the geniuses of British animation unpack their secrets – all in your weekly dispatch
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: Arresting portraits from Catherine Opie, exploring the past with paint and the geniuses of British animation unpack their secrets – all in your weekly dispatch
Content: Daniela, 2009, by Catherine Opie.Photograph: © Catherine Opie, courtesy Regen Projects, Los Angeles; Lehmann Maupin, New York, Hong Kong, London, and Seoul; Thomas Dane GalleryView image in fullscreenDaniela, 2009, by Catherine Opie.Photograph: © Catherine Opie, courtesy Regen Projects, Los Angeles; Lehmann Maupin, New York, Hong Kong, London, and Seoul; Thomas Dane GalleryArt Weekly newsletterArt and designNew faces, fresh memories and a grand day out with Aardman – the week in artArresting portraits from Catherine Opie, exploring the past with paint and the geniuses of British animation unpack their secrets –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 7 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekCatherine Opie: To Be SeenPowerful photographs that put people before you heroically, on tour from London’s National Portrait Gallery.Royal Scottish Academy, Edinburgh, from 8 AugustAlso showingEarth MattersArtists including Tania Kovats and Alberta Whittle explore the legacy of the 18th-century geologist James Hutton.Inverleith House, Edinburgh, until 1 NovemberVestigesPaintings by the talented and imaginative Laura Footes feature in this group show about memory.Annely Juda Fine Art, London, until 28 AugustInside AardmanThe geniuses of British animation invite you for a slice of wensleydale in the summer holidays.Young V&A, London, until 15 NovemberFfasiwnYoung people work with artists Clémentine Schneidermann and Charlotte James to deconstruct fashion.National Museum Cardiff until 4 April 2027Masterpiece of the weekVirgin and Child with Saints by Lorenzo Lotto, 1505View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Niday Picture Library/AlamyLotto is a wondrous portrait painter, and that feel for faces comes through here in the way he brings a gathering of saints to life. The two old white-bearded men at the left of the Virgin Mary – Saint Jerome and Saint Peter – are huddled as if they’ve been conversing passionately: while Jerome looks broodingly at Jesus, perhaps meditating on his destiny of crucifixion, Peter’s strong, almost angry face looks out at us. But the biggest departure from convention is Saint Francis of Assisi in his rough brown robe on the other side of Mary. He’s often shown as humble and gentle but here he looks more confrontational and impassioned. The female saint in the shadows hasn’t been identified: she is lost in introspection and melancholy in a way that holds you. This ability to give people intense, unexpected, mysterious character was to make Lotto one the greatest portraitists of all time. In this early work he sets out his wares and scouts for commissions. He also shows off his ability to paint pastorals like his contemporaries Giorgione and Titian: two woodsmen are chopping down a tree in the background, as if to prepare the cross on which Christ will die. This violent image is ironically set on a calm, green wooded hill under a stilled blue sky with silky white clouds. It’s a lovely vista but portraiture, not landscape would prove to be Lotto’s thing.Scottish National Gallery, Edinburghskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get in TouchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: AI, boy kibble and parasite cleanses: the 11 biggest wellness trends of 2026 | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Suggestions for improving your wellbeing are more plentiful than ever – and some may even be on to something
Author: Madeleine Aggeler
Headline: Suggestions for improving your wellbeing are more plentiful than ever – and some may even be on to something
Content: Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesWell actuallyAI, boy kibble and parasite cleanses: the 11 biggest wellness trends of 2026Suggestions for improving your wellbeing are more plentiful than ever – and some may even be on to somethingMadeleine AggelerFri 7 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery year, thewellnessindustry churns out new products and practices that it claims are finally – finally! – the real secret to being well. Sometimes, these trends are legitimate. Sometimes they’re utter nonsense. Often they’re somewhere in between.These are the wellness trends that have provoked controversy and interest in 2026.AIAI has rapidly become part of every area of life, including wellness routines. More and more people are turning to chatbots for nutrition advice, fitness routines and even guidance on how tonavigate relationshipsand grow as a person.In May, Guardian readers shared how they have incorporated AI into theirfitness routines. Some said the personalized information helped them stick to a routine and meet their fitness goals, but others acknowledged it was an imperfect tool. “It can be wrong, and confidently so,” said one AI user.As forpersonal growth, AI can lower the barrier to self-reflection, experts say; chatbot prompts may help you more clearly define your questions and goals. But because these technologies are trained on large-scale, human-generated data, their recommendations risk being over-generic, and reinforcing “dominant cultural narratives, rather than what is meaningful for an individual”.Read more on AI fitnessParasite cleansesIn an interview last year, supermodel Heidi Klum revealed that she and her husband were undertaking aparasite cleansebecause, as she put it, “everything on my Instagram feed at the moment is about worms and parasites.” The idea has trickled down through social media, where users have been making bold claims that deworming cleanses could help with everything from sleep, gut health, mood and skin.While parasitic infections are real, and common in communities where people lack access to clean water and sanitation, experts say they are far less common in areas with good sanitation. What’s more, such infections cannot be cleared up by the herbal supplements hawked on TikTok. Parasitic infections are diagnosed with stool samples or blood tests, and often treated with antibiotic or antiparasitic medications.Read more on parasite cleansesProteinmaxxingProtein has been having a moment, and the usual sources – meat, eggs, dairy – aren’t cutting it any more. Increasingly, consumers are supplementing their regular intake –proteinmaxxing– with protein-fortified foods: powders, cereal and even snacks like popcorn and pretzels.What’s the reason behind this seemingly bottomless appetite for a single macronutrient? Some credit it to the boom in GLP-1 medications: when people eat less, consuming an adequate amount of protein to maintain existing muscle becomes especially important.Experts add that there is a ceiling of how much protein can help with building muscle – it’s generally recommended that most adults aim for 0.8g of protein per kg of body weight. And even for those serious about weightlifting and building muscle, protein intake and muscle synthesis seems to plateau above 1.6g per kg of body weight.Read more on proteinmaxxingDivorce ringsSometimes known as “F-you rings”, divorce rings are the result of refashioning engagement and wedding rings after a marriage ends. The trend took off among celebrities too, with people like Emily Ratajkowski and Rachel Zoe flaunting their divorce rings.“It’s not an F-you to an ex-husband, necessarily,” said one woman who reworked her wedding ring into new jewelry. “It’s an F-you to the expectations, to the norms, to this belief that a woman’s sole purpose is to be a man’s wife, not their own person.”Read more on divorce jewelryOlive oil and lemon juiceThough this combination sounds like the base of a nice salad dressing, social media influencers started drinking it asa shot, claiming it improves skin and digestion.This isn’t complete nonsense. Olive oil in particular has a number of health benefits – it is a monounsaturated fat, meaning it helps lower bad cholesterol and keeps artery walls flexible and functional. It also contains polyphenols, a type of antioxidant that helps reduce inflammation.It’s a relatively low-risk trend to try. But experts agree you’d probably be better off eating the mixture with a salad.Read more on lemon shotsHyroxEvery once in a while, a new fitness method comes along that completely consumes young professionals with free time and disposable income. Before, it was CrossFit. Now,there’s Hyrox.Founded in 2017, Hyrox is a competition that occurs over several days. It consists of eight 1km runs and eight different workouts, including pulling and pushing sleds, farmer’s carry, burpee broad jumps and rowing. Training classes include sets of exercises that closely resemble these – and they’re hard. “I had hoped my baseline fitness and adrenaline would carry me through,” wrote Wilson Wong. “They did not.”Read more on hyroxskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBoy kibble“Boy kibble” describes a meal that has long been popular among fitness enthusiasts: rice, ground protein and some kind of vegetable.“This is essentially old-school bodybuilding nutrition repackaged,” said one nutritionist. It is a fairly nutritious meal option when it combines the right amounts of protein, fat, carbohydrates and fiber. Simple meal structures like this one can be helpful for some people trying to meet their nutritional needs.But it shouldn’t be the only meal structure one uses. Experts emphasized that other meals should provide a wider range of foods. Also, there are plenty of other meals that are equally nutritious, and a little more interesting.Read more on boy kibbleFunctional foodsIt’s not enough any more for chocolate to be chocolate, or chips to be chips – these days, chocolate now offers PMS relief, and chips now have added protein.So-called “functional foods” – foods that provide specific health benefits or enhance the body’s processes – are not new, but they have risen in popularity with the ascent of wellness influencers and increasingly health-conscious consumers. But experts agree functional food claims should be taken with a grain of salt. The amount of nutrients or probiotics added to functional foods tends to be far below what has been studied in clinical trials.Nutrition expert Dr Marion Nestle says most of the claims made by these foods have “nothing to do with science. It’s about marketing.”Read more on functional foodsThe burned haystack dating methodDeveloped by Dr Jennie Young, a professor of rhetoric, theburned haystack dating methodoffers an answer to the question, “How do you find a needle in a haystack?”: You burn it down.Applied to dating, this means blocking any person who doesn’t seem like a match. There are also 10 “rules of engagement” (for example, don’t spend too much time on the apps; don’t message for too long before meeting in person) and 33 red flag rhetorical patterns (for example, sending an inappropriately sexual first message). Critics argue the method is too unforgiving towards men, and that it doesn’t encourage enough self-reflection on the part of the person doing the burning. Followers of the method say it has helped them go on fewer but more promising dates.Read more on burned haystackVaginal wellnessThe billion-dollarvaginal probiotic industrysells supplements and suppository capsules which it claims can improve vaginal health and odor, and prevent infections.It’s clear why the industry is booming. For decades, little scientific progress has been made in treatments for vaginal microbiome-related conditions such as bacterial vaginosis and urinary tract infections. But there is little evidence the vaginal probiotic supplements on the market now help, and some may cause gastrointestinal side-effects.Read more on vaginal wellnessSpermmaxxingLike many wellness trends, this one starts from a place of truth and then quickly goes off the rails.Research has shown that men’s average sperm count and concentration has dropped significantly since the 1970s. Experts attribute this largely to modern lifestyle factors like poor sleep, stress and air pollution. To improve the quantity and quality of one’s sperm, online influencers have peddled a range of dubious solutions which they sometimes call “spermmaxxing”. These include eating more garlic and dipping your testicles in ice water.But according to experts, the best thing men can do for their reproductive health is to keep it simple: get enough sleep, eat healthy and move your body.Read more on spermmaxxingExplore more on these topicsWell actuallyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Experience: I dress up as rubbish | Life and style | The Guardian
description: On my TikTok I find trash that’s blowing in the wind, and mimic its movements using what I have to hand
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: On my TikTok I find trash that’s blowing in the wind, and mimic its movements using what I have to hand
Content: ‘I hope my videos influence people to look after the planet’: Shoji Yamasaki n Los Angeles.Photograph: Amanda Hakan/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I hope my videos influence people to look after the planet’: Shoji Yamasaki n Los Angeles.Photograph: Amanda Hakan/The GuardianExperienceLife and styleExperience: I dress up as rubbishOn my TikTok I find trash that’s blowing in the wind, and mimic its movements using what I have to handShoji YamasakiFri 7 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 05.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve always been interested in the concept of value and what is thought of as rubbish. When people throw things away, a perfectly good table, say, I think, “That’s still usable.” I’m a dancer and choreographer and hoard clothing – costumes from shows or pieces my mum has lent me. Sometimes, I’ll collect random things offered on Facebook.During the pandemic I was unable to perform but became hyper-aware of everyday movements around me. On daily walks in Los Angeles, where I live, I’d notice pieces of litter being blown about. I felt as if it was trying to get someone’s attention, but nobody was looking. I thought: “What if I start mimicking it? What if I used the trash as my choreographer?”So I started making “duet” videos; they featured a film of litter on one side and another of me dancing while dressed like it on the other. The first TikTok video I posted was in October 2023 – I recreated a dog poo bag blowing in the wind. I wore a green top and trousers, and sat on my knees, shimmying my upper body up and down.double quotation markI’ve made films of me as crisp packets, plastic bags and shopping receiptsThe duet videos didn’t take off. After a year of uploading them, I finally decided to post what I thought would be my last one. That featured me imitating anempty takeaway boxin a white plastic bag. I wore all white and hunched over a cardboard box with my hands clasped above me and the soles of my feet together on the ground to look like the bag’s handles. When that video got 3m views, I thought: “The universe has spoken.”Since then, I’ve posted more than 100 videos on TikTok and Instagram with the same caption: “PSA: Please pick up your trash”. I’ve dressed as crisp packets, plastic bags and shopping receipts. To recreate them, I layer different pieces of clothing and try to mimic any words or images. I have a rule about not creating additional waste. I don’t use glue or tape when making my costumes, only safety pins.My favourite video is also my most complicated. I dressed as an empty packet ofChex Mix (an American snack)that had been stuffed through a hole in a metal pole. I crouched on my knees on top of a swivel chair, my right arm dangling as I held another chair upside down on top of me with my left arm. That was tricky, as I kept falling off while trying to balance.The litter I choose to film must be moving in the wind and made of a synthetic material that won’t biodegrade.Once I’ve found something suitable, I record plenty of footage, later choosing the best 15 seconds to use. Then I put the litter in the bin – I want to leave a slightly cleaner place behind. After that, I go home and piece together an outfit that resembles it, then film myself wearing it and in a location that looks similar to where I found it. Then I edit the two videos together.People don’t realise how much work is involved. It’s a whole production, because every video I do is like putting on a little show. I am sore the day after filming as I have been contorting my body to the limits of what it can do. The videos may be only 15 seconds long, but I have to repeat moves over and over again to get a good shot. Sometimes, I feel self-conscious filming if other people are nearby, but I’m mostly used to it now. I’m often hunched over while recording, so people think I’m not feeling well. I’m like: “I’m OK! I’m just recording trash!”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExperience: I’ve found a four-leaf clover every day for three yearsRead moreI see social media as my virtual gallery space where people can come and scroll through. There will always be haters, but as long as they’re talking about my work, that’s all that matters. I have received some weird messages. As I’m barefoot in some of the videos, people have said things such as: “I love your feet, they’re beautiful.” You know you’ve made it online when you get noticed by the foot fetish community.It feels as if the world is choking on rubbish. We put things in the bin thinking it disappears, but, actually, most of it ends up in landfill. I know I’m not going to be able to change the world, but I hope my videos will help people notice rubbish. And maybe next time they see litter that’s moving, it’ll remind them to pick it up.As told to Annalise SmithDo you have an experience to share? title: Helen Goh’s giant shortcake with summer fruits and vanilla cream – recipe | Dessert | The Guardian
description: A jamboree of juicy stone fruit and summer berries with a crusty, sugary top brings a riot of textures and colour to your dessert table
Author: Helen Goh
Headline: A jamboree of juicy stone fruit and summer berries with a crusty, sugary top brings a riot of textures and colour to your dessert table
Content: Helen Goh’s giant shortcake with summer fruits and vanilla cream.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenHelen Goh’s giant shortcake with summer fruits and vanilla cream.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.The sweet spotDessertHelen Goh’s giant shortcake with summer fruits and vanilla cream – recipeA jamboree of juicy stone fruit and summer berries with a crusty, sugary top brings a riot of textures and colour to your dessert tableHelen GohFri 7 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAgiant American-style shortcake is one of summer’s great celebrations: tender, buttery shortcake, softly whipped cream and an extravagant tumble of fruit. Rather than prescribing a single combination, I like to let the market decide. Choose whatever looks and smells best: strawberries, raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, greengages, apricots, cherries, nectarines or peaches all work beautifully. Aim for a mix of juicy stone fruit and berries – it will bring different colours, textures and levels of sweetness to every bite. This is a dessert that embraces the glorious abundance of the season – a proper summer bonanza.Giant shortcake with summer fruits and vanilla creamWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep15 minChill1 hr+Cook1 hr 20 min, plus coolingServes8-10For the shortcake380g plain flour,plus extra for dusting70g caster sugar, plus 1 tbsp3 tsp baking powder½ tsp fine sea salt150g cold unsalted butter250ml cold double cream, plus 1 tbsp extra for brushing1 tsp vanilla extract1 tsp fennel seeds, lightly toasted and crushedA few small mintleaves, to garnishFor the fruit350g stone fruit of choice, stoned and cut into 5-7mm wedges350g berries of choice, halve or quarter strawberries, depending on size40g caster sugar, plus extra depending on the sweetness of the fruit2 tsp lemon juiceA pinch of fine sea saltFor the cream350ml double cream20g icing sugar1 tsp vanilla extractA pinch of fine sea saltCut a sheet of baking paper to fit a large baking tray, then, using a 20cm cake tin or dinner plate as a guide, draw a 20cm circle on it.Whisk the flour, caster sugar, baking powder and salt in a medium bowl to combine.Put the cold butter between two sheets of baking paper and give it a few firm whacks with a rolling pin, until it forms a rough sheet about 5mm thick. Tear the butter into irregular pieces and add to the flour mix, tossing to coat. Rub the butter lightly between your fingertips to flatten into smaller flakes of about 1-2cm across – some pieces will still be visible throughout the flour.Combine the cream and vanilla, then pour into the flour mix. Stir gently with a fork until the mix forms a shaggy dough, then use a flexible spatula to fold it over a few times, until there are no obvious dry patches. The dough will still look rough and that’s exactly what you want.Turn the dough out on to a lightly floured work surface, then flour your hands and gently pat and press the dough into a rough disc. Transfer to the baking paper, placing it on the side without the circle. Using the drawn circle as a guide, gently press the dough into an even 20cm round, about 2cm thick. Wrap the dough in the baking paper and chill for at least an hour, or up to three hours.To bake, heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Unwrap the dough, put it (still on the baking paper) on to a large baking tray and brush the surface with the remaining tablespoon of cream. Mix the crushed fennel seeds with the extra tablespoon of caster sugar and sprinkle evenly over the top.Bake for 30 minutes, then reduce the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5 and bake for a further 15 minutes, until deeply golden brown and cooked through. Transfer to a wire rack to cool completely.About 30 minutes before serving, combine the fruits, sugar, lemon juice and salt in a bowl. Toss gently and leave to macerate until the fruit has released some of its juices.Meanwhile, whip the cream with the icing sugar, vanilla and salt until it holds soft peaks.Put the shortcake on a serving plate. Using a serrated knife, slice horizontally to lift off the central crusty-domed cap (about 1cm in thickness). Don’t worry if it cracks into a few pieces – reserve on a plate for serving. Spoon the whipped cream over the shortcake and pile most of the fruit on top, along with a little of the syrupy juices. Finish with a few small mint leaves.To serve, cut the shortcake into wedges and transfer to plates. Spoon over the extra fruit and juices, then tuck pieces of the crisp fennel-sugar top alongside each serving.Explore more on these topicsDessertThe sweet spotCakeFoodBiscuitsSummer food and drinkFruitrecipesShareReuse this content
