title: How to explore Britain and Ireland’s most beautiful rivers on foot, bike or boat: readers’ travel tips | Travel | The Guardian
description: Our rivers may be running low at the moment, but they still offer an abundance of adventure and nature to explore. Here are your favourites, from the Tees to the Shannon
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: Our rivers may be running low at the moment, but they still offer an abundance of adventure and nature to explore. Here are your favourites, from the Tees to the Shannon
Content: Stepping stones over the River Wharfe at Bolton Abbey in the Yorkshire Dales.Photograph: Andy Aughey/AlamyView image in fullscreenStepping stones over the River Wharfe at Bolton Abbey in the Yorkshire Dales.Photograph: Andy Aughey/AlamyReaders' travel tipsTravelHow to explore Britain and Ireland’s most beautiful rivers on foot, bike or boat: readers’ travel tipsOur rivers may be running low at the moment, but they still offer an abundance of adventure and nature to explore. Here are your favourites, from the Tees to the ShannonTell us about a favourite holiday in the UK– the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 7 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 05.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Bolton Abbey and the Yorkshire Dales from the WharfeLast summer, I enjoyed a six-mile walk along the fast-flowing River Wharfe from Ilkley to Bolton Abbey, with calming vistas of the Yorkshire Dales every step of the way. I set out at Ilkley’sRiverside Gardenson the south bank, near the remains of a Roman fort. Trace the path to the ancient stone bridge and along to the picturesque village of Addingham with its Low Mill weir and views of late bronze age or early iron ageCastleberg fort. Simply carry on hugging the riverbank to the splendid remains of 12th-century monastery ofBolton Abbey, situated in wonderful woods and parkland.HelenProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Cruising the Bure in the Norfolk BroadsView image in fullscreenThe ruins of St Benet’s Abbey.Photograph: John Duckett/AlamyThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.A week cruising along the River Bure in Norfolk from Acle to Coltishall is an unforgettable experience. With a speed limit of 5mph, life is slow, and there is plenty of time to enjoy the ever-changing landscape and wildlife. Numerous stopping places give access to nature reserves, quintessentially English villages such as Belaugh, the romantic ruins ofSt Benet’s Abbey, as well as riverside pubs and the Broads themselves. Not to forget “the world’s largest village store”, Roys of Wroxham – an essential port of call to restock supplies before the atmospheric last stretch to Coltishall with its cafes and shops. Boats can be hired from several locations and are easy to handle – no experience needed.JohnWildlife in the city on Coventry’s River SoweView image in fullscreenHerons are a common sight on British rivers.Photograph: FLPA/AlamyFor a peaceful walk close to Coventry city centre, try theSowe Valley Footpath. This 8½-mile riverside trail runs from Hawkesbury Junction to Whitley Grove Wood, following the River Sowe – a tributary of the Avon – through woodland, waterways and urban landscapes. Look out for herons, moorhens and other wildlife along the way. I love that it shows how nature can be found in unexpected places.Deborah DixonEdinburgh’s sublime Water of LeithView image in fullscreenThe Water of Leith runs through Dean Village.Photograph: Jui-Chi Chan/AlamyTheWater of Leith Walkwayis a 13-mile riverside journey through Edinburgh from Balerno to Leith, lovingly cared for by the Water of Leith Conservation Trust. A good introduction is to walk from Roseburn (a mile west of Princes Street) downstream to Stockbridge. It’s about two miles and will take roughly 45 minutes through Dean Village and passing St Bernard’s Well. If you’re lucky, you might see a kingfisher.Keith CummingFrom the Midlands to the Fens and the sea along the WellandView image in fullscreenThe River Welland between Market Deeping and Crowland.Photograph: Tim Scrivener/AlamyI create my own long-distance walks using the Ordnance Survey app. My favourite was a five-day walk following the 65-mile long River Welland from source to sea. Starting at Sibbertoft, near Market Harborough in Leicestershire, I walked the Rutland-Northamptonshire border pastRockingham Castlenear Corby, through Stamford and the poet John Clare’s birthplace at Helpston. The route then headed out into the fens, stopping at the ruined medieval abbey at Crowland and the elegant canal-side town of Spalding. The final day was spent slowly watching the Boston Stump (St Botolph’s church) grow larger as I walked to where the river met the sea.AlexCruisng down the Shannon, Ireland’s ‘Mississippi Delta’View image in fullscreenThe Shannon at Banagher harbour, County Offaly.Photograph: Image Broker/AlamyShannon Harbour in the Irish Midlands marks the spot where the Grand Canal meets Ireland’s River Shannon. As children we often walked the canal, stopping inMcIntyre’s pubfor Irish tapas (Tayto crisps). But the biggest treat was when my father’s childhood friend would take us in his boat from Shannon Harbour to the Shannon proper. The landscape changes utterly. On a warm day it feels like leaving rural Ireland and going down the Mississippi Delta. On a wet day you can’t see the other side. But McIntyre’s will be open when you get back, whatever the weather.Eveskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRoman ruins along York’s OuseView image in fullscreenWalking the Ouse is a great way of exploring York.Photograph: Andrew Briggs/AlamyNorth Yorkshire’s River Ouse takes you on a gorgeous walk through York and beyond. You can start by crossing Scarborough Bridge before strolling down Dame Judi Dench Walk, then meander past Roman and medieval ruins at theMuseum Gardens. ThePerky Peacockcafe in a medieval tower on the riverside is a highlight. You can follow the river down to Rowntree Park and Millennium Bridge. Just beware of the cobbles and some step-only access along the way.MaryWaterfalls on the Tees in County DurhamView image in fullscreenKayakers tackle Low Force.Photograph: Malkin Photography/AlamyThe River Tees crashes over High Force waterfall amid dramatic moorland before bubbling over Low Force downstream. Park at Bowlees and cross the Tees at Low Force on the historic Wynch suspension bridge, built in the 1830s (it replaced Britain’s first suspension bridge, built by lead miners in 1741). It’s a good place to stop and watch kayakers tackle Low Force. Continue upstream through the moorland to the roar ofHigh Force. After all that fresh air, finish with cake atBowlees visitor centre, bliss!Hannah SWinning tip: along the Ouse through the South DownsView image in fullscreenThe River Ouse near Lewes, East Sussex.Photograph: Lemanieh/Getty ImagesFollowing the River Ouse (one of five British Ouses) to the sea is great fun, on foot or bike. I usually start near Horsham in West Sussex, and track theOuse Valley Waywhich passes through South Downs. This route lets you cross rolling fields and wander through woodland paths and you can even pause at the beautifulNymans, an extraordinary garden owned by the National Trust. The river walk goes under a 37-arch Victorian railway viaduct near Balcombe and leads to the historic town of Lewes in East Sussex, where you can have a break at theJohn Harvey Tavernand watch the waters flow past. The final part is an easy stretch of flat riverside walking as you the coast comes into sight, leading into Newhaven.PeterView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsTravelReaders' travel tipsTop 10sfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fancy fresh cabbages next spring? Then it’s time to get sowing | Gardening advice | The Guardian
description: Spring cabbages sown now will grow swiftly and then overwinter in your garden
Author: Claire Ratinon
Headline: Spring cabbages sown now will grow swiftly and then overwinter in your garden
Content: Spring cabbages take around six months to reach maturity.Photograph: Oscar D'Arcy/Gap PhotosView image in fullscreenSpring cabbages take around six months to reach maturity.Photograph: Oscar D'Arcy/Gap PhotosGardening adviceFancy fresh cabbages next spring? Then it’s time to get sowingSpring cabbages sown now will grow swiftly and then overwinter in your gardenClaire RatinonFri 7 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you told primary-school-age me that I’d one day love cabbage, I would have laughed and called you a liar. Despite how much school dinners tried to put me – and likely, you – off this green-leafed staple, I’m happy to say that my taste has been rehabilitated. Yet, for all the love I have for the humble cabbage, it is not a crop I grow. And it is for the same reason that lots of grow-your-own classics don’t make it on to my plot: I don’t have enough space. For a vegetable that is so inexpensive and ubiquitous, I simply can’t justify it.But if you’re fortunate enough to have a decent-sized patch – or just a strong desire to grow cabbages – then it’s a good time to get them started. Spring cabbages sown now – in good quality sowing compost in a modular tray – will grow swiftly in summer’s ideal conditions. They will then overwinter in the ground all the way through to next spring, when they will be ready to pick.double quotation markThey are edible from the off, so you could grow cabbages as microgreens should that interest youThere are plenty of brassica-hungry creatures around – from butterflies to pigeons – so I’d advise potting young cabbage plants on and keeping them protected until they are sturdy enough to survive a bit of munching. Even when they are ready to go in the ground, I’d use insect-proof mesh to protect them. Appropriate spacing is also important – 30-40cm between plants, depending on the variety – so they have room to grow, plus you can monitor their progress much more easily. If you do plant spring cabbages (like ‘Duncan’,pictured) closer together, harvest some as spring greens and leave the remainder to keep growing until they develop into full heads.From seed to harvest, spring cabbages – grown in plenty of sun and nutrient rich, well-draining soil – take around six months to reach maturity. This is another important consideration when deciding whether to dedicate an area to this delicious but time- and space-hungry crop.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI used to be intimidated by roses. But they are not as high-maintenance as you thinkRead moreIt is quite possible to grow cabbages pretty much year-round. Those ready for harvest in the summer months are sown in late winter or early spring, while autumn cabbages are sown from mid-spring but tend to be large and so need plenty of space. Winter cabbages are on the bigger side too. They’re the type that come to harvest when the veg patch is otherwise bare, and they boast a hardiness that can withstand a British winter, so they are poised to be picked as and when they are needed.My favourite thing about the brassica family to which cabbages belong is that they are edible from the off, so you could grow cabbages as microgreens should that interest you. More helpfully, it means that if you set out to grow cabbages and at any point change your mind, then you can eat what you’ve grown and call it a day.Explore more on these topicsGardening adviceGardensVegetablesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Blinded by War: documenting the aftermath of injury in Ukraine – photo essay | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Since 2025, Paula Bronstein has been photographing wounded Ukrainian servicemen as they learn to live with the loss of sight, hearing and limbs
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Since 2025, Paula Bronstein has been photographing wounded Ukrainian servicemen as they learn to live with the loss of sight, hearing and limbs
Content: An eye prosthetic worn by Andriy Onopriienko, who lost his eyesight when he was hit by tank rocket fire.Photograph: Paula BronsteinSince 2025, Paula Bronstein has been photographing wounded Ukrainian servicemen as they learn to live with the loss of sight, hearing and limbsByLuke Harding. Photographs by Paula BronsteinFri 7 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 04.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor more than four decades, the US photojournalist Paula Bronstein has travelled to places overlooked by the wider world, including countries scarred by war, such as Afghanistan andUkraine.Bronstein says her life’s mission has been to “bear witness to critical moments” and to “create images that evoke true empathy in others”.Her prize-winning photographs document political conflict, humanitarian crises and social injustice. Yet she is equally drawn to the quieter moments of everyday life: to “joy and happiness and the full spectrum of human experience”. She attributes her work to an “insatiable curiosity” and a desire to document people’s “enduring humanity” amid tragedy.View image in fullscreenAt a workshop in Lviv for blind veterans, Ivan Rozuman receives instruction from a mobility trainer as he learns to navigate the streets. Rozuman joined the military before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. He says he has been wounded twice and undergone more than 50 operations. So much shrapnel remains lodged in his body, he says, that he has lost count. He was first injured during a Kharkiv offensive in 2022 while serving with the 25th Brigade. Ivan lost his sight and has hearing loss. After leaving military service, he was caught in an explosion near his home in in Zaporizhzhia and almost died.Since 2025, Bronstein has been photographing wounded Ukrainian servicemen for a project, Blinded by War. Vladimir Putin’s 2022 invasion has left a generation of young Ukrainian men with life-changing injuries. Most have been hit by kamikaze drones, used extensively by both sides across a sprawling battlefield.View image in fullscreenOn 14 February 2023, Vitaliy Veres was injured in Bakhmut. His eyes were damaged, his chin was torn open and both tympanic cavities – the middle ear – were destroyed. He underwent more than 30 surgeries, beginning with military-funded care that left him disillusioned and frustrated. He hopes to popularise adaptive sports for Ukrainian veterans and become a motivational speaker. He is now a bodybuilder and trains in the gym every day.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreen‘Abroad, I’m a hero. At home, people look at me like I’m scary,’ Veres says. He met his partner, Victoria Lysachenko, in their hometown in 2012 and they have a daughter. Her unwavering support has been one of the cornerstones of his recovery.Ukraine is facing the immense challenge of providing medical care, rehabilitation and psychological support to a growing number of wounded military personnel. The country’s healthcare system is struggling to treat the many soldiers who have sustained vision loss.View image in fullscreenArtists at the Imatech medical eye clinic in Kyiv use 3D printers to create realistic eyes.Bronstein’s subjects include Artur Martosich, a competitive weightlifter who runs with a guide, and Serhii Chabanov, a father of three who was blinded and lost an arm in a drone attack near the eastern city of Bakhmut. “I learn something from each new story I do. The people in Ukraine are incredible. What fascinates me is their resilience,” she says.View image in fullscreenArtur Martosich is a war veteran who lost his sight as a result of his injuries. Since then, Martosich has dedicated himself to sport and personal growth. A passionate strongman and powerlifter, he also embraces endurance sports, combining strength training with running and other athletic disciplines, and has won numerous veteran sporting competitions.Martosich was shot in the head from three metres while on a combat mission. He lives with his father and describes sport as the “best form of rehabilitation – physical, spiritual and mental”, adding: “Before the war I used to wrestle. My current goal is to make it into the Ukrainian national team for strongman competitions.”View image in fullscreenAndriy Onopriienko takes dance lessons at a centre for the blind in Kyiv where he can also take part in rock climbing, cooking and learning braille.Another soldier, Andriy Onopriienko, 32, was hit two years ago by tank fire. He lost his eyesight and suffered several facial burns and hearing loss in one ear. “I was in so much pain I begged another comrade to kill me. Now I want to live my life to the fullest, one step at a time and to achieve small things every day,” he says. He lives in the Kyiv family apartment where he grew up.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenRecalling the aftermath of his injury, Onopriienko says: ‘I couldn’t see anything, I was worried about my family and had suicidal thoughts as well.’In July, Bronstein visited the Ukrainian capital’s regional hospital, where she photographed patients undergoing eye surgery. One of them, 30-year-old Rafael Akhmedov, lost his left eye in 2024 when a mortar hit him in the Kharkiv region. He was receiving a scleral implant. Last year, the hospital carried out eye operations on 100 soldiers.View image in fullscreenMariia Borkhalenko performs surgery on a veteran who lost his eye, inserting a scleral implant“I hope this is my last time here,” Akhemedov says. Asked about his plans for the future, he says: “My wife and I are working on having a kid.” The hospital’s ocular surgeon, Mariia Borkhalenko, says 70% of her patients have lost one or both eyes. “They are victims of FPV drones, bombs, explosions and blast waves.”Many blinded soldiers also lose their hands. “It’s a reflex. When there is a blast people raise their arms,” Borkhalenko says. While some veterans cope well, others become depressed and “asocial”, she adds. “It’s a big number of people, unfortunately. We have psychologists who talk to them and help them to learn to live without hands and sight.”View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenIlya Romantsov, 26, at the Protez Foundation in Kyiv, which provides free prosthetics. Romantsov lost his eyesightand both hands in a first-person view (FPV) Russian drone attack last year. There has been a devastating rise in traumatic hand amputations and loss of vision because FPV drones target individuals directly and detonate at close range.In recent months Russia has stepped up its drone and ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv. Many people shelter in basements and metro stations. Borkhalenko says: “I still get up in the morning and go to work. Doing surgery is my job. Our shared goal is to defeat the enemy and win this war.”Bronstein moves rapidly around the operating theatre, photographing Akhmedov from different angles. She is not squeamish about blood: “I’ve covered conflict for so many years, going back to the horrible bombings in Pakistan, to the war in Afghanistan, and to working in many many hospitals in Kabul. It’s how I want to tell the story.”View image in fullscreenAt a Lviv workshop supported by the non-profitLet’s See the Victory, for blind veterans, Yuliya watches as her father, Volodymr, dances with an instructor.She adds: “For me, photography is an intensely personal exploration, seen through my own eyes. I am incredibly fortunate that, at 72, what truly matters is my unwavering passion for my work. I remain deeply curious, always seeking, and profoundly proud to portray what’s possible, even in the darkest corners.”Bronstein’s latest book is calledWitnessing Life: A Retrospective. Her pictures have been published and exhibited globally. She spent 15 years as a staff photographer for US newspapers, before working for Getty Images in Asia from 2002 to 2013. Between 2001 and 2021 she covered the war in Afghanistan. Her book Afghanistan: Between Hope and Fear was published in 2016.View image in fullscreenSerhii Chabanov, right, takes part in a weightlifting competition in Brovary for veterans with disabilities. He was severely wounded in a drone attack that caused his to lose him sight and one arm. Chabanov took second place in his category.“My life has unfolded as a continuous conversation with photojournalism. I have given myself entirely to it, and in turn, it has profoundly shaped who I am today,” she says.Witnessing Life: A Retrospectiveby Paula Bronstein will be published in August by CDP EditionsExplore more on these topicsThe Guardian picture essayUkraineEuropeRussiaShareReuse this content

title: ‘Her face was beaten in’: how Taliban rule ushered in a new era of women being killed | Afghanistan | The Guardian
description: An investigation into 231 femicide cases highlights the dire situation in Afghanistan, where men are empowered to murder and face no punishment while the state covers up their crimes
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An investigation into 231 femicide cases highlights the dire situation in Afghanistan, where men are empowered to murder and face no punishment while the state covers up their crimes
Content: Liza Shams, who died in February. Her family believes she was murdered by her husband, Hasibullah Sarwari, in AfghanistanView image in fullscreenLiza Shams, who died in February. Her family believes she was murdered by her husband, Hasibullah Sarwari, in AfghanistanFive years of Taliban ruleAfghanistan‘Her face was beaten in’: how Taliban rule ushered in a new era of women being killedAn investigation into 231 femicide cases highlights the dire situation in Afghanistan, where men are empowered to murder and face no punishment while their crimes are covered up by the stateSupported byAbout this contentKhadija Haidary, Zahra Nader, Hura Omar* & Atousa Azar* for Zan TimesFri 7 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a voice message recorded weeks before she died, Liza Shams, 33, asks a relative to pray for her. “There’s no end to my days of misfortune,” she says. “Pray that God shames Hasib [her husband, Hasibullah Sarwari] in front of the whole world for what he has done to me.” In a second recording, she describes being beaten by Sarwari while pregnant, then kept isolated for days, injured to the point she couldn’t eat or speak. “I’m a woman, fine, I should not talk about what happens in my home,” she says. “But I can’t do this any more.”On the afternoon of 1 February, Liza’sneighbours heard screaming and alerted the police. A short while earlier, Liza’s father, Shamsuddin Shams, had received a video call from his daughter. Her injuries were shocking: “Her jaw was broken and she could hardly talk,” he says, but she had managed to pass the message that her husband had beaten her again. Shamsuddin immediately called his two other daughters who lived close by, who arrived at the house and took her to Rahmat hospital in Kabul. About an hour after arrival, Liza died.The report on her death shows that Liza’s face has been beaten in. The CT scan findings describe multiple fractures to her cheekbones and sinus walls, an injury pattern consistent with enormous blunt-force trauma to the face. Photographs of her body and the report’s physical examination, conducted the evening she died, document extensive bruising, injuries and swelling across her face and body.Despite the extensive nature of her injuries, the forensic report lists the likely cause of death as ingesting rat-poison, noting that an autopsy was not performed at the family’s request (Liza’s father says this request came from her in-laws).View image in fullscreenShamsuddin Shams, who believes his daughter Liza was murdered by her husband in Afghanistan.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianHer husband’s family did not respond to questions, but have argued that Liza took her own life, and that the bruising covering her body is a side-effect of poison. Suicide is frequently listed as the cause of death inAfghanistanin cases where women die in violent circumstances – a designation that typically means no one will be held accountable for the death. Liza’s father believes her death was murder.A clear patternTheTalibandoes not collect any data on how many Afghan women are killed each year. The attorney general’s office, which used to collate this information, was abolished in 2023.To measure what the state will not, reporters for Zan times, a collective of journalists who work under cover in Afghanistan, collected cases of women killed in 10 of Afghanistan’s 34 provinces since the Taliban came to power in August 2021, drawing on 174 instances reported by local media, as well as 57 cases documented directly by the journalists but previously unreported. The investigation found women across Afghanistan are being killed at home by husbands, fathers, brothers, in a system that all but guarantees impunity for the crime. Many cases are never entered into official records.View image in fullscreenA mural calling for women and children’s rights in Afghanistan in August 2022 in Bamian, west of Kabul, a year after the Taliban takeover.Photograph: Nava Jamshidi/Getty ImagesThe team documented 231 cases, of which 53 were declared suicide. The provinces with the highest recorded tolls were Jawzjan (36), Herat (32), Badakhshan (28) and Ghazni (26). The age of victims ranged from girls as young as five to women of 65. Seven out of 10 victims – 165 of 231 – were housewives with no independent income or institutional standing to pursue a domestic violence case. Most of the cases occurred in the victim’s home. Across the dataset, only 58 arrests were recorded. More than one in five were officially declared suicide, even when there was significant evidence of foul play. Only one in four of the 231 killings resulted in any arrest, but even in these cases, the suspect was often released – sometimes just one day after being detained.The reporters found a number of deaths that according to family or witnesses had resulted from domestic violence, but were being officially recorded as suicides.View image in fullscreenFreshta Emady, whose family and friends believe she was killed by her husbandA healthcare worker in Jawzjan said that many of the dead women that came to hospital and were labelled suicides had clearly been beaten, their bodies covered in wounds and bruises.Freshta Emady, 33, aUN agency employee in Kabul, was found dead in her home on 31 May. Her husband reportedly told Taliban police she had killed herself, citing a psychiatric condition.Her family and friends, however, believe she was killed by her husband. Five people who knew her said Freshta, who had been married off at 17, had spent 15 years being beaten, choked and controlled. A colleague said Freshta had described her husband repeatedly strangling her and telling her, “I’ll cut your throat.”Danger for families who interveneOften, the families of girls who try to intervene on behalf of their daughters can face deadly consequences. In Kandahar, a 14-year-old girl was killed after being given into marriage to a much older man. Her husband was violent, and she fled back to her father’s family. When he came to force her home in October 2024, she refused to go. He drew a pistol and killed her. Her younger brother, who ran to help, was also shot and died a week later.The Taliban opened a file but her husband, a serving member of the group, was never arrested.In May in Sar-e-Pol province, Sara, 16, and her mother, Chaman, an Iranian-trained doctor, wereshot deadby a local Taliban official who had forced an engagement on Sara. When Chaman refused to hand her daughter over without the agreed dowry, he beat her with his rifle and, as Sara ran to her mother, he shot them both. He was captured after a manhunt and remains in jail.The Taliban’s new criminal code means a husband’s punishment for beating his wife to the point of visible injury such as fracture or wounds is capped at 15 days’ imprisonment. If a wife goes to her family’s house without her husband’s permission, however, and her family does not return her on request, the wife and her family are subject to three months in prison. The code creates a legal structure in which seeking refuge from domestic violence brings a worse punishment than the violence itself.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenIn 2021, the Taliban dissolved the Ministry of Women’s Affairs, the special prosecutor’s office for violence against women, and the country’s shelter network.Photograph: Wakil Kohsar/AFP/Getty ImagesEven before the Taliban, Afghan women were experiencing gender-based violence nearly three times higher than the global average. UN Women’s 2024 AfghanistanGender Index, published in June 2025, found that in 2018, nearly 35% of Afghan women reported violence from a partner in the past year – compared with a global average of 13%.‘I don’t know how to save my daughter from her husband’: the brutal reality of the Taliban’s new marriage lawRead moreSince the Taliban took power, the existing scant protections for women facing violence have been stripped away. After August 2021, the Taliban dissolved the Ministry of Women’s Affairs, the special prosecutor’s office for violence against women, and the country’s shelter network. About250 female judges were removedfrom the bench; female prosecutors were sent home.Afghan law no longer permits a woman to be a direct party to her own legal case, so mothers cannot pursue justice for their daughters. In Takhar province, Shamsia (not her real name), the mother of a 23-year-old woman who was stabbed and set on fire by her husband in May 2025, said she was ordered by the local court to transfer power of attorney to her husband to pursue the case “because a woman cannot be a direct party to a petition or case file”. Months on, the case has gone nowhere.What the numbers don’t showOur reporters could not interview most of the families of the women killed. Fear closed many doors; in several provinces, the journalists received threats after even attempting to make contact. The 231 cases in this dataset are not Afghanistan’s femicide total – they provide only a snapshot of the potential killings, the dynamics that enable them and the impunity that many killers enjoy.View image in fullscreenLiza Shams and her family.Liza Shams’s case will probably be decided by a Taliban court. Her father, who has little hope of anyone being held responsible, has turned to social media, publishing recordings, hospital footage, and documents in a campaign for justice for his daughter.Shams says speaking up has already come with a cost. His daughters who took Liza to hospital were subsequently summoned by the Taliban and have now gone into hiding. “It is because we spoke to the media, the Taliban don’t want issues like this to become public.”Among the recordings her father released is a voice message Liza sent to her brother-in-law, in which she speaks about her marriage and her life.“I feel like I’m suffocating,” she says. “I suffer from these things. I’ll try every day, I’ll try every day, but this isn’t working. Our life can’t go on like this. I don’t want our life to be bitter. My children are growing up, they’ll look at us and see that we are fighting. But it can’t go on like this.”*Zan Times reporters inside Afghanistan write under pen names for their own safety. Sophia Malek, Tarana Mohammadi, Simon Danishjo, AtiaFarazar, Faranak, Horia, Roya, Tamga, Maria, Gawharshad, Raha and Nahid contributed to this report.Explore more on these topicsAfghanistanFive years of Taliban ruleViolence against women and girlsTalibanSouth and central AsiafeaturesShareReuse this content
