title: Spain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy | Spain | The Guardian
description: Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to Ceuta
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to Ceuta
Content: The checks, which come ‘amid the persistent irregular migration pressure’ facing Italy, will starts at midnight on Saturday.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/APView image in fullscreenThe checks, which come ‘amid the persistent irregular migration pressure’ facing Italy, will starts at midnight on Saturday.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/APSpainSpain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from ItalyMove comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to CeutaAgence France-PresseFri 7 Aug 2026 17.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 17.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpain has announced it will introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass rush of people fromMoroccointo Ceuta.The checks, which come “amid the persistent irregular migration pressure” facingItaly, will start at midnight on Saturday and last until 7 September, Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement.Hours earlier,Spainthreatened Italy with countermeasures if it did not swiftly lift its own border checks, drawing a rebuff from Rome.The rare spat between the EU and Nato allies came after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco to Spain’s north African territory on 30-31 July in an unprecedented, deadly rush.The scenes infuriated EU members that back a hard line on irregular immigration, including Italy, which imposed border checks on people arriving from Spain for one month.Russia-linked accounts spread far-right narrative online during Ceuta migration crisis, analysis findsRead moreThe Spanish government criticised the measure on Friday as “unfair, contrary to the EU’s interests and discriminatory for the Spanish population”.Foreign minister José Manuel Albares described it as “a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity”.“We urge the government of Italy to rectify, put an end to the checks and treat Spaniards like other European citizens,” he added.He threatened “proportional measures” in response by Sunday if Italy failed to comply.Within hours, the government of Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it “had no intention of revising the decision” before 15 August, when it said Spanish authorities “expected a new wave of migration” to hit Ceuta.Meloni’s office said in a statement: “Italy does not accept ultimatums or impositions from abroad regarding national security and border control.“Only when there is certainty that there are no security or terrorism risks to Italy, that no new wave is occurring, and that no irregular migrants are heading toward European territory, will the decision be reconsidered.”Spain’s interior ministry announced the reciprocal measures within hours.Spanish police have been monitoring online rumours and social media about possible fresh arrivals in Ceuta in mid-August, according to local media. But authorities have not expressly said they expect a repeat of last week’s rush.Border authorities would in the meantime “do their utmost to ensure maximum ease of movement for Spanish and European citizens” who are not affected by border checks, the Italian statement added.Italy, which does not share a land border with Spain, introduced border controls at maritime and air entry points for third-country nationals arriving from Spain.The move, announced on 31 July, was an “extraordinary measure” intended to “safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation”, Meloni said at the time.She was among several EU leaders who called for Spain to be suspended from the visa-free Schengen travel zone after the Ceuta incident, despite such a move being legally impossible.Italy’s coalition government has sought to stop the tens of thousands of people who land in small boats on the country’s shores each year.The Spanish government warned against “creating rifts and sterile conflicts driven by internal electoral motives” and said “we trust that pro-European sentiment, common sense and good faith prevail”.‘Morocco feels emboldened’: Trump’s influence in spotlight after Ceuta disasterRead moreOf the 72,000 people who entered Ceuta, 70,000 have returned to Morocco, according to official Spanish figures.Spanish authorities said 80 people died in the crossings.Moroccan rights groups, however, estimate the figure to be higher. The Moroccan Association for Human Rights and the European Coordination for Human Rights in Morocco on Friday said at least 141 deaths were recorded and that the toll was likely to rise.Morocco’s interior ministry has said 11 people died on its side of the border, all but one by drowning.Those who remain in Ceuta – including hundreds of unaccompanied children – face dire living conditions with little access to food, water and shelter.Explore more on these topicsSpainItalyMoroccoMigrationAfricaEuropeMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Judge approves Trump effort to end South Sudan TPS protections | US immigration | The Guardian
description: Decision follows supreme court ruling that allowed US government to strip protections for Haitians and Syrians
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Decision follows supreme court ruling that allowed US government to strip protections for Haitians and Syrians
Content: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) headquarters in Washington.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Department of Homeland Security (DHS) headquarters in Washington.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesUS immigrationJudge approves Trump effort to end South Sudan TPS protectionsDecision follows supreme court ruling that allowed US government to strip protections for Haitians and SyriansMaya Yangand agencyFri 7 Aug 2026 14.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 19.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTemporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of South Sudanese nationals in the United States is set to end after a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration can move forward with stripping their protections.How will the US supreme court’s ruling on TPS affect 1.3 million immigrants?Read moreOn Friday, US district judge Patti Saris of the district of Massachusetts rejected an attempt by immigrant rights organizations including the New York-based African Communities Together to keep TPS for South Sudanese nationals living in the US.Saris’s decision follows a6-3 supreme court rulingin June allowing the Trump administration to strip hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians of TPS, which granted them permission to work and live legally in the US.The supreme court’s conservative majority overturned lower court rulings in New York and Washington DC, which had blocked the administration from ending TPS for more than 350,000 Haitians and about 6,100 Syrians.ATPS designationallows eligible people from certain countries facing crises including civil war and environmental disasters to remain in the US temporarily, protects them from deportation and allows them to work legally.In her 15-page ruling, Sariswrotethat “as a logical matter, plaintiffs’ arguments rest upon a self-contradictory, self-defeating foundation”.According to Saris, the plaintiffs’ argument undermined itself, because if the homeland security department (DHS) lacked the authority to terminate South Sudan’s TPS designation, it also would have lacked the authority to issue the designation initially.“South Sudan’s original TPS designation would thus be invalid by the same token as its termination,” Saris wrote.In response to the ruling, James Percival, a DHS general counselsaidon X: “Every other TPS judge must do the same! Every day these ‘administrative stays’ are in effect is a day the American people are denied what they voted for.”The Guardian has contacted African Communities Together for comment.Meanwhile, in a statement to the Guardian on Friday, the immigrant advocacy organization Global Refuge condemned the ruling. The CEO, Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, said: “The reality of the situation is that South Sudan is on the brink of a return to an all-out-civil war. Roughly two-thirds of the population, some 10 million people, now depend on humanitarian aid to survive.“With only several hundred South Sudanese holding TPS in the US right now, this isn’t a policy forced by scale or strain on our system. To the contrary, this is the administration’s deliberate choice to send a small group of vulnerable individuals and families back into a country where civilians are bearing the brunt of intensifying violence and displacement,” Vignarajah added.The Trump administration’s effort to strip TPS protections from hundreds of thousands of immigrants comes despite the US government’s own highest-level travel warnings for Americans to several countries affected, including South Sudan, Haiti and Syria.In the case of South Sudan, the country has been ravaged by years ofcivil war and political instabilitythat have displaced millions. Since gaining independence in 2011, more than400,000 peoplehave been killed in conflict, with fighting and ethnic violence continuing toclaim civilian lives.The DHS moved in November to terminate TPS for South Sudan, saying the country ‌no longer met the conditions for the designation, which was first issued in 2011. The department’s action would have led to the end of protections for more than 232 South Sudanese and at least 73 South Sudanese with pending applications. An earlier order by Saris had blocked that from happening.After the supreme court’s ruling, lawyers for a group of South Sudanese nationals and the non-profit African Communities Together urged Saris to once again block the ‌end of TPS on new grounds that the justices had not addressed.That included an argument that the DHS lacked authority to terminate TPS because the statute that created the TPS program in 1990 referred ​only to the attorney general as the official who had authority to extend and terminate the deportation protections.The DHS was established later, in 2002, after the September 11 attacks.Most of the justice department’s immigration-related functions were transferred to it at that time. Saris, who was appointed by Bill Clinton, concluded Congress had likewise transferred authority over TPS to the DHS.Since 2001, TPS holders have paid $7.8bn annually in taxes and contributed $262bn to the US economy,according tothe advocacy organization Fwd.us. Many TPS holders areemployedin critical industries alreadyfacing worker shortagesacross the country, including construction, hospitality and healthcare.Losing TPS can leave immigrants without legal statusvulnerable to arrest, detention, and deportation, even with pending asylum or green card applications.Some may face immigration court proceedings with limited options to stay in the US. Those ordered removed could be deported and barred from returning for years.Reuters contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsUS immigrationSouth SudanAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: US police officer accused of killing three people in Mexico arrested at border | Texas | The Guardian
description: Chad Eberle of Texas charged over deadly shooting in Saltillo that officials say stemmed from custody dispute
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Chad Eberle of Texas charged over deadly shooting in Saltillo that officials say stemmed from custody dispute
Content: Members of the Mexican army at the border in Piedras Negras, Coahuila state.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMembers of the Mexican army at the border in Piedras Negras, Coahuila state.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesTexasUS police officer accused of killing three people in Mexico arrested at borderChad Eberle of Texas charged over deadly shooting in Saltillo that officials say stemmed from custody disputeMarina DunbarFri 7 Aug 2026 16.49 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 16.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleATexaspolice officer has been arrested inMexicoafter authorities there accused him of killing three people and critically injuring the mother of his child in what investigators say stemmed from a dispute over the custody of the minor.The Coahuila attorney general’s office said 35-year-old Chad Eberle was arrested on Wednesday at the border on a warrant accusing him of femicide and qualified homicide, according toLa Razonde Mexico, a newspaper based in Mexico City. Under Mexican law, femicide refers to the intentional killing of a woman or girl because of her gender.According to La Razon, the deadly shooting happened in July in Saltillo,Mexico, after an argument over Eberle allegedly not having permission to take his three-year-old son. Two women and one man were killed in the attack.The victims were identified by La Razon with the first names and ages of Ana Laura, 44; Laura Jaquelín, 22; and Emanuel, 44. The child’s 26-year-old mother was also shot in the head and remained in critical condition, officials said.Investigators said Eberle was arrested while attempting to cross from Mexico into Texas through the international bridge at Piedras Negras, across from Eagle Pass,KTXSreported. Eberle had left the residence with his son in a gray Chevrolet Silverado, prompting investigators to launch a manhunt as they tracked the vehicle toward the Texas border, theUS Sunreported.He was then intercepted before he could re-enter the US with the child. The three-year-old was unharmed and was later placed in the care of Coahuila’s child welfare agency.TheSan Antonio Expressidentified Eberle as a police officer in the central Texas town of Santa Anna. Before that, he worked as a deputy constable with Bexar county – which includes San Antonio – and also served as a police officer for the Northside independent school district.The Express reported that Eberle also held law enforcement positions in theTexascommunities of Somerset, Marble Falls, Gregory, near Corpus Christi, Lockney in the state’s panhandle, and Bangs in the west. According to the newspaper, a 2022 Facebook post from the Lockney police department described Eberle as an army veteran.In a social mediaposton Thursday, Coahuila attorney general Federico Fernández said: “It is reported that at [9.59p] Chad ‘N’ has been admitted to the Saltillo men’s penitentiary in compliance with [an] arrest warrant, where he has been placed at the disposal of the competent judicial authority, in accordance with the corresponding procedure.”He added: “Likewise, the minor is already in the city of Saltillo, under the custody and care of the prosecutor’s office for boys, girls and the family (Pronnif), in order to guarantee the comprehensive protection of his rights.”Texas news outletColeman Todayobtained a statement from Santa Anna city officials which described Eberle as “one of our reserve officers … [who] was on a personal leave of absence until December.“The Santa Anna police department has been in contact with the US consulate in Mexico and [the Texas commission on law enforcement].”That statement also said Eberle was “an unpaid reserve police officer hired in November 2025 and worked one weekend per month.“Due to the ongoing investigation, no other public comment will be made.”Explore more on these topicsTexasUS crimeMexicoUS policingAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Colombia on the brink: ELN guerrilla group prepares for return to war | Colombia | The Guardian
description: As Abelardo de la Espriella takes office as president vowing a new military offensive, the country’s last leftwing rebels are getting ready to fight back
Author: Thomas Graham
Headline: As Abelardo de la Espriella takes office as president vowing a new military offensive, the country’s last leftwing rebels are getting ready to fight back
Content: ELN members at a camp in southern Chocó, Colombia.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianView image in fullscreenELN members at a camp in southern Chocó, Colombia.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianColombiaColombia on the brink: ELN guerrilla group prepares for return to warAs Abelardo de la Espriella takes office as president vowing a new military offensive, the country’s last leftwing rebels are getting ready to fight backThomas Grahamin Chocó. Photography by Santiago MesaFri 7 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTFirst published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTShareAs the boat approached the riverbank, camouflaged figures watched from the tree line.Behind them, in the dim understory of the jungle, a commander of the National Liberation Army (ELN) sat with his rifle on his lap, amid the buzz and whine of insects and the thwacks of machetes on bamboo as his troops set up camp, hidden from enemy drones.Colombia’s 62-year old armed conflict is on the brink of a new chapter, with the country’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, who takes office on Friday,vowing an end to peace talks and launch a new military offensive. Colombia’s last guerrilla group says it is ready for whatever might come.“Where we can go on the offensive, we will,” said the commander of the group’s Western War Front, who goes by the moniker Yerson. “And if the ELN leadership says we have to carry out a military offensive at the national level, we will. Attacks in cities, in the countryside, wherever.”View image in fullscreenMembers of the ELN’s Western War Front take part in military exercises in southern Chocó, Colombia.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA member of the ELN’s Western War Front walks across a wooden raft on the San Juan River in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA member of the ELN’s Western War Front rests inside a shelter in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianYerson and his troops were deep in the Pacific department of Chocó, in an ELN stronghold accessible only after hours of river travel, where humid heat soaks through the cloud cover.Occasional communities, each a line of wooden shacks on stilts, broke the dense forest on the banks. Giant mining barges were moored on the river, with diggers clawing up the riverbed to extract the particles of gold it contains.The ELN and rival armed groups fight to control the San Juan River, its resources and its population. At one point in the journey, armed men from the Gulf Clan, a violent paramilitary group, stopped the Guardian’s boat to question the passengers, before promising to liberate the area from the ELN.Yerson was unfazed. “All of the ELN territories are being invaded by bands of mercenaries,” he said. “They are very violent, but they are not disputing political power.”View image in fullscreenCommander Yerson stands in front of an ELN flag at a camp in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianView image in fullscreenELN members listen as Commander Yerson reads the group’s regulations at a camp in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn ELN member poses for a photograph at a camp in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianColombia’s conflict began in the 1960s, rooted in extreme land inequality and exclusionary politics. Leftwing guerrillas emerged to challenge the state, battling government forces later allied with rightwing paramilitaries, forerunners of the Gulf Clan. Money from cocaine trafficking fuelled all sides. The conflict has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.Along with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc), the ELN was the most important of the guerrilla groups. Founded in 1964, it fused Marxism-Leninism with Che Guevara’sfocotheory – the idea that a small armed band in a remote rural area can eventually topple the state – and Liberation theology, which framed the struggle against poverty and oppression as an expression of Christian faith.National Liberation Army (ELN) train in the Colombian JungleIn their pursuit of revolution, the two groups have carried out killings and kidnappings, and forced the confinement and displacement of civilian populations.The Farc demobilised in 2016 after striking a peace deal with the Colombian state, but the ELN says its members will only lay down arms after the country’s political and economic system has been transformed.“The Farc surrendered in exchange for nothing,” said Yerson, adding that subsequent presidents have failed to fully implement the peace deal, while former Farc combatants have been killed.View image in fullscreenA female member of the ELN’s Western War Front at a camp in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn ELN member at a camp in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe hands of a member of an ELN member who lost a finger after being bitten by a snake while living in the jungle.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianGustavo Petro, a leftist who was a guerrilla with the defunct M-19 in the 1980s, was elected president in 2022 on a promise of “total peace”, vowing to make good on the Farcdeal and negotiate with all of Colombia’s remaining armed groups on the left and right.But after a few years, almost all the talks – including those with thelargest groups – the ELN, the Gulf Clan and Farc dissidents who refused to demobilise in 2016 – either stalled or collapsed.Yerson rejected the idea that the election of Colombia’s first leftist president meant that the ELN’s goals could be achieved through the current political system.“They handed out lands [to the poor]. They did a kind of pension reform. They were looking for ways to improve healthcare,” he said. “But in the end these are small things. They don’t help with the popular awakening.”View image in fullscreenColombia’s president-elect, Abelardo de la Espriella, speaks at a security summit in Barranquilla.Photograph: Charlie Cordero/ReutersIn Yerson’s telling, Petro was allowed to take power by the “Colombian oligarchy”, which needed to pacify the people after an explosion of inequality protests in2019and2021, but knew he “was never going to undertake fundamental reforms, that he could be controlled”.Colombia’s political system “is not the democracy it claims to be”, he said. “That is where the trap is.”Now the ELN faces a very different proposition in the form of De la Espriella, a Trump-admiring millionaire whorose to prominence as a criminal lawyer representing accused leaders of the AUC, a rightwing paramilitary group that fought the guerrillas and killed civilians accused of collaborating with them..De la Espriella has given Colombia’s armed groups a month to submit to him or face the consequences, while promising to deepen security cooperation with the US and build mega-prisons inspired by the Salvadoran president, Nayib Bukele.Security analysts, however, say armed groups have gathered strength and resources in recent years. The ELN has about 6,300 members between armed fighters and unarmed support,spread across Colombia and Venezuela.View image in fullscreenCommander Yerson reads out the ELN’s regulations to at a camp in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn ELN member operates a drone during exercises at a camp in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn ELN member wearing camouflage used by the group’s snipers with a precision rifle at a camp in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianThe 60 or so fighters in the camp were evenly split between men and women, indigenous and Afro-Colombian members. “The majority [of the ELN] has always been the poor, the lowest down,” said Yerson. “Here, as Chocó is more Afro-Indigenous, that’s what we are.”Each of them had a modern assault rifle, either an AK-47 or an AR-15, some with “Made in USA” stamped on the body. One also had a .50 calibre sniper rifle, the bullets of which can punch through vehicles,while another flew a drone.The camp was deep in ELN territory, and they were relaxed. When someone took out a portable speaker and began to playvallenatos– popular Colombian folksongs – they left their rifles resting against trees or slung them over their backs and paired up to dance, suddenly looking like the young Colombians they are.National Liberation Army (ELN) dance during a break from trainingVarious groups, including the UN and Human Rights Watch, have accused the ELN of recruiting minors – but Yerson said their rules only allow people over 16 to join.It was impossible to verify details of his troops’ backgrounds, as they had been told not to discuss anything sensitive. Yerson presented two women to be interviewed in his presence, who spoke about the hardship of their lives before joining the ELN, but struggled to answer questions, apparently afraid of saying the wrong thing.Yerson himself described the ELN as “a life choice” for Colombia’s poor, who have few options. “Maybe that’s why they join, but once they are here they come to understand why we are fighting,” he said.The ELN functions by taxing “every commercial entity” in the territory it controls, and in Chocó that means illegal gold mining and logging are their key sources of income, said Yerson. It also carries out kidnappings for ransom.View image in fullscreenTwo ELN members rest on the forest floor at a camp in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA female ELN member combs her hair at a camp  in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn ELN member adjusts another’s beret before military exercises in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian“We are an embryonic state, and every state takes taxes,” he said. “If they can strangle us economically, we will cease to exist as a rebel organisation.”Yerson claimed coca cultivation has disappeared in ELN territory in Chocó. He denied the group was involved in the drug trafficking, but acknowledged it taxes the business like any other.The US, which has given its military a new role to take on “narcoterrorism” across theAmericas, might not think much of that distinction.“The question of guilt doesn’t matter to the US. What matters to them are interests,” said Yerson. “We are the only guerrilla group with political principles left standing in Colombia and the world. We will always be something they want to destroy.”He says the ELN will not simply be on the defensive, but will strike back where it can. A car bomb attributed to the group exploded outside a police station near the border with Venezuela last week, injuring 12 police officers and three civilians, and drone attacks have become common.View image in fullscreenELN members listen as Commander Yerson reads the group’s regulations at a camp in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA fire burns at night at a camp in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The GuardianView image in fullscreenELN members in thick vegetation near a camp in southern Chocó.Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian“They have to be legitimate objectives. We don’t put car bombs where the civil population will die,” said Yerson, who pointed to the 2019 suicide car bombing of a police academy in Bogotá that killed 22 as a model. “The comrades could go and make kamikaze attacks of that impact.”Despite the election of De la Espriella and other rightwing leaders across the continent, Yerson was adamant that the ELN was not losing the ideological battle.Voters are being deceived, he said, before quoting the South American revolutionary leader Simón Bolívar: “An ignorant people is the blind instrument of its own destruction.“The ideological battle is not being lost,” he repeated, as if irritated by the phrase. “We are on the right side of history.”Asked whether Colombia was any closer to the ELN’s goals after decades of conflict, Yerson was unsure: “I don’t know. But I can tell you that the only way to win things for the people is through the struggle,” he said. “We’ve been in the struggle for 62 years, and there will be many more.”

title: Haitians face arrest and deportation after US removes TPS protections | US immigration | The Guardian
description: DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin says ‘We’re going after them right now’ despite threat of violence in home country
Author: Alexandra Villarreal
Headline: DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin says ‘We’re going after them right now’ despite threat of violence in home country
Content: A person worships at the St Jerome Catholic church in the Little Haiti neighborhood of Brooklyn.Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/ReutersView image in fullscreenA person worships at the St Jerome Catholic church in the Little Haiti neighborhood of Brooklyn.Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/ReutersUS immigrationHaitians face arrest and deportation after US removes TPS protectionsDHS secretary Markwayne Mullin says ‘We’re going after them right now’ despite threat of violence in home countryAlexandra Villarrealin New YorkFri 7 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of thousands of Haitians are faced with the prospect of imminent risk of arrest and deportation – to a home countryrackedwith crime, violence and political unrest – after the Trump administration officiallystrippedthem of humanitarian protections that had allowed them to live and work legally in the United States for years.US district judge Ana Reyesconfirmedon Wednesday that her order blocking the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from ending temporary protected status (TPS) for Haiti was no longer in effect. This followed thecontroversialsupreme courtrulingin June thatupendedjudicial review of the program and opened the door for immigration enforcement to track down and detain Haitians en masse.Supreme court conservatives accused of advancing ‘white-supremacist agenda’Read more“We’re going after them right now,” the DHS secretary, Markwayne Mullin,saidearlier this week. “These individuals can either self-deport or we’ll arrest you and send you back. It’s that simple.”Enacted by Congress in 1990, TPS protects people who are already in the US when a natural disaster, epidemic, armed conflict or other extraordinary and temporary circumstance affects their country of origin, making it unsafe for them to return home.‘Devastating’: lives of nurses and patients upended by Trump migrant crackdownRead moreTPS holders are eligible for work permits and have added an estimated $262bn to the US economy since 2001, according to theFWD.usadvocacy organization, often pursuing careers in essential industries such as construction andhealth and elder care.But since returning to office last year, the Trump administration has almost categorically terminated existing TPS designations for some of the most dangerous countries in the world – a policy change that eventually led the highest court to authorize ending the program forHaitiandSyria, despiteboth countriesbeing on the state department’s “do not travel” advisory list.“In a stunning contradiction, the administration advises Americans against all travel toHaiti– and instructs those who go anyway to draft a will and submit DNA samples so their remains can be identified,” said Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of the immigrant-serving non-profit Global Refuge.He continued: “That is the government’s own assessment of the danger. To then compel hundreds of thousands of Haitians into such dire circumstances is an unconscionable abdication of our moral responsibility.”More than 300,000 Haitians havelost TPS permission overnightand could endure deportation if they have not applied for another form of immigration relief, such as asylum in the US or a green card. For a wide swathe of people, no suchpathwayto citizenship exists, even if they have lived in the US for decades.Even so, the thought of returning to Haiti’s life-threatening conditions is “unimaginable” for many Haitians in the US,PBS News reported.“It’s not that we don’t want to go back to Haiti,” said Harriett Cecilia Joseph, a former TPS holder. “It’s just the situation [there] doesn’t allow us to.”Already, removal orders for Haitians in the immigration courts have soared by 96% between March and June, according to theTransactional Records Access Clearinghouse(Trac). And immigration officials have startedoutfittingHaitians with ankle monitors to track their movements, making them easy to find and detain.“They now face an impossible choice: remain without status and risk arrest and deportation, or return to a Haiti marred by gang violence, kidnapping and the collapse of basic services,” said Vignarajah.Thousands of Syrians,although a much smaller group in the US than Haitians, may be at similar risk ofrepatriationafter losing TPS and their affiliated work permits. At the same time, a US district court on Wednesday alsoallowedthe federal government to end employment authorization foractive TPS holdersfrom El Salvador, Ukraine and Sudan, jeopardizing their livelihoods despite their ongoing protections against deportation.With so many immigrants suddenly barred from the workforce,business ownersare being forced to let go of employees in industries already hampered by significant labor shortages.Meanwhile, Haitians and their champions are calling on the US Senate to extend TPS legislatively, througha proposalthat already passed the House of Representatives in April.“We work hard, we pay our taxes, we give back to our communities and we are a big part of the engine that keeps the United States workforce in many essential industries moving,” Josiane Valsaint, a Haitian who had TPS,wrotefor the Guardian. “We deserve to stay here, with our families and loved ones.”Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationTrump administrationUS foreign policyHaitiUS politicsCaribbeanAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thailand school shooting: eight killed including suspected attacker, police say | Thailand | The Guardian
description: Teenager killed his grandparents ⁠before opening fire at school near Bangkok, where more than 30 were wounded
Author: Natasha May
Headline: Teenager killed his grandparents ⁠before opening fire at school near Bangkok, where more than 30 were wounded
Content: Schoolgirls being carried away from the scene of the shooting in Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi province.Photograph: Wason Wanichakorn/APView image in fullscreenSchoolgirls being carried away from the scene of the shooting in Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi province.Photograph: Wason Wanichakorn/APThailandThailand school shooting: eight killed including suspected attacker, police sayTeenager killed his grandparents ⁠before opening fire at school near Bangkok, where more than 30 were woundedNatasha Mayin BangkokFri 7 Aug 2026 10.16 EDTFirst published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 00.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Thai teenager killed his grandparents before opening fire at his school, where he shot five people dead and took his own life, police have said, in an attack that has shaken a country struggling to deal with gun violence.The 14-year-old wounded more than 30 people in the ⁠shooting at the prestigious Debsirin Nonthaburi school northwest of Bangkok. Nine people were in a critical condition, the Thai health department said.For Prompong Namwong, an English teacher at the school, it was a normal morning until a panicked student from another class flung open the door, trying to find somewhere to hide. In the corridor, Prompong heard other teachers shouting that there had been a mass shooting downstairs.View image in fullscreenPrompong Namwong.Photograph: Natasha MayWhen Prompong recounted the ordeal to the Guardian, he hesitated between calling the 14-year-old, whom he saw run in front of his classroom, “killer” or “student”.At that moment, “I thought I was going to die, for sure,” he said.The suspected attacker fired at least 26 bullets with a gun belonging to his grandfather, and was found with 34 additional ammunition rounds.1:06Students seek safety during Thai school shooting – videoThe suspected shooter remained inside the school after reports of the attack emerged, Arsit Sampantharat, the permanent secretary of the interior ministry, told PPTV.A lockdown at the school was declared over in about half an hour. Prompong said that when he heard a knock, he thought it was the end of his life, but instead it was the police coming to their rescue.Images from the scene showed students running with only socks on their feet as they were evacuated from the school.Locator mapThe children, as is customary across Asia, had taken their shoes off outside their classrooms, but in the panic to escape the grounds, the shoes were left strewn around lunch tables and the stairs outside classrooms.By the afternoon, the sports area where the students would usually have been playing was filled with officials and the media, as the country’s leader vowed to implement new gun laws.The prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, told reporters the new law would allow only government officials on duty to carry guns, but did not provide any ⁠specifics, including whether the legislation would tighten gun ownership requirements.Thailand has thehighest rate of civilian gun ownership in south-east Asia, and in 2017 the Switzerland-based Small Arms Survey placed the country 13th worldwide for small-gun possession.A number of mass shootings have occurred in recent years in Thailand, including incidents at schools and a large Bangkok mall, and a 2022 attack in the country’s north-east that ‌killed 37 people including 22 children.The country’s licensing regime still lacks mental health screening for people applying to have a ⁠gun and does not require periodic reassessments ​for licence holders, according to Piyaporn Tunneekul, an ​associate professor at Nakhon Pathom Rajabhat University in Thailand.View image in fullscreenPolice at the scene in Bang Kruai district.Photograph: Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP/Getty ImagesPichanan Thiengtham was in the teachers’ lounge when she heard the shots at about 10am. But she said she could not believe at first that it was a gun: “There were so many shots and they lasted for a long time without stopping.”It was only when the art teacher saw one of the injured students that she realised what was happening. “I took the injured student to get first aid and then transferred them to the hospital [in the school] building.”Kiatikhun Verapongpradith, an emergency worker, described arriving as the shooting was taking place. He said his team had treated students with injuries to the back, chest and arms.They found a male teacher lying dead on an upper floor of the school, and in another room they found a female teacher with wounds to her chest and arm, Kiatikhun said.View image in fullscreenAn injured teacher receiving medical attention at the scene on the outskirts of Bangkok.Photograph: Chalinee Thirasupa/ReutersThe school is part of the Debsirin network, founded by the Thai royal family. Its alumni include prime ministers, scholars and writers.Prompong found out in the school’s group chat that some of his friends had not survived. “They’re all good teachers. I don’t know what to say.”He said: “My life has to go on, but right now … it’s a very great shock. I never thought to myself that it would happen – really happen – in my school.”Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsThailandGun crimeAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: David Brat bound for Australia as diplomat confirmed as next US ambassador | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: Former Republican state congressman, who once argued Christianity and capitalism should merge, confirmed by US Senate to fill long-vacant role
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Former Republican state congressman, who once argued Christianity and capitalism should merge, confirmed by US Senate to fill long-vacant role
Content: David Brat as a Republican congressman in 2014. The US Senate has confirmed him as the next US ambassador to Australia.Photograph: Steve Helber/APView image in fullscreenDavid Brat as a Republican congressman in 2014. The US Senate has confirmed him as the next US ambassador to Australia.Photograph: Steve Helber/APAustralian politicsDavid Brat bound for Australia as diplomat confirmed as next US ambassadorFormer Republican state congressman, who once argued Christianity and capitalism should merge, confirmed by US Senate to fill long-vacant roleGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorFri 7 Aug 2026 19.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 19.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFormer Virginia congressman David Brat has been confirmed by the US Senate to be the next US ambassador to Australia, after the role had been left vacant for 18 months.Brat’s confirmation was among more than 70 votes pushed through the Senate by Republicans on Friday, Washington time, before the summer recess.Brat was nominated by Donald Trumpin April. The 61-year-old served two terms in Congress until 2018 when he was defeated by a Democrat, and was vice-president of business relations at Virginia’s Liberty University.The ambassador role had been vacant since November 2024, when Joe Biden’s ambassador, Caroline Kennedy, left the post.Anthony Albanese in April said he would work with anyone Trump nominated, when asked to respond to Brat’s earlier claims that US intelligence agencies conspired to remove Trump from office.“We respect the sovereignty of countries to put forward ambassadors just like we expect our choices to be endorsed,” he said at the time.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailBrat was described by Time magazine in 2010 as a “Tea Party professor” and an enthusiast of the author Ayn Rand.In a 2011 paper, he argued that capitalism and Christianity should merge, writing: “If we all did the right thing and had the guts to spread the word, we would not need the government to backstop every action we take.”Brat was swept into the Senate in 2014 when he defeated the then House of Representatives majority leader, Eric Cantor, in a primary. He lost his seat in 2018 to Democrat Abigail Spanberger, who is now the governor of Virginia.The confirmation comes amid tense US-Australia relations, with Trump levelling12.5% tariffs on many Australian exportsin July. Australia was on a list of 54 economies hit with the tariffs due to what the US claimed was a failure “to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor”.At the time, the trade minister, Don Farrell, called for the tariffs to be removed, saying they were inconsistent with Australia’s free-trade agreement with the US.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDavid Brat, Ayn Rand expert who once argued Christianity and capitalism should merge, named as US ambassador to AustraliaRead moreBrat’s arrival in Australia will coincide with the 75th anniversary of the Anzus treaty, a security pact over defence of the Pacific, and comes after the Albanese government announced in May it would instead buythree second-hand American nuclear submarinesas part of the $370bn Aukus deal, instead of two second-hand and one new as originally intended.While the Albanese government has remained supportive of Aukus, there has been growing disquiet from some within Labor about the plan.Former cabinet minister Ed Husic said in Junethat the change meant “we are not going to get the deal that was promised to us”.The former defence secretary Greg Moriartyhas been Australia’s representative in Washingtonsince taking over from former prime minister Kevin Rudd in April.Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsLabor partyAukusAnthony AlbanesenewsShareReuse this content

title: Dogs to be euthanised after man dies following suspected animal attack at rural Sydney property  | New South Wales | The Guardian
description: Police say body of 23-year-old found at Eschol Park property with significant injuries, indicating he may have been attacked before death
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Police say body of 23-year-old found at Eschol Park property with significant injuries, indicating he may have been attacked before death
Content: NSW police found a dead man at an Eschol Park property in Sydney after a suspected dog attack.Photograph: David Gray/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNSW police found a dead man at an Eschol Park property in Sydney after a suspected dog attack.Photograph: David Gray/AFP/Getty ImagesNew South WalesDogs to be euthanised after man dies following suspected animal attack at rural Sydney propertyPolice say body of 23-year-old found at Eschol Park property with significant injuries, indicating he may have been attacked before deathFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressFri 7 Aug 2026 04.40 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 21.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA group of dogs has been taken to a shelter to be euthanised after a young man died following a suspected dog attack at a ruralSydneyproperty.Authorities were alerted to the discovery of the 23-year-old’s body at a rural property in Sydney’s south-west on Wednesday. Police found the body with what they described as significant injuries and established a crime scene.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“Initial inquiries indicate the man may have been attacked by animals prior to his death,”New South Walespolice said in a statement.Campbelltown investigators and council rangers attended an Eschol Park property on Friday morning and seized five dogs, who were taken to the animal shelter to be euthanised, police said.According to Sydney radio station 2GB, none of the animals were registered or microchipped.NSW police said a 53-year-old man was also treated at the scene for a minor hand injury.The NSW police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, said the reasons behind the 23-year-old’s presence at the house was unclear.“We don’t know the circumstances by which the male was on the premises,” he told reporters.“He certainly doesn’t appear to be a resident of that location.”Guardian Australia understands the incident occurred at a house on Badgally Road known as Saturn’s Rings or the Universal Power House.Based on the rings of Saturn, the circular building was designed by Stefan Dzwonnik in the 1970s and intended to serve as a home for him and his family, according to theCampbelltown City Library.MapBut Saturn’s Rings was never completed, and Dzwonnik died in 2018, according to the library.The Campbelltown council said it was assisting police.“Council is supporting police inquiries and will continue to assist as required, in accordance with its legislative responsibilities, including determining the registration and ownership status of the dogs,” a spokesperson said.Inquiries are ongoing and a report will be prepared for the coroner.Achol Arok contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsNew South WalesSydneynewsShareReuse this content

title: Complainant wants to ‘humiliate’ Alan Jones by revealing intimate details of alleged assaults, defence tells court | Alan Jones trial | The Guardian
description: Barrister alleges ‘account of penis wiggling is an attempt to humiliate’ broadcaster who has pleaded not guilty to 22 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching
Author: Amanda Meade
Headline: Barrister alleges ‘account of penis wiggling is an attempt to humiliate’ broadcaster who has pleaded not guilty to 22 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching
Content: Alan Jones (left) arrives at a Sydney court on Friday. He has denied indecently assaulting and sexually touching six men.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreenAlan Jones (left) arrives at a Sydney court on Friday. He has denied indecently assaulting and sexually touching six men.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPAlan Jones trialComplainant wants to ‘humiliate’ Alan Jones by revealing intimate details of alleged assaults, defence tells courtBarrister alleges ‘account of penis wiggling is an attempt to humiliate’ broadcaster who has pleaded not guilty to 22 charges of indecent assault and sexual touchingGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAmanda MeadeFri 7 Aug 2026 04.38 EDTFirst published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 01.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlan Jones’s defence barrister has told a Sydney court one of the broadcaster’s alleged victims invented details of alleged indecent assaults at a Fitzroy Falls farm to “humiliate” and “smear” the former media titan.Complainant J told the court during evidence-in-chief earlier this week that during one alleged incident in the property’s bedroom, Jones’s penis was not fully erect and “not very big”.On Friday, J, during cross-examination, denied fabricating his account of alleged indecent assaults at Jones’s farm in the southern highlands more than 20 years ago.Complainant J, aged in his 40s, is the first alleged victim to give evidence in the trial at Downing Centre local court. Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty to 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges involving six men.J this week alleged in court he did not consent to a kiss near the farm’s pigsty, the touching of his penis on a lounge room couch or sexual touching in the guest bedroom.Alan Jones’s alleged victim denies ‘fabricating’ claims against broadcaster during robust cross-examinationRead moreUnder cross-examination by defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC, complainant J on Friday denied inventing details about Jones’s genitals to humiliate the older man.Bashir asked: “This account you’ve given of ‘penis wiggling’ is an attempt to humiliate Mr Jones, isn’t it?”“No,” J replied.Bashir suggested in court that it was “an attempt to smear him, isn’t it?” J again said: “No.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailJ has previously alleged that when visiting the farm as a teenager, he heard a “tap, tap, tap” before Jones came into the bedroom. He told the court that, while they were both wearing robes, Jones wiggled his hips so their penises crossed.Bashir said: “You cast yourself as ‘impressive’ and Alan as not achieving an erection as part of the humiliation you are trying to describe, didn’t you? So too your comment on Tuesday that ‘it wasn’t very big’.”“No,” J replied in court on Friday.Bashir alleged: “You wouldn’t know because you have never seen Mr Jones’s penis.”Complainant J then said: “Yes, I have.” J said that Jones had remarked that the then teenager’s penis was “impressive”.He had earlier told the court that Jones’s penis was circumcised and his genitals were hairy. Bashir suggested that he guessed the details because circumcision was likely for an “Anglo-Saxon man of his age – and so too the hair on the genitals”.J disagreed that he had guessed.Throughout the cross-examination, Bashir alleged that J was forgetting key details because he had made the whole thing up.Bashir told the court: “Are you making your evidence up as you go along?”“No,” complainant J replied.Bashir challenged J’s memory of his visits to the southern highlands property in the mid-2000s, suggesting in court that he had mixed up occasions, dates and fellow guests.J agreed that his family was invited to visit the property, and he accompanied them. Bashir said there were inconsistencies in his police statement and his evidence in court regarding how many nights he stayed and which vehicle he drove.Bashir questioned J in detail about an alleged kiss by Jones while the two men were looking at a pigsty on the farm.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBashir told the court: “There was no kiss at the pigsty. It was a fabrication.”J replied: “No, it wasn’t.”The defence barrister said if J was afraid of being assaulted, as he claimed, he didn’t have to walk into the lounge room wearing a robe after Jones instructed him to shower and come back wearing the robe and nothing else.She pointed to inconsistencies between his police statement and evidence-in-chief.Bashir said: “There is nothing in your statement about a robe.” J replied: “I remember he was in a robe.”Bashir suggested he read about Jones wearing a robe in the media. J denied this but agreed there was no mention of Jones wearing a robe in his statement.The defence barrister said J’s account of the alleged assaults did not make sense because he was young and fit – and he could have pushed the older Jones away.Bashir asked if Jones had ever threatened to withdraw his stipend and J said no.Bashir said: “He never said to you he would pull the money if you didn’t do what he wanted, did he?” J replied: “No.”J agreed that there were “no repercussions” when he couldn’t make invitations from Jones and that Jones didn’t ask him for favours in return for financial supportBashir said: “All Mr Jones asked of you was that you dedicate yourself to your career.” J told the court: “That’s not all he asked me.”Bashir closed her cross-examination with two final questions.Bashir said: “Alan Jones never kissed you indecently.”J replied: “Yes, he did”Bashir said: “Alan Jones never indecently touched you.”J said: “Yes, he did.”The trial continues on Tuesday with J returning to the witness stand for a sixth day for a re-examination by the crown. There is a break in evidence on Monday.Explore more on these topicsAlan Jones trialAlan JonesAustralian medianewsShareReuse this content

title: Businessman was ‘preparing champagne’ to celebrate Caruana Galizia murder, court hears | Daphne Caruana Galizia | The Guardian
description: Taxi driver says he acted as middleman between Yorgen Fenech and three men already convicted of €150,000 contract killing
Author: Juliette Garside
Headline: Taxi driver says he acted as middleman between Yorgen Fenech and three men already convicted of €150,000 contract killing
Content: Melvin Theuma, centre, pictured in 2019, says he acted as a middleman in a plot to murder of journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.Photograph: Vincent Kessler/ReutersView image in fullscreenMelvin Theuma, centre, pictured in 2019, says he acted as a middleman in a plot to murder of journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.Photograph: Vincent Kessler/ReutersDaphne Caruana GaliziaBusinessman was ‘preparing champagne’ to celebrate Caruana Galizia murder, court hearsTaxi driver says he acted as middleman between Yorgen Fenech and three men already convicted of €150,000 contract killingJuliette GarsideFri 7 Aug 2026 13.40 EDTFirst published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe businessman accused of paying for hitmen to murder the journalistDaphne Caruana Galiziawas impatient for the killing to take place, and once texted from his boat to say he was “preparing champagne” to celebrate, a jury inMaltahas heard.Yorgen Fenech, the 44-year-old heir to a property empire that includes several Hilton hotels, is on trial in Malta for complicity in the murder of Caruana Galizia. She died in a car bombing in October 2017 after publishing a series of revelations about senior politicians that were so damaging they triggered a snap general election.The key witness in the case, a taxi driver who says he acted as middleman between Fenech and three men already convicted of accepting €150,000 (£128,000) to carry out the killing, took the stand on Friday to begin his testimony.Melvin Theuma, who has been living under witness protection since agreeing to testify in return for a pardon, said Fenech had told him to contact a known criminal and set up the killing because he wanted to protect his uncle Raymond Fenech, the head of the family business.View image in fullscreenFlowers placed in front of a portrait of murdered journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia during a vigil outside the law courts in Valletta, Malta.Photograph: Jonathan Borg/AP“Bring him here, I need him to kill Daphne because she’s going to publish information about Uncle Ray,” Theuma claimed Fenech had told him.Theuma has previously testified that over time the explanation changed, and the hit was designed to stop revelations about Yorgen himself.The conversation took place in April 2017. The two men were friends, having known each other for years, although Theuma told the jury it was not an equal relationship.“He’s a lion and I’m a mosquito,” Theuma said of the accused.The taxi driver, who had cultivated a friendship with Fenech over a shared interest in horseracing and betting, is regarded by the prosecution as key to securing a conviction. He has given police multiple recordings of conversations he had with Fenech after the murder.Before taking the stand, Theuma had to be certified as fit to give evidence, having previously tried to take his own life. In 2020, having already secured a pardon, he swallowed acid and slit his own throat. He will be allowed to give evidence seated, with his back to Fenech and his lawyers, having previously complained of intimidation.He began his testimony by apologising to the victim’s family, saying: “My cross was too much to bear; I can’t imagine what theirs was like.”After receiving the order from Fenech, Theuma said he went to the docks in Marsa, where the hitmen, brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio and their associate Vincent Muscat, used a warehouse known as the potato shed as a base.“Alfred got into my taxi and I told him ‘I have someone who wants to kill Daphne Caruana Galizia’.“He asked if the person could pay, and I said yes, of course.”View image in fullscreenYorgen Fenech pictured in 2019. He is on trial in Malta for complicity in the murder of Caruana Galizia.Photograph: Yara Nardi/ReutersTheuma said he never told the hitmen who had sent him. He told the court Fenech had agreed to the price, but then asked him to call off the attack after Malta’s then prime minister, Joseph Muscat, called a snap general election. Instead, he asked Theuma to place a €150,000 bet for him on Muscat securing a second term.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen Muscat was returned to power with a landslide victory in June 2017, Theuma said Fenech rang him that night. “He sounded tipsy. He told me to go ahead with the Daphne job. I didn’t do anything, he sounded drunk.”A few days later, he gave Fenech his winnings from the bet – €300,000, minus a commission. Nothing more was said about Caruana Galizia. But a few days later, Fenech summoned him and gave him an envelope stuffed with cash. “I asked him, ‘What’s this?’ He said: ‘It’s the €150,000 to have Daphne killed.’”The hitmen were given a €30,000 deposit and began scoping the journalist’s movements. Theuma was given a burner phone to contact them with. The witness said he took the phone with him to Disneyland for a family holiday, and that Fenech wanted reassurance he had not left Malta without it. The businessman became impatient as time passed.“Yorgen would ask me every few days: ‘When will they kill her?’ Once, he was on his boat and texted me to say he was preparing champagne in case it happened.”Theuma said Fenech helped to plot Caruana Galizia’s routine, identifying a cafe and restaurant that she frequented.Maltese politicians ‘involved’ in plot to kill Daphne Caruana Galizia, court hearsRead moreThe witness broke down as he described the moment he learned of the death from the television news. Wiping his eyes, he said: “I was living a normal life, I didn’t want for anything. Then I turned on the TV and saw that Daphne was dead. My life ended. When she was killed, my life was blown up.”He also revealed he had been in regular contact by text message with Caruana Galizia’s sons, Matthew and Paul. He said: “I was involved in their mother’s murder, and they speak to me. They tell me I will feel better after the trial. But I know I won’t. The remorse is too great.”Fenech, who is on trial for complicity in the voluntary homicide of Caruana Galizia, denies the charges. The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsDaphne Caruana GaliziaMaltaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia-linked accounts spread far-right narrative online during Ceuta migration crisis, analysis finds | Social media | The Guardian
description: Counter-disinformation group says social media channels connected to Pravda network helped amplify message
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Counter-disinformation group says social media channels connected to Pravda network helped amplify message
Content: Migrants cross into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in north Africa last month.Photograph: Jon Nazca/ReutersView image in fullscreenMigrants cross into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in north Africa last month.Photograph: Jon Nazca/ReutersSocial mediaRussia-linked accounts spread far-right narrative online during Ceuta migration crisis, analysis findsCounter-disinformation group says social media channels connected to Pravda network helped amplify messageAisha DownFri 7 Aug 2026 12.35 EDTFirst published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 10.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAccounts with links to the Russian military promoting far-right messages reached more than 500,000 people inthe days following the mass influx of people into Ceuta, according to an analysis by 411, a counter-disinformation group.Russia-linked social media accounts frequently spread destabilising narratives inEurope, often promoting far-right talking points about immigration.But 411 and other experts suggest the scale and coordination of the disinformation that followed the Ceuta crisis is significant. Groups spreading disinformation are more organised and powerful than they were several years ago.“We keep seeing this across Europe and we find it very interesting. It seems like there is some type of machinery in place, or structure,” said Saman Nazari, the lead researcher at Alliance4Europe, a Brussels-based nonprofit.“Quite regularly, we are seeing this escalation happening across Europe now, with these types of crises. It is too much of a coincidence to be a bandwagoning effect.”10:29How Ceuta migrant crisis exposes divisions within Europe - The LatestThe barrage began on 1 August, the day after tens of thousands of people reportedly attempted to cross into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta fromMoroccoovernight. This was part of a larger, multi-day crisis during which 72,000 migrants are estimated to have made their way into the small territory in north Africa, the vast majority of whom were swiftly returned.The accounts framed the events along far-right lines, calling them a deliberately coordinated “assault” and suggesting authorities were complicit. Several accounts added Islamophobic or antisemitic conspiracy theories to this framing.These narratives were rapidly reproduced in seven languages and reached more than 720,000 views over the course of six hours on 1 August, according to 411’s examination of roughly 4.5m social media posts.Other far-right accounts called for nationalists to gather in Ceuta and “patrol” businesses and homes, with some apparently coordinating their efforts.Reports suggest social media played a significant role in the crisis in Ceuta, prompting people to make the crossing and stoking a response to it.Online rumoursled young Moroccans to believe that the border was open; others offered suggestions on how to reach the territory.The analysis by 411 confirmed reports that there was substantive “peer-to-peer logistics chatter” between potential migrants on social media over how to make the crossing. Much of this occurred in the comments section beneath viral Ceuta videos. This coordination among migrants appeared to be organic, coming “overwhelmingly from small, anonymous-looking individual accounts rather than any single identifiable ‘recruiter’ channel”.A separate, rightwing backlash began on social media as the crossings continued. One origin of the propaganda barrage was Rybar, a Telegram channel withlinks to Russian intelligence. Rybar’s parent company has faced sanctions in Europe.A network of “repeater” accounts then amplified and spread Rybar’s posts. These included accounts linked to thePravda network, an operation spreading Kremlin propaganda worldwide.View image in fullscreenMigrant children queue outside a police station to be registered in Ceuta on Thursday.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersNazari suggested that disinformation efforts appeared coordinated and that investigations should be made to determine if there were closed forums or similar structures in which far-right influencers discuss how to spread talking points.Ned Mendez, the lead researcher at 411, said disinformation about the Ceuta crisis spread far more quickly than it did in May 2021, during a similar incident in which 8,000 migrants crossed the same border from Morocco intoSpain.‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon ValleyRead moreThe far right also seized on those events, but this time the amplification of far-right narratives happened more swiftly. The far-right mobilisation calls brought nationalist groups to the main square of Ceuta within days, 411 noted. In 2021, similar calls went out but it took much longer for nationalists to mobilise.“You could compare the process to a highly specific and organised information superhighway,” said Mendez. “If a piece of content or disinformation is placed on to that privileged superhighway, then it will receive a degree of amplification and boost that other types of content just don’t have access to. Events like this across Europe suggest that some pieces of content are being selected for the onramp, and those content pieces share similar characteristics.”The 411 analysis said: “That machinery is the real thing to worry about, more than this particular crisis. The next time there’s a border incident anywhere on the Mediterranean, those same relay networks are already in place, ready to pick it up and run with it again.”Additional reporting by Majida ChowdhuryExplore more on these topicsSocial mediaMigrationThe far rightSpainMoroccoRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Scramble to house hundreds camping in Rome heatwave after squat eviction | Italy | The Guardian
description: Officials try to find homes for residents as talks to save social assistance hub collapse amid government crackdown
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Officials try to find homes for residents as talks to save social assistance hub collapse amid government crackdown
Content: While some people were accommodated by friends and family, more than 200 have been sleeping in tents outside the building.Photograph: Claudia DeganuttiView image in fullscreenWhile some people were accommodated by friends and family, more than 200 have been sleeping in tents outside the building.Photograph: Claudia DeganuttiItalyScramble to house hundreds camping in Rome heatwave after squat evictionOfficials try to find homes for residents as talks to save social assistance hub  collapse amid government crackdownAngela Giuffridain RomeFri 7 Aug 2026 08.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRome authorities are scrambling to find homes for hundreds of peoplesleeping in tents in extreme heatafter talks aimed at saving Italy’s most high-profile centre for housing and social assistance collapsed amid a crackdown by Giorgia Meloni’s government on squatted buildings.The approximately 400 evicted residents of Spin Time Labs, located in a 10-floor building in Rome’s Esquilino district occupied by grassroots groups since 2013, will not be allowed to move back in after its private owner refused Rome council’s offer to buy the property. The residents were forced out at the end of last month.A spokesperson for Italy’s interior ministry, which had set its sights on shutting down Spin Time, confirmed that the owner had taken repossession of the building “in accordance with the law”.View image in fullscreenFormer residents of the Spin Time Labs building are sleeping in tents in extreme heat.Photograph: Claudia DeganuttiThe move has reignited political debate over occupied or squatted buildings, which Meloni’s government regard as dens for criminality – including those supported by leftwing associations. Critics have questioned why Meloni and her coalition allies have long been so decisively against Spin Time while the neofascist CasaPound has occupied a state-owned building in the same neighbourhood for more than 20 years, using the premises as its headquarters.People of all nationalities, about a quarter of them children, were forced to evacuate Spin Time on 29 July after a minor fire, which was quickly extinguished by a group of residents before it could spread.The building was locked up by police during safety checks, before being placed under two judicial seizure orders – one linked to the owner’s long-running legal battle to regain possession and the other to the fire.While some people were accommodated by friends and family, more than 200, including elderly people and those with ill health, have been sleeping in tents outside the building. One child was hospitalised this week after suffering breathing difficulties.View image in fullscreenThe Spin Time building was locked up by police amid safety checks before being placed under two judicial seizure orders.Photograph: Claudia DeganuttiRome’s leftwing council, supported by the Catholic church-run charity Caritas, is now seeking alternative solutions.In an interview on In Onda, a talkshow broadcast on the TV channel LA7, the mayor of Rome, Roberto Gualtieri, said the response to the council’s offer had been an “irrevocable no” and that despite presenting what he believed was the best possible deal he “had the impression that the decision had already been taken”.The owner had cited unspecified legal weaknesses in the proposal, Gualtieri said, adding that he felt “irritated” about the situation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenRome’s leftwing council is seeking alternative solutions for the former residents.Photograph: Claudia DeganuttiHe described Spin Time, which over the past decade has transformed into a space offering various social and cultural services, including a food bank, a restaurant and co-working, as “the mirror of a failure of Italy’s Second Republic, which stripped away a pillar of welfare”. The Second Republic is a political term for the era of government that began in the early 1990s.The initiative has provided a lifeline for hundreds of people, including Marco Perilli, an Italian construction worker who was one of the community’s first residents. He became homeless after a divorce.As of Friday, people were still camped outside. Perilli said they would continue to do so until a real solution was found. “We are trying to understand how things will proceed but we resist and will continue to resist. The owner refusing the offer means Spin Time is over, but for us it’s not over – we will find another space.”Explore more on these topicsItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Weather tracker: central and western Europe brace for more sweltering heat  | Extreme weather | The Guardian
description: High 30s celsius forecast for France, Spain and Italy next week, before affecting Germany, Poland and Czechia
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: High 30s celsius forecast for France, Spain and Italy next week, before affecting Germany, Poland and Czechia
Content: Low water levels in the Rhine River caused by hot weather and prolonged drought in Düsseldorf, Germany.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APView image in fullscreenLow water levels in the Rhine River caused by hot weather and prolonged drought in Düsseldorf, Germany.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APExtreme weatherAnalysisWeather tracker: central and western Europe brace for more sweltering heatEd WaltonHigh 30s celsius forecast for France, Spain and Italy next week, before affecting Germany, Poland and CzechiaFri 7 Aug 2026 07.59 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 12.14 EDTShareAnother pulse of heat is expected to affect central and westernEuropenext week. The latest forecast models show daily maximum temperatures well into the high 30s celsius widely across France, Spain and Italy during the first half of the week, while Germany, Poland and Czechiawill experience the highest temperatures towards the end of the week. The shift in the focus of the heat as the week progresses can be attributed to the movement of high pressure. At the start of the week, low pressure centred in the Atlantic and high pressure centred over the low countries will draw warm air from southern Europe northwards into parts of France. During the working week, the high pressure will slip a little farther south and east, enabling the warm air once situated over western Europe to make inroads into parts of Germany and central Europe.The heat in central and western Europe this summer has been unrelenting. Last week’sweather trackerhighlighted record-breaking temperatures for the month of July in Austria. However, only a few days later, on 4 August, the all-time record was shattered with 41.0C achieved in Stammersdorf, north-east of the capital, Vienna. This comfortably broke the previous all-time record set in August 2003 by 0.7C. Unbelievably, that record was broken again the following day when 41.2C was recorded in Deutsch-Altenburg. Slovakia also set an all-time record on the same day, of 41.4C. The continuing European heatwave, associated with a vertically extensive anticyclone, raised the freezing level above 4,000 metres across much of the Alpine region. This represents a level in the atmosphere well above many Alpine glaciers, accelerating the seasonal melting process. On the opposite side of the Atlantic, 51.8C was recorded in Badwater, California, the highest temperature in the US for 2026 so far.Although south-eastern parts of Europe have eluded the worst of the summer heat, wildfires have ignited in recent days. Extremely strong northerly wind gusts in excess of 70mph ripped through the Greek Islands on 29 July, causing medium-voltage power lines to sway and produce sparks that set fire to vegetation below. Part of the palm forest at Preveli beach, Crete, was damaged by a wildfire but the centre of the forest was spared from the worst of the destruction.Explore more on these topicsExtreme weatherEuropeanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Buried for not being Brueghel: overlooked masterpiece by still-life pioneer discovered in storage area | Art | The Guardian
description: The curator of Norway’s national museum in Oslo is bringing the work by the Flemish baroque artist Clara Peeters out of obscurity in a major exhibition of female artists
Author: Joanna Moorhead
Headline: The curator of Norway’s national museum in Oslo is bringing the work by the Flemish baroque artist Clara Peeters out of obscurity in a major exhibition of female artists
Content: Revivified … Still Life with Small Game and Grapes on a Gilded Tazza by Clara Peeters, c1620, Nasjonalmuseet, Oslo.Photograph: Børre Høstland/The National MuseumView image in fullscreenRevivified … Still Life with Small Game and Grapes on a Gilded Tazza by Clara Peeters, c1620, Nasjonalmuseet, Oslo.Photograph: Børre Høstland/The National MuseumArtBuried for not being Brueghel: overlooked masterpiece by still-life pioneer discovered in storage areaThe curator of Norway’s national museum in Oslo is bringing the work by the Flemish baroque artist Clara Peeters out of obscurity in a major exhibition of female artistsJoanna MoorheadFri 7 Aug 2026 04.51 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 05.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnonymous was often a woman: so said Virginia Woolf. And so thought Cynthia Osiecki one day in 2022, when she chanced on an unattributed still life in the storage area of the National Museum ofNorwayin Oslo.Osiecki had been studying the work of a renowned 17th-century Flemish artist, Clara Peeters, one of the earliest practitioners of still life painting. Works by Peeters hang in the Prado in Madrid, the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford and the Metropolitan Museum in New York.The Oslo painting, Still Life with Small Game and Grapes on a Gilded Tazza, was created around 1620 and features nine freshly dead birds, hazelnuts, apricots and a fly perched on a bunch of grapes. It had once been regarded as the work of a member of a famous family of Antwerp artists, Ambrosius Brueghel. But in the early 20th century the attribution was reassessed, and the work reclassified as being by “anonymous”. Since then it had mostly been consigned to storage.Osiecki began to wonder whether the work – some details of which have been obscured by many layers of varnish – could be by Peeters, an enigmatic but prolific artist who pushed the boundaries of still life painting in the Northern European baroque period. Osiecki began to compare the work with other pieces by the painter, who is thought to have been born in Antwerp around 1594. “I looked at the panel the Oslo work is painted on, and discovered it was from a supplier Peeters often used,” she says. “Then I looked at other paintings by Peeters, and I noticed some of them had atazza[a saucer-like dish on a pedestal] very similar to the one in the Oslo painting.” Osiecki noticed, too, similarities in the way the dead birds, the grapes and the hazelnuts were positioned in the composition.One problem, though, was that Peeters was well known for signing her works, and the Oslo piece had no signature. But the panel had been damaged by woodworm, and the area eaten away was the bottom edge of the work – the very area where Peeters usually signed her pieces.View image in fullscreenAlongside Peeters … Judith and her Maidservant with the Head of Holofernes byArtemisia Gentileschi, c1640.Photograph: Børre Høstland Annar Bjørgli/Kunstner: Gentileschi ArtemisiaIt seemed more and more likely that the painting was a work by Peeters – but a piece of the jigsaw was missing. Peeters is famous for including miniature self-portraits in her work, often reflections of herself in pewter or glass objects, or on shiny fruit or vegetables. “I could see a shape on some of the grapes, and on closer examination I realised they look like outlines of human figures,” says Osiecki. These might be the artist herself, and it could be that the image has been lost during conservation work.Earlier this year the painting was officially reattributed to Peeters, and it will be one of the star exhibits inWomanPainterat the National Museum of Norway opening 8 October, curated by Osiecki.
