The show features the work of female artists working across northern Europe and Italy between 1550 and 1650, with paintings by 19 artists including Artemisia Gentileschi, Lavinia Fontana and Judith Leyster, as well as Clara Peeters.Peeters was known for intimate still lifes reflecting the transience of this world, says Osiecki. “Her paintings, including the newly attributed work, are all about the brevity of life. We see recently dead birds, who will be part of a feast for humans, and grapes that will soon either be eaten or will decay. And though the work includes luxurious objects such as thetazza, Peeters is making the point that you can’t take anything with you when you die. In the end we’re all equal.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe reattributed work demonstrates how art history is expanding to include women whose work has been lost or ignored, says Nora Ceciliedatter Nerdrum, director of exhibitions and collections at the National Museum of Norway. Over recent years, Europe’s major museums have been opening up to shows of women’s work – in 2016, Peeters became the first woman ever to be given a solo show at the Prado.Nerdrum agrees that the quest to correct the omission of women from the canon of art history began by retrieving known works by women from storage; now, the search is on for women whose work has been labelled “anonymous”. “Watch this space, because there will be lots more of these finds in the future,” says Osiecki. “The more we look, the more archival research we do, the more women we’re going to find.”Explore more on these topicsArtNorwayEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel indicts settler over death of Palestinian activist who worked on No Other Land | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Yinon Levy charged with manslaughter in first exception this decade to culture of impunity for Israelis who kill Palestinians in the occupied West Bank
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Yinon Levy charged with manslaughter in first exception this decade to culture of impunity for Israelis who kill Palestinians in the occupied West Bank
Content: A demonstrator holds a photo of Awdah Hathaleen during an August 2025 protest in Tel Aviv over his death.Photograph: Tamir Kalifa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA demonstrator holds a photo of Awdah Hathaleen during an August 2025 protest in Tel Aviv over his death.Photograph: Tamir Kalifa/Getty ImagesWest BankIsrael indicts settler over death of Palestinian activist who worked on No Other LandYinon Levy charged with manslaughter in first exception this decade to culture of impunity for Israelis who kill Palestinians in the occupied West BankEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemFri 7 Aug 2026 09.49 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 10.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProsecutors in Israel have indicted an extremist settler for shooting a Palestinian activist last July, the first attempt this decade to hold an Israeli responsible for killing a Palestinian in the occupiedWest Bank.Yinon Levy, who was under western sanctions, is charged with manslaughter over the death of Awdeh Hathaleen, an English teacher and peace activist. In his last moments, Hathaleenfilmedthe settler drawing his weapon and opening fire towards him.Hathaleen’s family said Levy should have been charged with first-degree murder over the well-documented attack in the village of Umm al-Khair.Reckless manslaughter carries a maximum prison sentence of 12 years, far less then murder.“This was not an accident,” said his cousin Tarek Hathaleen. “Yinon Levy must be held fully accountable for Awdeh’s killing.”The charges nevertheless represented a “significant development”, Hathaleen added, after years of near-total impunity for Israelis who attack Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.0:53Palestinian activist recorded moment he was killed by settler in West Bank – videoMy sweet friend Awdah Hathaleen was murdered by a West Bank settler. May his memory be a revolution | Emily GlickRead moreIsraeli settlers and soldiers have killed more than 1,500 Palestinians this decade, according torights group B’tselem. Levy is the first person indicted over any of those deaths.Military prosecutors last brought charges over a 2019 shooting of a young man who stopped to help victims of a traffic accidentThe last time civilian prosecutors brought charges was in 2018 over the killing of a mother of eight, hit by a rock as she was driving.Settler violence and ethnic cleansing has surged in the occupied West Bank over the past three years, supported by far-right Israeli cabinet ministers who hold security, defence and finance portfolios.Levy’s indictment over one of the highest-profile killings in that period does not represent a policy shift for Israel, rights groups said.Hathaleen had worked onNo Other Land, the Oscar-winning documentary about his community’s decades-long struggle against the Israeli state and settlers, to stay in their homes and lands in the south Hebron hills.“It’s important to see this killing as part of an ongoing and systematic situation in the West Bank,” said Ziv Stahl, executive director of Yesh Din, an Israeli rights and advocacy organisation.“I don’t think these charges are an indication of increased law enforcement or accountability. It is more likely due to the fact that [Awdeh Hathaleen] was a well-known activist and the case got a lot of media exposure and public critique. It’s more about an appearance of law enforcement, rather than actual law enforcement.”Levy, who was under sanctions for violence against Palestinians by the UK, EU, Canada and Australia at the time of the attack, was briefly detained last year but policereleasedhim after three days under house arrest.He spent the last year free and continued establishing illegal outposts in the occupied West Bank, said Yair Dvir, spokesperson for B’tselem.“The decision to indict Yinon Levy is the exception that proves the rule,” Dvir said. “The impunity Israel grants to soldiers and settlers who harm Palestinians is not a failure of the system – it is a central component of a policy designed to allow the violence to continue and escalate.”The culture of impunity spurred the former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert tocallfor the International Criminal Court to bring charges against “Jewish terrorists”, saying intervention was needed to halt the violence.Levy is also charged with armed trespassing and malicious property damage in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair.Before Hathaleen was shot, another settler drove a bulldozer through Palestinian land, destroying trees and property. When a resident approached and asked him to stop, the driver knocked the man down with the bulldozer blade.Even if the case goes to trial, any verdict could be many years away, and Israeli judges have a record of lenient treatment of Israelis who attack Palestinians.The Israeli soldier who shot 23-year-old Ahmad Manasrah dead in 2019pleaded guiltyto the equivalent of negligent homicide and was sentenced to three months community service for the killing. He has not been publicly named.Eight years after a 2018 attack that killed 47 year-old Aisha Rabi, an Israeli courtruledthat a settler had thrown the stone that killed her.Judges did not hand down a conviction or sentence, instead ordering a review because the man, who was not named, was 16 at the time of the attack. No further details have been made public.Hathaleen’s family say they will continue to fight for Levy to face full trial. “Justice requires more than simply bringing a charge,” said Tarek Hathaleen. “Awdeh was not only my cousin. He was my childhood friend and someone very dear to me. His absence has left a pain that will never go away.”Sufian Taha contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineIsraelMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran plots to deal Trump a blow in midterms by keeping him entangled in war | Iran | The Guardian
description: By dragging out talks, Tehran aims to damage the US president politically – but some fear a bruised and weakened Trump could lash back
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: By dragging out talks, Tehran aims to damage the US president politically – but some fear a bruised and weakened Trump could lash back
Content: Iran has distrusted the US since the 1979 Islamic revolution, but their anger is now focused personally on Trump.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreenIran has distrusted the US since the 1979 Islamic revolution, but their anger is now focused personally on Trump.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APIranAnalysisIran plots to deal Trump a blow in midterms by keeping him entangled in warPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorBy dragging out talks, Tehran aims to damage the US president politically – but some fear a bruised and weakened Trump could lash backFri 7 Aug 2026 07.47 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareTehran has set out a protracted negotiating timetable designed to keepDonald Trumpembroiled in the Iran conflict until the midterm elections, in the hope of inflicting the same ruinous blow on his presidency as Jimmy Carter suffered over the 1979-81 US embassy hostage crisis.For many insideIran, inflicting meaningful revenge on Trump is a legitimate and self-standing war aim, reflected in the mood of those attending the funeral of the supreme leader Ali Khamenei where demands for retribution were ubiquitous.While Iranian officials since the 1979 Islamic revolution have never trusted the US, that animus is now also directed personally towards Trump. He not only tore up the painfully negotiated nuclear deal in 2018, but he sanctioned the assassination of the military leader Qassem Suleimani and twice involved Iran in negotiations on its nuclear programme only to launch wars against it. He shows no remorse for the killing of the country’s supreme leader, or for the attempt on the life of Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian.As the countdown to November’s midterms begins, what could be Trump’s political demise has become a subject of obsessive speculation in Tehran. Iranian media track the US president’s waning ratings, attributing the decline to thewar’s unpopularity and high oil prices. The changing politics of the Democrats is minutely examined.But the focus on the midterms became more obvious this week when the deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, told the official IRNA news agency thatafter agreeing a route for commercial shippingthrough the strait of Hormuz, it would take two to four months to reach the second phase of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme. The original plan – to commence the nuclear phase of the talks within 30 days of signing June’s memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the US – had been jettisoned by the Trump administration, Gharibabadi said.To get to that second stage, he laid out an obstacle course including the lifting of sanctions, the end of the US blockade of Iranian ports, the unfreezing of Iranian assets and new commitments on non-belligerence in a process that could last well beyond the midterms.If Tehran gets its way on this timetable, Trump will be going to the polls with no Iranian commitment on nuclear weapons, only a hefty economic bill for a failed war. “This raises the very likely scenario of continued cycles of conflict between the US and Tehran over the strait,” said Jason Brodsky from United against a Nuclear Iran, an advocate of the war. “There won’t be any true quiet before the midterm elections – Tehran has no interest in giving this to theTrump administration… It will continue to play games.”Mehr News, an agency close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, published a piece saying Iran had given Trump a major dilemma. “Continuing the war could increase political and economic pressure on the government and exacerbate the decline in his popularity. On the other hand, backing down, or moving towards reducing tensions, could also be interpreted by some of Trump’s supporters as a retreat from his campaign slogans,” it said.From this perspective, the outcome of this war will not be played out on thebattlefield, but at the ballot box. The agency suggested the outcome could affect the course of American domestic and foreign policy for years to come.View image in fullscreenHardliners want to expel the US from the area not by negotiation but by using control of the entry points to the strait of Hormuz.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesFew in Iran take Trump’s statements at face value. But his denials that the midterms affect his Iran strategy are treated with special scepticism. Iranian media point to comments from Marc Zell, chair of Republicans Overseas Israel, who has said: “It’s all about the midterms … the American public simply is tired of war and the administration is navigating the pre-election waters adroitly in order to avoid a Democratic takeover of Congress.”Such remarks fuel the debate inside Iran about how much the midterms should be part of Iran’s calculus. Some believe the loss of Congress will inhibit Trump or lead to his impeachment; at the very least, it may mark the end of the war’s funding. Mostafa Zahrani, a former Iranian diplomat, argued electoral defeat “will make it inevitable that Trump will not be able to go back to war and will take the negotiations seriously”.Others such as Nasser Hadian, a professor of international relations at Tehran University, disagree, advocating cashing in on Iran’s victories now rather than waiting for Trump to become weaker. “If he loses, he’ll have less incentive to reach an agreement with Iran, because in that case he’ll be weakened, and Israel and others will find it much easier to attack him – something they don’t dare do now,” he said. “Those who say we should wait for the midterm elections have no understanding of politics in America.”Iran’s pleasure in seeing Trump defeated would indeed be reduced if he felt he had nothing left to lose, but its diplomats overall believe the US president’s freedom to act will be constrained by the unpopularity of more conflict and by Republican presidential candidates’ anxiety to wrap this up. Trump would also be at risk of seeing his whole second term consumed by a disastrous war.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe bigger question is what Iran itself wants to achieve. Agreeing to keep the dispute simmering until November is not an answer to that question – one that Iranians are better at debating than resolving.Pezeshkian, working in alliance with Mohammad Ghalibaf, the chief negotiator, repeatedly says he does not want endless war, and insists that almost all the supreme national security council concur. He still has faith in the MoU, saying it should be the cornerstone of Iran’s foreign policy.But the conservative newspaper Kayhan describes the memorandum as worthless since the US always breaks its commitments. “Accordingly, officials should know that the strait of Hormuz is not a bargaining chip and should not be opened as a passage for America,” it said.Both hardliners and moderates envision the war leading to a new regional security architecture. But the hardliners put the emphasis on America’s expulsion and see this as something less to be negotiated and more to be enforced using control of the entry points to the strait of Hormuz as a lever to close US bases.Pezeshkian says he sees a place for legitimate US investment in Iran, while the former foreign minister Javad Zarif, in an essay this week, argued Iran in “a post-polar era would benefit from not depending solely on Russia and China in future”.If Iran developed “a balanced and multifaceted foreign policy”, Tehran would not be forced into relationships based on necessity, he wrote. “Continuing uncontrolled tensions with the United States not only imposes direct costs on Iran, but also makes it more difficult for other countries, even close partners such as China and Russia, to cooperate with Iran.”Just as Trump cannot resolve from one sentence to the next what he thinks of Iran, nor can Iran agree what it thinks it can get from America.Explore more on these topicsIranDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS-Israel war on IranUS politicsMiddle East and north AfricaStrait of HormuzanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Wasted medicine in England could fill 75 swimming pools a year, pharmacy group says | Pharmaceuticals industry | The Guardian
description: Industry body calls for greater scrutiny of patients with multiple repeat prescriptions to tackle ‘growing problem’
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Industry body calls for greater scrutiny of patients with multiple repeat prescriptions to tackle ‘growing problem’
Content: The National Pharmacy Association estimated that wasted medicine costs the NHS more than £480m annually.Photograph: Flavio Brancaleone/AAPView image in fullscreenThe National Pharmacy Association estimated that wasted medicine costs the NHS more than £480m annually.Photograph: Flavio Brancaleone/AAPPharmaceuticals industryWasted medicine in England could fill 75 swimming pools a year, pharmacy group saysIndustry body calls for more regular reviews of repeat prescriptions to tackle ‘growing problem’Nadeem BadshahFri 7 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe amount of wasted medicines thrown away inEnglandin one year could fill 75 swimming pools, according to a pharmacy group.The National Pharmacy Association (NPA) estimated that 3,400 tonnes of partly used medicines were disposed of in England in 2024-25.The organisation, which analysed data from regional health bodies, also estimated that the problem costs theNHSat least £480m annually.Olivier Picard, chair of the NPA, said: “Wasted medicines cost theNHSsignificant sums of money every year that could be invested in better services for patients.“More than this, wasting medicines can have environmental and health consequences, and we can do much more to tackle this growing problem.“As soon as a medicine leaves apharmacy, even if it is not used and is unopened, it must be disposed of, so it is important patients only get medicines they are sure they will use.”The NPA, which represents 6,000 independent community pharmacies in the UK, called for patients with several repeat prescriptions to have more reviews so that medicines that were no longer needed could be identified.It also urged the public not to “over order” medicine.Picard added: “We are urging patients only to request medicines if they really need them when ordering repeat prescriptions.A bitter pill: are you wasting your money on supplements?Read more“As well as this, patients who are prescribed multiple medicines should have these more regularly reviewed to ensure they are being fully utilised.“If a patient has any concerns about their medicines, they should speak to their pharmacist who can help them get the most out of their medicines.”Dr Rasha Abdelsalam Elshenawy, a senior lecturer at the University of Hertfordshire, said surplus medicines “aren’t only a financial and environmental problem – it’s a patient safety and resistance problem”.She added: “Leftover antibiotics kept at home are often taken later without medical advice, which fuels antimicrobial resistance, one of the biggest threats to modern medicine.“Regular medication reviews and only ordering what is needed protects patients, the NHS and the environment.”An NHS England spokesperson said it had taken action to ensure people could better manage their prescriptions on their mobile phones through the NHS app, including repeat prescriptions.“We know there is more to do, which is why several local NHS services are running campaigns to reduce medicines waste, alongside wider efforts to optimise medicines use that have also seen the total number of dependency-forming medications prescribed fall over the last decade,” they added.In June, health leaders warned that Britons were facing some of the“most severe” shortages of NHS medicines on record, including common painkillers, epilepsy drugs and HRT.The NPA and the Royal College of GPs highlighted long-lasting supply issues affecting Estradot, a hormone replacement therapy (HRT) medicine used by menopausal women, and Creon, a drug taken by people with pancreatic cancer and cystic fibrosis to help them digest food.Explore more on these topicsPharmaceuticals industryEnglandNHSHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police investigating Ann Widdecombe murder reopen attempted burglary case from 2025 | Ann Widdecombe | The Guardian
description: Failure to pursue line of inquiry ‘which may have been relevant’ now being investigated by police watchdog
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Failure to pursue line of inquiry ‘which may have been relevant’ now being investigated by police watchdog
Content: Ann Widdecombe was found dead with serious injuries at her home in Devon on 9 July.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAnn Widdecombe was found dead with serious injuries at her home in Devon on 9 July.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianAnn WiddecombePolice investigating Ann Widdecombe murder reopen attempted burglary case from 2025Watchdog examines alleged failure to pursue a line of inquiry ‘which may have been relevant’Nadeem BadshahFri 7 Aug 2026 18.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCounter-terrorism police investigating the death ofAnn Widdecombesay they have reopened an old investigation into an attempted burglary last year.The incident at an address in Greater London was reported in April 2025.Since the case was reopened, CTP London said it had identified a line of inquiry “which may have been relevant” but was “not identified and pursued by [counter-terrorism police] at the time”.The police watchdog said it is now investigating the conduct of a CTP London staff member over allegations they “failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry” related to the attempted burglary.Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism policing, said: “As part of the ongoing investigation led by counter-terrorism policing south-east into the murder of Ann Widdecombe, officers have reopened an investigation into an incident reported to police last year.”CTP London made a “mandatory conduct referral” to the Independent Office forPoliceConduct (IOPC) on Friday.A spokesperson for the IOPC said: “We can confirm that the IOPC has decided to independently investigate the conduct of a counter-terrorism policing London staff member following a referral received earlier today.“The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025.“Counter-terrorism policing London has been notified of our decision, and no further information is available at this early stage.”Widdecombe, 78, a former Conservative minister, was found dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.Last month, a 28-year-old man was charged with the former MP’s murder.Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July.He was also arrested on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism but has not been charged with this offence.Devon and Cornwall police initially arrested a 26-year-old man from Newton Abbot in Devon, but later released him and said he was no longer part of the investigation.Widdecombe served as Conservative MP for Maidstone, Kent for 23 years. She subsequently represented south-west England as a member of the European parliament for the Brexit party and in 2023 joined Reform UK as a party spokesperson.Explore more on these topicsAnn WiddecombePoliceUK security and counter-terrorismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thetford residents remain on edge after days of ‘mob rule’ over asylum plans | Norfolk | The Guardian
description: People voice frustration with officials’ failure to engage with community over placement of asylum seekers in area
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: People voice frustration with officials’ failure to engage with community over placement of asylum seekers in area
Content: Sue, 68, and her son Tommy, 32, with other protesters outside RAF Barnham, near Thetford, where the government is considering accommodating asylum seekers.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSue, 68, and her son Tommy, 32, with other protesters outside RAF Barnham, near Thetford, where the government is considering accommodating asylum seekers.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianNorfolkThetford residents remain on edge after days of ‘mob rule’ over asylum plansPeople voice frustration with officials’ failure to engage with community over placement of asylum seekers in areaBen QuinnPolitical correspondentFri 7 Aug 2026 15.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 15.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA smashed window pane and some broken eggshells on a footpath were some of the tell-tale signs of events that took place this week on a residential street at the edge of Thetford.On Friday afternoon it was not hard to find local people with a sense of foreboding after the latest disorder in theNorfolkmarket town which has seen crowds attempt to break into properties believed to be housing asylum seekers.“The main concern is safety, the proximity of children and that people just have not been consulted about this,” said Jenny Hollis, a former councillor, who indicated the proximity of a local school and nursery to a – now seemingly vacant – house on the targeted street in the north of the town.View image in fullscreenJenny Hollis: ‘Thetford is a small town.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian“Thetford is a small town where people know each other, but if you are putting young men who people know nothing about into an area, sometimes in the dark of night, then it will be a cause of concern,” she said in reference to asylum seekers.For three nights, Thetford was the scene of protests and disorder, with police officers being subjected to violence, windows smashed, fences broken and people attempting to break into a residential property, police said.However, after unrest which the local MP said had “put Thetford back decades”, there was also deep unease among residents and others about the prospect of racism poisoning local relations, fuelled by disinformation and the role of the far right in seeking to exploit tensions.“I have lived here for more than a decade and have come to call it home,” said a woman, originally from eastern Europe, around the corner from where the latest unrest took place. “The people are lovely, but last week was the first time that my partner was shouted at by someone who derided him as a ‘migrant’.”Amid chants of “We want them out” from a crowd of up to 200 people on the targeted street on Wednesday night, a male police officer was hit by a brick and a female colleague was seriously bitten, Norfolk constabulary said. The number of arrests in connection with disorder in different parts of the town had risen to six as of Friday.Asylum seekers had been removed from properties on Thursday for their safety, according to the police, and there was no answer at a number of homes believed to have been used for that purpose when the Guardian visited.“I have HMOs [houses of multiple occupancy] with asylum seekers in them on both sides of my house,” said one man. They had tended to keep to themselves, he said, but he had concerns about tensions in the area and what it would do to property prices.The three nights of disorder threaten to become the spark for the type of anti-immigration tensions that boiled over last year around a hotel outside the Essex town of Epping and spread elsewhere.If the unrest in Thetford is different, however, it is that it marks the first time HMOs in England have become the target of concerted and organised anger.Terry Jermy, the MP for South West Norfolk and a rare Labour presence in what has traditionally been a Conservative-leaning region, has criticised what he described as a lack of engagement by theHome Office, and given voice to people’s unease that cheaper, working-class areas have been chosen as the location for housing asylum seekers in HMOs.“The lack of engagement both with the community and elected officials has been a huge concern, along with the apparent lack of a strategy, in terms of a cohesive plan, but also to close down rumours and the spread of misinformation,” said Jermy.View image in fullscreenTerry Jermy: ‘What we have seen … is outright criminality, mob rule and vigilante-style antics.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian“I have been happy to acknowledge people’s concerns and support peaceful protest but what we have seen over the last few days is outright criminality, mob rule and vigilante-style antics which go way beyond the rule of law. These people – and in many cases I’m talking about those who have travelled to Thetford – claim to be proud to be British, but to be proud to be British is to support the rule of law.”Criticism has persisted over the use of HMOs and the choice of locations to house asylum seekers, with protesters in Thetford targeting a list of houses believed to be used by Serco, a company that has a multimillion pound contract with the Home Office.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSocial media accounts operated by prominent far-right activists, including Stephen Yaxley-Lennon – who calls himself Tommy Robinson – have disseminated footage from the protests. In one clip, a man can be seen directing crowds to an address where he said there were “invaders”, a term used by Robinson and others.View image in fullscreenDamage to the homes of people believed to be asylum seekers in Thetford.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianIn answer to the allegation it had mishandled its contract, a spokesperson for Serco said it worked under the direction of the Home Office, which tells it the number of people it expects to house in local authority areas based on overall national levels of demand.The Home Office has insisted the use of “large sites” is a key part of its strategy, and said the population of asylum seekers in hotels fell by 35% in the past year and by 63% from the peak of 56,000 in 2023.Figures from Reform UK have taken a prominent interest in the opposition to the use of HMOs.Scott Hussey, a member of the cabinet on Reform-controlled Norfolk county council, was at the scene on Friday, and said residents were frustrated at seeing their town being turned into “a dumping ground for illegal immigrants”.He said his understanding from meeting with the Home Office was that more HMOs were going to be sited in Thetford,and that this would add to tensions over proposals to use a nearby RAF base to house asylum seekers.Those who protested in Thetford this week included participants in a regular protest outside RAF Barnham, outside the town. Plans to house 3,750 migrants at the former base were revealed in June.Anna Turley, the minister for border security and asylum, said on GB News on Friday that people had a right to protest but that the disorder in Thetford had been “horrendous”.“What we’ve seen is spilling over into violence, which is just not acceptable,” she said. “Nobody should feel harassed, intimidated or threatened in their home, and certainly we shouldn’t see our emergency workers and our police attacked in the way that we have seen.”Explore more on these topicsNorfolkImmigration and asylumFar rightHome OfficeMigrationProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Millions in England face longer waits for mental health care as NHS providers plan cuts | Mental health | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Seven in 10 survey respondents expect services to be reduced or shut, while more than half anticipate job losses
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Exclusive: Seven in 10 survey respondents expect services to be reduced or shut, while more than half anticipate job losses
Content: Demand for NHS mental health services has risen rapidly amid growing pressure on existing provision.Photograph: Roos Koole/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDemand for NHS mental health services has risen rapidly amid growing pressure on existing provision.Photograph: Roos Koole/Getty ImagesMental healthMillions in England face longer waits for mental health care as NHS providers plan cutsExclusive: Seven in 10 survey respondents expect services to be reduced or shut, while more than half anticipate job lossesAndrew GregoryHealth editorFri 7 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMillions of adults and children inEnglandface being forced to wait longer for mental health care, with more than two-thirds of NHS providers planning to cut services and half expected to axe jobs, the Guardian can reveal.With mental health services already under extraordinary pressure amid soaring demand for support, experts warned the proposed cuts – drawn up by trusts to plug holes in their finances – would also have “significant” consequences for the widerNHS, the economy and public services.Key services such as child and adolescent mental health care, talking therapies, addiction support, help for adults undergoing a mental health crisis and community programmes, including those for ethnic minorities and low-income groups, areamong those that may be affected.Seven in 10 (68%) NHS trusts providing mental health services are likely to reduce or shut some of their services in 2026-27, according to the results of a national survey conducted by the NHS Alliance and seen by the Guardian.Of respondents, 59% said they expect to freeze vacancies, with more than half (57%) likely to cut the number of clinical staff they employ this year.Earlier this week, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, announced plans to create a network of nearly 200 community mental health centres and mental health A&Es by 2029. Writingon LinkedIn, he said: “These services will make it much easier for people to get the right support, at the right time, in the right place.”View image in fullscreenThe UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, announced plans to launch additional community health centres this week.Photograph: Jack Taylor/Reuters Pool/APMental health charities welcomed the ambition but said if funding for staff and services was being cut, meaningful improvements to care would be “impossible”.One of the NHS mental health trusts affected, East London foundation trust, plans to cut a wide range of services and axe hundreds of jobs to close a £25m hole in its finances,the Guardian reportedon Monday.NHS mental health professionals at other trusts said similar plans were being drawn up where they work. They fear the cuts will strip back services so much that they will not be able to properly perform their duties or guarantee safe care in their areas.An NHS consultant psychiatrist, speaking on condition of anonymity, said: “This is not an isolated example in east London. Many mental health trusts are in a similar, if not worse, situation and are responding in similar ways through cutting jobs and compromising service delivery.”A mental health service manager at a third NHS mental health trust said: “Many mental health trusts are in a similar position. They have faced declining funding for the last couple of years alongside cost reduction targets.”Alex Stewart, assistant director of the NHS Alliance’s mental health network, said: “Mental health services are coming under extraordinary pressure as a result of rapidly rising demand for care and very tough financial conditions.“Despite this, we see many examples of innovation and great care which give real grounds for hope. But it’s increasingly evident that the trade-offs and difficult decisions over jobs and services which we warned about are making their mark.“Mental health leaders face particular pressures when finances are tight because a higher proportion of their expenditure goes on staff.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStudy finds three midlife health factors that could delay dementia for 13 yearsRead moreThe NHS Alliance survey, conducted in March before the new financial year, revealed widespread concerns about the need to make record efficiency savings in 2026-27.There were also concerns among the 37 NHS mental health providers responding to the poll that the focus on balancing the books would impede progress on providing more care outside hospital settings and increasing preventive mental health care.One NHS mental health trust leader told the survey there was “no investment for mental health community services” and their teams were “under resourced” to manage the rise in demand.Stewart said: “We welcome recent announcements on capital funding for community mental health centres and the confirmation of targets to improve access to mental health care. But in the face of rising demand, the share of national NHS spend on mental health is expected to reduce for the third year in a row.“It is essential that mental health investment is not allowed to fall behind, as the consequences of underfunding mental health for the wider NHS, the economy and public services will be significant.”Tom Pollard, the head of policy, public affairs and campaigns at Mind, said the results of the survey showed “the huge uphill battle we face” to save mental health services in England and ensure everyone could access high-quality care.He said: “The government set out a welcome ambition to move towards a more open access model of support through neighbourhood mental health centres. But if funding for staff and services is being cut, meaningful improvements to the mental health system will be impossible.”Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the trade union Unite, said: “We cannot balance the books on the backs of the most vulnerable in society and by underfunding mental health provision you simply kick the can down the road and it costs more in the long term.“Our members at health trusts across the country are outraged at attempts to cut jobs and services and will be fighting back with the full support of their union.”A Department ofHealthand Social Care spokesperson said: “As well as investing a record £16.1bn into mental health services this year, we have recruited more than 8,500 additional mental health workers since this government came into office, and only this week, we announced the rollout of 159 new NHS mental health facilities across England, backed by £343m in funding.“Later this year, our mental health strategy will outline how we plan to future-proof the mental health system, including responding earlier and reducing waiting times for support.”Explore more on these topicsMental healthHealthHealth policyNHSEnglandAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: French officers halted small boats at sea 10 times since spring | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Disclosure challenges Conservative and Reform claims that police are refusing to intervene
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Disclosure challenges Conservative and Reform claims that police are refusing to intervene
Content: A French warship and navy rib alongside an inflatable ‘small boat’ carrying migrants across the Channel after leaving northern France.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA French warship and navy rib alongside an inflatable ‘small boat’ carrying migrants across the Channel after leaving northern France.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesImmigration and asylumFrench officers halted small boats at sea 10 times since springDisclosure challenges Conservative and Reform claims that police are refusing to interveneRajeev SyalHome affairs editorFri 7 Aug 2026 13.46 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 14.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe French authorities have halted small boats at sea in the Channel on 10 occasions since the spring, officials said on Friday.Despite claims from the Conservatives and Reform that the French were refusing to intervene in small boat crossings, maritime prefect officers were using “intervention tactics” to board or control vessels at sea and take asylum seekers back toFrance.The disclosure comes as political parties are once again attempting to seize the initiative over small boats over the summer.Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, last week confronted French police on a beach near Boulogne and uploaded footage to X of an officer saying: “Our order is to let them go. We just have to say to them, ‘Don’t do that. It’s dangerous.’”Earlier this week, Reform MP Lee Anderson visited Calais and said the French police were “literally waving these people on to boats”.In an unusual intervention, the director of maritime and small boats at Border Security Command, Charlie Eastaugh, said: “The incidents we have seen in the Channel over the last few weeks are a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting people for profit. It is easy to look at out-of-context images and think little is happening to stop these crossings – this is simply not true.Has the UK government’s strategy on small boat crossings been effective?Read more“I know personally how tirelessly French officers have been working to disrupt launches before they reach UK shores. Their efforts include facing violent people with weapons, dispersing huge crowds, arresting smugglers, seizing equipment and collating vital evidence to help our prosecutions.”Every confrontation with asylum seekers was assessed by commanders as well as individual police officers and gendarmes, who were expected to balance the safety of their officers with that of the public, including large groups of often agitated people and gang members, officials said.On Sunday, when Andy Burnham visited HM Coastguard in Dover, Border Force officers had been warned that it was a “red day”, when conditions were calm enough for several small boat crossings.Two small boats attempted to launch from France, but one was intercepted at sea, while the other was halted on land.Small boats crossing the Channel were down by 43% compared with January to mid-July 2025 – from 21,690 people who crossed last year to 12,469 over the same period this year.The drop has come despite hot and dry conditions, which are usually associated with an increase in crossings.UK officials believe that government initiatives to “stop the boats” by financing the French authorities with another £660m in April have disrupted the business model of people smugglers in northern France and reduced the number crossing to the UK.Gangs are adapting their tactics. Boat launches have spread further along the coast, with some leaving from Belgium and others from as far south as Dieppe, a journey of 70 miles (113km) to the UK, compared with the Calais to Dover route of 27 miles.Officials are concerned the trend towards “mega-dinghies” – larger motorised boats – is putting more people at risk. More than 170 migrants were rescued on Tuesday after the boat they were using to cross the Channel caught fire.The sustained drop in crossings was a welcome development for Burnham, allowing him to focus his early weeks in government on setting out his policy agenda.Shabana Mahmood, who Burnham has kept in post as home secretary, has been reluctant to celebrate the recent drop because she is conscious the trend could change if there is an increase in arrivals in the late summer and autumn months.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeFranceChris PhilpMigrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Idaho police release video of In-N-Out Burger mass shooting that killed three | Idaho | The Guardian
description: Officials praise unarmed employee from nearby store for engaging 24-year-old gunman who later killed himself
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Officials praise unarmed employee from nearby store for engaging 24-year-old gunman who later killed himself
Content: A woman at a candelight vigil for the victims of the Twin Falls shooting.Photograph: Andrew Eakin/APView image in fullscreenA woman at a candelight vigil for the victims of the Twin Falls shooting.Photograph: Andrew Eakin/APIdahoIdaho police release video of In-N-Out Burger mass shooting that killed threeOfficials praise unarmed employee from nearby store for engaging 24-year-old gunman who later killed himselfGuardian staff and agenciesFri 7 Aug 2026 17.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice released video on Friday of a mass shooting that killed three people at anIdahoIn-N-Out Burger restaurant last weekend, and praised an unarmed employee from a nearby store who engaged the gunman outdoors, slowing him down and possibly preventing more deaths as authorities were catching up.The video released by the police also showed at least three people confronted the gunman with their own weapons during the incident.“What happened here was violent, frightening and deeply traumatic,” the Twin Falls police chief, Matthew Hicks, said during a news conference before screeningan eight-and-a-half minute compilationof surveillance camera and bodycam video of the incident.The distressing video, which was edited by the police to blur faces and omit graphic images, revealed more details of the chaotic scene last weekend. It shows that the gunman walked up to the drive-thru window four times and opened fire, killing an In-N-Out employee, police said.Ten people were shot – inside the restaurant, directly outside, on an adjacent busy road and at a car charging station in a Twin Falls visitor center lot, Hicks said.Hicks said investigators still do noty have a motive for the shooting. The gunman, identified as Chad Williams, 24, killed himself when police officers caught up to him on a nearby walking trail.It should have been a “normal Saturday afternoon”, Hicks said atthe televised news conference. “Employees showing up for work. Visitors coming to see our beautiful city. Instead they were confronted with chaos, fear and now loss.”As the shooting unfolded, employees from nearby stores fled to a walking trail. When the gunman headed to the trail, he came across two people, including one with his hands in the air who spoke to him, the video shows.That man distracted the gunman from possibly pursuing others on the trail. Williams subsequently killed himself as police closed in. His body was found near a canyon.“To that young man, you are a hero,” Hicks said of the bystander who slowed the gunman down. “Your courage, your composure, your selflessness in that moment likely gave others the time they needed to escape harm. This community is grateful for you, and we will never forget what you did that day.”Hicks also praised the work of an off-duty state trooper, who shot at Williams from inside the restaurant, and a former police officer, AJ James, who was wounded while confronting him.Authorities had previously credited an armed civilian who fired back and diverted Williams from the restaurant.James ran toward the sound of gunfire from the drive-thru window, while the off-duty officer inside the In-N-Out exchanged gunfire with Williams through the window and directed workers out of the building, Hicks said.He acted “heroically and unbelievably” to try to slow down the shooter, the police chief said, declining to release the off-duty officer’s name.Braxton Steube said he was the person who encountered Williams on the trail after fleeing a Dick’s Sporting Good store.“I said, ‘I have a family.’ I said, ‘You don’t have to do this. I’ll tell you whatever you want. I’ll do anything,’” Steubetold KMVT-TVin Twin Falls.“He started to like tear up a bit, it seemed. And he said to me, ‘Just get away from me, man.’”Steube said the gunman shot at him and missed.Police identified those killed as Ashley Garibay, 23, of Stockton, California; Dale Schultz, 66, of Salt Lake City; and Christopher Claunch, 59, of Hagerman, Idaho.Williams had briefly attended the College of Southern Idaho and previously lived in Arizona.Explore more on these topicsIdahoGun crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Prosecutor fired over blogposts critical of Trump sues US justice department | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Will Rosenzweig’s defunct blog was publicized online by conservative pundit who tagged senior DoJ officials
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Will Rosenzweig’s defunct blog was publicized online by conservative pundit who tagged senior DoJ officials
Content: The September 2025 termination was part of a sweeping personnel purge inside the justice department.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/APView image in fullscreenThe September 2025 termination was part of a sweeping personnel purge inside the justice department.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/APTrump administrationProsecutor fired over blogposts critical of Trump sues US justice departmentWill Rosenzweig’s defunct blog was publicized online by conservative pundit who tagged senior DoJ officialsAssociated PressFri 7 Aug 2026 17.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA federal prosecutor fired last year over critical comments he had written as a private citizen about Donald Trump sued the justice department on Friday, saying his termination violated his first amendment rights.Will Rosenzweig was two weeks away from trying a multimillion-dollar Medicare fraud case when a blog he had written years earlier covering a broad range of topics was publicized online by a conservative political commentator who also included a screenshot of Rosenzweig’s LinkedIn account and tagged senior justice department officials for their awareness.Less than three hours after the post, the lawsuit says, Rosenzweig received an email signed by then attorney generalPam Bondiinforming him that he had been fired. The news came as Rosenzweig was out of town with his family observing the Jewish holiday of Rosh Hashana.The September 2025 termination was part of a sweeping personnel purge over the last year and a half inside the justice department, which has fired prosecutors who worked on investigations into Trump and others seen as being against the administration’s efforts.A lawsuit filed in federal court in Miami, where Rosenzweig worked as a federal prosecutor for five years, seeks reinstatement to the job as well as backpay and a court order declaring his firing unlawful.The complaint says Rosenzweig was a highly respected prosecutor who received “consistent praise and awards” and was so highly valued in his office that he was told just weeks before his firing that he would be getting a special parking spot due to his performance.“Will Rosenzweig was an excellent prosecutor who returned millions of dollars to the taxpayers by prosecuting healthcare fraud cases,” said a statement from his lawyers, Margaret Donovan, Daniel Fridman and Adam Fels.“Yet the Department of Justice fired him on the eve of trial because, years ago as a private citizen, he published criticisms of President Trump. Since the current Department of Justice will not stand up for the first amendment and the American people, we will. We look forward to vindicating Will’s rights in court.”The blog Rosenzweig had maintained had been defunct for over six years at the time of his firing and included his thoughts on travel, sports and other “apolitical, anodyne topics” in addition to critical observations about Trump and other political candidates, the lawsuit says.The conservative commentator, Natalie Winters, who has a large online following, characterized Rosenzweig as “a rogue Trump hater” as she posted screenshots of some of his political musings, according to the complaint, which characterizes the firing as a direct assault on Rosenzweig’s free-speech rights.“The department’s conduct rests on a single premise: a citizen must forever refrain from criticizing the government and its leaders to remain eligible to serve it,” the lawsuit says.“That rule would force every American who might one day serve to choose between speaking freely now and working for the government later. Conditioning public employment on political loyalty, where a party card rather than merit opens the door to a government job, is a way of life in Havana and Caracas. It has no place here.”A justice department spokeswoman declined to comment, citing pending litigation.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationPam BondiUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US airfares expected to stay high even if Iran ceasefire drops oil prices, experts say | US economy | The Guardian
description: Domestic flights cost 26.5% more than last year, data shows, amid demand for travel and reduced oil refining capacity
Author: Debbie Carlson
Headline: Domestic flights cost 26.5% more than last year, data shows, amid demand for travel and reduced oil refining capacity
Content: An American Eagle Embraer E175LR plane, operated by Republic Airways, approaches Reagan National airport on 13 May in Washington DC.Photograph: Al Drago/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn American Eagle Embraer E175LR plane, operated by Republic Airways, approaches Reagan National airport on 13 May in Washington DC.Photograph: Al Drago/Getty ImagesUS economyUS airfares expected to stay high even if Iran ceasefire drops oil prices, experts sayDomestic flights cost 26.5% more than last year, data shows, amid demand for travel and reduced oil refining capacityDebbie CarlsonFri 7 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEven if a lasting ceasefire between theUS and Iranlowersoil prices, travelers hoping to snag cheaper airfare should buckle their seatbelts andexpect continued turbulence.US domestic airfares are 26.5% higher than a year ago, according to June’sconsumer price indexdata, and analysts say prices globally are up 25-30% compared with 2025.Strong demand for travel and reduced global oil refining capacity caused jet fuel prices to spike during the early weeks of the Iranian war. While prices are off their highs, they remain elevated. Jet fuel was trading about $149 a barrel as of 4 August, up from $90 at the start of 2026 – a 65% increase. Crude-oil prices are up about 30% since January, trading around $76 a barrel.Jet fuel costsrise slightly higher than oil prices because on average, only about 10% of refined oil can be turned into jet fuel. “The more limited the product, the more vulnerable it is to these supply shocks,” saidLouise Burke, the global head of aviation atArgus Media, a commodities data provider.US gas prices edge up again as US-Iran tensions heighten over strait of HormuzRead moreThere have been a “substantial” amount of refinery closures, Burke said, a key to why jet fuel prices have soared so much higher than standard crude oil. A new refinery in west Africa has helped bring on supply, and refiners are making tweaks to boost output to about 12-14% to take advantage of the higher jet fuel prices, which has helped to alleviate some of the shortages.Jet fuel prices are the biggest operating cost for airlines and the hardest to control, saidJohn Grant, the chief analyst at OAG, an aviation data firm. Cost can range between 30% and 35%.Airlines have little wiggle room to control the impact of higher jet fuel prices. Some airlines may hedge their fuel costs to limit losses, but others buy on the volatile spot market. Each carrier has a strategy to control costs, such as how they use aircraft or cut routes.But risingjet fuel prices are just part of the reason for expensive plane tickets. Capacity constraints at Boeing and Airbus have delayed some aircraft deliveries, while the US Federal Aviation Administration’s (FAA) continued staffing issues has led to fewer flights from some of the biggest airports.The ongoing US-Iran conflict gives carriers cover to pass along more of the costs. “For the airlines, there’s no better time to do it. When there’s a war on, they’ve got a great excuse,” Grant said.Demand for flying has also persisted despite higher airfares, giving airlines more leeway to continue charging higher prices.Burke said demand for jet fuel may be peaking with the summer travel season wrapping up, and if there’s a lasting ceasefire, prices could start to normalize. But the impact on energy prices seen after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has shown that it could take a year or so for prices to normalize.The current US-Iran conflict may play out differently since there is much more volatility, she added, noting that US jet fuel inventories are at the lower end of a five-year average.Legacy carriers such as American Airlines, United Airlines and Delta Air Lines said in recent earnings calls that higher airfares helped to offset some of the higher fuel costs, but the volatility of prices makes it hard to forecast the effects, according to aReutersreport.While some airlines are profitable, many aren’t. In the best cases, airlines have margins of about 15%, Grant said. Globally, there are about 50 airlines who are very profitable, but many are “surviving on cashflow and revenue generated”.Spiritless summer: Americans feel squeeze of costly fuel amid busy travel seasonRead moreIt’s why he doesn’t expect any significant reduction in airfares in the next year. “There isn’t sufficient capacity to come back into the system to create any sort of price war or discounting,” he said.Katy Nastro, a spokesperson for the travel service websiteGoing.com, concurred. With Spirit Airlinesclosingearlier this year, she is watching other low-cost airlines, which have largely not been profitable after the pandemic. The loss of Spirit means less competition for other airlines and potentially higher fares for flyers.The shoulder season of September into October will be a test to see if travel demand continues. Nastro said travel deals come and go more quickly, a signal that airlines are testing consumer appetite in real time as they try to recoup some of their fuel costs. Airlines could trim some routes this fall in anticipation of people traveling less.For those wanting to travel during the popular fall and winter holidays, Going is seeing Thanksgiving fares up 19% compared with 2025, which she said, “is pretty stark”.She also recommends not waiting to buy tickets. “Hoping at this point that the flight price that you’re looking at for Thanksgiving is going to drop by $100 is, I think, wishful thinking,” she said.Explore more on these topicsUS economyUS-Israel war on IranAir transportAirline industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Bari Weiss’s overhaul of CBS News has been rocky. But her 60 Minutes revamp will be the ultimate test | Bari Weiss | The Guardian
description: Ten months into her tenure as editor in chief, Weiss’s biggest – and riskiest – bet is getting closer to taking flight
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Ten months into her tenure as editor in chief, Weiss’s biggest – and riskiest – bet is getting closer to taking flight
Content: Bari Weiss in Sun Valley, Idaho, on 10 July 2026.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersView image in fullscreenBari Weiss in Sun Valley, Idaho, on 10 July 2026.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersBari WeissAnalysisBari Weiss’s overhaul of CBS News has been rocky. But her 60 Minutes revamp will be the ultimate testJeremy BarrTen months into her tenure as editor in chief, Weiss’s biggest – and riskiest – bet is getting closer to taking flightFri 7 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 09.46 EDTShareBari Weiss is 10 months into her tenure as editor-in-chief of CBS News, but her biggest test is right around the corner.The newest season of 60 Minutes is set to premiere next month after Weiss overhauled the show’s correspondent corps and production staff in the spring. Long considered the gold standard in television news,the show still generates a staggering nine million average viewersper night at a time when linear television’s core audience is either ageing out or turning to digital alternatives.A drop in ratings for 60 Minutes would be devastating for bothCBSand Weiss, and her track record at the network has raised concerns about whether her changes – which included ousting several top correspondents and producers – will be well-received by viewers.Under Weiss, the network’s journalists have continued to break big stories about the Trump administration. But her first programming move, bringing in a new anchor for CBS Evening News, has not meaningfully increased the show’s audience, and the network’s morning show has also struggled mightily to attract viewers, recently hitting new weekly lows in viewership.CBS News insiders worry how 60 Minutes will endure after firings: ‘What are they going to put on the air?’Read moreOne of her new hiresto the 60 Minutes lineup, the British commentator Sir Trevor Phillips, laid out the high stakesin an eyebrow-raising interview this weekwith the Telegraph.“Bari and her team have a huge tanker of a network news organization to turn around, and they are assembling a little team on the bridge,” he said. “The great thing about her is that she’s one of those people who will either change the world or crash and burn. But when they crash and burn, it’s in Technicolor.”Weiss was appointed editor-in-chief of CBS News in October 2025 after Skydance Media, owned by David Ellison, son of the billionaire Larry Ellison, acquired CBS parent company Paramount and then bought Weiss’s website, the Free Press, for a reported $150m.CBS News has long trailed behind ABC and NBC in both its morning and evening newscasts, and while some at the network may have hoped she could jolt the shows out of third place, that goal always seemed far-fetched.That didn’t stop Weiss from attempting a shake-up. She tapped the well-coiffed Tony Dokoupil to lead a relaunch of CBS Evening News in January and was hands-on in thechaotic startto the show.But the early returns on her changes have been modest. Over the first three months of 2026, the CBS Evening News was the only show to lose viewers (-7%) compared with the same period last year.In July, CBS Evening News averaged 3.81 million total viewers per night, compared with 6.44 million viewers for the NBC Nightly News and 8.27 million viewers for ABC’s nightly news show, according to Nielsen data. It was the lowest-rated month yet for Dokoupil. And among viewers in the coveted 25-to-49 age demographic, CBS Evening News attracted just below 500,000 average viewers. Still, the network sees growth from last year, and the show has recently averaged over 4 million viewers on several nights.Although CBS Mornings is seen as more under the purview of the network president, Tom Cibrowski, the show – now hosted by only two personalities, star anchor Gayle King and former NFL player Nate Burleson – has declined in viewership under Weiss. Last month, the show averaged 1.62 million total viewers, compared with 2.77 million for NBC and 2.79 million for ABC. Between 27 July and 31 July, CBS Mornings drew its smallest audience in the program’s history: 1.57 million average total viewers. (It hasn’t helped that the network no longer ends the day with Stephen Colbert, after his show was cancelled and replaced with a cheaper but less popularalternative.)Ratings for 60 Minutes remained strong under Weiss, finishing its 58th season with an industry-leading 9.1 million average viewers per show. But soon after the latest season ended in May, Weiss completely upended the show, ousting star correspondents Scott Pelley, Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega along with executive producer Tanya Simon.Amid the turmoil in the spring, the show’s other three full-time correspondents, Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker and Jon Wertheim, agreed –with some obvious trepidation– to “stay and fight”.Still, with roster spots to fill, her hand-picked executive producer, Nick Bilton,announced the hiringlast week of the New York Times opinion columnist Ross Douthat as a full-time correspondent, along with the addition of three new contributors: Sebastian Junger, an author and documentarian best known for writing the 1997 book The Perfect Storm; Gianna Toboni, a video journalist who spent 10 years at Vice News and gets high marks from her peers and future colleagues at CBS News; and Phillips, a British political commentator who is not well known in the United States.“I think that they’re all talented people in their own right,” Steve Kroft, who retired in 2019 after 30 seasons as 60 Minutes correspondent, said in an interview with the Guardian. “I have trouble seeing how they’re going to be 60 Minutes correspondents, mainly because nobody really knows what the show’s going to look like.”While Douthat’s lack of experience in television journalism, and clear partisan lean, made himan odd choiceas a 60 Minutes correspondent to many media observers, some CBS News staffers were relieved that Weiss didn’t move further in the conservative direction. “At least he isn’t Nick Fuentes,” one staffer joked,referring to the white supremacist. “That shows both where we are mentally and where the bar is.”The tumult at the network has led to questions about Weiss’s long-term future at CBS.In May, the networkoffered a statement of supportfor Weiss aftera report in industry publication Puckthat her “mandate” at CBS might be changed “in ways that would give her less control over the linear product”.“Bari has the full support of Paramount and David Ellison as the editorial leader overseeing CBS News and 60 Minutes,” a Paramount spokesperson said at the time.According to Puck’s Dylan Byers, Ellison contacted him directly to push back on the story, telling him: “Bari is a singular talent, and she is the person we have empowered to run our newsroom. Any reports that suggest otherwise are false.”But concerns about her performance have only increased amid speculation that she could be asked to oversee CNN if and when Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of parent company Warner Bros Discovery, currently held up by a multi-state lawsuit, goes through.In June, the Guardian briefly spoke with Ellison as he arrived for a brunch in Washington DC ahead of a UFC fight that was to be held in front of the White House. (Paramount Skydancesigned a huge dealto obtain the rights to broadcast UFC matches).Ellison exchanged pleasantries with this reporter, who asked for his thoughts on “how Weiss is doing at CBS News” and whether he was “happy” with her leadership.Instead of discussing Weiss, Ellison turned and walked straight into the venue. But a member of his entourage said: “She’s doing really well, thanks for asking.”Explore more on these topicsBari WeissCBSUS televisionUS television industryanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘This is where I belong’: Katelyn Ohashi’s Olympic comeback is fueled by joy, not redemption | Gymnastics | The Guardian
description: A decade after leaving elite gymnastics behind, the viral UCLA star is chasing a spot at LA 2028 on her own terms – and inspiring a new generation
Author: Helen Li
Headline: A decade after leaving elite gymnastics behind, the viral UCLA star is chasing a spot at LA 2028 on her own terms – and inspiring a new generation
Content: Katelyn Ohashi (left) with Val Kondos Field, her former coach at UCLA.Photograph: Shayne Smith/UCLA AthleticsView image in fullscreenKatelyn Ohashi (left) with Val Kondos Field, her former coach at UCLA.Photograph: Shayne Smith/UCLA AthleticsGymnastics‘This is where I belong’: Katelyn Ohashi’s Olympic comeback is fueled by joy, not redemptionA decade after leaving elite gymnastics behind, the viral UCLA star is chasing a spot at LA 2028 on her own terms – and inspiring a new generationHelen LiFri 7 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery morning, Katelyn Ohashi gets up and makes a smoothie and then walks her four-month-old puppy. She drives to the gym and begins with a moment of gratitude before warming up with gymnasts half her age. She trains four days a week, around four hours per day, while also dabbling in her various hobbies. It’s a routine that maybe a decade ago she didn’t envision but is now undertaking.When Ohashi left elite gymnastics in 2013, it was no longer a place where she found joy. Although she was seen as an Olympic hopeful (she was the last gymnast to beat Simone Biles in the all-around finals at the American Cup), a back injury took her out of the running for the Games. She slowly found her joy for the sport in NCAA gymnastics at UCLA, where she was known forher perfect 10 floor routines that often went viral, garnering millions of views from around the world.Now 29, she is chasing a lifelong dream: a spot on the US team for a home Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028.View image in fullscreenKatelyn Ohashi competes at the US Classic earlier this month.Photograph: USA GymnasticsOhashi first had inklings of a return to elite gymnastics back in 2021. She, along with former Tokyo gymnasts and others, participated in Simone Biles’s Gold Over America tour across the country. With a three-year runway, Ohashi said she started to get into shape but “never really took it seriously”. Paris 2024 came and went. Last year, the conversation shifted.“This time around, it just felt like: OK, LA, home soil. For gymnastics, I’m definitely getting up there in age,” Ohashi said. The average age on the women’s national team in Paris was about22– the oldest since 1952 – with Biles the oldest member at 27. “It just felt like if I really wanted this to be something real, I needed to move out of LA.”A Seattle native, Ohashi moved repeatedly during her childhood in pursuit of gymnastics, relocating with her mother and one of her brothers from Missouri to Texas before heading to California for college. Finding the right training gym this time was a stroke of luck thanks to her connections at UCLA. Cale Robinson, a friend and former Stanford men’s gymnast, owned Pacific ReignGymnasticsin Woodinville, Washington, where Ohashi would play around some skills when visiting family. Catching up at dinners together over the years, Robinson and Ohashi would joke about how easy her flips still felt. At one point, the conversation about coming back to elite got more serious.“We, like, loosely mapped things out,” Robinson recalled. Ohashi started working with a personal trainer and lifted weights daily to get stronger and build her muscle strength back.“Get a team of people around you, like your physical therapist, all of the people that you need to make sure that you’re healthy first and foremost,” Robinson said.Katelyn Ohashi’s perfect 10 reminded America life could be fun againRead moreOhashi gathered her team, including talking to Valorie Kondos Field, the former UCLA head coach known as Miss Val. While there might have been initial doubts about Ohashi getting all of her skills back, Kondos Field said Ohashi has “one of the strongest minds of any athlete that’s ever played sport”.“At the end of the day, Katelyn is not fixating on a score. Yes, she has a goal. She’d love to make the Olympic team or whatever that is. We don’t even talk about that. It’s like: what is today going to look like for you? How are you going to go home at the end of the day with no regrets?”Kondos Field flew up to Seattle for three days this summer to help Ohashi refine the last touches on her floor routine before the US Classic competition in July. The two developed a “badass” character for Ohashi to portray. The routine is a two-and-a-half pass floor to jazz-inspired music that marries the “contemporary feel of artistic gymnastics in this era while respecting the classical essence of elite gymnastics”, Kondos Field said. It includes elements such as a split jump into a straddle split, a classic Ohashi if you’ve watched her previousMichael Jacksonviral routines. Her athleticism was even praised by the likes of Kobe Bryant, Kondos Field noted.College taught Ohashi gratitude and gave her the reps in front of crowds every week to know how to be more precise with her practices. Since she is still regaining her full range of skills, she and Robinson tweak routines now to her advantage for the code of points.The United States’ depth makes Ohashi’s comeback all the more difficult. Jade Carey, Olympic floor champion and vault bronze medalist, and world champion Leanne Wong remain in the mix for 2028, while Tokyo all-around champion Sunisa Leeannounced her own comebacklast month. Only five gymnasts will make the US Olympic team for Los Angeles.In June, Ohashi competed in her first senior meet at the American Classic. She walked into the gym and saw the familiar faces of past judges and even some of the fellow competitors. She hopped on to the beam and threw out a standing Arabian.“When I saluted, it was like, ‘Oh yeah, this is where I’ve always been. This is where I belong,’” Ohashi said.View image in fullscreenKatelyn Ohashi performs a floor routine during the 2019 NCAA Division I women’s gymnastics championship.Photograph: Tim Nwachukwu/NCAA Photos/Getty ImagesAt July’s US Classic, she competed on beam and floor, finishing four-tenths shy of qualifying for this weekend’s US national championships.For Ohashi, creativity has also returned to other areas of her life. She sews, knits and makes jewellery.“I’ve found myself writing a lot more, especially just going through so many different life changes. It’s starting to spark the creativity again,” she said.In January, she moved from Los Angeles back to Seattle in January this year to live and train. As life would have it, it was an important move as her father started struggling with heart conditions.“This is, I guess, the harsh realities of having parents that are ageing,” she said on Zoom while calling in from the hospital; her mother had also just fractured her hip the day before our call.Ohashi attributes her strong mind to her Japanese father, an avid bowler and former Seattle City Light employee who died in May. She never told him her goals.“I’m sure he would be very proud. He always wanted it to be my dream. My mom probably wanted it to be her dream, and he was just along for the ride and supported in any possible way he could, and I’m sure he still is,” she said.Two years out from Olympic selection, even if she does not make the team, there are no regrets.“I don’t want to shy away from [LA 2028], but I also want to be realistic with where my body is every day and make sure I’m still doing it for me and for the love of the game,” she said.The ripple effects are already there.Intergenerationally, Ohashi’s presence models what can be possible for the young girls and boys who are learning how to understand their bodies and assert themselves.Simone Rose, 18, another athlete from Pacific Reign and a member of the US national team, remembers being 10 years old and watching Ohashi compete for UCLA. A signed Ohashi autograph meet and greet still hangs on the wall of her room.Now training alongside her for LA 2028, Rose said that meets are a lot more fun because of Ohashi’s positive energy in the gym and competitions that make experiences “even more special”.“It’s pretty incredible to go from looking up to her as a young gymnast to now calling her my teammate,” Rose said.For a sport that has historically been high-pressure and focused on skinny, young athletes, having someone like Ohashi in the gym can make a positive difference in showing that it’s never too late to chase your dreams.“The energy shifts in any room that Katelyn walks into. I imagine that as the arenas get bigger, that energy is going to just permeate through more people,” Kondos Field said.Ohashi won’t be at this year’s US nationals. But don’t count her out at the next one.Explore more on these topicsGymnasticsLA Olympic Games 2028US sportsCollege sportsSimone BilesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Will Lankshear starts off in style to see Middlesbrough past Wrexham | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: The £10m summer signing from Spurs scored a fine volley on his debut for Boro, who by advancing to the second round have improved on last year already
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The £10m summer signing from Spurs scored a fine volley on his debut for Boro, who by advancing to the second round have improved on last year already
Content: Will Lankshear (centre, wearing No 7) instantly endeared himself to the Riverside faithful.Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWill Lankshear (centre, wearing No 7) instantly endeared himself to the Riverside faithful.Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesCarabao CupWill Lankshear starts off in style to see Middlesbrough past WrexhamPA MediaFri 7 Aug 2026 17.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 19.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWill Lankshear’s debut strike ensuredMiddlesbroughmade a winning start to the season as they beat Wrexham 1-0 in the Carabao Cup first round. Lankshear, a £10m summer signing from Tottenham, scored the only goal of the game in the 61st minute as he hooked home an excellent first-time volley.Middlesbrough almost claimed a seventh-minute opener but when Adilson Malanda prodded Sebastian Berhalter’s cross goalwards from close range, Danny Ward kept the ball out with a superb point-blank save.Middlesbrough 1-0 Wrexham: Carabao Cup first round – liveRead moreDanny Imray wasted a decent chance forWrexhamwhen he failed to make a proper connection from Callum Doyle’s cross and the visitors went close again six minutes before the break when Sam Smith fired a low shot into the legs of Sol Brynn after he was rolled into space by Nathan Broadhead.Lankshear came close with an effort that was curled just over the bar at the start of the second half, but the 21-year-old did not have to wait too much longer for his first goal in a Boro shirt. Leo Castledine headed Jeremy Sarmiento’s cross into Lankshear’s path, and the striker swivelled neatly before hooking a superb first-time volley into the far corner.Boro almost doubled their lead with three minutes remaining but Morgan Whittaker’s low strike rebounded off the post.After the match the Middlesbrough manager, Kim Hellberg, expressed his delight with the instant impact Will Lankshear has made since joining the club. “He was very impressive and the most impressive thing has been seeing how well he has worked on the training ground,” Hellberg said. “How hard he works on the training ground and how much he wants to learn.“It’s a joy to watch and when you add the person he is to the quality he has as a footballer on the pitch, you have a very good striker. I’m happy to have him here.”Wrexham’s manager, Phil Parkinson, felt his side had given a decent account of themselves just four days after returning from a pre-season tour of the US. Parkinson said: “I thought we had enough half-chances, particularly in the first half, to have progressed in the competition. The game really separated from one quality finish from their lad.
