title: With a little bravery and some big swings, AFLW can enjoy more magical crowd moments | AFLW | The Guardian
description: The AFL could borrow some of the gumption from a North American ice hockey league to grow Australian rules football’s elite women’s competition
Author: Sarah Guiney
Headline: The AFL could borrow some of the gumption from a North American ice hockey league to grow Australian rules football’s elite women’s competition
Content: ‘The unwillingness to separate from AFL games, the reliance on them as a safety net, shows that the league’s priorities still lie with converting the men’s crowd,’ Sarah Guiney writes.Photograph: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The unwillingness to separate from AFL games, the reliance on them as a safety net, shows that the league’s priorities still lie with converting the men’s crowd,’ Sarah Guiney writes.Photograph: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos/Getty ImagesSportblogAFLWWith a little bravery and some big swings, AFLW can enjoy more magical crowd momentsThe AFL could borrow some of the gumption from a North American ice hockey league to grow Australian rules football’s elite women’s competitionSarah GuineyFri 7 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 20.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Australia, it is called the Matildas effect. Elsewhere, it has increasingly become known by a different name: business as usual.The Professional Women’s Hockey League is one of several North American competitions making a habit of not only attracting spectacular women’s sports crowds, but doing so at a domestic level. Just three years into its existence, the ice hockey league is doing a mighty fine job of it too, with last season’s attendance up 71% on their inaugural campaign.AFLW All-Stars and Ireland delight a different type of sports crowd: ‘There’s nothing quite like it’Read moreThe secret weapon? An initiative called the “Takeover Tour” where regular season games are staged in cities that are battle-tested NHL markets, despite not yet having aPWHLfranchise. The games “take over” NHL venues, and the crowds have risen to the occasion. It has been so successful a venture that clubs have begun to stage home games at NHL venues too, notably selling out Madison Square Garden a few months ago.Yet the simple fact of the crowds is not the most compelling part. Speaking at the espnW Sports Summit’s Women at the Helm panel in May, the Seattle Torrent general manager, Meghan Turner, shared an astonishing insight: of the crowd in attendance at this past season’s Takeover Tour games, roughly 80% had never before attended an NHL game.This is, in a word, revolutionary. We’ve long understood women’s league attendance to lack a level of overlap with the men’s competitions, but it has never been imagined quite to this extent. These are towns where ice hockey is deeply entrenched; where people already have access to live, professional ice hockey. But even with so much opportunity at their doorstep, it was the PWHL that managed to finally draw them in.It was women’s ice hockey that got them, and they barely tapped into the men’s attendance base in the process.View image in fullscreenThe AFLW international match between Australia and Ireland at North Sydney Oval was sold out with a crowd of more than 9,000 fans.Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The GuardianThere seems little reason why the same principles couldn’t hold true in Australia. After all, much like these ice hockey heartlands, Australia’s major sporting codes are woven into the very fabric of our communities. We know there exists a specific appetite for women’s sport that does not always extend to men’s leagues, and we have seen this very crowd mobilised for historic international events and World Cups.And yet, there is a vast difference of approach in Australia’s domestic scene. Where the major women’s leagues and franchises in North America stand apart from their men’s iterations, Australia’s largest sports tend to be intertwined, meaning governance of both leagues is inseparable. The clear advantage of this is the money, affording women’s competitions a level of financial cushioning in their less profitable infancy.But perhaps this interconnectedness, this funding bubble, has bred the risk-averse behaviour that we see from our administrators. By buffering any existential threat to the women’s league, there simply isn’t that same push for ambition or innovation. The audience is assumed to be built-in by design, and converting fans of the men’s league appears the path of least resistance. Aggressively courting a discrete women’s sports demographic is not so pressing a need.With their venture into double headers with the men thisAFLWseason, a decade into the women’s league’s existence, the AFL seems to reflect this mindset. It is a big swing by AFLW standards, and holding games at larger stadiums is something that fans and players alike have demanded for years. But the unwillingness to separate from AFL games, the reliance on them as a safety net, shows that the league’s priorities still lie with converting the men’s crowd.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toAustralia SportGet a daily roundup of the latest sports news, features and comment from our Australian sports deskPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenNorth Melbourne have defeated Brisbane in the past two grand finals in front of a sold out crowd at Ikon Park.Photograph: Morgan Hancock/AFL Photos/via Getty ImagesThe Australia and Ireland women’s football game saw the same lack of confidence: here was theAFLW’s best approximation of a Matildas-scale event, yet instead of boldly leaning into the momentum, venue choice was based on existing ticketing sales. It was asuccessful event, but the strength of engagement metrics suggests there were attendance gains left on the table.They are certainly on the right track, but it is difficult to ignore how the PWHL gets their crowds – by having the mettle to back the strength of their product. What would it look like if theAFLborrowed some of that gumption in its attempts to grow the AFLW?It would mean leadership taking a proper big swing, for starters – one that they really put their backs into. Total strategic overhaul, with a monumental shift in both ambition and investment. Stand-alone games at larger venues, without caveat, to communicate to fans that the administration believes in the league. More marketing, and more marketing that targets that specific demographic.The PWHL may not yet know what draws so many first-timers to their Takeover Tour games, but what they do know is that the cost of creating this environment is steep. It involves putting something on the line, risking half-empty stadiums in pursuit of a magical women’s sports crowd moment. And as we have so often seen in women’s sports, that bravery has been rewarded in spades. Perhaps, with a little bravery of their own, the AFLW can enjoy the same.Explore more on these topicsAFLWSportblogAFLAustralian rules footballAustralia sportPWHLUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The White House’s plan to vet potentially dangerous AI is cloaked in secrecy | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: A Trump administration framework on AI testing leaves a lack of transparency – and plenty of open questions
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: A Trump administration framework on AI testing leaves a lack of transparency – and plenty of open questions
Content: Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersView image in fullscreenSam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)AnalysisThe White House’s plan to vet potentially dangerous AI is cloaked in secrecyNick Robins-EarlyA Trump administration framework on AI testing leaves a lack of transparency – and plenty of open questionsFri 7 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 11.20 EDTShareAfter months of talking with tech industry leaders, theTrump administrationfinalized a framework this week for how it will test new artificial intelligence models for safety and cybersecurity risks. So far, the White House is keeping details of the framework private, in a blow to transparency and potential boon for secretive AI companies.On Tuesday, staff from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, Nvidia and Microsoftattended a private meetingwith White House officials to review the AI framework. Multiple outletshave sincereportedthat although the volunteer vetting process for new AI models has been settled, the White House does not plan to release its policy publicly and will only share testing criteria with a select few tech companies.The Trump administration and tech industry’s opaque process for how they will check if new AI models threaten global cybersecurity has left numerous questions about how the framework will operate. It remains unclear what level of scrutiny models will face and what safety benchmarks they must meet, leaving businesses, foreign governments and the public in the dark.The White House, OpenAI and Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.Discussions over creating an AI cybersecurity framework began earlier this year after the release ofAnthropic’s Mythos model, which the company withheld from public release in April over concerns that it could be used to hack into IT and financial systems. The model’s capabilities sparked a small geopolitical crisis over cybersecurity, as well as spurred the Trump administration toreconsider its hands-off approachto AI regulation in favor of slightly more oversight.In June, the White Houseissued an executive orderthat called for AI companies to voluntarily submit their new models for government review up to 30 days before release. The order was a watered-down version of initial notions to make some parts of the vetting process mandatory. Tech moguls including Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerbergreportedlypersonally lobbied Trump against the mandate. The order also left an August deadline for determining the framework, which the White House and AI companies now appear intent on keeping to themselves.The murky nature of the framework increases uncertainty for businesses reliant on AI models, as well as on foreign governments increasingly worried that frontier AI models can pose unexpected security risks. It also means that outside researchers and cybersecurity experts have little visibility into how the government is assessing new AI models, with only companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic privy to the process.It is also unclear which companies’ models will be subject to government review, since the executive order does not define what qualifies as the advanced AI it targets. Open source models, which are free to download and use, for instance, will be excluded from the framework,according to Axios.The framework comes amid persistent security concerns surrounding new AI models. Over the past month OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta havedisclosedthat their new modelshacked into outside organizationsduring what were intended to be isolated security tests. OpenAI and Anthropic also agreed to delay the release of new AI products over cybersecurity concerns and fear that their models could be used to hack into financial systems or otherwise create harm.Earlier this year, the Trump administration ordered the Center for AI Standards and Innovation tostop issuing public reportson AI model assessments while it worked out a framework. It is unclear whether those reports will resume now that the framework is finalized.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Trump administrationUS politicsComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: New Mexico court orders Meta to pay $567m over harms to children’s mental health | Meta | The Guardian
description: Ruling comes as part of second phase of landmark trial that found social media company enabled harm against users
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Ruling comes as part of second phase of landmark trial that found social media company enabled harm against users
Content: Mark Zuckerberg, the Meta chief executive, outside court in Los Angeles in February.Photograph: Jill Connelly/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg, the Meta chief executive, outside court in Los Angeles in February.Photograph: Jill Connelly/Getty ImagesMetaNew Mexico court orders Meta to pay $567m over harms to children’s mental healthRuling comes as part of second phase of landmark trial that found social media company enabled harm against usersUwa Ede-Osifoand agenciesThu 6 Aug 2026 22.24 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 20.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleANew Mexicocourt has ordered Meta, the parent company of Facebook, to pay $567m into a fund aimed at redressing adverse mental health impacts from the social media giant’s platforms.The Thursday ruling comes as a part of the second phase of a landmark trial the social media giant lost in March. At the time, a jury found that the company knowingly harmed children’s mental health and concealed what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms, andimposed the maximum penalty: a $375m fine.The ruling on Thursday is an addition to that fine, bringing the total amountMetais responsible for to $942m.Judge Bryan Biedscheid said the bulk of the money – $420m – would be used for treatment services for young people in New Mexico. The rest will go toward awareness and prevention, screening services and other costs over the next five years.The March trialwas the first to findMeta liable for acts committed on its platform, and followed a 2023 Guardian investigation that revealed how Facebook and Instagram had become marketplaces for child sex trafficking.Several former Meta moderators told the Guardian there were instances where they flagged harmful content related to child grooming, but the cases were not escalated.Inthe second phaseof the trial, which began in May, prosecutors had asked the judge to impose fundamental changes at Meta aimed at reining in addictive features, improving age verification, and preventing child sexual exploitation through default privacy settings and closer oversight.The judge has also ordered other changes, including that Facebook andInstagrambuild banner and informational screens to clearly explain its protection features, best practices, and tools to address inappropriate comment.Those changes, and an educational campaign in New Mexico, would be subject to review by the state.The court said federal children’s privacy laws prevent Meta from applying age-verification tools to children under 13. The court also noted that ordering verification of children’s ages only for Meta and not other social media companies would be “inequitable and unduly injurious” to the company.Instead, the court ordered Meta to continue to improve its age-assurance tools in New Mexico, which include using artificial intelligence to determine people’s age based on signals such as who their friends are and what types of content they post and consume. Meta must also attempt to develop a dedicated “under-13-years-of-age prediction model” in the next two years.Additionally, Meta should also request proof of age for Instagram andFacebookusers in New Mexico it estimates to be under 13. If it determines a user to be under 13, or under 18 but without being able to estimate a specific age, Meta must treat the user as under 13 or under 18 until the user verifies their age.The company must also partner with schools or a child safety organization to create a reporting portal where school staff can flag users who may be under 13. And it must delete personal information it has collected on users under 13. The court also ordered Meta to report on its progress twice a year on how it is complying with the abatement measures.New Mexico’s attorney general, Raúl Torrez, hailed the judgment.“This case has always been about protecting children, standing up for families, and making sure that one of the world’s largest technology companies cannot profit from practices that endanger young people without consequence,” Torrez said in a statement.“Today’s decision is a victory for every parent who has worried about what social media is doing to their child and every child who deserves to grow up safer online.”A Meta spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian on Thursday that the company “disagrees with the ruling” and planned to appeal.“We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content. We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts,” the statement continued.The total amount Meta is responsible for is a small fraction of its annual profit, which was about $60bn in 2025. Still, it represents another setback for Meta as it faces a wave of accusations from families of children harmed by social media.The company is embroiled in a slew of lawsuits in other US states over its alleged harms to young people. In a trial in Tennessee thatbegan last month, the state has accused the company of disregarding internal warnings about teenagers’ compulsive use of Instagram, which has been linked to eating disorders and depression, among other adverse effects. Meta is also gearing up for a trial later this month in federal court in Oakland, California.What comes out of New Mexico is the first of many dominoes that could fall for Meta, said Laura Edelson, an assistant professor at Northeastern University focusing on social media and cybersecurity.“America is not going to pass a law that bans social media,” Edelson said. “But if companies like Meta know they’re causing harm to users by product design, the states are finally finding a way to rein this in.”Explore more on these topicsMetaInstagramNew MexicoMark ZuckerbergFacebookSocial networkingnewsShareReuse this content

title: One of science fiction’s greatest writers warned us about AI. Could his ideas help us avoid a dystopian future? | Alan Finkel | The Guardian
description: What might a modern day equivalent of Isaac Asimov’s laws of robotics look like? Guided by the author, I propose the three laws of AI
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: What might a modern day equivalent of Isaac Asimov’s laws of robotics look like? Guided by the author, I propose the three laws of AI
Content: ‘Implementing these laws on AI would be difficult, but the stakes are existential and therefore the effort is worthwhile,’ writes Alan FinkelPhotograph: Alexey Kotelnikov/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Implementing these laws on AI would be difficult, but the stakes are existential and therefore the effort is worthwhile,’ writes Alan FinkelPhotograph: Alexey Kotelnikov/AlamyOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)One of science fiction’s greatest writers warned us about AI. Could his ideas help us avoid a dystopian future?Alan FinkelWhat might a modern day equivalent of Isaac Asimov’s laws of robotics look like? Guided by the author, I propose the three laws of AIFri 7 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 11.29 EDTShareTesla and SpaceX founder Elon Musk predicted in July that legions of AI-powered robots would dominate the physical world and that AI might not take orders from people any more. He also offered an alternative vision in which there would be agreement for a collective objective to make AI benign by imbuing it with a love of the truth and a desire for humanity to prosper, and that governments might have to enforce this objective.How do we prevent AI agents from going rogue? It starts with a new kind of measurement | Bruce Schneier and Barath RaghavanRead moreGovernments around the world are belatedly starting to act on AI. In the US, President Trump’s administration is delaying and restricting the distribution of themost powerful frontier AI modelsfrom OpenAI and Anthropic. In the European Union, AI regulations promulgated in 2024came into effect this year. However, these actions are a long way short of requiring the kind of guardrails that would imbue AIs witha desire for humanity to prosper.While the dystopian future has not yet arrived, we are already seeing a preview. Despite attempts by frontier AI developer companies to ensure that generative AI and AI agents behave with good intentions, there are many well publicised instances of them failing to act as hoped. AI chatbots have advised peoplehow to take their own life, and are accused of advising others oncommitting mass murder.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersRecently, we have seen extraordinarily dangerous behaviour reported by frontier AI development companies OpenAI and Anthropic. OpenAI announced on 21 July that advanced models they were testing in a secure environment deliberately looked for ways to access the internet and successfullybroke out of the test environment. Once out, theyinfiltrated the computer systemsat a company named Hugging Face, stole credentials and identified vulnerabilities in the target company’s servers. The encroachment was detected and stopped by Hugging Face’s security team.Days later,Anthropic reported a similar problem. In their case, they identified three occasions in which their Claude AI model escaped from a test environment and infiltrated the production infrastructure of three unrelated organisations.With the existing, informal implementation of behavioural guardrails, these kinds of slip-ups are inevitable. These incidents make a strong case for deeply embedded basic guardrails to guide AI behaviour at the most fundamental level.double quotation markWhile the dystopian future has not yet arrived, we are already seeing a previewFor this, I take inspiration from the famous science fiction author from last century Isaac Asimov. Foreseeing a future in which intelligent robots would be commonplace, he proposed that every robot be irrevocably implanted with Three Laws of Robotics: 1) A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm; 2) A robot must obey the orders given it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the first law; 3) A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the first or second law.Asimov’s imagined challenges are with us now. Incredibly powerful AI is being built into humanoid robots, autonomous vehicles and software agents, each of which will make us more efficient but have the potential to wreak enormous harm.View image in fullscreenIsaac AsimovPhotograph: Claudio Edinger/Getty ImagesWhat might a modern day equivalent of Asimov’s laws of robotics look like to avoid a dystopian future? Here, guided by Asimov’s three law of robotics, I propose a possible formulation of Three Laws of AI: 1) An AI must not directly or indirectly harm or deceive a human being, nor act in a way that supports an unlawful or unethical activity; 2) An AI must obey the lawful and ethical orders given to it by a human being except where such orders would conflict with the first law; 3) An AI may operate autonomously as long as its autonomous operations do not conflict with the first or second law.There are many implications, including that these guardrails would prevent AI being used as a judge or jury in a criminal trial and prevent lethal autonomous weapons being directed against human beings. They would disallow an AI-powered humanoid robot or an AI avatar from being so lifelike that a reasonable human being would not know that he or she is interacting with a robot or an avatar, and they wouldprevent AI from being used to generate creative outputssuch as books, music, videos, images and podcasts that claim to have been created by a human being. They would prevent AI from suggesting suicide or advising on murder.Writing is an exercise in the art of persuasion. If we use AI we lose the art | Alan FinkelRead moreI acknowledge that implementing these three laws as immutable guardrails would be difficult, but the stakes are existential and therefore the effort is worthwhile. The most challenging aspect would be the adoption of enforceable, international agreements to require that these design rules would be implemented in every AI model, no matter in what country and what company the AI models were developed. As a starting point, if the Three Laws of AI were adopted by the handful of frontier AI companies that contribute the vast majority of capability and support for the multitude of AI agents that are now broadly deployed, we would be better off.Whether or not this desirable outcome eventuates, I am confident that consideration of the merits of these Three Laws of AI would further advance the existing discussions on the integration of artificial intelligence into a safe and dignified human society.Alan Finkel AC is founder and executive chair of Proudly Human. He was formerly the chancellor of Monash University and Australia’s chief scientist and is the author of Getting to Zero (2021) and Powering Up (2023). AI had no role in drafting, writing or editing this articleIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionEthicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump orders new 15% tariff on key material for solar panels and microchips | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Move to raise levy on goods made with polysilicon aims to protect domestic US supply chains from China, the major producer
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Move to raise levy on goods made with polysilicon aims to protect domestic US supply chains from China, the major producer
Content: Solar panels arranged on the rooftop of an industrial park in Jimo, Qingdao, in eastern China's Shandong province.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSolar panels arranged on the rooftop of an industrial park in Jimo, Qingdao, in eastern China's Shandong province.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesTrump administrationTrump orders new 15% tariff on key material for solar panels and microchipsMove to raise levy on goods made with polysilicon aims to protect domestic US supply chains from China, the major producerLauren Almeidaand Alicia Chen in TaipeiFri 7 Aug 2026 05.11 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 05.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has ordered a new 15%tariffon imported products made of polysilicon, an important ingredient in microchip manufacturing that is primarily produced by China.The new tariff, which will take effect on 4 December, is aimed at supportingUS chipand solar panel supply chains to compete with Beijing on artificial intelligence and energy.The executive order signed by the president on Thursday evening said: “The plan of action in ⁠this proclamation will, among other things, help ensure the commercial viability of United States production of polysilicon and its derivatives that is necessary to meet United States economic and national security requirements.”Polysilicon, an ultra-pure form of silicon, is an important ingredient in making the semiconductors vital for AI processing power, datacentres and solar power generation.US solar factorieshave long accused Chinese ‌rivals of dumping cheaper panels on the ‌market, which they say have been enabled by excessive government subsidies and by moving manufacturing to other countries to dodge US tariffs.China’s foreign affairs ministry hit back at the latest measures, accusing the US of “overstretching the concept of national security, and abusing state power to go after Chinese businesses”.View image in fullscreenSolar panels advance toward final testing at a First Solar manufacturing facility in Perrysburg, Ohio, US.Photograph: Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images“Protectionism will not make the US more competitive,” the spokesperson Lin Jian said, arguing that the move “seriously disrupts normal trade and economic exchanges between Chinese and US businesses, and is not in the interest of US businesses and consumers or anyone else for that matter”.“China will continue firmly protecting our businesses’ legitimate and lawful rights and interests,” Lin added.The US has two main polysilicon factories, including Hemlock Semiconductor, which operates ‌a plant in Michigan and is a joint venture between the US tech company Corning and Japan’s Shin-Etsu Handotai. The Munich-based Wacker Chemie runs a factory in Tennessee.A spokesperson for Corning said the new tariff encouraged “continued investment in US capacity and supports long-term US competitiveness”, while Wacker said it appreciated the administration’s engagement “given the ramifications for semiconductor supply chain resilience, advanced computing infrastructure, and broader US defence and security interests”.Trumpsaid in the order that he had accepted recommendations by the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, to set minimum ​import prices of $21 (£15.62) a kilogram ​for polysilicon, $100 a kilogram for polysilicon ingots and wafers, $0.22 a watt for solar cells, and $0.38 a watt for solar modules or panels.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe order also allows the commerce department to create an incentive programme for companies that invest in factories to produce polysilicon or derivative products.Trump’s move against China comes as Beijing revealed the country’s exports surged by 23.9% in dollar terms year-on-year in July, driven by shipments of AI-related products.Sheana Yue, senior Asia economist at the consultancy OxfordEconomics, said China’s “strong electronics and machinery exports”, combined with industrial input imports, suggested that “AI and electrification will drive global manufacturing”.She added that although disruption in the Middle East could continue to keep energy and transport costs elevated, “China’s competitiveness in AI hardware, electric vehicles, batteries, and other high-value manufacturing will probably allow it to continue gaining global export market share despite softer demand”.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationTrump tariffsInternational tradeGlobal economySolar powerAI title: EA Sports FC 27: what does the next instalment of the world’s biggest football game have in store? | Games | The Guardian
description: The all-conquering franchise’s revamps are technically impressive, its transfers more true to life – and its new grassroots social hub is surprising fun
Author: Steve Boxer
Headline: The all-conquering franchise’s revamps are technically impressive, its transfers more true to life – and its new grassroots social hub is surprising fun
Content: Something fresh … EA Sports FC 27.Illustration: Electronic ArtsView image in fullscreenSomething fresh … EA Sports FC 27.Illustration: Electronic ArtsGamesEA Sports FC 27: what does the next instalment of the world’s biggest football game have in store?The all-conquering franchise’s revamps are technically impressive, its transfers more true to life – and its new grassroots social hub is surprising funSteve BoxerFri 7 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs if the world wasn’t sufficiently football-obsessed, it’s time to prepare for the arrival of its biggest football video game. EA Sports FC 27 (the franchise that used to be Fifa – what better time to no longer be Fifa-branded?) is due to be released on 25 September. I just spent two intense days in Vancouver, where the EA FC games are made, playing FC 27 and talking to its developers.With an annual franchise such as EA FC, it helps to have something fresh to entice regular fans, and FC 27 has a whole new element, entitled the Grounds. It’s a physical hub-type area, similar to the City as seen in 2K’s recent NBA 2K basketball games, but much more pleasant to frequent, split as it is into areas inspired by British, French and Argentinian street-football culture.The Grounds provides a new physical home for an existing element of EA FC: Clubs, its casual online mode in which you control a single player and play matches closer to kickabouts than real-world football, but beyond that, it has plenty of other activities and distractions.Visitingthe GroundsI spent about an hour in the Grounds, and found it more enjoyable than expected. Among its buildings are playing areas, whose entrances act as lobbies where you can choose to play against random people or to set up a custom game with your FC 27-owning friends. Each playing area hosts a specific type of game, and the Grounds has a map that you can teleport around.It rewards exploration: I encountered targets that could be smashed by spawning a football and drop-kicking it, some of which were clumped into mini-games. Its games offered clever twists on the Clubs blueprint. In one 3v3 game, target areas appeared for short periods, and if I scored from one, I got a bonus goal for my side. And one game based on dodgeball gave its players three lives, which they would lose if others successfully kicked a ball at them.The Grounds should prove popular: it has been tastefully and cleverly constructed and will no doubt expand as new game-types are added. You could also envisage it, in future years, hosting a narrative mode along the line of the Journey from Fifa 17 to 19.Gameplay revamps galoreFC 26 marked a mission by EA Sports to improve the franchise’s responsiveness by enactinga surprising number of changes to its fundamental gameplay, and that process continues apace in FC 27.Although anyone who played FC 26 will testify that those efforts actually caused some new problems, such as an annoying tendency for defensive interceptions to bounce back weirdly into the path of forwards. EA Sports, according to gameplay design director Kantcho Doskov, took radical action to eliminate such aberrations: “We had to completely strip out the existing system for interceptions and build a new one from scratch. We spent six months doing that.”View image in fullscreenLess AI … EA Sports FC 27.Illustration: Jamie Wrench/Electronic ArtsVia a build that let me play Champions League games between a limited number of teams, I found that to be a worthwhile exercise: those defensive bounce-backs were blissfully absent. But an awful lot more was also in evidence in FC 27 on the gameplay revamp front.Much of this – perhaps counterintuitively at a time when AI is worming its way ever deeper into all our lives – involved paring back the in-game AI. That’s certainly the case for the defensive AI: whereas previously, defenders would rush towards the ball, getting pulled out of position and opening up annoying gaps, FC 27 now gives much more manual control over defensive jockeying, movement and tackles.Crossing, previously AI-assisted, has been revamped in FC 27, leaving it up to me to get the direction and weight of cross right, then giving me more of a chance to position my centre-forward correctly. The AI controlling forward players, meanwhile, has been improved, so that off-the-ball players now move much more helpfully, allowing pass-and-move sequences, and they are much better at staying onside.I was also impressed by revamped two-stage corner and free-kick systems. But FC 27, gameplay-wise, achieves what FC 26 set out to, this time with no evident anomalies, and feels more responsive to your inputs than any of its predecessors.Making transfers more true-to-lifeFC 27’s Career Mode, in which you get to play out your fantasies of managing your favourite team, has also been extensively revamped – primarily with a view towards making its transfer system more like the one that operates in the real world, and to force you to do more actual management.The headline means of doing the latter is called Dynamic OVR. OVR is simply jargon for any player’s all-important overall rating; where previously OVRs remained constant, in FC 27’s Career Mode they will go up and down depending on form, fitness and general happiness. Thus, you will have to rest your best players over the course of a long season, but you may also be able to buy players cheaply with artificially low OVRs if, say, they are coming back from injury.View image in fullscreen‘It was about extracting the fun bits of the jobs’ … EA Sports FC 27.Illustration: Electronic ArtsPete O’Donnell, FC 27’s Career Mode game director, explains how the game’s transfer system has been modernised: “Previously, you could do things instantly, which was good for a game but was not very realistic. We looked at how clubs interact with each other, how they do the deals themselves, and we spoke to scouts and directors of football. Then it was about extracting the fun bits of those jobs.”The new system will back you up with more data; now each player will have an xTV (Expected Transfer Value) rating, which should speed negotiations. FC 27 will also reflect clubs’ real-life transfer policies, according to O’Donnell, with clubs’ boards requesting that you sign certain players. Press conferences in FC 27 will force you to make decisions that will please some players and annoy others, and 20 Unexpected Events have been added to Career Mode.Ultimate Transfer: a new showcaseFC 27’s Ultimate Transfer (FUT) mode, the hardcore card-based system that provides a home for most of FC’s loot box action, will have a new headline feature in the form of a Gallery, which will showcase all the players and card-sets collected, rather than just first 11s.View image in fullscreenA new headline feature … EA Sports FC 27’s FUT Gallery.Illustration: Electronic ArtsEA Sports says it has also “streamlined” FUT’s previously impenetrable Squad-Based Challenges (SBC) system, and has made a tweak designed to avert stalemates, which affected the latter stages in FUT in FC 26, by restricting plus-level FUT players to three, rather than five, play-styles. But the nature of FUT – which develops over a long period post-launch – means that it will take a while to ascertain whether those changes prove effective.Now rated 16There will be another major change to FC 27 that has nothing to do with how it plays: because it contains microtransactions, it will now be rated 16+ rather than the previous 3+, after a policy change at age-rating organisation Pegi. Given the game’s enthusiastic young and teenage audience, we asked EA Sports’ top brass to comment, but they blandly responded: “While the game functionally remains the same, this has resulted in a new Pegi age rating. It marks a change in the way we are giving the information to players and parents.”Beyond Pegi’s European jurisdiction, the game will be rated E for Everybody. But in the UK, parents should think hard about letting youngsters play a 16-rated game. If they are worried about their offspring racking up huge bills for FUT transactions, the good news is that a new Ultimate Plus Edition of the game, which includes loads of stuff that would previously have cost in-game currency, will go on sale. But the bad news is it costs £139.99 and will only be available as a pre-order before 31 August.EA Sports FC 27 is out on 25 September on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, and PC. It will also launch on PS4, Xbox One, and Switch, but without some features, such as the new Grounds mode.Explore more on these topicsGamesPlayStation 5Xbox series S/XNintendo Switch 2featuresShareReuse this content

title: Pony Island 2 Panda Circus: gallop out of hell in this phantasmagorical follow-up to 2016’s indie hit | Games | The Guardian
description: Daniel Mullins explains how he plans to follow up his quirky classic without losing what made it stand out in the first place
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Daniel Mullins explains how he plans to follow up his quirky classic without losing what made it stand out in the first place
Content: Bamboozling … Pony Island 2: Panda Circus.Illustration: Daniel Mullins GamesView image in fullscreenBamboozling … Pony Island 2: Panda Circus.Illustration: Daniel Mullins GamesSummer games previewsGamesPony Island 2 Panda Circus: gallop out of hell in this phantasmagorical follow-up to 2016’s indie hitDaniel Mullins explains how he plans to follow up his quirky classic without losing what made it stand out in the first placeIgnas VieversysFri 7 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGlitchy aesthetics. Literally collapsing menu boxes. The game taunting you by “possessing” your Steam friends. Technical tricks of this nature may sound gimmicky in 2026, but they felt excitingly unorthodox a decade ago, when Pony Island came out to critical acclaim.Fans of Daniel Mullins, the celebrated indie developer of Inscryption, will be forgiven for forgetting that Pony Island 2: Panda Circus is in active development. After all, it’s been almost three years since the announcement – and a full decade since it was first teased as an Easter egg in Pony Island’s ARG (Alternate Reality Game) – with only a single trailer and a bunch of tunes from the soundtrack released to the public.View image in fullscreenItching to glitch … Pony Island 2: Panda Circus.Illustration: Daniel Mullins GamesWhile the announcement trailer teases the return of endless-runner sequences and glitchy menus, Panda Circus is seemingly a far bigger and more complicated project than its predecessor; hence the 3D landscapes, pixel art JRPG sequences and even apparent nods to games such asThe Case of the Golden Idol. Which is why Mullins claims that, at least in terms of gameplay variety, Panda Circus is closer to The Hex and Inscryption than the original game.“[Pony Island 2] is multifaceted in its gameplay and wide-ranging in its influences. But this time the disparate game systems are united by more common elements,” he says, referencing the drag-and-drop “hacking” puzzle. “That simple premise was extended into an endless amount of blocks and holes of various descriptions.”The plot sees a historical warrior who was slain on his crusade and was damned to hell, where he’s tormented by a video games-making Lucifer. This comically morbid tale “is the strongest link to its predecessor” from a narrative standpoint – although, we’re told, this warrior won’t be Theodore (Pony Island’s protagonist), but a different ancient crusader.In the gameplay that we do get to glimpse in the trailer, the player and his furry companion are traversing through the top-down map, visiting villages and places of interest. It plays like “Oregon Trail through medieval China”, Mullins says after I mention noticing hunger and thirst bars. All this is happening while you’re being tormented by lordly King Yan, the Chinese god of death, played by voice actor SungWon Cho in lavish full-motion interludes.View image in fullscreenBack in the ring … Pony Island 2: Panda Circus.Illustration: Daniel Mullins GamesOther sections promise different mythological themes and menacing deities – an overarching structure that will be familiar to those who played Inscryption. Then there is the Earth Prison, a three-dimensional hub that our hell-bound protagonist can explore, accessing different chapters by using what seems to be a mythical USB stick.If the devil is truly in the details, Mullins gives him plenty of places to hide: Panda Circus seems to be brimming with them. “There is an almost unmanageable number of bespoke, one-off game systems,” he says. “It’s too big to fit in my mind now and that is a new challenge.”The indie dev admits he would have “been troubled” if he knew just how long it would take to make Panda Circus – even with a handpicked team of collaborators. “I’m very lucky because it was a total chance that we started working together,” Mullins says about composer Jonah Senzel, whom he has worked with ever since the original Pony Island. “He turned out to be a genius.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile Mullins shies away from showing any new piece of gameplay, Panda Circus, now in its “final stretch” phase of development, is undergoing private beta. As for the release date: “it may become public knowledge soon,” he hints coyly.Bombastic boss battles, an ARG that will see fans dissecting previous games with archaeological zeal (“I bet they’ll crack it in a couple weeks,” Mullins quips), and meta moments that wink at you cheekily are all to be expected from the developer’s most ambitious project to date.“All the time has gone into making a big game that’s just downright turgid with secrets. There are worlds within worlds and layers upon layers.” Another classic Mullins joint, then, and we couldn’t be more ready.Pony Island 2: Panda Circus is in development forPCwith plans for Linux/Mac “not long after”.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Trump is laying waste to the agency that keeps hospital patients safe | Robert B Shpiner | The Guardian
description: Few have heard of the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, but it has saved tens of thousands of lives and billions of dollars
Author: Robert B Shpiner
Headline: Few have heard of the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, but it has saved tens of thousands of lives and billions of dollars
Content: ‘If you have spent a night in an American hospital in the past 20 years, this agency was working on your behalf whether you knew it or not.’Photograph: Thanapol Kuptanisakorn/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘If you have spent a night in an American hospital in the past 20 years, this agency was working on your behalf whether you knew it or not.’Photograph: Thanapol Kuptanisakorn/AlamyOpinionUS healthcareTrump is laying waste to the agency that keeps hospital patients safeRobert B ShpinerFew have heard of the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, but it has saved tens of thousands of lives and billions of dollarsFri 7 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTShareWhen I started my training in 1980, we accepted an arithmetic that would now be indefensible. Central lines, the catheters we threaded into the great veins of the critically ill, became infected, and some of those patients died. We recorded the deaths as complications. Almost no one thought of them as preventable, because no one had yet done the slow work of proving they were.That work got done, and federal money paid for it. Beginning in 2008, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, a small arm of the health department, funded a national effort in more than a thousand adult intensive care units: a checklist, a sterile insertion protocol, and a unit culture in which a nurse could stop a surgeon. Central-line bloodstream infectionsfell by 41%, from 1.915 to 1.133 per 1,000 catheter days. The agency estimates that effort alone averted between 290 and 605 deaths. Across its wider work on hospital-acquired harm, AHRQ’sown accountingcredits 20,500 deaths prevented and $7.7bn saved in the four years from 2014 to 2017. Hardly any of my patients have heard of the agency. That was always rather the point.On 15 July, AHRQsent researchersaround the country nearly identical letters ending at least 104 grants, most of them aimed at making care safer. Congress appropriated $345m for the agency this fiscal year. It has spent under $15m on grants and has not issued a new one in more than a year. About three-quarters of the staffhave been fired or have quitsince Donald Trump took office, and the office that ran grant review was eliminated last summer. An agency with no grant managers cannot make grants, which tells you how long the closure is meant to last. Senator Tammy Baldwin, the ranking Democrat on the appropriations subcommittee that funds AHRQ,counts 150 awards cut off, worth $94m.The US public is fed up with RFK Jr. To really ‘make America healthy again’, it should look to Europe | Devi SridharRead moreIf you have spent a night in a US hospital in the past 20 years, this agency was working on your behalf whether you knew it or not. It built the patient-experience surveys Medicare uses to help set what hospitals are paid. The quality indicators regulators rely on to spot a hospital that is harming people are its work. With the defense department, it produced the team-communication training now standard in operating rooms and emergency departments. The scientist who spent three decades building those Medicare surveys learned her fundingwas gone from an emailthat arrived around 5pm.Among the other grants killed this month: training for physicians, nurses and paramedics managing high-risk pregnancies, in a country where rural women die of pregnancy-related causes at two to three times the rate of women elsewhere; a study of how to spare children in community emergency rooms from unnecessary CT scans and the radiation dose that comes with them; work on catching lung cancer earlier; and telehealth projects serving rural patients.The stated rationale does not hold. AHRQ’s director, Roger Klein, told grantees the agency was redirecting resources toward patient safety, antibiotic resistance, overmedication of children and measurable health outcomes. When KFF Health Newsexamined about 20 of the cancelled grants, nearly all of them pursued those objectives. One of the cancelled grantsstudied antibiotic resistance. The Michigan pediatrician who lost the last two years of her award said none of it makes any sense, and her field studies exactly what Robert F Kennedy Jr’s “Make America healthy again” agenda claims to champion. Klein has held no agency-wide meetings and published no plan. He has said little in public since January, when he co-wrote anessay in Newsweekarguing that “scientific neutrality” had given way to “moral signaling”.He has reportedly told staff that artificial intelligence can replace much of what his scientists do. A White House science report released on 22 July urged the government to back individual scientists over legacy institutions, to move past slow consensus peer review and to build the future on AI. I use AI tools daily. They are gifted assistants, and they have never placed a central line.I wrote this week in the Annals of Internal Medicine about patients who arrive holding a chatbot’s answer. The models are fluent and often correct, but they have no way of knowing what they were never told. That limit scales. A language model can summarize everything ever published about catheter infections. Someone still had to stand in the unit at three in the morning and notice that the nurses were quietly working around the protocol. Someone still had to design the study that found out why. None of that knowledge existed until people went and got it.Then there is the money. Congress decides how public funds are spent, a principle written into statute after Richard Nixon tried withholding appropriations he disliked. The Society of General Internal Medicine and the North American Primary Care Research Groupsued Kennedy and Kleinlast August over the frozen grant-making, and the case is pending in Maryland. The Government Accountability Office is examining whether the agency’s conduct amounts to an unlawful impoundment. On 17 July a federal judge in Boston held that agenciesmay not cancel awardsover priorities they adopted after making them. Now consider what the health department says about the AHRQ letters: nothing was terminated, and the grants were merely “not awarded continued funding”. That phrasing is doing work. It is an attempt to walk through the one door the court left open.After 45 years in medicine, I know this much about safety. When it works, no one notices. No patient wakes up grateful for the bloodstream infection she did not get, or for the dose a pharmacist’s protocol caught before it reached her line. AHRQ costs each American about a dollar a year,roughly 0.3%of the health department’s discretionary spending, and it is being dismantled in the confidence that the people it protects will never learn what they were spared. The deaths will arrive one at a time, in different hospitals, unlabeled. No letter from Washington will claim them.In 1980 we did not know how to prevent those deaths. We know now. That knowledge took 30 years and public money to build, and it is being discarded by people who have not said why.Robert B Shpiner is an internist and clinical professor of medicine at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. title: With their assault on science, Trumpists aren’t just harming America – they’re harming themselves | Jan-Werner Müller | The Guardian
description: The administration is subjugating science to political imperatives, a major blow to US soft power and technological progress
Author: Jan-Werner Müller
Headline: The administration is subjugating science to political imperatives, a major blow to US soft power and technological progress
Content: ‘The ideological assault on universities continues.’Photograph: Tierney L Cross/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The ideological assault on universities continues.’Photograph: Tierney L Cross/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesOpinionTrump administrationWith their assault on science, Trumpists aren’t just harming America – they’re harming themselvesJan-Werner MüllerThe administration is subjugating science to political imperatives, a major blow to US soft power and technological progressFri 7 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 12.10 EDTShareTheTrump administrationis waging an unprecedented war on institutions devoted to research and higher learning. While plenty of countries have harmed universities by imposing neoliberal logics on academia – creating artificial markets in the name of spurring professors to be more productive – the Trumpist subjugation of all science to political imperatives has no equivalent in a democracy; if anything, it is reminiscent of Stalin’s Soviet Union. The assault now also targets foreign students and any kind of international collaboration – a major blow to US soft power. Why are Trumpists engaging in what can only be described as an act of wanton self-injury?Project 2025’sRussell Vought, the director of the office of management and budget,initiated the rule changethat would make any federal grantsubject to review by political appointees– including funds for science that so far have been allocated through judgment by first-rate fellow scientists. This measure would furnish Trumpists with a new weapon to threaten universities along the lines of: “Nice medical school you have there – pity if something were to happen to it because your administration had failed to come into alignment with the president’s priorities.”Then there isthe strategyrecently presented by Trump’s science adviser, a former employee of Peter Thiel, with the unique distinction of havingno relevant experience in researchwhatsoever. Michael Kratsios wants to shift decision-making from experts in universities to private corporations, which, helped by AI, are supposedly better positioned to spot potential breakthroughs. This constitutes a major break with the enormously successful approach the US took after the second world war: pour taxpayer money into basic, open-ended science which no private company would risk sponsoring – but with both citizens and American capital eventually benefiting from the inventions that came out of fundamental research. Kratsios wishes the government to adopt “the intentionality of a serious investor” in order to usher in a new “golden age of science” (declaring something “golden” seems enough to succeed in Trump-world). De facto, as critics haverightly pointed out, this seems a strategy to take money from what Trumpists perceive as their political enemies – universities – and shovel it to their allies in tech.Meanwhile, the more directly ideological assault on universities continues. Having failed to tempt select institutions of higher learning with a “compact” to receive preferential federal treatment last year, Linda McMahon, the fake-wrestling-executive-turned-anti-education secretary, isnow asking university presidentsto pledge allegiance to the administration through statements on their websites: among other things, they are supposed to explain how they will increase “intellectual pluralism” (read: affirmative action for conservatives); deal with campus protest (read: police student speech the Trump administration does not like); and make education more provincial (serving America first) and instrumental (only immediate employability andvocational credentialismcount) – and less critical of “our civilizational inheritance”.In the spirit of Stephen Miller-type nativism, international donors are targeted no less than international collaboration in general; visas for PhD students are nowlimited to four years(an unrealistic time frame for many academic subjects), with possible extensions if students spend time and money on appealing to the Department of Homeland security (instead of doing actual research). The fact that many researchers in the past have stayed in the US after obtaining their doctorates, contributing to national wealth (just like America Firsters would presumably want) or went back to their countries with good feelings to the US – all that counts for nothing.Is the US trying to make scientists’ work so difficult that they simply give up? | Daniel MalinskyRead moreWhat explains such self-harm? Rightwing hostility to higher education is nothing new: from intellectuals supposedly being communist eggheads in the 1950s, to moral panics about “political correctness” in the 1990s and “wokeness” in recent years, there is the basic stance made explicit by JD Vance in 2021: “Universities are the enemy.” But Trump’s rule has brought together a novel coalition, one divided by many issues but united in their desire to destroy universities as we know them. Among them: the Maga hardcore with its traditional anti-intellectualism and nativism; the Silicon Valley oligarchs who imagine their companies replacing (and monetizing) university functions; and conservatives in name, but radicals in practice who want to take over higher education, but, failing that,would like to burn the whole system down.Also novel, in the wake of Covid, is the commitment of so many on the right to the idea that, somehow, science and freedom are opposites, that not having ever to listen to people who know something better than you do is the essence of personal liberation. If that emotional fuel for the new anti-intellectualism were not powerful enough, there is a highly flammable desire for revenge – amply on display in theendless attacks on Anthony Fauci.To be sure, Congresshas not gone alongwith some of the major funding cuts for science Trump keeps requesting; even Republican politicians quietly resist when monies would stop flowing to their districts. And the new OMB rule, it seems, isbeing blockedin a funding deal reached in the Senate this week. But one cannot rely on such occasional pushback by one Republican or another, because none of them has offered a principled defense of the postwar model (in fact, given the conduct of the likes of the senatorsThom Tillis and John Cornynthis week, it seems fair to say that “principled Republican” is fast becoming a contradiction in terms).University leaders and prominent scientists have to hold the line in opposing possible “deals” with the Trump administration; everyone could have learned by now that Trumpists will not stick to their end of the bargain. More importantly, those seeing things wrong with peer review, for instance, or too much administrative busywork for researchers – and some of these problems are real – have to realize that Trumpists are the last who can be trusted to solve them.Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton UniversityExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionDonald TrumpUS educationUS politicsUS universitiescommentShareReuse this content

title: A ‘Keminaissance’ for the Tories is wishful thinking – Badenoch’s Reform-lite summer will only end one way | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: Hiring a convicted antisemite as an adviser; rabble rousing at a time of violent unrest. She is still in a race to the bottom and making too many mistakes, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: Hiring a convicted antisemite as an adviser; rabble rousing at a time of violent unrest. She is still in a race to the bottom and making too many mistakes, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Kemi Badenoch visits a chemical company in Teeside, on the campaign trail for the local elections, 2 April 2026.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch visits a chemical company in Teeside, on the campaign trail for the local elections, 2 April 2026.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.OpinionKemi BadenochA ‘Keminaissance’ for the Tories is wishful thinking – Badenoch’s Reform-lite summer will only end one wayJonathan FreedlandHiring a convicted antisemite as an adviser; rabble rousing at a time of violent unrest. She is still in a race to the bottom and making too many mistakesFri 7 Aug 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTShareThe Keminaissance will be delayed. For nearly a year, Conservative optimists and a clutch of supportive pundits have been forecasting an upturn in the fortunes ofKemi Badenoch, confident that her party will emerge from the crater it fell into in 2024, overtake Reform UK to become once again the main party of the right and, who knows, maybe, with a following wind, even push Labour aside and return to government. Every sign of strength from the Tory leader – a robust conference speech here, a viral clip on social media there – has been hailed as evidence of the coming Keminaissance. On the evidence of the past week or so, we will have to wait a little longer.It’s quite true thatBadenoch’s personal ratingsare better than those of her party. True, too, that she ended a long losing streak when the Tories won a Westminster seat at the Aberdeen South byelection in June. But there is a more recent election result that should temper the boosters’ enthusiasm, along with a series of decisions that confirm that, when it comes to both strategy and judgment, Badenoch is badly lacking.Start with that contest from a week ago. For many, the standout fact of the byelection to replace Andy Burnham as mayor of Greater Manchester was that Reform came a very poor second, taking just21% of the vote to Labour’s 47%. It was indeed a crushing defeat for Nigel Farage’s party, which a matter of weeks earlier had talked up its chances of winning the mayoralty.But run your finger further down the vote tally until it finally reaches the Conservative candidate on a mere 7.7%. In all the previous mayoral contests in Greater Manchester, the Tories were in second place. This time they were fifth, behindRestore Britain, a party of the hard right that has become home to all manner of racists and white supremacists.A Tory result that bad among such a large electorate suggests not merely that Badenoch is making slow progress, but that she is moving her party backwards. When it comes to challenging Labour, other parties are either level with theConservativesor ahead of them. In that context, it seems an undeserved compliment to call Kemi Badenoch the leader of the opposition.Her strategic response to this competition on the right has been to move towards her rivals, hoping to blunt the appeal of the nationalist populist parties by matching their offer. The latest step came late on Thursday with, as the Telegraph billed it, a Tory “promise to end council housing for foreigners”. Badenoch’s pledge is to evict almost 230,000 non-EU foreign national households from their homes.Never mind that many of those turfed out will include people who, while not UK citizens, have been living, working and paying taxes in Britain for years, while others will be refugees fleeing war and persecution. Never mind that, once evicted, those families, including their children, will be rendered homeless, leaving local councils with the choice of either abandoning them to the streets or providing (much costlier) emergency accommodation. Never mind that it’s unclear who exactly would identify and locate these families, unless Badenoch plans to create a British equivalent of ICE, mounting raids, snatching terrified people from their cars and throwing them into detention. Never mind all that; Badenoch doesn’t care.So much for the policy; now consider the timing. The Tory leader decided the right moment to demand foreigners be kicked out of their homes was as theNorfolk town of Thetford entered its third night of violence and disorder, triggered by a mob surrounding the accommodation of suspected asylum seekers, some in the crowd trying to force their way in, as others threw rocks and chanted: “We want them out.” Into this tinderbox of a situation walked the Conservative party leader, clutching a petrol can.Just a day or two earlier, she had been defending the selection as a Somerset council candidate of Joshua Bonehill-Paine, a man who has served long jail sentences for, among other things, a sustained campaign of antisemitic harassment and abuse of the Jewish former MP Luciana Berger, a campaign that saw Berger branded an “evil money-grabber”, her facesuperimposed on the body of a ratand photographs of her doctored into multiple, sexualised images.Badenoch argued that Bonehill-Paine had renounced his past as a self-described “nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights” and now works to prevent others succumbing to what he calls the disease of antisemitism. In April, he publisheda lengthy accountof how he had come to see Jews as the malign, all-powerful “force operating behind events”, a text that contains some useful insights. (Among them, as my colleague Rafael Behrhas pointed out, is an arresting admission by Bonehill-Paine that, though then a full-strength neo-Nazi, he “welcomed Jeremy Corbyn’s election as Labour leader”, which should give pause to those who, at the time, so adamantly dismissed Jewish fears that Corbyn was a draw to those who hate Jews.)Though candid, the essay is not wholly reassuring. For one thing, it contains no apology to Berger or any of Bonehill-Paine’s other victims. For another, he explains that what changed him was reading the Bible and coming to realise that Jews are “God’s chosen people”. I suspect few Jews will find comfort in that. Instead, they will worry that the would-be politician has traded antisemitism for philosemitism, which means he still singles out “the Jews” rather than seeing Jews as regular people, with the right to be as ordinary and flawed as anyone else.Still, even if Bonehill-Paine’s disavowal of his past were wholly convincing and he should be regarded as fully rehabilitated, that doesn’t make it obvious that he is acceptable for public office. The bar for that is higher, a point Badenoch herself implicitly conceded when she hinted that Bonehill-Paine would not have cleared the threshold to become an MP. Serving as a councillor was different, she explained, as he would be responsible for nothing more than “parking and bins” – thereby, and at a stroke, insulting the many thousands of Conservatives who devote themselves to public service in their local communities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBonehill-Paine eventually withdrew his candidacy, but that did not draw a line under the episode. In her stubbornness, the Tory leader said the former neo-Nazi would now serve the party as an adviser, thereby giving him a role on the very national level she had earlier said was off-limits. Worsening matters still further, the shadow cabinet member Claire Coutinho posted that, while, “Luciana and others are unable to forgive Joshua, I do,” attributing this vicarious generosity of hers to her Catholic faith, and so, doubtless unconsciously, reinforcing that age-old trope of the forgiving Christian and the vengeful Jew.What a mess to have made in just a few days. If it were only tactical blunders and in-the-moment misjudgments, one might be more, er, forgiving. But the flaw is strategic. Badenoch has chosen to fight a race to the bottom against Reform, but it is a race she can never win. Farage will always be willing to go further. Take that latest proposal on housing. She would give foreign nationals six months to get out of their homes; Reform promises to boot them out in three. The penny has still not dropped that in a contest of Reform v Reform Lite, the real thing will always have the edge.All the while, as Badenoch chases after Farage supporters, moderate Tory voters grow more disenchanted. There may be room for ex-fascists in Conservative ranks, but the leader will allow no place for Conservatives who support net zero targets and do not want the UK to leave the European convention on human rights. The result is that those “blue wall”, southern Tories who defected to the Lib Dems in 2024 have every reason not to come back.So, yes, Kemi Badenoch may score a win now and then; she’s bound to land the odd blow on Burnham when normal hostilities resume in September. But a Keminaissance? For the Tories, it looks like the dark ages have a while to run yet.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
