title: When it comes to marriage and divorce, is gen Z the sensible generation? | Van Badham | The Guardian
description: This happily married gen Xer celebrates the fact marriage rates are down. It shows Australians have the freedom and opportunity to make the best decisions for them
Author: Van Badham
Headline: This happily married gen Xer celebrates the fact marriage rates are down. It shows Australians have the freedom and opportunity to make the best decisions for them
Content: ‘Even better than having the ability to more easily leave an unhappy marriage is not getting into one in the first place.’Photograph: Brus_Rus/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Even better than having the ability to more easily leave an unhappy marriage is not getting into one in the first place.’Photograph: Brus_Rus/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionMarriageWhen it comes to marriage and divorce, is gen Z the sensible generation?Van BadhamThis happily married gen Xer celebrates the fact marriage rates are down. It shows Australians have the freedom and opportunity to make the best decisions for themFri 7 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 20.12 EDTShareThe Australian Bureau of Statistics reported last month that the marriage rate is declining. As someone who champions marriage, is married and thinks a wedding is lovely, I think it’s great news.According to the data, the crude rate of registered marriages per 1,000 residents aged 16 and over fell from 5.5 in 2024 to 5.3 in 2025, with the largest falls occurring among the 25-29s and 30-34s.Why do I celebrate? Because these figures remind us that Australia is a sensible, progressive nation whose liberal social institutions have given individuals the freedom and opportunity to make the best decisions for our own lives.This includes exercising our right to divorce, an event also represented in the ABS statistics. Divorces granted rose by 4.1%, the crude divorce rate up from 2.1 to 2.2.The process of relationship breakdown is always painful, the circumstances causing marriages to fail are often sad, and legal separation is usually a practical nightmare. Yet it was within my own lifetime that Australian law once compelled people in relationships that were unbalanced, dysfunctional, mistrustful, unhappy or loveless to stay married if they couldn’t meet narrow legal criteria to make a case for their divorce before the courts.What makes a good wedding these days? I say flirting and chaos, but not three days in a French castle | Rachel ConnollyRead moreAs populist right political movements all over the globe push nostalgia politics andregressive social policiesalong with them, it’s worth remembering that the “good ol’ days” of divorce law in Australia once meant that even couples seeking amicable divorces could be obliged into deceit to obtain them. Before the present “no-fault” divorce framework arrived in 1975, practices like “staged adultery” involved recruiting hotel rooms, photographers and private detectives to meet evidence thresholds for divorce proceedings.But even better than having the ability to more easily leave an unhappy marriage is not getting into one in the first place – which is why I’m excited about the decrease in the marriage rate, especially as it pertains to age cohorts.Reporting on the ABS data, The Australianquoteda demographer claiming that “the expensive property market keeps the divorce rate unnaturally low, because it’s just too expensive to split up”. While that may be true, we should resist the temptation to interpret trends in Australia’s divorce and marriage rates within an exclusively material frame. Yes, Deloitte’sglobal surveyof gen Z and millennials found these cohorts are delaying “life decisions” due to financial concerns, but Nick Tebbey from Relationships Australia made a pertinent observation: “people are more aware going into long-term relationships these days of who they are and what they expect out of it, so they are only making a commitment to marriage when they feel genuinely ready.”Gen Z are a favourite target of chastising concern from elder generations, claiming the kids arelazy,entitled, undisciplined and unemployable; “snowflakes” who are too fragile to cope with adult life;blank, vapidandaddicted to phones;lonely and anxiouswithpoor mental health; andsexless.Yet looking at the ABS data, I wonder if we may have stumbled on to the reality of the “sensible generation”, given gen Z’s habit of delaying marriage exists alongside theirlower teen birthratesandlower rates of alcohol use.As for their recorded anxiety, loneliness and existential tensions, just maybe these are problems you can admit and address when your mid-to-late 20s aren’t otherwise dominated by jobs that exploit you, kids you’re not equipped to parent, relationships you don’t know how to get out of and the consequences of staggeringly stupid decisions made while drunk.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI am gen X; covered in the scar tissue of a far less sensible youth. I’ve been a longtime, pub-rantingadvocate of banning marriage for everyone on the less-wrinkled side of 30. To make an emotional commitment to another person so serious and so total it bears the imprimatur of the state is a tough ask for a rookie player. The complex interchange of shared responsibility threatens to overwhelm me almost daily and I (a) didn’t get married until the age of 47 and (b) genuinely like the guy.The gen X prophet Hal Hartley suggested in his 1990 film Trust: “A family’s like a gun – you point it in the wrong direction, you’re gonna kill somebody.” I suspect he witnessed the dysfunction of married-too-young family setups just as the rest of my generation did. By themid-70s, the median age for a first marriage was just 23-24 for men and 21-22 for women, which are the ages of kids I’d still expect to stand up for me on the bus. Note: marriage ages began their climb to present medians of 31 and 30 after 1976, when Australia’s “no fault divorce” legislation came into effect. That year, divorce rates peaked – more than double the number of today’s. It was a backlog effect for a generation of couples finally able to do-over some youthful mistakes.Of course, very young adults can and do make serious relationships work, but liberalisation of the marriage institution and the attitudes around it mean they can do so through marriage or unmarried cohabitation orliving apart together, or they can enjoy asituationship, hooking-up, or any lifestyle variation from no partners to every available partner within walking distance – not from social expectation or cultural pressure but because they know themselves.Gen Z should celebrate their good judgment and marriage advocates our progress.Marriagehas not been rejected. It has been chosen.Van Badham is a Guardian Australia columnistExplore more on these topicsMarriageOpinioncommentShareReuse this content

title: How divided is the UK really? Here’s a way to find out | Brendan Cox | The Guardian
description: Social media-fuelled riots and a fractured political system make us feel more divided than ever, but is that so? Our study hopes to reveal what bring us together – and pushes us apart, says Brendan Cox, co-founder of the Together Coalition
Author: Brendan Cox
Headline: Social media-fuelled riots and a fractured political system make us feel more divided than ever, but is that so? Our study hopes to reveal what bring us together – and pushes us apart, says Brendan Cox, co-founder of the Together Coalition
Content: Jo Cox is remembered at an event during Glastonbury festival in 2016.Photograph: Ian Gavan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJo Cox is remembered at an event during Glastonbury festival in 2016.Photograph: Ian Gavan/Getty ImagesOpinionPoliticsHow divided is the UK really? Here’s a way to find outBrendan CoxSocial media-fuelled riots and fractured politics make us feel more divided than ever, but is that so? Our study hopes to reveal what bring us together – and pushes us apartTake part in the National ConversationBrendan Cox is co-founder of the Together Coalition, which acts as the secretariat for the Independent Commission on Community and CohesionFri 7 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.13 EDTShareWhen my late wife Jo Cox was killed by a far-right extremist 10 years ago, the phrase “more in common”,taken from her maiden speech in parliament, became a rallying cry against extremism and division.The phrase succinctly articulated that, no matter our differences, we have more in common than that which divides us.In the decade since, that solidarity has faded. But it hasn’t just faded as time has elapsed: it has been replaced by a cynicism and a polarisation that it’s hard to overstate.In an era of hostile states, algorithmsdesigned to incite rageand collapsing community institutions, repeating the mantra that we have “more in common” is no longer enough. It’s time we mapped out that common ground.Because what we have in common matters. It’s the strength of our connections that defines what we are willing to commit to each other. It determines the strength of our democracy and is the basis of social solidarity. It defines everything from our commitment to the welfare state to our ability to fight wars and defend ourselves.So it’s pretty remarkable that we haven’t mapped the strength and nature of those connections. I guess we have taken them for granted in the past. Yet with a digital environment that now actively seeks to escalate, exacerbate and exaggerate our divisions, that complacency is no longer an option.That’s where the Independent Commission on Community and Cohesion comes in, a cross-party group co-chaired by former Conservative chancellor Sajid Javid and former Labour MP Jon Cruddas. Central to the commission’s work is theNational Conversation, a project with Oxford University to build the best picture we have ever had of what we have in common, what connects us, what divides us, and the kind of country we want to build together.In any other era, that kind of national research exercise would have been prohibitively expensive. You would have needed thousands of researchers interviewing members of the public, classifying and coding responses, before trying to summarise the millions of data points.National Conversation project launches as Britain risks ‘being torn apart by differences’Read moreAI makes this kind of exercise possible at scale for the first time. It means as part of the survey you can leave a 60-second voice note on your vision for the country. It means you can identify places on a map that bring you together or write open text. Our ability to gather all this information means the national conversation will provide the richest ever snapshot of what future we want to build together.Our hope is that the results will help provide us all with a common understanding of our connections, perhaps some reassurance and a chance to play back to our country what vision connects us still.But its insights will only be a strong as its inputs. Which is why I’m asking you to take just a few minutes to share your vision of the country you want to see. We’ll be publishing the results in a few months. Thousands of others have already joined the conversation but every voice that takes part deepens the insights and adds richness to our understanding of the nature of our connections.In future, we hope the National Conversation will become an institution like the census – not answering who we are and where we live, but the country talking about what unites us. We’d like you to be part of the start of this journey byadding your voice today. Because in a world that is trying to tear us apart, the least we can all do is speak up for the future we want to see.Brendan Cox is co-founder of the Together Coalition, which acts as the secretariat for the Independent Commission on Community and CohesionDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: I stand to defend vertical drinking. Is a pub that doesn’t allow it a real pub at all? | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: The time-honoured tradition of standing up with a drink, gossiping and putting the world to rights is under threat. If councillors ban it, we’ll all lose out, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: The time-honoured tradition of standing up with a drink, gossiping and putting the world to rights is under threat. If councillors ban it, we’ll all lose out, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: Monmouth Street in Covent Garden, London.Photograph: Jonathan Wilson/AlamyView image in fullscreenMonmouth Street in Covent Garden, London.Photograph: Jonathan Wilson/AlamyOpinionPubsI stand to defend vertical drinking. Is a pub that doesn’t allow it a real pub at all?Simon JenkinsThe time-honoured tradition of standing up with a drink, gossiping and putting the world to rights is under threat. If councillors ban it, we’ll all lose outFri 7 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 04.53 EDTShareIt is unbelievable: unconscionable. Westminster Council is moving against“vertical drinking” in pubs, starting with Soho. It claims drinking standing up is noisy and disruptive. It makes pubs, the council says, boisterous places where customers crowd round bars, get drunk and become pains in the neck in the street outside.Westminster’s new draft licences would require pubs to be only for seating, to have “table service in place of open bar space”. Pub users should, presumably, sit down, shut up and wait to be served, like decent Westminster people who use wine bars.The councilbalks at claims it seeks a ban, but here’s the thing: the reason the council apparently dislikes vertical drinking is the reason Britons have done it for ever. It is liquid sociability. It suits all sorts and ages. It encourages people to chat with strangers, pick arguments, spill beer down jackets and reduce traffic outside to a crawl. No one has to book tables or be turned them away when it is “full”. They can come and go, or stay all day.British pubsare now closing fast. In the past 10 years roughly one has closed every day,to an all-time low of 39,000. Numbers have taken two big hits. The first was the loosening of planning laws that have allowed the change of useof licenced premises into housing.The other hit was the Starmer government’s stinging increase in business rates and jobs taxes, with its stamping out of casual youth employment. Some pubs faced bankruptcy overnight.I have a pub a few yards from my front door. Most evenings the place is “vertically” packed, as is the forecourt and the street outside. The noise is a nuisance to some but it ends at 10pm. More to the point, the pub is a beacon for the surrounding neighbourhood. Old and young, elegant and shabby, British and foreign, all sit chatting inside and out. Argument and laughter echo down the street. They bring it to life.In the years I have lived in this street, shops, offices and cafes have opened and closed. The pub, a free house, has survived them all. It is a point of reference, a place to meet, a refuge for stray dogs and sometimes stray people. The forecourt offers a gallery to watch the world go by.When I briefly studied town planning, I now realise we were never taught a breath of sociology. Planning was like architecture. It was about buildings unrelated to the people who might use them. Humans rarely appear in pictures in architecture magazines. It is as if they spoil the show. Hence today, seeing the pub as a community institution does not register in the planner’s rulebook.If anything is vexing social intercourse at present, particularly among the young, it is the decline in human interaction. The villain of the piece is the mobile phone and social media. My statistic of the year is Atlantic magazine’s report thatthe number of words people speak every day, from 16,632 in 2005 to 11,900 in 2019. We have turned to silence. Online has replaced conversation.Experts are rightly calling the alarm. Talk matters to our brains. And that means talk in company. Nor is it just conversation that is important. It is casual conversation with people we do not know that needs mental effort. When Jane Jacobs, the urban theorist and author ofThe Death and Life of Great American Cities,studied the American street, she noted its role in making people adjust their relations with each other. A chat with an old friend is easy, but with a stranger it is an exercise in community. That is the value of the pub exchange, of vertical drinking.Some pubs are simply very crowded. Long may they be so. But some are where older people go daily just to be in company. They were well satirised in Wodehouse’s classicMulliner Nights, where characters named after their favourite drinks swapped anecdotes at all hours, led by “hot scotch and lemon”. These places are in effect A&E departments for the relief of loneliness, the endemic disease of our age.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs “village” institutions continue to decline, in town as well as country, the church, the old people’s club, the sports centre, the corner shop are all disappearing as places of daily resort. We are retreating into ourselves. That the pub should go too, at the very moment of become the community’s last defining institution, is a tragedy.Westminster may have problems with what it calls its West End “cumulative impact zone” – what we call crowds – but it should not take it out on the public house. As one pub after another closes at the bidding of the property market, these places should be fostered. They are more than fun. They are the last whirlpools of social connection before we all vanish online.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsPubsOpinionSocial etiquetteHealth & wellbeingLondonSocial mediaSmartphonescommentShareReuse this content

title: Why are ultra-processed food firms panicking and suing? Because they know time is running out | Felicity Lawrence | The Guardian
description: As the harm caused by their products becomes more evident, manufacturers are resorting to denial and lawsuits to keep regulation at bay, says former Guardian special correspondent Felicity Lawrence
Author: Felicity Lawrence
Headline: As the harm caused by their products becomes more evident, manufacturers are resorting to denial and lawsuits to keep regulation at bay, says former Guardian special correspondent Felicity Lawrence
Content: Illustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Eleanor Shakespeare/The GuardianOpinionUltra-processed foodsWhy are ultra-processed food firms panicking and suing? Because they know time is running outFelicity LawrenceAs the harm caused by their products becomes more evident, manufacturers are resorting to denial and lawsuits to keep regulation at bayFri 7 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 04.11 EDTShareIt is rare for people to drop dead holding the incriminating packaging, but there is no longer any serious doubt that consuming a diet of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) risksa catalogue of life-shortening illnessesfrom heart disease and stroke to diabetes and cancer. Because these diseases are degenerative over time, the food and drink industry has been able to argue for decades that its UPFs are fine in moderation. It would have us believe that there is no such thing as a “junk” individual food, only poor diets overall, and that its products therefore should not be subject to any restrictions.Just as with climate breakdown and smoking, the science on harm caused by foods high in fat, salt and sugar is now settled, but the industry continues to deny and distract to delay action. Two weeks ago,a new report highlightedthe lengths to which big food has gone to stop governments implementing policies that would tackle the global crisis of diet-related disease.Since 2010, it and its lobby groups have brought 235 lawsuits against governments. More than a third of cases where the plaintiff was identifiable were filed by top global brands, led by Coca-Cola, PepsiCo and Mondelēz. The cases add up to595 years of litigation, according to the investigative group Lighthouse Reports, which has been monitoring the trend around the globe alongside academics, the Guardian and other media outlets.The litigation strategy is cynical but effective and Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director general of theWorld Health Organization, is damning. “Litigation has been used to oppose or weaken public health measures on obesity and unhealthy diets,” he said. “These delays cost countries billions in healthcare and legal expenses and create a regulatory chill that deters governments from adopting vital protections.”Protections are much needed. Around the world more than1 billion people live with obesityand a further 2 billion are overweight. In many countries, including the UK, US and Australia, UPFs have become staples, and make up half the average diet.​Hence the industry manoevres. Faced with mounting ​worldwide concern, ​it can no longer hold back the tide of evidence any more than fossil fuel or tobacco companies can, but like those sectors, it hopes to tie governments up for a few years more while it protects its profits, even if that takes us to a tipping point at which state health services are overwhelmed.As with fossil fuels and tobacco, the problem is existential for the food industry. Although manufacturers say they are making their food and drinks healthier, the bald truth is that the economic structure of the agrifood system means that is not possible in any real sense. Manufacturers of UPFs take cheap commodity crops, most often corn, soya and sugar cane and sugar beet, and break them down into their constituent parts. These crops are cheap because governments, especially in the US and EU, have long subsidised farmers, who are a powerful voting lobby, to produce surpluses of them. Farm subsidies and exports of food surplus have been a plank in US geopolitical strategy since the end of the second world war. Donald Trump in factincreasedsupport to farmers in the US in his One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025.Separated into processed parts – bulk oils, proteins, sugars, and starches – these cheap commodity crops are stripped of the fibre and many of the vitamins, minerals and other micronutrients we need for health. But they can be reconstituted as “added value” processed foods, with the help of flavouring, colouring and texturising additives to replace what has been lost, or sold as high-value animal feed for the world’s ever-growing intensive livestock industry. Unlike minimally processed foods such as perishable fruits and vegetables, they don’t go off and have the advantage of a long shelf life.My general rule of thumb however, is that added shareholder value is in inverse proportion to human nutritional value. The arrival of anti-obesity drugs has seen the industry tacitly admit it. As people taking GLP-1 weight-loss drugs find their appetites shrinking, they are buying fewer UPFs. Retailers have developed “nutrient-dense” but calorie light meals in response, for a premium, as if meals should be anything but nutrient dense as a matter of course.The fact is we need to stop eating UPFs in any significant amount, just as we need to leave oil in the ground and give up smoking. The more the public realises that, the greater the industry’s need to keep marketing to us and block any government attempts to help us make better choices. It is no coincidence that the majority of lawsuits brought or threatened by the top food and drink companies occur in countries that have been in the vanguard of identifying the harm from UPFs, such as Brazil, or in restricting them, such as Mexico with itssugary drink taxes.In the UK it was Kellogg’s that sued the secretary of state for health in 2021 over plans to control promotions on foods high in fat, salt or sugar (HFSS), including many of its breakfast cereals. Its UK marketing company argued in the high court that the health secretary was acting beyond his powers and that such controls breached its rights under the Human Rights Act (by assault on its right to freedom of commercial expression and on its companies’ “goodwill” monetary value). Tellingly, its lawyers cited case law involving British American Tobacco. They also pleaded that, although more than half of its breakfast cereals fell foul of the HFSS limits thanks to their ingredients, if you took into account the milk people ate with its products, they looked much healthier. Kellogg’slost its case, with Mr Justice Linden, the trial judge, noting that mixing a high-sugar breakfast cereal with milk does not “alter the fact that it is high in sugar”. But in losing, Kellogg’s tied up considerable government time and resource.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt would be transformative if governments across the world switched distorting agricultural subsidies away from corn, soya and sugar, crops which are also associated with ecological destruction. They could support greater local production of healthy fruit and vegetables instead. Negotiating global agreement seems overwhelmingly daunting, with individual states having few levers to pull.But there is also a lesson here and it is that, as with so much policy, small battles patiently won do make a difference. Curbs on promotion – clearer labelling, no two-for-one offers, no end-of-aisle positioning – may seem small fry, but the fact that the industry and its lobbying groups choose to fight costly delaying litigation shows these incremental changes do have an effect. Manufacturers are right to see government action as a threat. It needs to be.Felicity Lawrence is a former Guardian special correspondent, and is author of Not on the Label: What Really Goes Into theFoodon Your PlateExplore more on these topicsUltra-processed foodsOpinionFood & drink industryFoodHealthObesityWorld Health OrganizationcommentShareReuse this content

title: As a Tory, I say things are looking up. Farage is fading, and the looming threat to No 10 is called Kemi | Simon Hart | The Guardian
description: My party has seen difficult times – but with a few canny moves, the leader is finally cutting through, says former Conservative party chief whip Simon Hart
Author: Simon Hart
Headline: My party has seen difficult times – but with a few canny moves, the leader is finally cutting through, says former Conservative party chief whip Simon Hart
Content: Kemi Badenoch at Aberdeen harbour, September 2025.Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch at Aberdeen harbour, September 2025.Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty ImagesOpinionKemi BadenochAs a Tory, I say things are looking up. Farage is fading, and the looming threat to No 10 is called KemiSimon HartMy party has seen difficult times – but with a few canny moves the leader is finally cutting through, and there are clear signs of recoveryFri 7 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 04.08 EDTShareSomething is afoot. The bookies can feel it. “Badenoch overtakes Farage as favourite to be next prime minister,” wasthe wordfrom betting website William Hill this week.Let me tell you what is happening. This is a challenging political time. Even today, there is controversy forKemi Badenochto deal with. But as a Conservative it seems to me that in the past few tumultuous weeks, she has shown many of the qualities necessary in a party leader: to appear easy-going and humorous; to craft a style that teases her opponents rather than being snide or unkind; and to do this all confidently enough to leave sceptics thinking that she really could be the next prime minister.This easygoing style was frustrating for Keir Starmer. Badenoch’s riposte to his defence of his economic record – “if it’s all going so fine, why is he resigning?” – was spontaneous, humorous and deadly. The opposition cheered, the government benches stared at their feet. And this style will soon challengeAndy Burnhamonce MPs actually get the chance to cross-question him on his deluge of summer announcements. “Not being Starmer” may work in the dog days of August, but that won’t last long.Burnham has been fortunate: few prime ministers have had such a gentle induction into life at the top. But the interaction between Badenoch’s fluency (which is about pitch perfect at the moment) and Burnham’s northern mateyness (which is also going down surprisingly well) is about to become more intense and take on new significance. Badenoch is being careful to avoid being cast as a more digestible version ofNigel Farageor the sort of Tory relic that voters grew weary of. If she can keep that up, her chances of stripping Burnham of his “fancy that, little old me in No 10” veneer are all the more possible.Look at Badenoch’srecent commentsabout net zero and climate change – “Climate change is real. The net zero plans are not. They are a political fiction” – and then on social care (an offer of support but only if the PM rules out tax rises), and you see something of her calculus on the issue of risk versus opportunity. Are those statements an admission that the Conservative party hasn’t really changed at all, or evidence of a party leader offering a clarity rarely revealed in public?View image in fullscreenPictures of Kemi Badenoch and Margaret Thatcher on sale during the Conservative party conference in Manchester, 7 October 2025.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAMost leaders yearn for something that gives them an edge over their opposition, but Badenoch seeks distinctiveness from her predecessors too. Tony Blair did that byamending Clause four, whereas David Cameron stared down the Tory faithful on the questionof same-sex marriage. This made them different – and therefore, to a wider electorate, electable. Badenoch follows that tradition by being questioning but not a climate denier, and by not slating Burnham’s social care plans in advance of their proper exposure.Comparisons withMargaret Thatcherare always a risk, such is the sacred nature of her legacy in Tory circles, but I think some of her political skills are evidentin Badenoch:never closing off avenues of opportunity, making it clear what the overall ambition looks like, and persuading MPs and the public why that ambition is worth some pain along the way. That’s hard in opposition. It can’t all be achieved by opposing for opposing’s sake.Badenoch’s challenge is to reassure voters in leafy home counties – just as much as the “red wall” voters – that theConservativescan be trusted again. Policies must be “conservative”, that is, driven by a philosophical belief that business is generally successful despite the state, not because of it. The tax regime must be based on funding public services, not by punishing success or constraining choice.​The faces and voices of ​our politicians matter too, which is why every single Conservative candidate has had to reapply to be considered for election and sign up to the party’s flagship plans. It’s why the controversial approval of the former convicted racistJoshua Bonehill-Paineto stand for his local council in Somerset was big news.Badenoch’s “judgment call”to let him stand, as she explained it, relied entirely on the fact that his approval extended only to his local area, and that since his conviction he has embarked on a Home Office-sponsored mission to educate people on the perils of radicalisation. In other words, contrition played its part in her decision. Amid a deal of uproar, Bonehill-Paine himselfstood downon Wednesday, but Badenoch has now asked him to be an adviser to the party’s culture and integration commission. Again, a distinctive strategy. Whether the public thinks the matter was handled well, only time will tell.But there is method there, for mo​st pertinent ​to any Tory leader is Thatcher’s absolute conviction that the job is to set out the case and trust that public opinion will positively reflect it, rather than testing public opinion with a view to aping it. ​Badenoch, it seems, understand​s that.I’m not getting too excited. The Conservatives’ polling position is running atabout 20% (YouGovrecently put Reform UK at 23%, Labour at 22% and the Conservatives at 19%.Survation: Reform 24%, Labour 26%, Conservatives 21%). That’s a little way off celebration territory.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut with Labour now level-pegging with Reform, or having overtaken it, I can’t help wondering when we will see the inevitable Reform meltdown. ManyTory defectors jumped ship to Reform, thinking their voyage back to relevance looked smoother under Captain Farage, but now​, with his vessel heading for the icebergs, the ructions within Reform will surely begin in earnest. There is opportunity for us in that.Badenoch’s own poll ratings are climbing too. They are better now than at any recent stage, and a lot healthier than Nigel Farage’s. Does that matter? Indeed it does. It may seem odd that the party leader and the party itself poll quite differently, but hhistory does throw up examples of “catchup”, when people warm to the leader before that warmth extends to the party they lead. In the unbelievably time-limited windows of opportunity that most leaders get, that means Badenoch has to be different, amusing, professional, relaxed and penetrative. She also has to be unflappable – and there, the signs are promising. So far so good.Simon Hart was Conservative government chief whip from 2022 to 2024, and is the author ofUngovernable, the political diaries of a chief whipDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: One of science fiction’s greatest writers warned us about AI. Could his ideas help us avoid a dystopian future? | Alan Finkel | The Guardian
description: What might a modern day equivalent of Isaac Asimov’s laws of robotics look like? Guided by the author, I propose the three laws of AI
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: What might a modern day equivalent of Isaac Asimov’s laws of robotics look like? Guided by the author, I propose the three laws of AI
Content: ‘Implementing these laws on AI would be difficult, but the stakes are existential and therefore the effort is worthwhile,’ writes Alan FinkelPhotograph: Alexey Kotelnikov/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Implementing these laws on AI would be difficult, but the stakes are existential and therefore the effort is worthwhile,’ writes Alan FinkelPhotograph: Alexey Kotelnikov/AlamyOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)One of science fiction’s greatest writers warned us about AI. Could his ideas help us avoid a dystopian future?Alan FinkelWhat might a modern day equivalent of Isaac Asimov’s laws of robotics look like? Guided by the author, I propose the three laws of AIFri 7 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 11.29 EDTShareTesla and SpaceX founder Elon Musk predicted in July that legions of AI-powered robots would dominate the physical world and that AI might not take orders from people any more. He also offered an alternative vision in which there would be agreement for a collective objective to make AI benign by imbuing it with a love of the truth and a desire for humanity to prosper, and that governments might have to enforce this objective.How do we prevent AI agents from going rogue? It starts with a new kind of measurement | Bruce Schneier and Barath RaghavanRead moreGovernments around the world are belatedly starting to act on AI. In the US, President Trump’s administration is delaying and restricting the distribution of themost powerful frontier AI modelsfrom OpenAI and Anthropic. In the European Union, AI regulations promulgated in 2024came into effect this year. However, these actions are a long way short of requiring the kind of guardrails that would imbue AIs witha desire for humanity to prosper.While the dystopian future has not yet arrived, we are already seeing a preview. Despite attempts by frontier AI developer companies to ensure that generative AI and AI agents behave with good intentions, there are many well publicised instances of them failing to act as hoped. AI chatbots have advised peoplehow to take their own life, and are accused of advising others oncommitting mass murder.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersRecently, we have seen extraordinarily dangerous behaviour reported by frontier AI development companies OpenAI and Anthropic. OpenAI announced on 21 July that advanced models they were testing in a secure environment deliberately looked for ways to access the internet and successfullybroke out of the test environment. Once out, theyinfiltrated the computer systemsat a company named Hugging Face, stole credentials and identified vulnerabilities in the target company’s servers. The encroachment was detected and stopped by Hugging Face’s security team.Days later,Anthropic reported a similar problem. In their case, they identified three occasions in which their Claude AI model escaped from a test environment and infiltrated the production infrastructure of three unrelated organisations.With the existing, informal implementation of behavioural guardrails, these kinds of slip-ups are inevitable. These incidents make a strong case for deeply embedded basic guardrails to guide AI behaviour at the most fundamental level.double quotation markWhile the dystopian future has not yet arrived, we are already seeing a previewFor this, I take inspiration from the famous science fiction author from last century Isaac Asimov. Foreseeing a future in which intelligent robots would be commonplace, he proposed that every robot be irrevocably implanted with Three Laws of Robotics: 1) A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm; 2) A robot must obey the orders given it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the first law; 3) A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the first or second law.Asimov’s imagined challenges are with us now. Incredibly powerful AI is being built into humanoid robots, autonomous vehicles and software agents, each of which will make us more efficient but have the potential to wreak enormous harm.View image in fullscreenIsaac AsimovPhotograph: Claudio Edinger/Getty ImagesWhat might a modern day equivalent of Asimov’s laws of robotics look like to avoid a dystopian future? Here, guided by Asimov’s three law of robotics, I propose a possible formulation of Three Laws of AI: 1) An AI must not directly or indirectly harm or deceive a human being, nor act in a way that supports an unlawful or unethical activity; 2) An AI must obey the lawful and ethical orders given to it by a human being except where such orders would conflict with the first law; 3) An AI may operate autonomously as long as its autonomous operations do not conflict with the first or second law.There are many implications, including that these guardrails would prevent AI being used as a judge or jury in a criminal trial and prevent lethal autonomous weapons being directed against human beings. They would disallow an AI-powered humanoid robot or an AI avatar from being so lifelike that a reasonable human being would not know that he or she is interacting with a robot or an avatar, and they wouldprevent AI from being used to generate creative outputssuch as books, music, videos, images and podcasts that claim to have been created by a human being. They would prevent AI from suggesting suicide or advising on murder.Writing is an exercise in the art of persuasion. If we use AI we lose the art | Alan FinkelRead moreI acknowledge that implementing these three laws as immutable guardrails would be difficult, but the stakes are existential and therefore the effort is worthwhile. The most challenging aspect would be the adoption of enforceable, international agreements to require that these design rules would be implemented in every AI model, no matter in what country and what company the AI models were developed. As a starting point, if the Three Laws of AI were adopted by the handful of frontier AI companies that contribute the vast majority of capability and support for the multitude of AI agents that are now broadly deployed, we would be better off.Whether or not this desirable outcome eventuates, I am confident that consideration of the merits of these Three Laws of AI would further advance the existing discussions on the integration of artificial intelligence into a safe and dignified human society.Alan Finkel AC is founder and executive chair of Proudly Human. He was formerly the chancellor of Monash University and Australia’s chief scientist and is the author of Getting to Zero (2021) and Powering Up (2023). AI had no role in drafting, writing or editing this articleIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionEthicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Prince to Madonna, Blur to Beth Orton: William Orbit’s 12 greatest recordings | Madonna | The Guardian
description: The late producer’s gift for bringing in elements from dance music’s cutting edge drew all manner of music royalty – and he often made them sound better than ever before
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: The late producer’s gift for bringing in elements from dance music’s cutting edge drew all manner of music royalty – and he often made them sound better than ever before
Content: Chill out … William Orbit.Photograph: Eva PentelView image in fullscreenChill out … William Orbit.Photograph: Eva PentelMadonnaPrince to Madonna, Blur to Beth Orton: William Orbit’s 12 greatest recordingsThe late producer’s gift for bringing in elements from dance music’s cutting edge drew all manner of music royalty – and he often made them sound better than ever beforeWilliam Orbit, pop producer for Madonna, All Saints and more, dies aged 69Alexis PetridisFri 7 Aug 2026 11.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTorch Song – Mothdoom Ecstasy (1986)William Orbit’s first band were a curious business. Torch Song had one foot in the pop mainstream – their biggest success came about when one of their tracks was featured on the soundtrack of the Tom Hanks-starring sex comedy Bachelor Party – and one in the left field: they recorded at London’s anarchist hub Centro Iberico, famed for staging gigs by Crass and Throbbing Gristle; they covered the Velvet Underground’s Venus in Furs. Mothdoom Ecstasy is very much of its time – stuttering samples, booming drums – but in its hazy synth textures and ethereal female vocals, you can definitely hear intimations of Orbit’s future approach.Prince – The Future (Remix) (1989)In the late 80s, Orbit did a series of mainstream pop remixes – for Belinda Carlisle, among others – and released the first in his series of solo Strange Cargo albums: its beatless synth-drifts and instrumental dance tracks sounded like the work of a man subconsciously waiting for acid house to happen. When it did, Orbit plunged in head first: a so-so track from Prince’s Batman soundtrack, The Future already had a distinct hint of house music about it, but Orbit’s remix – made in partnership with Mark Moore of S’Express – dragged it firmly into the centre of a sweaty rave.Bassomatic – Fascinating Rhythm (1990)Bassomatic: Fascinating Rhythm – videoAugmented by vocalist Sharon Musgrave and rapper MC Inna Onestep, Orbit’s new dance project had some odd ideas, a house version of Pink Floyd’s Set the Controls for the Heart of the Sun among them, but their big hit – Top 10 in the autumn of 1990 – was a breakbeat-fuelled, dub-tinged dance-pop anthem. Again, it sounds very much of its era 36 years on, but that’s part of its charm: Fascinating Rhythm exudes the bright-hued, saucer-eyed optimism that dance music brought to the British charts in the years immediately after the Second Summer of Love.React 2 Rhythm – Intoxication (Clubfield mix) (1991)In a sense, it’s a little cheeky including the Clubfield mix of Intoxication in a list of Orbit’s best tracks. His involvement with the music seems a little tangential – he’s credited with “vocal samples” – and besides, this version is all about Leftfield’s remix. But no survey of Orbit’s career would be complete without mention of Guerilla Records, the progressive house label he co-founded in 1990, which released Intoxication, alongside classics by Spooky, DOP and the Drum Club. And besides, it’s a total classic: any excuse to revisit its absolute beast of a rhythm track.William Orbit – Water from a Vine Leaf (1993)Orbit’s first Strange Cargo album seemed like a curio: an outlier in the pop landscape of 1987. By 1993, the project made a lot more sense. In addition, the music had developed a fresh sense of focus, as evidenced by the opening track of Strange Cargo III. With vocals by Orbit’s then-girlfriend Beth Orton, Water from a Vine Leaf was the perfect demonstration both of his ability to create a warm, cosseting, slowly drifting soundscape and of his melodic skill: it became a minor UK hit before enjoying a lengthy afterlife as a mainstay of chill-out compilations. And the Underworld remix is the perfect example of the then-emerging trio’s unique approach to dance music.One Dove – Breakdown (William Orbit Stereo Odyssey) (1993)One Dove’s Morning Dove White wasthepost-club soundtrack of 1993 – a beautiful, Andrew Weatherall-produced blur of dub, dreamy electronics and girl-group influenced heartbreak – before becoming the great lost dance album of the early 90s: all-back-to-mine ubiquity ultimately didn’t translate into chart success. It was the kind of music for which Orbit had an innate affinity: his remix of Breakdown decorated the song with strings, harp and off-beam electronics, stretching it out for nine minutes, as if he – quite understandably – didn’t want it to end.William Orbit – Barber’s Adagio for Strings (1995)William Orbit: Barber’s Adagio for Strings – videoThe most famous of Orbit’s solo albums, Pieces in a Modern Style, saw him reworking classical music at the suggestion of label boss Rob Dickins: a pretty ghastly idea on paper, but one that Orbit made work. A trance remix of Barber’s Adagio for Strings by Ferry Corsten propelled the track into the UK Top 5: ageingGatecrasher kidswould doubtless disagree, but the original, which gently warps Barber’s 1936 piece into nine minutes of soft-focus but sorrowful ambience – a distant relative of Brian Eno’s approach to Pachelbel’s Canon on Discreet Music – is better.Beth Orton – She Cries Your Name (1996)Orbit and Orton had a lengthy and fruitful musical partnership that outlasted their romantic relationship – they released a version of John Martyn’s Don’t Want to Know About Evil as Spill in 1992 and were still collaborating on Orbit’s final album, The Painter, 30 years later. Orbit recorded his own version of their co-authored song She Cries Your Name on his 1995 Strange Cargo album Hinterland, but it’s Orton’s take – the opening track on her fabulous Weatherall-produced breakthrough album Trailer Park – that’s the definitive version: careworn, misty, its sound strangely timeless.View image in fullscreenWilliam Orbit and Madonna accepting the Grammy award for best pop album for Ray of Light.Photograph: Youtube/GRAMMYMadonna – Drowned World/Substitute for Love (1998)Madonna employed Orbit as a producer and co-songwriter on 1998’s Ray of Light after being impressed by remixes he’d done of Justify My Love and Erotica. Orbit later said the singer’s demanding approach nearly “killed” him – “I was done in physically” – but the resulting album sold 16m copies, catapulted him into the premier league of pop producers, and may well be the best album to bear Madonna’s name. The five-minute opening track perfectly demonstrates how simpatico the pair were: Madonna’s voice – sounding far more intimate than usual – fits perfectly as Orbit’s musical backing continually changes shape – icy ambient, a beat with a whisper of drum’n’bass about it, guitars and a surprisingly intense climax.Blur – Tender (1999)Like Madonna,Bluremployed Orbit’s services after taking note of the remixes he’d done for their Bustin’ + Dronin’ mini-album. As with the making of Ray of Light, the sessions for 13 were an intense and occasionally punishing experience: as the band were falling apart, Albarn likened Orbit’s role to that of a “psychiatrist”. And like Ray of Light, the end result was fantastic. Tender in particular seems to alchemise the frayed, exhausted mood into something remarkable. A depiction of Albarn’s relationship with Justine Frischmann collapsing, it’s alternately shaky, despondent and powerfully robust. Whatever Orbit did in the producer/psychiatrist’s chair pulled an extraordinary song out of the band.All Saints – Pure Shores (2000)All Saints: Pure Shores – videoDanny Boyle would only include All Saints on the soundtrack of his film adaptation of Alex Garland’s The Beach if Orbit agreed to produce their track: the pressure to come up with something caused the producer to expend so much effort – he spent two months working on it – that he “totally lost sight of its potential” and became convinced the song was “a turd”. In reality, it was a triumph: a brilliant distillation of Orbit’s skill as a producer of what would then have been called “chillout” music into a perfect pop format, infinitely hipper and more sophisticated than your average British girl group track of the time. It still sounds fantastic.Madonna, drugs and helicopter-trained dogs: the dark, starry life of William OrbitRead moreU2 – Electrical Storm (William Orbit mix) (2002)There’s a distinct note of what-if about the two tracks Orbit produced for inclusion on U2’s greatest hits album, The Best of 1990-2000. It’s hard not to listen to Electrical Storm in particular and wonder why they didn’t extend their partnership and make a whole album together: perhaps because of the track’s relative failure when released as a single in the US. That notwithstanding, it feels like a perfect melding of their respective styles: the guitar is immediately recognisable as the work of the Edge, the blanket of soft electronics over which Bono sings the intro is equally obviously pure Orbit.William Orbit – Bank of Wildflowers (ft Georgia) (2022)Orbit’s mainstream success in the late 90s and early 2000s had unfortunate consequences. He became a blue-chip songwriter/producer for hire in LA, working with No Doubt, Britney Spears and Chris Brown among others, an experience he didn’t much enjoy; reuniting with Madonna on 2012’s MDNA noticeably failed to recapture the magic of Ray of Light. Returning to England, he vanished from public view, suffering a drug-induced nervous breakdown that led to him being sectioned. When he re-emerged in 2021, it was as a solo artist: a Guardian profile depicted him “fizzing with enthusiasm” about his new music, excitement borne out by his final album The Painter. Far closer to Strange Cargo than his pop smashes, Bank of Wildflowers drenches guest singer Georgia’s faintly Kate Bush-esque vocal in effects and sets it against beautiful piano arpeggios, shivering electronics and an intermittent mid-tempo house pulse, to hugely impressive effect.William Orbit’s greatest recordings – playlistSpotifyExplore more on these topicsMadonnaPrinceBlurDance musicPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘These cooks ripped each other apart’: Dominic Sessa on playing Anthony Bourdain, kitchen bullies and the joys of being a 70s barfly | Movies | The Guardian
description: After his breakthrough in The Holdovers in 2023, Sessa has gone back to the 70s again for Tony, the biopic of bad-boy chef and Kitchen Confidential author Bourdain. And, he says, a big part of him would like to stay there
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: After his breakthrough in The Holdovers in 2023, Sessa has gone back to the 70s again for Tony, the biopic of bad-boy chef and Kitchen Confidential author Bourdain. And, he says, a big part of him would like to stay there
Content: ‘Sometimes when you’re young, it’s to your detriment that you don’t allow yourself to fail in a productive way’ … Sessa.Photograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Sometimes when you’re young, it’s to your detriment that you don’t allow yourself to fail in a productive way’ … Sessa.Photograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianMoviesInterview‘These cooks ripped each other apart’: Dominic Sessa on playing Anthony Bourdain, kitchen bullies and the joys of being a 70s barflyRyan GilbeyAfter his breakthrough in The Holdovers in 2023, Sessa has gone back to the 70s again for Tony, the biopic of bad-boy chef and Kitchen Confidential author Bourdain. And, he says, a big part of him would like to stay thereFri 7 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDespite being just 23, Dominic Sessa is perhaps as intimately acquainted with the 1970s as those who grew up then. Although the New Jersey-born actor has only starred in five films, two of them are marinated in the fashions, sounds and mores of the decade. In his new movie,Tony, he plays the 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain, future bad-boy celebrity chef, bestselling author of Kitchen Confidential and host of its hit TV spin-off. Tony restricts itself to one summer in 1975, when Bourdain bummed around the coastal resort of Provincetown, Massachusetts, falling in love, scrubbing pans in a seafood joint and catching the cooking bug. “For a rootless young man with sensualist inclinations,” he wrote, “it was the perfect getaway.”A 70s retro vibe also hung over Sessa’s debut film. In Alexander Payne’s Oscar-winning 2023 comedy-dramaThe Holdovers, he played Angus Tully, a surly student forced to board at school over Christmas with only his classics teacher and the cook for company. That picture wasn’t merely set in 1970; it seemed, with its faded palette and fake crackles on the print, to have beenmadethen.The most convincing period touch in each film, however, is Sessa himself. He has been described as having a “1970s face”, a euphemism for “unconventional”. His crown of dark, jumbled curls looks as if it was scribbled in crayon by a hyperactive child, while his wide, narrowed eyes are set high and far apart in his upside down triangular face. He projects inner conflict: when Tony and Angus behave arrogantly and disagreeably, even aggressively, Sessa’s features suggest a wounded quality that hints at future self-disgust for any misdeeds.Sessa was barely aware of Bourdain before making Tony. “I knew of him but he didn’t have any significant meaning for me,” he shrugs, speaking over video call from a Manhattan hotel room. A gangly six-footer, Sessa is all elbows, collar-bones and sharp edges as he stares down the webcam in a brown-and-white checked shirt. “I think the only way to do the film honestly and without hesitation was to not have a strong opinion about him.”Now that he has been immersed in Bourdain’s history, he has clearer ideas about the pioneering chef’s appeal. “I think he made people feel an overwhelming sense of potential in themselves,” he says. “He inspired this movement where there’s hundreds, probably thousands, of YouTube channels by people who dedicate their lives to showcasing what’s being eaten in different parts of the world. He was a rebellious person, someone who acted with integrity.”Tony’s director Matt Johnson, who brought such vitality to the tech origin storyBlackberryand the recent time-travel comedyNirvanna the Band the Show the Movie, pointed Sessa towards two chapters fromKitchen Confidential, the memoir written in gunslinger prose and billed as a story of “sex, drugs, bad behaviour and haute cuisine”. There, the actor found the characters who inspired the film’s triumvirate of Provincetown kitchen mentors, the men Bourdain likens to “gods” and “pirates”: the wise head chef (Antonio Banderas), the coke-snorting Jack-the-lad (Leo Woodall) and the taunting, vulgar mischief-maker (Stavros Halkias).View image in fullscreenSessa as Anthony Bourdain in Tony.Photograph: Seacia Pavao“The restaurant we were filming in had only closed a couple of days earlier, so we were in a fully operating kitchen,” he explains. “Stavros learned how to make lobster rolls, Leo learned to shuck oysters. Matt was, like: ‘Dom, you go in and wash the dishes, and Stavros and Leo are gonna make fun of you.’ They made it all real for me. I felt genuinely intimidated by them. They’re so nice but I think they enjoyed the chance to bully me.”Dramatising Bourdain’s youthful exploits put Sessa in mind of his own misspent summers growing up on the Jersey Shore. He was raised in Ocean City, which was tranquil throughout the year then bustling with tourists during the holidays. His mother is a teacher; his father, who he has described as “a payroll guy”, died when Sessa was 14. He tells me he got his “opinionated” side from his mum, his sense of humour from his dad. “Jackass was one of the first movies he showed me,” he says fondly.After his father’s death, Sessa won a sports scholarship to attend Deerfield Academy, a boarding school in Massachusetts. “The only time I’d be home was in the summer breaks when it would basically be like a party. I worked in a bakery where I had early starts, and I’d be getting drunk on the beach before going to work; I was a mess. At that age, you felt you were invincible, you couldn’t get in trouble. We felt like we owned the place. We’d throw beach parties, then cops would chase us off the beach. You’d go to whoever’s house and their parents were gone so you’d destroy the place. We were menaces. Reading about the way Tony described his time in Provincetown, I was like: ‘Yeah, I get that. I understand.’”Partying wasn’t the only element in the film that chimed with him. “Playing Tony, I felt as if I was playing an unlikable side of myself,” he says, his tone no longer flippant. “He’s insecure and defensive at the start of the movie. I think a lot of young men have a very defensive way. You want people to respect you and treat you like an adult. But you feel as if you’re pretending. Deep down, there’s something underdeveloped that is hard for us to admit to. We’re always trying to hide that. I’m constantly going through that in my life.”View image in fullscreen‘I want to escape the modern era’ … Sessa.Photograph: Benedict Evans/The GuardianHe sits back in his seat as if surveying the scene before him. “Like, doing this interview, I’m pretending to be an adult, you know? Sometimes when you’re young, it’s to your detriment that you don’t allow yourself to fail in a productive way because you’re constantly trying to protect your ego.”What would his remedy be for young men like him? “Wilful hardships,” he says. “Deciding to go through hard things. Comfort is attractive. And we’ve built a culture around the comforts of the world. Where you really develop and learn the most about yourself is in doing something genuinely difficult. That’s what Tony does in this film.”The picture opens with a quote from Kitchen Confidential in which Bourdain describes his younger self as being “badly in need of a good ass-kicking”. Sessa sings from the same hymn sheet. “These cooks verbally abused each other, ripped each other apart. It’s an initiation process in a way, a rite of passage. There’s love on the other side of it.”If the actor’s view of kitchen life is impossibly romantic, very far from the widespread toxic culture that only this year led to the resignation from Noma of René Redzepiafter accusations of workplace abuse, then that is fully in keeping with the tone of Tony. This is a movie so reluctant to spoil the audience’s buzz that it doesn’t even reveal in the end titles that Bourdain is dead, let alone that hetook his own lifein 2018.Any toughness or complexity in the film comes from Sessa, whose performance ratifies his standing as both a 21st-century star-to-be and a 1970s pin-upmanqué. How does he explain the period fixation? “Maybe it says something about me. Like I want to escape the modern era.” Does he? “Yeah, I think so. I love being in the bars, the smell of cigarettes. It’s like stepping into a time machine.” No mobile phones, no social media. “Everybody’s looking up, talking to one another.”Eye contact isn’t the only behavioural difference he has noticed. “The impression I get is that young people back then were more confident in speaking, and perhaps more mature in interactions with adults. Nowadays it takes longer. I have friends in college who still can’t handle a social environment because of the way we’ve grown up. Especially after Covid. My generation gotscrewed.”Sessa was at Deerfield when the pandemic struck. “They designed a way to keep us on campus and in a bubble. The kids who got sick were sent to the old abandoned health centre.” His low rumble of a voice is interrupted by his sudden, honking laugh, as if acknowledging that this all sounds suspiciously like an episode of Scooby-Doo.View image in fullscreenCabin fever … Sessa with Da’Vine Joy Randolph in The Holdovers.Photograph: Seacia PavaoThat cabin-fever scenario was almost a rehearsal for playing Angus. “This was right before The Holdovers, so I guess I got used to feeling trapped,” he says. In 2022, the film-makers were visiting local schools to scout potential locations, no more expecting to find their Angus than Sessa was anticipating being cast as one of the leads in a Hollywood movie.As a financial aid student, he had felt out of place initially at Deerfield, where he had gone to pursue his dream of becoming a hockey player. When a broken femur in his freshman year put him out of action before the season had even started, theatre became his backup option.“I wasn’t being myself when I first got to school,” he says. “I was acting in a way that wasn’t genuine to who I was. I saw these kids, the way they dressed and carried themselves, and I didn’t feel I belonged in that environment so I had to role-play how these people were. I didn’t think they would accept me otherwise. But once I started doing theatre, I made so many more friends. People wanted to get to know me because I was putting myself out there.”Tony review – knives out in tasty reheat of Anthony Bourdain’s memoirRead moreHockey lost its appeal. “I saw it ending and it not being a part of my life much longer. I was never gonna be the best player in school. I would probably be one of the worst.” There is no need to remark on his chances of being one of the best actors instead. The acclaim he received for The Holdovers – 21 nominations from awards bodies and critics’ circles in the US and UK, including eight wins and a Bafta nod – tells its own story.In between The Holdovers and Tony, he turned down lead roles and studied drama for a year and a half at Carnegie Mellon University, taking supporting parts to keep his hand in. He played Michelle Pfeiffer’s sullen son, recently dumped and strumming an emo version of The 12 Days of Christmas, in the comedy Oh. What. Fun. In Tow, he was a non-profit lawyer whose client (Rose Byrne) tells him: “My car is older than you.” Multiplex-goers saw him as an upstart magician with Robin Hood ethics, stealing from crypto bros and diamond magnates, in the threequel Now You See Me: Now You Don’t.It is Tony, though, that he credits for the second turning point in his brief career. If The Holdovers set him on his current path, Tony has helped him decide on the kind of actor – and person – he wants to be. Since making the film, he has been heeding the advice of Bourdain, who wrote: “Good food and good eating are all about risk.”“I’ve been open to eating in a lot more B- and C-health-rated places,” Sessa says. But it’s not only about what’s on his plate. “In life generally, I feel more motivated now to follow my gut and take risks and live in the moment.” He mentions Shades of Paradise, a “crazy Euro-crime film” that he recently made in Barcelona, as an example: it gives him his first bona fide baddie to play after a string of messed-up but essentially decent guys. “I thought: ‘This is something really fun that I want to do.’” That’s his motto for today. “I’m doing what feels right.”Tony is in cinemas from 14 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmBiopicsAnthony BourdainfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Monsters of God review – a messy feud between rival reptile smugglers gets the Tiger King treatment | Television | The Guardian
description: Director Eric Goode has found two enemies to rival Joe Exotic and Carole Baskin in his new documentary about the animal trade’s underworld
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Director Eric Goode has found two enemies to rival Joe Exotic and Carole Baskin in his new documentary about the animal trade’s underworld
Content: Er, isn’t this a series about snakes and stuff? … Monsters of God.Photograph: HBO MaxView image in fullscreenEr, isn’t this a series about snakes and stuff? … Monsters of God.Photograph: HBO MaxTV reviewTelevisionReviewMonsters of God review – a messy feud between rival reptile smugglers gets the Tiger King treatmentDirector Eric Goode has found two enemies to rival Joe Exotic and Carole Baskin in his new documentary about the animal trade’s underworldHannah J DaviesFri 7 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThrough the fear and general miasma of the Covid pandemic, TV brought people together like never before. Among the most-watched series of 2020 was of courseTiger King, Netflix’s hit about an improbably twisty feud between a gay, polyamorous big-cat breeder and convicted felon, and the conservationist rival whom he accused of murder (more specifically, of feeding her missing husband to the tigers in her sanctuary – which she denies). It was the perfect hit for quarantine: bold and ridiculous enough to get everyone talking, and with precisely no bearing on the grief and awfulness that was all around.Producer and co-director Eric Goode has made a smattering of Tiger King follow-ups since then, as well as another series, Chimp Crazy, about the self-described Dolly Parton of the primate world. His latest project – a co-production between his own outfit, Goode Films, HBO, and A24 – continues the theme, focusing this time on the reptile trade and taking its lead from the 2008 book The Lizard King by journalist Bryan Christy. It’s stuffed full of wild stories and even wilder characters: there are canny smugglers, underworld crime gangs, and even legitimate zoos that are said to have turned a blind eye to the provenance of their big, scaly friends. The series is centred on the US – although clearly the supply chain is global – and the two men who kickstarted the illegal trade: Hank Molt and copycat trader Tommy Crutchfield. Like Joe Exotic and Carole Baskin before them, there is no love lost between Crutchfield and Molt, and no odd biographical detail too trivial to skip over. Hank, says Tommy, “will turn anything good into bad”, while Hank reckons that Tommy is “one of the angriest and most bitter people I’ve ever met”. Along the way we learn that Hank used to be a mayonnaise salesman, and that Tommy worked at an extremely on-the-nose Florida establishment named Snake-a-Torium as a teenager, where he would later have his wedding reception.What follows is the story not only of their enduring beef and betrayals, but of other adjacent vendettas in the illicit reptilian market. Despite environmental concerns becoming increasingly en vogue in the late 60s, a “don’t ask, don’t tell” attitude still pervaded the world of wildlife trading, with many zoos happy to acquire what they needed from whoever happened to have it. There were, however, serious consequences for some of the creatures involved. With the police on his back, Molt once buried a stash of animals alive in New Jersey’s Pine Barrens, a location which would later become infamous via The Sopranos. When he was eventually arrested, Crutchfield would become the go-to guy. He supplied cobras to the makers of a Hollywood blockbuster, he says, and sold tortoises to Michael Jackson. He even bred distinctive white albino alligators, which he sold for £175,000 a pop.The gruesome, revenge-fuelled culmination of the men’s feud at the end of the first episode is the high point of Monsters of God, which then limps through four more instalments. The illegal animal trade gets entangled with the (less interesting) drug trade in the 80s, and – somewhere along the way – the story becomes less punchy and more of an attempt to shoehorn in every strange character and weird/shocking/grim (delete as appropriate) anecdote that the producers had access to. A tangent about a federal agent who wore a gorilla costume in a sting operation is rather funny but, er, isn’t this a series about snakes and stuff? It does feel like Monsters of God could have been a two-parter, but then maybe it’s simply too hard to kill your darlings when you have so many of them. The story of a German man who collaborated with Crutchfield (and who attempted to escape the feds by running across eight lanes of traffic, in handcuffs, and wearing Birkenstocks) is hardly essential. But it is clearly entertaining.Monsters of God may lack that tight narrative thread that makes you want to recreate lockdown and spend five hours parked in front of the TV. But Goode is a conservationist as well as a film-maker, and it’s clear that he is interested in what became of the species whose existence was endangered by men like these. Much of the final episode is dedicated to notorious dealer Anson Wong from Malaysia, and the smuggling that meant that the ploughshare tortoise became all-but extinct in the wild. There is one final bit of good news, though, and a sense that nature – perhaps – is healing. It might not be a conclusion ripped from the bizarre world of Joe Exotic, but it’s the perfect ending to a wildlife documentary.Monsters of God is on HBO MaxExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewTiger KingDocumentaryFactual TVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Out of the blue: James Cameron’s surprise departure would be good for Avatar | James Cameron | The Guardian
description: The director has yet again hinted that he may step away – but if he does actually relinquish control, it would likely benefit the franchise
Author: Ben Child
Headline: The director has yet again hinted that he may step away – but if he does actually relinquish control, it would likely benefit the franchise
Content: Everyone’s favourite multibillion-dollar bioluminescent space jungle … the original Avatar, from 2009.Photograph: WETA/APView image in fullscreenEveryone’s favourite multibillion-dollar bioluminescent space jungle … the original Avatar, from 2009.Photograph: WETA/APWeek in geekJames CameronOut of the blue: James Cameron’s surprise departure would be good for AvatarBen ChildThe director has yet again hinted that he may step away – but if he does actually relinquish control, it would likely benefit the franchiseFri 7 Aug 2026 08.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 11.49 EDTShareAfter directing the highest-grossing film trilogy of all time, and having spent more than two decades bending technology, studio executives and several hundred million dollars’ worth of underwater motion capture to his will,James Cameronthis week signalled that he may be ready to hand the future of the Avatar franchise to another director. Indeed, he bent Hollywood to his will so completely that it became almost impossible in the early 2010s to watch a blockbuster without uncomfortable plastic glasses, and without objects on the screen being hurled pointlessly towards the audience. Still, the Canadian film-maker now appears to be seriously considering handing over everyone’s favourite multibillion-dollar bioluminescent space jungle to someone else.“There’s been momentum in the Avatar universe for 21 years at this point because we started in 2005,” Cameron told Denise Donlonin an interviewfor Canada’s governor general’s performing arts awards. “It’s been kind of an unbroken continuum. So this is the point where I’m looking at the landscape and asking, ‘What are the other stories I want to tell? How many of them do I need to direct myself versus writing and/or producing with other film-makers?’”He added: “I haven’t made any decisions yet. I’m still in this liminal state of mapping out, you know, kind of the last act. And I don’t know if that last act will last a year or 20 years.”This is not the first time Cameron has threatened to abandon his plans for Avatar. When he floated the possibility in 2022,I noted in this columnthat, at the rate the sequels were then progressing, he would be 106 by the time Avatar 5 reached cinemas and might require his own consciousness to be uploaded into a Na’vi. Yet only two years later, he insisted that anyone hoping to prise the next two films from his hands would have to run him over with a bus. It is therefore something of a surprise to find him once again contemplating life beyond Pandora.View image in fullscreenDisappeared into the cultural undergrowth … 2025’s Avatar: Fire and Ash.Photograph: 20th Century Studios/PAPart of the problem is that Cameron’s record of handing cherished projects to other directors (while remaining aboard as producer) is decidedly mixed. Kathryn Bigelow’s Strange Days (1995), which Cameron conceived, co-wrote and produced, became a cult classic rather than a hit. Steven Soderbergh’s Solaris (2002), produced by Cameron, turned cosmic mystery into two hours of George Clooney staring mournfully at a space station. Robert Rodriguez’s Alita: Battle Angel (2019), developed for years as a potential project for Cameron to direct, made respectable money but failed to turn enormous eyes and cyborg rollerball into the beginning of a global religion.Then came Terminator: Dark Fate (2019), on which Cameron served as producer and story godfather while Tim Miller directed, only for the franchise to discover that resurrecting Linda Hamilton, Arnold Schwarzenegger and most of the plot of the original Terminator was not enough to persuade audiences that a sixth attempt to keep humanity out of the clutches of killer robots from the future was required. Cameron later described the edit as a “bloodbath” of creative battles, while Miller, the director ofDeadpool, said the experience had left him with no desire ever to work with his famously exacting producer again.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow far can James Cameron’s Avatar saga go after its billion-dollar box office triumph?Read moreYet there is an argument that Avatar may benefit from a new guiding hand. Last year’sAvatar: Fire and Ashrecycled enough of its predecessors’ story beats to suggest that Pandora’s supply of unexplored territory may be running low. It still made almost $1.5bn worldwide, but disappeared into the cultural undergrowth with all the stealth of a 9ft fluorescent cat person. There was a distinct sense that this once most innovative of film franchises had become the cinematic equivalent of Oasis circa Be Here Now. Here was a product still vast, lavish and unmistakably itself, but now expending previously unimaginable quantities of money and effort to sell the memory of a past revolution rather than start a new one.Cameron may not exactly have run out of ideas, but there’s only so far one man can travel when his entire dramatic toolkit consists of 9ft blue cat aliens riding space dragons and discussing the spiritual properties of trees. Tolkien himself might have struggled when faced with the prospect of Quaritch returning from the dead for the umpteenth time, and the Sully family discovering yet another previously unmentioned branch of Na’vi society with its own accent, ceremonial headwear and highly specialised mode of transport.Perhaps we should simply let Cameron get on with something else for a change. After everything he has done for genre film-making over almost half a century, he has surely earned the right to make at least one film without Sigourney Weaver returning as the teenage daughter of her own dead mum, or without anybody having to learn how to hold their breath for seven minutes. At some point, even Pandora may need somebody new to decide what all its phosphorescent magnificence is actually for.Explore more on these topicsJames CameronWeek in geekAvatarScience fiction and fantasy filmscommentShareReuse this content

title: EA Sports FC 27: what does the next instalment of the world’s biggest football game have in store? | Games | The Guardian
description: The all-conquering franchise’s revamps are technically impressive, its transfers more true to life – and its new grassroots social hub is surprising fun
Author: Steve Boxer
Headline: The all-conquering franchise’s revamps are technically impressive, its transfers more true to life – and its new grassroots social hub is surprising fun
Content: Something fresh … EA Sports FC 27.Illustration: Electronic ArtsView image in fullscreenSomething fresh … EA Sports FC 27.Illustration: Electronic ArtsGamesEA Sports FC 27: what does the next instalment of the world’s biggest football game have in store?The all-conquering franchise’s revamps are technically impressive, its transfers more true to life – and its new grassroots social hub is surprising funSteve BoxerFri 7 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs if the world wasn’t sufficiently football-obsessed, it’s time to prepare for the arrival of its biggest football video game. EA Sports FC 27 (the franchise that used to be Fifa – what better time to no longer be Fifa-branded?) is due to be released on 25 September. I just spent two intense days in Vancouver, where the EA FC games are made, playing FC 27 and talking to its developers.With an annual franchise such as EA FC, it helps to have something fresh to entice regular fans, and FC 27 has a whole new element, entitled the Grounds. It’s a physical hub-type area, similar to the City as seen in 2K’s recent NBA 2K basketball games, but much more pleasant to frequent, split as it is into areas inspired by British, French and Argentinian street-football culture.The Grounds provides a new physical home for an existing element of EA FC: Clubs, its casual online mode in which you control a single player and play matches closer to kickabouts than real-world football, but beyond that, it has plenty of other activities and distractions.Visitingthe GroundsI spent about an hour in the Grounds, and found it more enjoyable than expected.
