Among its buildings are playing areas, whose entrances act as lobbies where you can choose to play against random people or to set up a custom game with your FC 27-owning friends. Each playing area hosts a specific type of game, and the Grounds has a map that you can teleport around.It rewards exploration: I encountered targets that could be smashed by spawning a football and drop-kicking it, some of which were clumped into mini-games. Its games offered clever twists on the Clubs blueprint. In one 3v3 game, target areas appeared for short periods, and if I scored from one, I got a bonus goal for my side. And one game based on dodgeball gave its players three lives, which they would lose if others successfully kicked a ball at them.The Grounds should prove popular: it has been tastefully and cleverly constructed and will no doubt expand as new game-types are added. You could also envisage it, in future years, hosting a narrative mode along the line of the Journey from Fifa 17 to 19.Gameplay revamps galoreFC 26 marked a mission by EA Sports to improve the franchise’s responsiveness by enactinga surprising number of changes to its fundamental gameplay, and that process continues apace in FC 27.Although anyone who played FC 26 will testify that those efforts actually caused some new problems, such as an annoying tendency for defensive interceptions to bounce back weirdly into the path of forwards. EA Sports, according to gameplay design director Kantcho Doskov, took radical action to eliminate such aberrations: “We had to completely strip out the existing system for interceptions and build a new one from scratch. We spent six months doing that.”View image in fullscreenLess AI … EA Sports FC 27.Illustration: Jamie Wrench/Electronic ArtsVia a build that let me play Champions League games between a limited number of teams, I found that to be a worthwhile exercise: those defensive bounce-backs were blissfully absent. But an awful lot more was also in evidence in FC 27 on the gameplay revamp front.Much of this – perhaps counterintuitively at a time when AI is worming its way ever deeper into all our lives – involved paring back the in-game AI. That’s certainly the case for the defensive AI: whereas previously, defenders would rush towards the ball, getting pulled out of position and opening up annoying gaps, FC 27 now gives much more manual control over defensive jockeying, movement and tackles.Crossing, previously AI-assisted, has been revamped in FC 27, leaving it up to me to get the direction and weight of cross right, then giving me more of a chance to position my centre-forward correctly. The AI controlling forward players, meanwhile, has been improved, so that off-the-ball players now move much more helpfully, allowing pass-and-move sequences, and they are much better at staying onside.I was also impressed by revamped two-stage corner and free-kick systems. But FC 27, gameplay-wise, achieves what FC 26 set out to, this time with no evident anomalies, and feels more responsive to your inputs than any of its predecessors.Making transfers more true-to-lifeFC 27’s Career Mode, in which you get to play out your fantasies of managing your favourite team, has also been extensively revamped – primarily with a view towards making its transfer system more like the one that operates in the real world, and to force you to do more actual management.The headline means of doing the latter is called Dynamic OVR. OVR is simply jargon for any player’s all-important overall rating; where previously OVRs remained constant, in FC 27’s Career Mode they will go up and down depending on form, fitness and general happiness. Thus, you will have to rest your best players over the course of a long season, but you may also be able to buy players cheaply with artificially low OVRs if, say, they are coming back from injury.View image in fullscreen‘It was about extracting the fun bits of the jobs’ … EA Sports FC 27.Illustration: Electronic ArtsPete O’Donnell, FC 27’s Career Mode game director, explains how the game’s transfer system has been modernised: “Previously, you could do things instantly, which was good for a game but was not very realistic. We looked at how clubs interact with each other, how they do the deals themselves, and we spoke to scouts and directors of football. Then it was about extracting the fun bits of those jobs.”The new system will back you up with more data; now each player will have an xTV (Expected Transfer Value) rating, which should speed negotiations. FC 27 will also reflect clubs’ real-life transfer policies, according to O’Donnell, with clubs’ boards requesting that you sign certain players. Press conferences in FC 27 will force you to make decisions that will please some players and annoy others, and 20 Unexpected Events have been added to Career Mode.Ultimate Transfer: a new showcaseFC 27’s Ultimate Transfer (FUT) mode, the hardcore card-based system that provides a home for most of FC’s loot box action, will have a new headline feature in the form of a Gallery, which will showcase all the players and card-sets collected, rather than just first 11s.View image in fullscreenA new headline feature … EA Sports FC 27’s FUT Gallery.Illustration: Electronic ArtsEA Sports says it has also “streamlined” FUT’s previously impenetrable Squad-Based Challenges (SBC) system, and has made a tweak designed to avert stalemates, which affected the latter stages in FUT in FC 26, by restricting plus-level FUT players to three, rather than five, play-styles. But the nature of FUT – which develops over a long period post-launch – means that it will take a while to ascertain whether those changes prove effective.Now rated 16There will be another major change to FC 27 that has nothing to do with how it plays: because it contains microtransactions, it will now be rated 16+ rather than the previous 3+, after a policy change at age-rating organisation Pegi. Given the game’s enthusiastic young and teenage audience, we asked EA Sports’ top brass to comment, but they blandly responded: “While the game functionally remains the same, this has resulted in a new Pegi age rating. It marks a change in the way we are giving the information to players and parents.”Beyond Pegi’s European jurisdiction, the game will be rated E for Everybody. But in the UK, parents should think hard about letting youngsters play a 16-rated game. If they are worried about their offspring racking up huge bills for FUT transactions, the good news is that a new Ultimate Plus Edition of the game, which includes loads of stuff that would previously have cost in-game currency, will go on sale. But the bad news is it costs £139.99 and will only be available as a pre-order before 31 August.EA Sports FC 27 is out on 25 September on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, and PC. It will also launch on PS4, Xbox One, and Switch, but without some features, such as the new Grounds mode.Explore more on these topicsGamesPlayStation 5Xbox series S/XNintendo Switch 2featuresShareReuse this content

title: ‘It might be one of the most unpopular tunes ever written!’: kids’ TV composers tell all | Television | The Guardian
description: Big cheques, standing ovations, irate adults – there are surprising sides to composing a children’s TV theme tune. From Bluey to Byker Grove, the creators of the best reveal the secrets
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: Big cheques, standing ovations, irate adults – there are surprising sides to composing a children’s TV theme tune. From Bluey to Byker Grove, the creators of the best reveal the secrets
Content: Dog whistle … Bluey is one of the biggest kids’ shows in the world today.Photograph: DisneyView image in fullscreenDog whistle … Bluey is one of the biggest kids’ shows in the world today.Photograph: DisneyTelevision‘It might be one of the most unpopular tunes ever written!’: kids’ TV composers tell allBig cheques, standing ovations, irate adults – there are surprising sides to composing a children’s TV theme tune. From Bluey to Byker Grove, the creators of the best reveal the secretsMichael HoganFri 7 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 16.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow do you write TV theme music for children? Does it make you mega-rich? And does the tune itself eventually drive you (and parents everywhere) nuts?We tracked down the creators of half-a-dozen of TV’s greatest children’s show themes in order to find out. As Bluey’s Joff Bush told us: “The key lesson is that if you’re going to write a theme tune, make sure you really like it because you’re going to hear it a helluva lot!”From nostalgic cult classics to current hits, from cartoon animals to live-action school soaps, six composers confess the secrets of kids’ TV music …‘Parents get woken up at 6am by it’View image in fullscreenOn the hoof … a demo track was used as the Peppa Pig theme for 20 years.Photograph: Album/AlamyComposerJulian NottscoresPeppa Pig, as well asWallace & Gromit,BingandBen & Holly’s Little Kingdom.It all started at the National Film andTelevisionSchool’s animation department. Two fellow students became friends: Nick Park, who did Wallace & Gromit, and Mark Baker, who did Peppa Pig. They’ve been collaborators ever since.Peppa was just another job that came along. I worked on the pilot episode for free as a favour. It wasn’t just the same theme tune as today, it was the same recording. We finally updated it last year but for two decades they used the demo version. It’s only 10 seconds long which is shorter than most title sequences. It was a challenge to write a short, sharp, catchy tune. It had to be fast and fun with a memorable melody. The gaps in it were exploited by Mark, who inserted oinking sound effects.We classical musicians tend to laugh at pop writers for only knowing three chords but Peppa has two, which is probably a musical outrage. There was zero budget, so it’s all played on synthesisers and samplers. The instrumentation which became associated with Peppa – marimbas, timpani, glockenspiel, vibraphone – were only chosen because they were the most convincing samples you could get back then.Peppa took over the world, so I hear my music all the time. I’m often in a cafe or airport and a child will be playing it on their iPad. I’m tempted to lean over and say: ‘I wrote that!’ but never have. There was a time when I couldn’t get on a train without hearing it. It’s a strange feeling. Kids watch their favourite shows on repeat, so it can drive parents mad. Toddlers work out how to switch on Peppa Pig and their parents get woken up at 6am by the theme music. It might be one of the most unpopular tunes ever written! But I’m very lucky that it’s given me financial security. Peppa Pig was like winning the lottery. It’s enabled me to sustain a career. It’s all upside and it’s marvellous.‘It was the luckiest two minutes of my life’View image in fullscreenRing of success … the cast of Saved By the Bell.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyScott Galewrote the theme song forNBC’s 1990s teen sitcom Saved Bythe Bell.I was music coordinator onThe Golden Girls. One Friday, the producer of this new teen comedy called and asked me to try out for the theme tune. My wife had left me that morning but I put down the phone, picked up my guitar and, bingo, it just poured out of me. It was the luckiest two minutes of my life. We recorded it over the weekend at my partner Rich Eames’s home studio.On Monday morning, we handed in our cassette. Little did I know that executive producer Peter Engel had told all the other prospective composers not to include “saved by the bell” in the lyrics because he wasn’t sure the name would stick. But I never got that message, so the title appeared five times in mine. Peter later admitted he was glad I didn’t get his instructions.Saved By the Bell was the first live-action Saturday morning kids’ show. Everything else was cartoons. I thought it’d be lucky to last seven episodes but it ran for four seasons. And the show, thank goodness, was heavy on music. We wrote it all. If there was a jukebox playing, we’d write the songs. The characters formed a rock group. We wrote what they played. There was something new every week.Saved By the Bell was very good to me. I still get royalties from Spain, South Africa, everywhere. Those gigs are hard to get but it’s the gift that keeps on giving. I never tire of hearing it. I’ll chance across it while channel surfing and it whisks me back to those wild times. Nearly four decades later, I still get to talk about it. It’s nothing but wonderful.‘I ended up writing songs with Ant and Dec’View image in fullscreenLimitless win … regular royalties from Byker Grove – the show that launched Ant and Dec – are a boon for theme composers the Kane Gang.Photograph: ITVMartin Brammeris the frontman of pop triothe Kane Gang, whose track became the basis of the theme tune to Byker Grove.We’d already reworked our song Small Town Creed to be the jingle for Radio 1 DJ Gary Davies’s show. The makers of this local teen drama – a sort of Geordie version of Grange Hill – asked if the Kane Gang fancied doing the theme tune. Either out of expedience or laziness, we thought: “Hang on! Maybe we can get a third version out of it.”It’s a challenge to create something impactful in 45 seconds. It became this tongue-in-cheek funk workout, a bit edgier than the average kids’ TV tune. A dozen of the cast came down to do the “Ooh, Byker Grove!” chants. That little laugh at the end was from Lyndyann Barrass, who played Spuggie. We liked it and left it in. People tend to remember that laugh. A few years ago, I got a request from another artist – Professor Green or someone – to sample it.The show ran for 18 series, so royalties make a handy annual bonus. It’s not a life-changing amount of money but it’s hard making a living in music nowadays, so sidelines that tick over are invaluable. Midway through the run, we redid it slightly. Put a funky drummer sample on it to make it more contemporary. Byker Grove led to all sorts of connections. I did some work with Donna Air’s pop duo Crush and songwriting sessions withAnt and Decas they were moving away from being PJ & Duncan. Lovely lads.I’ve written hundreds of proper songs but the Byker Grove tune always gets a reaction. I write with Olly Murs now and he flipped when he found out. Now there’s a reboot in development. It would be madness to change the theme tune, right? Fingers crossed we get the call from Ant and Dec.‘Kids are disappointed that I’m not a six-year-old girl’View image in fullscreenHeeler dealer … Daley Pearson wrote the Bluey theme tune.Photograph: Ludo StudioJoff Bushwrote the theme music and composes most of the soundtrack for globally loved animation Bluey.I met Daley Pearson [Bluey’s executive producer] when we were students. In 2017, he said: “Would you be interested in coming up to Brisbane for this side project we’ve got? It’s called Bluey, for four to six-year-olds.” I was like: “I doubt I’m the right fit but I’ll check it out.” I’ll be forever grateful that I did. I met [Bluey’s creator] Joe Brumm and we clicked. I watched the rough pilot episodes and just fell in love. I had do it.I knew exactly what the show’s sound should be. A bit hand-made with an almost chamber ensemble sound. It’s hard to describe but I could hear the chord progression in my head. When the writing’s that good, it’s relatively easy to score. Joe Brumm makes my music look better. I suggested building a library of music which we could reuse but Joe wanted something new for every episode. I was like: “That’s a lot of work!” But it became one of the beauties of Bluey.They were going to license a track for the theme tune but I said: “Can I have a go at it?” And then I had 10 goes at it! Version eight unlocked it. Now it’s hard to imagine without the theme song. It probably sounds simpler than it is. There are little details in it that only I notice. Parents tend to be more impressed than children. If I tell a kid that I write the music for the show, they’ll ask: “Are you Bluey?” “No.” “Oh, OK.” They’re disappointed that I’m a 41-year-old man, not a six-year-old girl. That keeps your ego in check.I’m fortunate that my work’s more famous than me. Bluey’s been great for opening up career opportunities and pretty lucrative. The albums have topped the charts. It’s enabled me to work on strange projects that I want to do, rather than taking adverts to pay the rent. I’m just starting on a ballet.I recently became a father and suddenly understood why dads find Bluey so emotional. I messaged Joe saying: “I get it now!” My daughter’s two and last week, she came back from daycare going: “Doo doo doo doo, Bluey and Bingo!” I was like: “Do you like that song?” She said: “It’s pretty good.” We rerecorded it last year and I got some cute photos of her conducting the orchestra. I’ll surprise her with them someday. Then again, I was singing Wagon Ride to her to help her go to sleep. She woke up, put her hand over my mouth and went: “Different music.” She’s my harshest critic.‘My fee definitely wasn’t Scrooge McDuck money’View image in fullscreenQuacked it … the DuckTales intro is known worldwide.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyPop and musical theatre songwriterMark Muellercomposed the theme tune forlate 80s Disney seriesDuckTales.I’d just had my first top 10 single, having writtenNothin’ at All by Heart. That’s how I got the meeting at Disney for DuckTales. The execs told me: “Write a radio song, not a cartoon song,” with lots of action in the lyrics they could animate to. That’s why I came up with “race cars, lasers, aeroplanes ... it’s a duck blur”. I jammed as many moving images as possible into 60 seconds.After the meeting, I drove back to my tiny apartment and wrote the song in 45 minutes on a second-hand Roland synthesiser. I was in a groove and it spilled out of me. I took the demo back to Disney and played it to them in person. They sent it all the way up to the head of the studio, who loved it. My head was spinning. Seldom does anything happen that quickly in Hollywood.There are so many hooks in DuckTales. Everything from the intro bass lick to the “d-d-dangers” were meant to worm into your brain. The “woo-hoos” fitted perfectly into three empty beats. Vanity Fair called it “history’s catchiest single minute of music”. To me, catchy isn’t a dirty word. It’s what I strive for. My initial fee was $1,250, which definitely wasn’t Scrooge McDuck money. It barely paid for a month’s rent but thankfully, the royalties were good and they keep coming in.After the show aired, I received a letter from the mother of an autistic child. She told me that she and her husband had never been able to communicate with their young son until he heard the DuckTales song. They would sing it to each other and it was the first time they truly connected. That touched me.Its global reach is heady stuff. I went to South Korea and my rather somber tour guide had it as his ringtone. A few months ago in Portugal, a strait-laced female banker launched into it. I heard it from tinny speakers on a rickshaw in London. The impact that this minute-long song had on my life is immeasurable. The experience has been a perfect whirlwind – or should I say “duck blur”?‘I got a £14,000 cheque for ringtones from Japan’View image in fullscreenDanger money … Mike Harding did well out of his kids’ TV scores.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyWriter, comedian and musicianMike Hardingcomposed the scores forDanger Mouseand its spin-offCount Duckula.“Manchester studio Cosgrove Hall Films were fans of my standup, so they asked if I had any ideas for animations. We made a pilot about a busking frog called Far-Out Fred and I did the music for The Reluctant Dragon. Then they said they’d got this mouse super-agent but it wasn’t quite working. I took a look and said: “You’re trying to make him a James Bond character, too rooted in the real world. You realise this is a mouse living in a pillar box? He can do whatever we like.”I went away and wrote some scripts. I based arch enemy Baron Greenback on this real-life nemesis of mine called Alan Greenbank and made him an evil toad. When it came to the theme music, I studied 60s spy films and wrote a pastiche. Sort of Bond meets Dick Tracy. We dragged in local session musicians and put it together.Danger Mouse became a classic of its time. David Jason and Terry Scott were terrific at the voices. The animators were amazing. It was a joy to be part of. People felt real warmth towards it. I once stood in for Seamus Heaney at short notice, giving the opening speech at an Irish school arts festival. When I said I wrote the music for Danger Mouse, the kids went wild. I got what my grandad used to call a “standing ovation”.We still get royalty cheques. The biggest was one year when we got £14,000 from Japan for ringtones. There was a CBBC remake a decade ago which went worldwide but the royalties from Kuala Lumpur are tuppence. I only get a standing ovation from old people nowadays. But I still have a T-shirt saying “The bloke who wrote the music for Danger Mouse”!Explore more on these topicsTelevisionBlueyPeppa PigAnt and DecfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘There is an alternative to capitalism’: after addiction and losing a home to LA wildfires, indie rockers Diiv start again | Music | The Guardian
description: No stranger to rebuilding after disaster, the US band’s frontman Zachary Cole Smith now sees the entire capitalist project as ripe for reinvention, on a surprisingly upbeat new AG Cook-produced album
Author: Jazz Monroe
Headline: No stranger to rebuilding after disaster, the US band’s frontman Zachary Cole Smith now sees the entire capitalist project as ripe for reinvention, on a surprisingly upbeat new AG Cook-produced album
Content: Diiv, from left: Zachary Cole Smith, Colin Caulfield, Ben Newman and Andrew Bailey.Photograph: Louie KovatchView image in fullscreenDiiv, from left: Zachary Cole Smith, Colin Caulfield, Ben Newman and Andrew Bailey.Photograph: Louie KovatchMusicInterview‘There is an alternative to capitalism’: after addiction and losing a home to LA wildfires, indie rockers Diiv start againJazz MonroeNo stranger to rebuilding after disaster, the US band’s frontman Zachary Cole Smith now sees the entire capitalist project as ripe for reinvention, on a surprisingly upbeat new AG Cook-produced albumFri 7 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZachary Cole Smith used to be a miserable interviewee. He had plenty to say – always generous, always voluble – but spoke with grim introspection, chastising himself and cataloguing his misdeeds with a fervour that engulfed him like his oversized T-shirts. A decade later, the Diiv frontman who materialises on my screen seems well rid of that old self. Suspiciously well rid of it, perhaps. He looks as if he has stepped out of a middle management meeting.“Precisely!” Smith concurs cheerfully, speaking via video call from a back garden in La Cañada, California. “We’re trying to have a visual language, which is fun. We’ve never done that with what we wear.” The singer-guitarist, 41, wears thick-rimmed square glasses, slicked-back black hair and a pinstripe shirt, its neck clasped by a tie printed with stock market emblems. He has an earnest but pranksterish energy. He uses the word “fun” so many times – more than a dozen within 10 minutes – that I suspect he is testing some sort of subliminal PR strategy.The Diiv album he is promoting is called Zirp! (meaning “zero interest-rate policy”) and produced by Alex “AG” Cook, the bubbly, neon pop accelerationist and co-conspirator of Charli xcx. Cook is by no means a natural fit for Diiv, who are one of the least garish bands around. Their buzzy early albums set 80s goth to a motorik pulse, with dream-pop riffs refracted like sunlight into a cobwebbed drawing room. Though they have likely benefited from the TikTok-aided shoegaze revival, their fourth album, 2024’s Frog in Boiling Water, waded into the swamp of anti-capitalist ennui. Cook has helped airlift them out: on Zirp!, for the first time in years, Diiv sound like they are finally having – hang on a minute …Diiv: The Fountain – video“It’s fun to do something fun,” proclaims Smith, smoking the first of several cigarettes. Today’s costume, accordingly, is based on a darkly comic figure: “the recession-era, stock market crash guy”. Smith strikes a pose like Rodin’s Thinker if he had just cost his hedge fund a billion dollars. “This kind of vibe, with the dishevelled suit.”To go with the look, the band coined a tongue-in-cheek genre dubbed the New Alternative. It reminds Smith of both the loathed Thatcherite slogan “there is no alternative” and the influential Mark Fisher book Capitalist Realism: Is There No Alternative? “I really want to reclaim that word,” Smith says. “Thereisan alternative to capitalism.”For starters, he dreams of a publicly owned streaming library that could operate as an alternative to the current ecosystem, particularly Spotify. “I do feel that that company absolutely should not exist and should be dismantled,” he says. “For Spotify, [music] is just fodder in their ecosystem. They’re selling tech. Apple is a company that’s selling phones. And music is this resource that they can pillage and plunder.”View image in fullscreenZachary Cole Smith at FYF Fest 2016 in Los Angeles.Photograph: Kevin Winter/Getty ImagesNew songs Evangelizer and The Crash are similarly forthright: the former, a wraithlike monologue, depicts “BlackRock master keys” and “Palantir-Pfizer collab pills” in what Smith calls a “post-capitalist hellscape”; the latter is a wonky, end-of-days art-pop screed by a narrator determined to “throw the billionaires screaming in an alligator pit”. As to what a New Alternative might be, he concedes that the term, for now, describes nothing beyond a break from “some kind of norm”. He shrugs helplessly, then seems to remember he is wearing a tie. “Alternative stocks are up!” he declares.One afternoon in January 2025, Smith invited his bandmates to his home in Altadena to demo My Star, a thrashing alt-rock love song to his one-year-old son. As they left, a windstorm was brewing. When nearby Eaton Canyon went up in flames in the wildfires, Smith and his wife, who was seven months pregnant, decided to gather their son’s belongings. “We gotta do bedtime,” he remembers thinking. “Let’s just pack up his little crib and his little jammies and get a hotel room, and then the power won’t go out.”By 3am, their hotel secured, Altadena was ablaze. “Our neighbours were describing the scene: it’s raining orange, it’s snowing orange.” Three hours later, “everything was gone. Then at 6.30am, our son woke up and was just like, ‘What are we doing today!’” As their adrenaline ebbed, the gravity of the loss struck. “All of a sudden, we had nothing. But once he woke up, we just had to make everything be normal.”Their home was now a pile of rubble beside the burnt-out carcass of a car. Finding a new place was hard “because so many people were displaced”, says Smith. A series of temporary lodgings led the family – now including their second child – to the La Cañada house where they have lived for the past six months, awaiting a distant peaceful life. “Where we’re at now feels like where we’ll be until we rebuild our house, which is a slow process,” he says. “But one that, I think, at some point, will become fun.”View image in fullscreenDiiv in 2016, from left: Devin Ruben Perez, Zachary Cole Smith, Ben Newman, Andrew Bailey and Colin Caulfield.Photograph: David A Smith/Getty ImagesWork on Zirp! swiftly resumed. Inspired by a 2023 arena tour supporting Depeche Mode – and a dip into the band’s 1980s catalogue – Smith had already decided to “surrender perfectionism, work quickly and not be precious”. Having run into Cook at a party, he cemented the partnership after hearing the grunge anthem Bewitched from the producer’s triple album Britpop. Cook renders Diiv’s shoegaze textures as if in arcade mode: portentous riffs wriggle like pop-punk earworms; feedback harbours micro melodies like radio jingles. “Knowing the songs were gonna wind up in front of Alex made it so much more fun to take risks,” says Smith.There were other benefits to recruiting an auteur producer. Though Smith single-handedly produced and masterminded the first two Diiv albums, the band gradually became more collaborative as he treated, and finally cut out, his drug use. “Addiction is all about control,” he says. “You want to block out what anybody else is saying, so it lends itself really well to dictatorship.”His addiction had become a minor scandalin 2013, when Smith and then-girlfriend Sky Ferreira were arrested for possession of heroin and ecstasy (he took full responsibility). He went to rehab, left and relapsed. He spent four years talking up Diiv’s second album and playinglacklustre showsin a period of heightened scrutiny: drummer Colby Hewitt was dealing with his own substance use and bassist Devin Ruben Perez had been exposed for bigoted messageboard posts. (Both left the band.) As Diiv threatened to slip through his fingers, Smith became preoccupied with collecting rare coral reefs in a 50-gallon saltwater tank at his Brooklyn apartment.View image in fullscreenChannelling a ‘spirit of fun and playfulness and risk and experimentation’.Photograph: Louie KovatchWith the help of his girlfriend (whom he married in 2020) and mother-in-law, Smith kicked drugs in 2017. The “ego destruction” of sobering up prompted him to democratise the band. “I’ve worked to repair the trust with my bandmates and whoever I damaged during my active addiction,” he says. “I just want to utilise that to get us to where we want to be,” moving forward in a “spirit of fun and playfulness and risk and experimentation”.Indie music has been invaded by fake fans and cynical viral campaigns​. Here’s how deep it all goesRead moreSmith has spoken relentlessly about all those he has let down and lied to. After all that, I ask, how did it feel to receive $100,000 in crowdfunded wildfire aid for his family, from a community that trusts and supports him? “I want to cry just thinking about it,” he says, choking up. “It taught me something, you know? It was profound. I’ve never experienced love like that. And it did feel like …” He sighs. “I felt like I deserved it.” As part of his recovery, Smith has helped others living with addiction and maintained a network of the similarly afflicted. “I feel like we earned it through being good to our friends, family and communities,” he says, “being available to people or letting a band borrow the van. I don’t know how I would have learned that lesson any other way. But it was probably the most meaningful thing that’s ever happened to me, on an interpersonal level.”The rebuilding of Smith’s family home remains clogged up in various city-planning departments. “But the Altadena community is stronger than it’s ever been,” he says, lighting another cigarette. “The relationships we have with other families that lived on our street is remarkable. Even the crowdfunding – the silver lining is how it showed this sense of community, lifting each other up.” For a little while, it seemed as if the fire would consume their whole world. “It could have felt really alienating, but luckily, we had each other.”Zirp! is released via Fantasy Recordings on 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMusicDrugsPsychedeliaIndiePop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Buried for not being Brueghel: overlooked masterpiece by still-life pioneer discovered in storage area | Art | The Guardian
description: The curator of Norway’s national museum in Oslo is bringing the work by the Flemish baroque artist Clara Peeters out of obscurity in a major exhibition of female artists
Author: Joanna Moorhead
Headline: The curator of Norway’s national museum in Oslo is bringing the work by the Flemish baroque artist Clara Peeters out of obscurity in a major exhibition of female artists
Content: Revivified … Still Life with Small Game and Grapes on a Gilded Tazza by Clara Peeters, c1620, Nasjonalmuseet, Oslo.Photograph: Børre Høstland/The National MuseumView image in fullscreenRevivified … Still Life with Small Game and Grapes on a Gilded Tazza by Clara Peeters, c1620, Nasjonalmuseet, Oslo.Photograph: Børre Høstland/The National MuseumArtBuried for not being Brueghel: overlooked masterpiece by still-life pioneer discovered in storage areaThe curator of Norway’s national museum in Oslo is bringing the work by the Flemish baroque artist Clara Peeters out of obscurity in a major exhibition of female artistsJoanna MoorheadFri 7 Aug 2026 04.51 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 05.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnonymous was often a woman: so said Virginia Woolf. And so thought Cynthia Osiecki one day in 2022, when she chanced on an unattributed still life in the storage area of the National Museum ofNorwayin Oslo.Osiecki had been studying the work of a renowned 17th-century Flemish artist, Clara Peeters, one of the earliest practitioners of still life painting. Works by Peeters hang in the Prado in Madrid, the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford and the Metropolitan Museum in New York.The Oslo painting, Still Life with Small Game and Grapes on a Gilded Tazza, was created around 1620 and features nine freshly dead birds, hazelnuts, apricots and a fly perched on a bunch of grapes. It had once been regarded as the work of a member of a famous family of Antwerp artists, Ambrosius Brueghel. But in the early 20th century the attribution was reassessed, and the work reclassified as being by “anonymous”. Since then it had mostly been consigned to storage.Osiecki began to wonder whether the work – some details of which have been obscured by many layers of varnish – could be by Peeters, an enigmatic but prolific artist who pushed the boundaries of still life painting in the Northern European baroque period. Osiecki began to compare the work with other pieces by the painter, who is thought to have been born in Antwerp around 1594. “I looked at the panel the Oslo work is painted on, and discovered it was from a supplier Peeters often used,” she says. “Then I looked at other paintings by Peeters, and I noticed some of them had atazza[a saucer-like dish on a pedestal] very similar to the one in the Oslo painting.” Osiecki noticed, too, similarities in the way the dead birds, the grapes and the hazelnuts were positioned in the composition.One problem, though, was that Peeters was well known for signing her works, and the Oslo piece had no signature. But the panel had been damaged by woodworm, and the area eaten away was the bottom edge of the work – the very area where Peeters usually signed her pieces.View image in fullscreenAlongside Peeters … Judith and her Maidservant with the Head of Holofernes byArtemisia Gentileschi, c1640.Photograph: Børre Høstland Annar Bjørgli/Kunstner: Gentileschi ArtemisiaIt seemed more and more likely that the painting was a work by Peeters – but a piece of the jigsaw was missing. Peeters is famous for including miniature self-portraits in her work, often reflections of herself in pewter or glass objects, or on shiny fruit or vegetables. “I could see a shape on some of the grapes, and on closer examination I realised they look like outlines of human figures,” says Osiecki. These might be the artist herself, and it could be that the image has been lost during conservation work.Earlier this year the painting was officially reattributed to Peeters, and it will be one of the star exhibits inWomanPainterat the National Museum of Norway opening 8 October, curated by Osiecki. The show features the work of female artists working across northern Europe and Italy between 1550 and 1650, with paintings by 19 artists including Artemisia Gentileschi, Lavinia Fontana and Judith Leyster, as well as Clara Peeters.Peeters was known for intimate still lifes reflecting the transience of this world, says Osiecki. “Her paintings, including the newly attributed work, are all about the brevity of life. We see recently dead birds, who will be part of a feast for humans, and grapes that will soon either be eaten or will decay. And though the work includes luxurious objects such as thetazza, Peeters is making the point that you can’t take anything with you when you die. In the end we’re all equal.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe reattributed work demonstrates how art history is expanding to include women whose work has been lost or ignored, says Nora Ceciliedatter Nerdrum, director of exhibitions and collections at the National Museum of Norway. Over recent years, Europe’s major museums have been opening up to shows of women’s work – in 2016, Peeters became the first woman ever to be given a solo show at the Prado.Nerdrum agrees that the quest to correct the omission of women from the canon of art history began by retrieving known works by women from storage; now, the search is on for women whose work has been labelled “anonymous”. “Watch this space, because there will be lots more of these finds in the future,” says Osiecki. “The more we look, the more archival research we do, the more women we’re going to find.”Explore more on these topicsArtNorwayEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: In the Black review – rewarding drama about the Faustian pact of big business | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Quaz Degraft draws on his knowledge of high finance for these misadventures in a material, misogynist world
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Quaz Degraft draws on his knowledge of high finance for these misadventures in a material, misogynist world
Content: Sweetly told … Quaz Degraft in his play In the Black.Photograph: Matt Dale/Fern PhotographyView image in fullscreenSweetly told … Quaz Degraft in his play In the Black.Photograph: Matt Dale/Fern PhotographyEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewIn the Black review – rewarding drama about the Faustian pact of big businessUnderbelly, Bristo Square, EdinburghQuaz Degraft draws on his knowledge of high finance for these misadventures in a material, misogynist worldMark FisherFri 7 Aug 2026 12.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou don’t hear much about the American dream these days, but for Kofi Grady, a first generation Ghanaian American, the opportunity for betterment in the land of the free is real. Brought up by a disciplinarian father whose definition of success is not just money but job security, he is a young graduate who puts his mathematical skills to work in a trillion-dollar financial company.Driving him is the sense of comfort and control he experienced as a teenage joyrider in a high-performance car. What he never had he craves the most.Actor and writer Quaz Degraft knows the world he describes. Like Kofi, he worked in high finance, but rather than end up in an orange jumpsuit helping fellow prisoners with their sums, as his character does, he jumped ship and reinvented himself as a performer. His solo show – back on the Edinburgh fringe after a well-received run last year – paints an insider picture of a corporate culture in which profit and personal success override all other considerations.Target Audience review – zingy satire puts media types in an apocalyptic pickleRead moreIn a sweetly told piece of storytelling, featuring a rollcall of colleagues, friends and double dates, Degraft describes the implicit Faustian pact of big business: put in the hours, say the right things, keep quiet about the abuses and wait for the bonuses to roll in.Above all, this is a #MeToo play told from the male perspective. Kofi is not directly connected to the assault of a female worker but is complicit in its cover-up, much as anyone would be who chooses silence over confrontation, private gain over honourable whistleblowing.That Degraft makes it seem like an everyday tale of a young man innocently trying to settle into a new job belies his deeper purpose: to reveal the insidious nature of male power. The insight is not new but, in Abigail Onwunali’s stripped-down production, it is subtly done.AtUnderbelly, Bristo Square, Edinburgh, until 31 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Target Audience review – zingy satire puts media types in an apocalyptic pickle | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: With characteristic wit, Dan Bishop’s comedy develops from a jolly send-up of the vacuous TV industry into a politically astute play about power
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: With characteristic wit, Dan Bishop’s comedy develops from a jolly send-up of the vacuous TV industry into a politically astute play about power
Content: An industry beholden to charismatic bullshitters … from left: James Coward, Molly Windust, Henry Calcutt and RhéAna Kamalu in Target Audience.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn industry beholden to charismatic bullshitters … from left: James Coward, Molly Windust, Henry Calcutt and RhéAna Kamalu in Target Audience.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewTarget Audience review – zingy satire puts media types in an apocalyptic picklePleasance Courtyard, EdinburghWith characteristic wit, Dan Bishop’s comedy develops from a jolly send-up of the vacuous TV industry into a politically astute play about powerMark FisherFri 7 Aug 2026 06.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 15.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘I’ve never read anything Greek, but I bet if feels exactly like this,” says Isabelle (RhéAna Kamalu) at the apocalyptic height of this zingy comedy. She is a gen Z intern whose end-of-times neuroses have suddenly become justified after she receives a government alert to stay indoors. Maybe she did not want to die young, after all.The line has the characteristic wit of playwright Dan Bishop, author of last year’sBrainsluts, but the scene itself is unexpected. Wind back to the start of Target Audience and you will find something much more ephemeral.It begins as a jolly send-up of a vacuous screen industry, one beholden to charismatic bullshitters such as Angie – short for Angus (James Coward) – and the tyranny of audience data. We could be watching the BBC satireW1Aor David Mamet’s Speed-the-Plow as a production company brings in Tobias (Henry Calcutt), a politically sensitive writer, to see if he can add an edge to their scripts in development.Edinburgh festival 2026: 10 terrific shows we’ve already reviewedRead moreOne of these is called Citizen 54, the other Thorns. If it were not for the poster for Horizon (tagline: “The future is round”), you could believe they had never made a film, preferring endless days of platitudes and statistics. With his sidekick Bruiser (Molly Windust, also starring inRockpoolsat the fringe), Angie flatters Tobias as quickly as he undermines him. He is not an artist but a cog in the wheel.If the material is familiar, the actors make it seem fresh in Bishop’s entertaining production. If he got rid of the scene changes, it would be more pacy still. But the playwright is playing the long game and what emerges from the airhead character comedy is a satire about moral compromises that affect not just the telly we watch but the late-capitalist power structures we inhabit. Funny, yes, but also politically astute.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s a Pan-African story’: the artists telling the amazing true tale of Zambia’s mission to reach space  | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The nation’s audacious 1960s rocket programme was met with ridicule. Now, more than 60 years on, this curious episode is inspiring film-makers, playwrights and a circus show at the fringe
Author: JN Benjamin
Headline: The nation’s audacious 1960s rocket programme was met with ridicule. Now, more than 60 years on, this curious episode is inspiring film-makers, playwrights and a circus show at the fringe
Content: Moonage daydream … the cast of Astronauts.Photograph: Circus Zambia & Wake The BeastView image in fullscreenMoonage daydream … the cast of Astronauts.Photograph: Circus Zambia & Wake The BeastEdinburgh festival 2026‘It’s a Pan-African story’: the artists telling the amazing true tale of Zambia’s mission to reach spaceThe nation’s audacious 1960s rocket programme was met with ridicule. Now, more than 60 years on, this curious episode is inspiring film-makers, playwrights and a circus show at the fringeExplore the rest of our Edinburgh festival 2026 coverageJN BenjaminFri 7 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn February 1960, Harold Macmillan, the UK’s Conservative prime minister, gave his seminal “wind of change” address to the Parliament of South Africa in Cape Town, announcing the end of the age of colonial rule on the African continent. He had given the same speech in Ghana a month earlier but the South Africa speech received significantly more press attention because of its perceived confrontation with the apartheid regime. The speech began a chain reaction: four years later, the British Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland was dissolved, establishing a newly independentZambia.Amid the hopeful energy of the nation’s birth emerged Edward Mukuka Nkoloso, the father of the Zambia National Academy of Science, Space Research and Philosophy, with an announcement that the young country would officially join the space race.Many thought this was a bizarre move – the competition for space primacy was originally part of a rivalry between the cold war superpowers. But now Zambia, in its infancy and without a fully functioning government, was not only set to join them; Nkoloso vowed to beat them into space and on to the moon. He was roundly ridiculed from all angles. Western media commentary took a particularly savage tone, calling the group “a bunch of crackpots”.View image in fullscreenLift off … A scene from Circus Zambia and Wake the Beast’s Afronauts.Photograph: Meshach/Circus Zambia & Wake the BeastIn his 1965 book, The New Unhappy Lords, the far-right British journalist AK Chesterton used the Zambian space programme as “proof of the absurdity in the idea that Africans should be ready for self-rule”.But Nkoloso was undeterred. He wrote an op-ed titled We’re Going to Mars! With a Spacegirl, Two Cats and a Missionary, asked Unesco for a £7m grant, and continued work on his mission with 12 young men and women handpicked for his training programme. The curriculum was mostly delivered on a remote farm a few miles outside the capital city, Lusaka. It included swinging the “Afronauts”, as they were so named, on ropes that were then cut as they reached their height, dunking them in rivers, and rolling them down hills in barrels.double quotation markNkoloso’s space project is a vehicle to imagine beyond traditionally western conceptions of what the future could look likeThere were at least some scientific principles behind the exercises: the rolling barrels had an effect similar to being in a centrifuge; the rope cutting was a crash course in freefalling, and the river dunks simulated a splashdown. “Some people think I’m crazy, but I’ll be laughing the day I plant Zambia’s flag on the moon,” Nkoloso told reporters.The space programme never did take off. Nkoloso’s application for funding from Unesco was unsuccessful and further requests for money from countries including Israel, the Soviet Union, the United States and the (then called) United Arab Republic went unanswered. Without financial resources, the idea was unsustainable. The negative press attention also affected morale – it was reported at the time that some of the trainees went on a drinking spree and never returned; 17-year-old Matha Mwambwa – Nkoloso’s most promising recruit – became pregnant and returned home to raise the baby. The Zambian government formally distanced itself from the mission and the programme was eventually quietly abandoned, with Nkoloso pivoting to a career in politics.View image in fullscreenAstro-futurism … Circus Zambia and Wake the Beast’s Afronauts.Photograph: Circus Zambia & Wake The BeastIn the years since, there has been some debate about whether or not the Zambian space mission was a genuine endeavour. In an interview with the Zambian-American writer and academic Namwali Serpell, Kenneth Kaunda – the first Zambian president and a close friend of Nkoloso – laughed when he was asked about the space mission. “It wasn’t a real thing! He wasn’t a scientist … it was more for fun than anything else,” he told her. A common theory is that Nkoloso was satirising the absurdity of the United States and Soviet Union spending billions of dollars to go to space when the money could have been better used to solve problems on Earth. He probably knew he couldn’t compete and his aim was actually to get the world talking about Zambia.Whatever the truth, it is clear that Nkoloso’s endeavours have made a significant impact on Zambia’s space exploration ambitions. Last year, the African Union formed the African Space Agency, with Zambia part of the group representing the south. And in 2024, the country completed a significant milestone in its journey to space by installing its first ground-receiving station. Nkoloso died in 1989, but the country is on its way to achieving his dream.Despite its downfall, the Zambian space programme continues to influence artists the world over, particularly in the past decade or so. One of the most well-known interpretations of the Afronauts story is the science fiction short film of that name by Ghanaian film-maker Nuotama Frances Bodomo, which premiered at the Sundance film festival in 2014. “I feel very connected to it as a Ghanaian,” says Bodomo. “Edward Nkoloso’s story is a Ghanaian one too. He’s of the generation of soldiers who went abroad to fight in the second world war for the British army, being promised land back, and when he returned he didn’t get those things – that’s also my grandfather’s story. It’s a Pan-African story of that time.”View image in fullscreenUp in the air … Circus Zambia and Wake the Beast’s Afronauts.Photograph: Meshach/Circus Zambia & Wake the BeastMore recently, Company Christoph Winkler, a Germany-based dance theatre ensemble, produced a two-part short film series, respectively titled We’re Going to Mars and We’ll Unite the Galaxies. Filmed in Uganda and the US in 2021, part one celebrates the spirit of optimism that fuelled the space programme, while the follow-up imagines blackness unbound from a single planet, let alone a single continent, through a fever dream of space travel.The fascination with the mission continues later this year as writer Ryan Calais Cameron teams up with director Monique Touko to deliver a “true-ish” take on the nation’s defiant dream. Their production,The Afronauts, has its UK premiere at west London’s Royal Court in November.double quotation markI was excited to find a story that is Zambian. It felt just like raw materialAll these works use Nkoloso’s vision of space exploration as a way to imagine beyond traditional western conceptions of what the future could look like, repositioning black Africans as leaders and trailblazers. In many ways, Nkoloso was an early – though perhaps largely forgotten – pioneer of Afrofuturism, a term coined in the 90s by cultural critic Mark Dery.While there has been considerable attention from outside the country, it’s clear that these historic events mean a great deal to Zambians too. This month, Circus Zambia, a Lusaka-based social enterprise that offers circus- and life-skills training to young people from marginalised backgrounds, brings its showAfronautsto the Underbelly at Edinburgh festival fringe. The production is a collaboration with UK-based theatre company Wake the Beast, co-founded by the Irish theatre-maker Adam McGuigan, and combines aerials, juggling and partner acrobatics to share this epic piece of African history.View image in fullscreenParallel universe … Circus Zambia and Wake the Beast’s Afronauts.Photograph: Circus Zambia & Wake the BeastThe partnership between the two companies goes back many years. McGuigan – who previously lived in Zambia for a decade and still regularly works within the country’s theatre industry – also co-founded BarefeetTheatre, a cultural movement that seeks to empower vulnerable children living on the streets of Lusaka through theatre workshops. It was through this programme that he met a young Gift Chansa, who would go from service user to facilitator at Barefeet, and eventually go on to co-create Circus Zambia. The two of them co-direct the Underbelly production, which also appeared at the UK’s Wilderness and Latitude festivals in July.“We started working on the show in 2019 and were planning to bring it to Edinburgh that year, then Covid came,” Chansa tells me over Zoom during a break from rehearsals last month. Before that, most of its shows were adaptations of well-known western works such as West Side Story and The Emperor’s New Clothes. “I was excited I found something that is Zambian,” he says. “It felt just like raw material, nobody had done a theatre production of it at that time. We are Zambians who are pushing the Zambian narrative with something that feels authentically Zambian – made for Zambia, by Zambia. We call that Zambia Ku Chalo.” A saying that literally translates as “Zambia to the world”.Circus Zambia performsAfronautsat the Underbelly, Edinburgh, to31 August;touring the UK and Ireland, 4 to 12 September,with the support of the Irish embassy, Lusaka, Zambia;tour starts Liverpool.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreEdinburgh festivalPerformance artZambiafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Not afraid of controversy’: Edinburgh fringe rejects calls to cancel Amanda Knox comedy | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Festival organisers defend show after criticism from sister of Meredith Kercher, Knox’s murdered former flatmate
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Festival organisers defend show after criticism from sister of Meredith Kercher, Knox’s murdered former flatmate
Content: Amanda Knox said a petition against Cartwheel  contained ‘many false assumptions and completely mischaracterises the show’.Photograph: Matt Licari/APView image in fullscreenAmanda Knox said a petition against Cartwheel  contained ‘many false assumptions and completely mischaracterises the show’.Photograph: Matt Licari/APEdinburgh festival 2026‘Not afraid of controversy’: Edinburgh fringe rejects calls to cancel Amanda Knox comedyFestival organisers defend show after criticism from sister of Meredith Kercher, Knox’s murdered former flatmateCaroline DaviesandNadia KhomamiFri 7 Aug 2026 09.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Edinburgh festival fringe has said it is “not afraid of controversy” after it faced calls to cancel a sold-out show byAmanda Knox, who was wrongfully convicted for the 2007 murder of her flatmate Meredith Kercher in Italy.Knox’s comedy show, Cartwheel, has been condemned by Kercher’s family, with her sister, Stephanie, saying it “normalises and trivialises violence against women”. Apetitioncalling for it to be cancelled has been signed by more than 9,000 people.Knox, from Seattle in the US, and her then Italian boyfriend, Raffaele Sollecito, were convicted in 2009 for the murder and sexual assault of Kercher, a British foreign exchange student living in Perugia. They maintained their innocence and, after years of legal battles, were acquitted by Italy’s highest court in 2015.In a statement posted on Instagram, Knox, 39, said of the petition: “Cartwheel is a show about motherhood, raising a daughter in a world that is unfair and dangerous for women, and what it costs to be the kind of mother who tells her the truth about that. Neither the author of this petition nor anyone who signed it has seen Cartwheel.”View image in fullscreenA poster advertising Knox’s show in Edinburgh.Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty ImagesKnox, now a married mother of two, said the petition contained “many false assumptions and completely mischaracterises the show”. She added: “Cartwheel honours Meredith Kercher’s memory and calls out the violence that was done to her and to me.”Knox has previously said the show did not “joke about Meredith’s death”.Cartwheel is a reference to a story that alleged Knox did cartwheels in the police station after Kercher’s death.Tony Lankester, the director of theFringe Society, told BBC Radio Scotland: “We’re not afraid of controversy. The decision as to whether or not [the show] goes ahead lies with herself and it lies with the venue.”He added: “As sympathetic as we are to individual cases that crop up, and absolutely as a parent I can relate to the pain that they describe, but that can’t be a criteria, it can’t be one of the lenses that we look through.”Gilded Balloon Teviot, the show’s venue, said in a statement: “TheEdinburgh festivalfringe is an open-access festival. As a fringe venue, we provide a platform for a wide range of voices, in line with the fringe’s longstanding commitment to freedom of expression (within the confines of the law) and ensure our audiences can make informed choices.View image in fullscreenMeredith Kercher was murdered in 2007 in Perugia, Italy.Photograph: PA“Artists and companies choose to participate at our venue and take on the financial and creative responsibility for their work. Amanda’s show is a one-woman piece exploring themes of motherhood, presented independently by her.”Stephanie Kerchertold BBC Breakfastthat Knox was “naturally free to continue with her life as she wishes, but I think the problem with this particular project is that it is comedy”.“And whilst I appreciate comedy is there to push the boundaries … it very much normalises and trivialises violence against women and Meredith in particular.”Rudy Hermann Guede wasconvicted of Kercher’s murder in 2008. He was released from prison in 2021 after serving 13 years of a 16-year term.Claire Cochrane, a professor emeritus of theatre studies at the University of Worcester, said: “What happened to both Meredith Kercher andAmanda Knoxwas dreadful and of course I understand the Kercher family’s continuing grief.“However, vociferous campaigns mounted against artistic product based on unexamined assumptions about content and motivation undermines genuine attempts to deal with the personal legacies of violence and tragedy.“Comedy thoughtfully deployed can be both cathartic and therapeutic. I’m not going to be able to see Knox’s performance inEdinburgh. But I think it should go ahead and be properly and thoughtfully scrutinised.”Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Amanda KnoxMeredith KercherEdinburgh festivalFringe theatreFestivalsTheatrenewsShareReuse this content

title: Sam Neill filmed role in Legend of Zelda film adaptation before his death  | Movies | The Guardian
description: The New Zealand actor, who died last month aged 78, will appear in live-action movie of popular video game, which is set for release next year
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: The New Zealand actor, who died last month aged 78, will appear in live-action movie of popular video game, which is set for release next year
Content: The King of Hyrule? Sam Neill pictured in 2016.Photograph: Variety/Penske Media/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe King of Hyrule? Sam Neill pictured in 2016.Photograph: Variety/Penske Media/Getty ImagesMoviesSam Neill filmed role in Legend of Zelda film adaptation before his deathThe New Zealand actor, who died last month aged 78, will appear in live-action movie of popular video game, which is set for release next yearLaurence PhelanFri 7 Aug 2026 09.57 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe New Zealand actor Sam Neill completed filming of a role in the forthcoming adaptation ofThe Legend of Zeldavideo game before he died, which will be one of his final screen appearances.According toa report in Deadline, Neill, whodied of pneumonia last month aged 78, will appear in the live-action movie, which finished filming in April this year and is set for release next May. Which role Neill plays has not been announced, but fans of the games have suggested that he would be a good casting choice for the King of Hyrule, the fictional fantasy realm in which the Zelda games are primarily set.Neill had also filmed parts in Godzilla x Kong: Supernova, which is scheduled for release in next March, and The Last Resort, a romcom in which he plays the father of the female lead, Daisy Ridley, also scheduled for release next year.Sam Neill obituaryRead moreSince the original Legend of Zelda game was published by Nintendo in 1986,more than 20 titlesin the main series have been released, along with various spin-offs and remakes. An estimated 170-190m copies have been sold, making it Nintendo’s most popular franchise after the Super Mario Brothers and Pokémon series. There have already been manga adaptations and an animated TV show based on Zelda, but the forthcoming production will be the first film adaptation.Two English actors, Benjamin Evan Ainsworth and Bo Bragason, play the lead roles of Link and Princess Zelda. The film is directed by Wes Ball, who is also responsible for the YA Maze Runner trilogy and, most recently, Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes.Neill had an extensive and varied career in film and television spanning five decades, but was especially loved for his work in horror and fantasy cinema, including Possession, Omen III, In the Mouth of Madness and three Jurassic Park films.Explore more on these topicsFilmSam NeillScience fiction and fantasy filmsThe Legend of ZeldaNintendoGamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alley Cats review – the genital jokes in Ricky Gervais’s sweary cartoon are just exhausting | Television | The Guardian
description: There are glimmers of potential in this comedy about a potty-mouthed feline gang. But not even the great voice cast or a cute kitten can save it from being lazy, crude and boring
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: There are glimmers of potential in this comedy about a potty-mouthed feline gang. But not even the great voice cast or a cute kitten can save it from being lazy, crude and boring
Content: Animal edgelord … David Earl as Puke in Alley Cats. Cr. Courtesy of Netflix © 2026Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenAnimal edgelord … David Earl as Puke in Alley Cats. Cr. Courtesy of Netflix © 2026Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixTV reviewTelevisionReviewAlley Cats review – the genital jokes in Ricky Gervais’s sweary cartoon are just exhaustingThere are glimmers of potential in this comedy about a potty-mouthed feline gang. But not even the great voice cast or a cute kitten can save it from being  lazy, crude and boringLucy ManganFri 7 Aug 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsuppose the question is really: what do you do after redefining comedy for your era? After The Office, that exquisitely observed, agonising, heartbreaking, hilarious examination of the human condition co-created with Stephen Merchant,Ricky Gervaismanaged Extras – off-peak but still great – and then continued a downward trajectory that his latest offering, Alley Cats, does nothing to arrest.You can see what the six-episode animated series about a gang of homeless cats wants to be. It wants to be an exquisitely observed, agonising, heartbreaking, hilarious examination of the human condition. But it can’t be bothered. Easier by far, especially as it’s on Netflix and unshackled from mainstream broadcasters’ rules about swearing, to call everyone a C-word and sigh at the inevitability/sweet release of death every five minutes. Nihilism – gotcha! So dark, man, so edgy!Gervais plays Gus, the corpulent, complacent (“I’m probably the best cat in the neighbourhood”) misanthropy-maxxing leader of the ragtag group. His right-hand man, Fang (Andrew Brooke) is the gang’s bruiser and not much beyond that and Puke (David Earl) is the disgusting one, providing the lads with all the material they require about anal sex, fingering and the varying states in which genitals can be found. A regular visitor to their squat is the cat they call “Ponce” (Tom Basden) – real name Rupert (of course) – who is a pedigree, lives with a family, enjoys regular meals, brushing and puddings (“You fucking ponce!”). He has also, of course, been neutered, which fills in the joke-gaps left when the anal sex/fingering/genitals stuff runs out. Ponce himself remains unbothered by his testicular lack. “They cloud the judgment,” he explains serenely, in one of the handful of lines that could raise a smile rather than a weary checking of how long is left.But, for now, we’re in the dark alley with these cats, plus the girl who lives upstairs – Olive (Diane Morgan), who is, Gus notes with glee, really thick. In a further sign of the laziness of the whole endeavour, though, she’s not. After a few token tries to establish her as such, she simply becomes a perfectly ordinary cat (it would also, it seems, have been too much effort even to make her a smart cat they only think is stupid), with a bit of a thing for Ponce until she finds out he doesn’t have the urge or the equipment to provide her with the kittens she wants.Into the mix is brought a lost kitten, Kitten (Jo Hartley), who – I am sorry to tell you – awakens fatherly instincts in Gus and begins to teach him and the rest of the gang about love and what it means to be a family. Gervais the sentimentalist is always a far more unnerving proposition than Gervais the misanthrope, so you are best advised to approach Kitten’s scenes with the utmost caution. There are several in which Gus has to comfort Kitten, who has not yet mastered the cool nihilism thing, about the fact of death. “I don’t want to not exist. I want to live for ever!”, says Kitten. Gus replies – and I think here we are aiming for “tenderly and awkwardly” – that although a cat may no longer be around physically, he “lives on in the memories of friends and family”. Kitten brightens. “So you’ll live on through all the things you’ve taught me!” And lo, Gus himself is comforted. The viewer – for whom this is an entirely unearned attempt at an emotional beat because Gus has not yet taught Kitten a single, solitary thing – is not.On we go, through an equally unmoving death of Gus’s mother, innumerable diatribes about obvious targets like spiders (“Maybe it’s the eight fucking legs and10 fucking eyes the cunts have got!” “Fucking shit creatures, mate!”), lengthy descriptions of Puke’s baroque proclivities that are usually a way of Gervais trying to engineer some kind of controversy (one involves Aids monkey rape that I’m honestly too tired to detail further).There are a handful of moments in which you can see, maybe, what might have been. Gus in front of his love interest Lara (Kerry Godliman) has echoes of David Brent’s eternal vulnerability and evokes memories of Gervais’s talent for a kind of compassionate skewering of male frailties. Ponce provides some moments of relative subtlety (“And where is that in the league tables?” he enquires politely after Gus and Fang’s lauding of the university of life. “Quite low, I’d imagine”) and some shelter from the hail of uninventive swears and pointless rants. But otherwise Alley Cats feels like a creative cul de sac, leaving you not consumed by laughter but the wish that Gervais could stop indulging himself in lesser projects, go away, rest up and let his genius ferment once more, however long it takes. Author: Hollie Richardson
