Content: Easy laughs … Marvin Flute in Grimsburg on Sky One.Photograph: Fox MediaView image in fullscreenEasy laughs … Marvin Flute in Grimsburg on Sky One.Photograph: Fox MediaTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Jon Hamm’s offbeat adult animation lands in the UKThe star voices a maverick cop in new cartoon Grimsburg. Plus: the finale of Scottish crime drama Granite Harbour. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Graeme Virtue,Priya Elan,Jack SealeandEllen E JonesFri 7 Aug 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGrimsburg10.15pm, Sky OneA triple bill of this adult cartoon starring Jon Hamm, which quietly debuted in the UK last week. Hamm plays police detective Marvin Flute, who has moved back to his home town to reconnect with his family and continue solving bizarre crimes. This time, there are easy laughs to be had as he finds himself accused of murdering a judge and tries to clear his own name.Hollie RichardsonView image in fullscreenRomario Simpson in Granite Harbour.Photograph: LA Productions/BBC ScotlandGranite Harbour8pm, BBC OneThe Scottish cop drama wraps up its third series with youthful duo DS Bartlett and DC Lindo determined to untangle the motives behind a teenage girl’s murder on a country estate. But with their prime suspect dead and the special police investigations service scrutinising their conduct, it won’t be easy.Graeme VirtueSurgery Secrets of the Super Rich8pm, Channel 4Do we all live inside the “circle of shame” now? In this chillingly dystopian testament to beauty standards, Hannah is celebrating her engagement with a “bridal package” of treatments for her big day. These include inserting threads in her cheeks and up her nose for a liquid rhinoplasty. All for a cool £3k. Congratulations!Priya ElanCorsica: Jewel of the Mediterranean8pm, Channel 5Joanna Lumley’s velvety tones narrate this look at the good life in Corsica, an island off the south coast of France. We meet a banker turned baker who makes irresistible biscuits, and a university lecturer who is also a chestnut farmer. Plus, the citadel gets a facelift.HRBergerac9pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenAlluring … Damien Molony in Bergerac.Photograph: BBC/UKTV/Joss BarrattDamien Molony is an alluringly unstable and impassioned detective in this smart reboot of the 1980s Jersey crime drama. This week, Jim Bergerac alarms his colleagues with a manic whiteboard presentation, fuelled by his obsessive desire to bring down supercilious bigwig Arthur Wakefield (Philip Glenister).Jack SealeAnn Droid9.30pm, BBC OneAn endlessly laugh-out-loud episode of the comedy about a widow and her robot carer. Sue (Sue Johnston) invites her son and his girlfriend over for wine and crisps, but she’s still not convinced about them: “Not eating prawn cocktail crisps? He’s forgotten who he is.” Meanwhile, unbearable frenemy Phyllis gets bad news.HRFilmThe Last House (Louis Leterrier, 2026), NetflixThe population has been confined indoors because of a little-understood external threat, meaning parents must homeschool their children, supplies are rationed and communication with neighbours can happen only at a distance … sound familiar? The Last House comes on like a Covid lockdown flashback but it’s actually an intriguing sci-fi horror, with a plot reminiscent of 2007 film The Mist. It benefits greatly from the presence of charming leads Wagner Moura (The Secret Agent) and Greta Lee (Past Lives), as a couple forced to extremes for their family’s survival.Ellen E JonesHoard (Luna Carmoon, 2023), 11.05pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenFetid … Joseph Quinn (left) and Saura Lightfoot-Leon in Hoard.Photograph: VertigoIf a film-watching experience can be described as “fetid”, then Hoard is that – but in a good way. Writer and director Luna Carmoon was only 26 when she made her debut feature, announcing herself as a thrillingly distinctive talent in British cinema. Saura Lightfoot Leon stars as Maria, a young, care-experienced woman whose loving but unstable childhood is revealed in the detritus of her chaotic present. Hayley Squires (I, Daniel Blake) plays Maria’s bin-diving, hoarder mother and Joseph Quinn (Stranger Things) is her foster brother turned love interest.EEJLive sportEFL Cup: Middlesbrough v Wrexham, 7.30pm, ITV1The first-round tie at the RiversideExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightAnimation on TVTravel TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Now, Autonomy by Max Easton review – a sardonic yet compassionate take on millennial apathy | Fiction | The Guardian
description: The author’s third novel to chronicle life in Sydney’s west follows a group of flawed friends trying to sustain meaning amid an ‘erosion in the world’
Author: Jack Callil
Headline: The author’s third novel to chronicle life in Sydney’s west follows a group of flawed friends trying to sustain meaning amid an ‘erosion in the world’
Content: Max Easton and his latest book Now, Autonomy.Composite: Lauren Eiko/GiramondoView image in fullscreenMax Easton and his latest book Now, Autonomy.Composite: Lauren Eiko/GiramondoAustralian book reviewsFictionReviewNow, Autonomy by Max Easton review – a sardonic yet compassionate take on millennial apathyThe author’s third novel to chronicle life in Sydney’s west follows a group of flawed friends trying to sustain meaning amid an ‘erosion in the world’Supported byAbout this contentJack CallilThu 6 Aug 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 02.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf any part of Australia can lay claim to being the country’s literary nexus, it is westernSydney. The wide wing of suburbia is both home to and the subject of granular attention for an ever-growing list of acclaimed writers: Yumna Kassab, Peter Polites, Luke Carman, Michael Mohammed Ahmad, Felicity Castagna – to name just a few. Each of them reflects a culturally diverse landscape in which social class and suburban identity are forever intersecting, animating the lives of those often neglected in the margins of Australia’s projected self-image.A key figure in this discourse is Max Easton, whose latest novel – Now, Autonomy – is the third instalment of his multi-decade series that chronicles working-class struggle and its subcultural undercurrents in Sydney’s west. Beginning with the Miles Franklin-longlistedThe Magpie Wingin 2021, and followed byParadise Estatein 2023, this ambitious, compelling quasi-trilogy – each title can be read and appreciated on its own – depicts people navigating Australia’s class hierarchies, hyper-gentrification, rental housing pressures and ever-diminishing spaces for community and collective activism.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Magpie Wing by Max Easton review – a bleak, exceptional portrait of millennial flailingRead moreWe continue as Easton started, thrown into an ecosystem of progressively minded, albeit flawed, friends trying to sustain a meaningful existence. The shrewd Helen Coleman, who started as a teenager in The Magpie Wing, is now in her late 30s. Among her friends these days is her reclusive flatmate Pat, a middle-aged sound guy who can’t seem to shake the past; her off-kilter former housemate Sunny, whose restlessness for radical change is as irksome as it is imperative; Sunny’s partner, Sio, the only one of them with a somewhat put-together life; and Helen’s partner, Maria, who is caring yet increasingly despondent amid the holding pattern of their relationship.Everyone is varyingly disillusioned and struggling to reorient themselves while fending off financial insecurity, creative inertia and interpersonal disaffection. Helen senses an “erosion in the world”: Israel’s genocide in Gaza continues unabated despite global protest, the economic gulfs of the 21st century are becoming yawning chasms and the commodification of artistic expression is even infecting the DIY scenes that sprang up in opposition to it. Collectively, there is a psychic strain: everyone cares for each other but is also exhausted by the emotional labour; everyone is quick to speculate about other people’s problems yet uninterested in addressing their own.Paradise Estate by Max Easton review – a layered, aching portrait of millennial malaiseRead moreWhen not numbed before this “great defeat”, the gang seek to reorient themselves around a sense of agency and purpose. Reclamation of autonomy – personal and collective – is the novel’s focal point, as is the tension in doing so meaningfully. When everyone haphazardly tries to set up a new music venue called The Quarterly, it’s unclear how much it’s really to save “Sydney from itself” or themselves from the void. When that ambition is cut short and as fragments of Pat’s activist history are unearthed, a more radical project emerges. But what is really motivating each person? And is being part of an insignificant attempt at change itself still significant?Now, Autonomy may sound like a jaded novel – but though it holds a mirror to cynicism, it is far from cynical itself. Indeed, it is a deeply compassionate work, more interested in diagnosing the causes of apathy than deriding it. As Eastonhas said, a driving motivation for him has been to address his fellow millennials who “bemoan the city and cultural milieu we’ve been handed without realising we’re not providing much more to those who come after us”. His writing is acerbic and sardonically funny while reflecting this, and is palpably alive to the strains of contemporary life while striving to give a voice to the means of resistance.In a similar vein to what Emmett Stinsonpointed outin The Magpie Wing, there are occasions in Now, Autonomy when Easton overtly expounds a point, as if intent on eschewing subtext. For example, when Pat is describing a certain condemned building to Sunny: “Everything is rotting in there. I dunno, I guess everything’s rotting now. The only things doing well are the things that feed on rot. Real estate. Banks. Internet.” Message received. Whether intentional or not, amid what is otherwise a novel of richly rendered place and nuanced characters, these moments at best flatten things and at worst dislodge you from the narrative.But as a whole, Easton’s newest addition to his remarkable tapestry of western Sydney is tantalisingly alive. It is an ode to people who reach towards change – even in ways conceited or delusional – as they struggle to get by in a world increasingly resistant to accommodating them. You fall effortlessly into their lives and find yourself in them. For that Now, Autonomy should be applauded.Now, Autonomy by Max Eastonis out now (Giramondo, A$32.95)Explore more on these topicsFictionAustralian book reviewsAustralian booksSydneyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The best recent science fiction, fantasy and horror – review roundup | Science fiction books | The Guardian
description: The Salt Kingby Natasha Pulley; A Trade of Blood by Robert Jackson Bennett; Netherwood by Jake Arnott; Fawn by CN Vair
Author: Lisa Tuttle
Headline: The Salt Kingby Natasha Pulley; A Trade of Blood by Robert Jackson Bennett; Netherwood by Jake Arnott; Fawn by CN Vair
Content: Visions of saltwater in Natasha Pulley’s The Salt King.Photograph: Jose A Bernat Bacete/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVisions of saltwater in Natasha Pulley’s The Salt King.Photograph: Jose A Bernat Bacete/Getty ImagesScience fiction booksThe best recent science fiction, fantasy and horror – review roundupThe Salt King by Natasha Pulley; A Trade of Blood by Robert Jackson Bennett; Netherwood by Jake Arnott; Fawn by CN VairLisa TuttleFri 7 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenThe Salt King byby Natasha Pulley (Gollancz, £22)The latest from the author of The Watchmaker of Filigree Street blends an apocalyptic end-of-the-world tale with folk horror and two slowly developing love stories. Avelyn Brocken is a trainee priest at the Vatican, sent to check out a possible miracle in the fens of East Anglia. His only qualification for the job is that he was born and raised in Hreodwater, a strange community based around a salt mine with its own language, religion and rituals. But what begins in Hreodwater, involving the mysterious salt light and a sleeping king deep in the mine, threatens civilisations. An original, rich and gripping tale that’s also an interesting exploration of the power of faith.View image in fullscreenA Trade of Bloodby Robert Jackson Bennett (Hodderscape, £25)A new case for Ana and Din, the crime-solving team introduced in the Hugo and World Fantasy award-winning novel The Tainted Cup, focuses on a murder among the cattle-ranching gentry of the Empire of Khanum. The murderer has been caught red-handed, unable to remember what happened. The victim was his lover, and their families were enemies; he is the last of his line, and fears his family is cursed. The detectives suspect a more material and dangerous adversary behind the scenes, with access to a terrifying weapon. This is the sort of other-world fantasy with close ties to speculative fiction, based on natural laws and science rather than any magical system, and some of the issues it raises are of immediate concern in today’s world of shrinking resources. Great world-building and a masterfully conceived mystery make for a compelling cross-genre blend.View image in fullscreenNetherwoodby Jake Arnott(Titan, £18.99)London is too expensive, so artist Adam and his partner Justine buy a house in Hastings. The room at the top will make the perfect studio for Adam, whose career has stalled after drink, drugs and quarrels. They’re intrigued by the property’s “special feature” – a cave hidden behind a locked door in the back wall. After they move in they discover a Latin phrase carved into the wall, layers of candle wax, a mysterious sealed bottle: evidence of occult rituals? It turns out the previous owner was a devotee of chaos magic, inspired by the notorious Aleister Crowley, who died in a Hastings boarding house called Netherwood. Justine fears they could be in danger, sensing the ghostly presence of a frightened girl, but at the same time, their new home is inspiring Adam to create his most powerful paintings, winning back the support of his agent and the promise of big money. A wonderfully unnerving, evocative horror in which Hastings looms large as the most uncanny place in England.Fawnby CN Vair (3AM, £20)This debut begins with deceptive gentleness, introducing the reader to Tess, a witch in present-day America who sold her soul to the devil in 1935, the price for surviving a murderous attack. She hardly seems to have aged, but is careful to keep the locals from noticing, using spells to turn unwanted attention away and keep herself and her animal sanctuary safe. Things start to go wrong when she rescues a fawn, born at the wrong time of year with teeth and a thirst for blood. She ignores advice to put it down, but when the local cop insists it must be destroyed, and a new preacher arrives in town, seeming to turn her friends against her, she struggles to maintain control. Just when she needs them most, the old spells are failing her. Like a newborn fawn, she’s doomed to be seen as prey. Tess refuses to accept defeat, on any level; she will do whatever it takes to survive in this disturbing, seductively written fiction about power and female rage.Explore more on these topicsScience fiction booksFantasy booksFictionHorror booksShareReuse this content

title: The Last House review – post-Covid apocalyptic lockdown thriller is a solid night in | Science fiction and fantasy films | The Guardian
description: Oscar nominee Wagner Moura and Greta Lee lead Netflix’s sci-fi tale of a family trapped in their house as something sinister arrives
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Oscar nominee Wagner Moura and Greta Lee lead Netflix’s sci-fi tale of a family trapped in their house as something sinister arrives
Content: Noah Alexander Sosnowski, Wagner Moura, Greta Lee and Riley Chung in The Last House.Photograph: Netflix/PAView image in fullscreenNoah Alexander Sosnowski, Wagner Moura, Greta Lee and Riley Chung in The Last House.Photograph: Netflix/PAScience fiction and fantasy filmsReviewThe Last House review – post-Covid apocalyptic lockdown thriller is a solid night inOscar nominee Wagner Moura and Greta Lee lead Netflix’s sci-fi tale of a family trapped in their house as something sinister arrivesBenjamin LeeFri 7 Aug 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost of us aren’t truly ready for films that directly cover the recent horrors of Covid and, well, why would we be? There was a need back in 2021 for something strict and journalistic like Matthew Heineman’s excellent documentaryThe First Waveand there have been other variously illuminating docs since, but it’s been tough for narrative storytellers to address and confront – and even tougher for audiences to engage. It’s partly why Ari Aster’s intermittently excellent 2020-set satireEddingtonfizzled at the box office, released five years after the pandemic began but still five years too soon.One Night Only review – sex is legal for 12 hours a year in bizarre romcomRead moreThe most effective ways in have usually been through the back door. Mike Leigh’s 2024 dramaHard Truthsmight have only mentioned the pandemic once and included just one mask but its portrait of a psychologically fractured, permanently on-edge woman, terrified of what lies outside her chillingly sterile house, was very much about the difficult after-effects of the disease. Next week sees the release ofThe End of Oak Street, an 80s-set fantasy adventure about a family trying to survive a prehistoric invasion from the safety of their own home and this week, sneaked out by Netflix just days before is The Last House, another high-concept genre tale that sees homes across the world locked off from the outside as something terrifying attacks.We’re focused on just one home, inhabited by a financially struggling Seattle family (although the film is clearly shot in the UK, note the extremely British brickwork), living on an average suburban street. A torrential pre-Christmas downpour brings with it a nasty twist: the rain has somehow forced everyone inside, some sort of mysterious sealant adding magical power to the water. Jason (Wagner Moura, fresh off his recent Oscar nomination) and Riley (Greta Lee) and their two children must figure out the initial, milder concerns – where will the dog shit and without wifi, what DVDs do we have left? – before days turn into months and eventually even longer (something spoiled byan over-eager trailer).There’s a satisfying and relatable itch being scratched in the lighter moments of early makeshift togetherness, that familiarly cosy process of making do with what we have and, in this case, also forcing a family away from their devices, but grimness is never far away. Elderly neighbours stop appearing at their windows, food becomes harder to eke out and, in a rather shocking chain of events likely to traumatise a certain sensitive subset of viewers, extreme measures are taken when the dog’s medication runs out. Then there’s the matter of what’s outside.The film works best when sticking to a more grounded survival thriller, mum preserving and reusing food waste while dad’s skills as both engineer and fisherman lead to a nifty sequence of using the oddly un-blocked chimney to hunt (even in the apocalypse, gender roles persist!). As teased by what happens to the family pet, there’s also a willingness to embrace the horrible reality of the situation as resources dwindle and mental health starts to disintegrate (as the son threatens to go full We Need to Talk About Kevin, any conservative notion that the film is suggesting family is all we need is swiftly binned). It’s less successful when it becomes a gloopier sci-fi horror, juicy big questions fumbled with unsatisfying and underwritten answers. There’s something Shyamalan-adjacent about so much of the intriguing set-up but the film gradually switches from skirting the highs of Signs to, almost, reaching the lows of The Happening (what if … nature?) with a sloppy and disappointingly un-twisty last act. Like so many buzzy genre movies, the initial pull of the pitch is left a little dampened by the half-assed follow-through and writer Matthew Robinson’s dialogue is frequently a little too neat and trailer-packaged to rise above cliche (“What do we do?” “We survive” is uttered within mere seconds of “Are monsters real?” “They are now”).While there’s an above-average sheen to so much of it (Louis Leterrier, the director, is more familiar with studio over streaming fare having made Clash of the Titans, The Incredible Hulk and Now You See Me), for a film that eventually most resembles A Quiet Place, the creature design is immediately unmemorable and entirely unscary while the editing of a theoretically ambitious last set – piece is far too scrappy to push us to the edge. Moura keeps us onboard with some confident leading man command but a rather unconvincing Lee remains unsteady and either goes too small or too big, admittedly left stranded by a script that gives her a character with very little distinction. For two actors more recently associated with weightier material, there are worse paycheque roles to take and, for a platform that often struggles to produce convincing mockbusters, far worse recent examples (it ranks above their recentdodgy Pixar rip-offandeven dodgier Crawl rip-off). It does in many ways represent the ideal of a Netflix Friday night movie, not good enough to warrant a bigger screen but, if stuck at home for reasons supernatural or not, just about good enough for a low-stakes click.The Last House is now available on NetflixExplore more on these topicsScience fiction and fantasy filmsNetflixHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Cats review – it’s a jellicle jumble as Andrew Lloyd Webber’s moggies get the zoomies | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Macavity and co are back, with the balance in Drew McOnie’s stylish revival tipped in favour of dance and acrobatics over storytelling
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Macavity and co are back, with the balance in Drew McOnie’s stylish revival tipped in favour of dance and acrobatics over storytelling
Content: Glimmering and glittering … Melanie La Barrie and the cast of Cats.Photograph: Mark SeniorView image in fullscreenGlimmering and glittering … Melanie La Barrie and the cast of Cats.Photograph: Mark SeniorTheatreReviewCats review – it’s a jellicle jumble as Andrew Lloyd Webber’s moggies get the zoomiesRegent’s Park Open Air theatre, LondonMacavity and co are back, with the balance in Drew McOnie’s stylish revival tipped in favour of dance and acrobatics over storytellingArifa AkbarFri 7 Aug 2026 10.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndrew Lloyd Webber’s cats are back and they could not inhabit a more feline-friendly space than this lush green corner of Regent’s Park. The trees swish around their nocturnal prowls and the brilliant moon on the steel crescent set shines down on their song and dance. The big cats up the road in London Zoo would surely approve?Up to a point. These animals, directed and newly choreographed by Drew McOnie, are more balletic and graceful than those in the 1981 original and the production definitely reclaims the musical’s reputation fromTom Hooper’s filmwhich many found to be a dog’s dinner (although some of us really didn’t mind it). Sami Fendall’s set glimmers and glitters while her costumes rise from earthy colours to flamboyant leotard and catsuit get-ups.This perky crew don’t just sit and sit like the Old Gumbie Cat, they dance and dance and dance through the flimsy and patchwork story of “Jellicle cats” convening for an annual ball in which one will be reborn for another chance at life. Using TS Eliot’s playful 1939 collection Old Possum’s Book of Practical Cats as its lyrical basis, Lloyd Webber’s musical is only slightly less strange in concept than his singing train carriagesin Starlight Express, also recently revived. As with the poems, the musical is constructed as an introduction to each cat contender in a series of vignettes, which here resemble an elegant feline variety show at times, an old-school film fantasia at others.View image in fullscreenAn elegant feline variety show … The cast of Cats.Photograph: Mark SeniorThat is partly the problem: it is a hodgepodge in style, although always very stylish. The musical’s sung-through nature does not lend itself to cohesive storytelling and the balance here is tipped too much in one direction so it seems like Cats: TheDance, with extended choreographed sequences and circus-like acrobatics. It results in some lovely expressive scenes but makes the structure even more disjointed, with less of a story to bind it.Some of the cats are more characterful than others: Old Deuteronomy (Melanie La Barrie) plods around a little generically, Macavity (Dianté Lodge) is sufficiently mysterious, the criminal duo Mungojerrie (Danny Nattrass) and Rumpleteazer (Briana Craig) come as a classic variety hall double act. The highlight, without doubt, is Rum Tum Tugger with his eponymous song, which Jaydon Vijn sings with the hip-thrusting swagger of a young Mick Jagger, David Bowie and an alley cat on heat, rolled into one. Vijn brings such a lot of (c)attitude and personality that you wish the others could all be a little more Rum Tum.View image in fullscreenUnused comic chops … Gary Wilmot as Gus.Photograph: Mark SeniorGumbie Cat (Charlotte Riby) is endearing when her eponymous number comes up but Gary Wilmot’s comic chops seem redundant for his turn as the old, nostalgic theatrical cat, Gus (why not cast him in a more playful role?). Mr Mistoffelees (Jet Yau) also comes on to showcase some street dance, spinning on his head.Taziva-Faye Katsande, an understudy stepping in as Grizabella, builds to a storming final rendition of Memory, the signature song of the show. Her vocal abilities are faultless but her characterisation is less polished and you are left wondering who Grizabella is, exactly, and what has got her back up.They fall out of character and become a preening, prowling chorus, too much of an ensemble. Some of the movement between cats has a slow, ritualistic quality which verges on corny and slows the pace considerably. By the end, you well and truly know how to address these cats but you would also quite like them to curl up and take a nap now.AtRegent’s Park Open Air theatre, London, until 19 September. Thentouring the UK and Irelanduntil 19 June 2027.Explore more on these topicsTheatreAndrew Lloyd WebberMusicalsDanceTS EliotCatsAnimalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Silence of the Lambs review – Hannibal Lecter’s daring stage outing is a shock to the system | Theatre | The Guardian
description: There are electrifying – and also queasy – moments in this version of the classic 90s horror about the interrogation of a psychotic psychiatrist by an FBI rookie
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: There are electrifying – and also queasy – moments in this version of the classic 90s horror about the interrogation of a psychotic psychiatrist by an FBI rookie
Content: Avoiding the hissy lip-sipping … John Partridge as Hannibal Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenAvoiding the hissy lip-sipping … John Partridge as Hannibal Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs.Photograph: Marc BrennerTheatreReviewThe Silence of the Lambs review – Hannibal Lecter’s daring stage outing is a shock to the systemCurve, LeicesterThere are electrifying – and also queasy – moments in this version of the classic 90s horror about the interrogation of a psychotic psychiatrist by an FBI rookieMark LawsonFri 7 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSoon after the hostile reception of thetheatrical version of Trainspotting, another landmark 1990s movie, The Silence of the Lambs, attempts a similar manoeuvre. In this case, director Nikolai Foster is surely sensible not to turn this source material into a musical. And adapter Gina Gionfriddo is working not from Jonathan Demme’s film but Thomas Harris’s 1988 novel about the dangerous interrogation of psychotic psychiatrist Dr Hannibal Lecter by FBI rookie Clarice Starling for his insight into serial killer Buffalo Bill.The biggest risk of theatricalised movies is that the acting becomes a form of karaoke. Mollie Gallagher, making a confident stage debut in effectively the lead role, echoes Jodie Foster’s Virginia accent and ramps up the pugnacious posture and walk. John Partridge’s Lecter, who is more sonically American than Hopkins’ variation on his Welsh register (the character is actually Lithuanian), avoids the hissy lip-sipping and also injects less charm and culture.Another jeopardy of staged films is that much of a cinema director’s job is moving the camera in, out and around while the frame of a stage is essentially a default wide shot. Nikolai Foster, however, impressively varies the perspective. He creates a sort of split-screen by bracketing the main scene with a silent tableaux of other characters.View image in fullscreenOliver Farnworth (Jack Crawford), Mollie Gallagher (Clarice Starling), Andrew Joshi (Lamar) and Sam Jackson (Buffalo Bill) in The Silence of the Lambs.Photograph: Marc BrennerIn the Lecter-Starling scenes, Howard Hudson’s lighting subtly directs our gaze, encouraging a sort of tight focus. Careful placing of characters also allows a clever approximation of a two character shot.Another moment interrogates the relationship between audiences and the horror stories. The genre-standard autopsy scene feels rawly appalling when played downstage without the protection of a multiplex screen or the camera cutting away from views. The brief touch between the two main characters also electrifies live.But, for all Foster’s imaginative presentation of the action, the content can feel queasy. The Buffalo Bill strand, sometimes more a main than subplot, means that much of the evening consists of watching women stalked and tortured.Gionfriddo is a front-rank dramatist – twice a Pulitzer prize finalist, including for Becky Shaw, a London success – and intelligently addresses this problem. Stressing the pervasive sexism of the 1983 setting, she also, reflecting changes in attitudes across the four decades since novel and film, gives the female victims – neatly differentiated by Lottie Amor – more plot-time and agency. A shocking new line (spoken twice) reflects the devastating calculations a victim may make with the aim of survival.Most daringly, while all versions of the Lecter-Starling narrative have seen it as a sort of love story, the stage version maximises the romantic context, albeit on a scale from warped to desperate. Buffalo Bill targets single women on the dating scene. The status of FBI boss Jack Crawford (Oliver Farnworth) as a recent widower is emphasised and haunts his mentorship of Starling.A risk of such crossovers is that they will encourage streamer searches for the film instead, but it’s a show worth seeing.AtCurve, Leicester, until 15 August. title: Olivia Rodrigo review – crushing riffs and infectious hooks at secret New York show | Olivia Rodrigo | The Guardian
description: Playing to just 1,000 fans, Rodrigo’s pop-up show is a thrillingly intimate showcase of her tour de force talent
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: Playing to just 1,000 fans, Rodrigo’s pop-up show is a thrillingly intimate showcase of her tour de force talent
Content: Olivia Rodrigo performs at Warsaw in Brooklyn, New York, on Thursday.Photograph: Bryan Armen GrahamView image in fullscreenOlivia Rodrigo performs at Warsaw in Brooklyn, New York, on Thursday.Photograph: Bryan Armen GrahamOlivia RodrigoReviewOlivia Rodrigo review – crushing riffs and infectious hooks at secret New York showWarsaw, Brooklyn, New YorkPlaying to just 1,000 fans, Rodrigo’s pop-up show is a thrillingly intimate showcase of her tour de force talentBryan Armen GrahamFri 7 Aug 2026 12.36 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 18.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 10am on Thursday,Olivia Rodrigoannounced in an Instagram post that she would play a concert in Brooklyn later that night. Tickets went on sale at precisely the same moment – for the princely sum of $25 a pop – not through a Ticketmaster presale code or a virtual waiting room or one of the other digital gauntlets numbingly familiar to today’s concertgoer but in-person only from the box office at Warsaw, the century-old Polish community hall turned music venue in Greenpoint.That made admission less a transaction than a delicate equation of geography, endurance and luck. Fans who lived in the neighborhood or happened to be nearby made a beeline to Driggs Avenue where the growing queue – including many “remote workers” cradling slightly ajar MacBooks – curled around the block as the heat index reached toward 100F. People arriving around 11.20am were already being turned away. By 11.40am, the roughly 1,000 wristbands had all been snapped up. Hours later, those fortunate few punters found themselves improbably close to one of the biggest pop stars on the planet. Maybe 90% of life really is showing up.A pressing issue: why are vinyl albums becoming so different from their digital versions?Read moreFourteen months since she put a bow on the Guts era with afestival-stealing Sunday-night headline seton Glastonbury’s Pyramid stage, Rodrigo is performing before barely 1,000 people in a Brooklyn ballroom best known for hosting punk shows and a pierogi bar off stage right. The contraction in scale brings about a sense of whiplash. The 23-year-old’s progression from Disney Channel alumna to generational pop star is by all relevant metrics complete: her third LP,You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love, debuted at No 1 in June with the year’s biggest opening week by a female artist. In a few weeks, she will launch an 86-date world tour that includes a 10-night run at the nearby Barclays Center and concludes in May with 11 shows at London’s O2. Her well-documented gen X bona fides remain intact: only days earlier shehad materialized beside Billy Corganin the rain at Lollapalooza for a spectral rendition of the Smashing Pumpkins’ Thirty-Three, one of a scant few live appearances since the onset of the album cycle.At Warsaw, there are no high-profile guests and nowhere to hide. Rodrigo emerges at 8.20pm in a pink floral minidress with puffed sleeves and a white Peter Pan collar, its prim 1960s silhouette undercut by black knee-high boots. She seems galvanized by the absence of distance, at one pointplucking a phone from a fan’s handsand filming herself from the stage in a thoroughly contemporary bit of crowd work. The result sits somewhere between a tour preview and a basement show, polished but relaxed enough to let a little air in.The lean, hour-long set makes no attempt to miniaturize an arena production while leaving some of her biggest crowd-pleasers on the table (Ballad of a Homeschooled Girl, Vampire, Traitor and Get Him Back! are notably absent tonight). Nine of its 15 songs came from You Seem Pretty Sad, including the opening four-song sequence of Drop Dead, U + Me = <3, Stupid Song and My Way. It is a confident decision to treat the new album as the evening’s premise rather than something to be endured between familiar hits, and it pays off. Bad Idea Right? is the first older song played this evening, but even Drivers License, slotted seventh, feels less like an inevitable centerpiece than another turn in a deliberately plotted sequence.‘It sounds good next to almost anything’: how Choosin’ Texas became the biggest song of the yearRead moreRodrigo’s songs, mostly co-written with longtime collaborator Dan Nigro, repeatedly make the same sharp turns, moving from confessional balladry to pop-punk abrasion, saccharine sweetness to venom, the tear-stained bedroom to the slammed door. In a room this compressed, every swerve felt heightened. The spare performances of Drivers License and Making the Bed draw the audience inward before Maggots for Brains and All-American Bitch snap the tension; later, Less and Expectations clear space for the closing rush of Good 4 U and Deja Vu. Her still-excellent all-female and non-binary band – almost entirely holdovers from the Sour and Guts tours – play with enough kinetic force to make the old ballroom feel smaller, while the spartan staging and clipped transitions keep the emphasis squarely on the tightly composed material.There is no encore, nor much need for one. After 60 minutes, the house lights come up and she is gone as quickly as she’d appeared, leaving behind an exhilarated crowd that had spent the morning earning the right to say they were there. Pop-up concerts are invariably exercises in manufactured scarcity and Thursday’s was no exception, but the performance itself never felt like a promotional stunt. If Glastonbury was a demonstration of Rodrigo’s reach, Warsaw laid bare the charisma and precision beneath the scale.Explore more on these topicsOlivia RodrigoPop and rockBrooklynNew Yorklive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the anxiety-ridden sugar rush of Tiffany Day and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Day’s latest album Halo is all high-energy exhaustion, injected with a crushing electroclash chaos that illuminates her insecurities in bright neon
Author: David Renshaw
Headline: Day’s latest album Halo is all high-energy exhaustion, injected with a crushing electroclash chaos that illuminates her insecurities in bright neon
Content: Breakthrough and burnout … Tiffany Day.Photograph: Ally WeiView image in fullscreenBreakthrough and burnout … Tiffany Day.Photograph: Ally WeiAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the anxiety-ridden sugar rush of Tiffany Day and the week’s best new tracksDay’s latest album Halo is all high-energy exhaustion, injected with a crushing electroclash chaos that illuminates her insecurities in bright neonDavid Renshaw,Ben Beaumont-ThomasandLaura SnapesFri 7 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromLos AngelesRecommendedif you likeSlayyyter, Charli xcx, UnderscoresUp nextHaloout now. UK and Ireland tour starts in DecemberRight now popstar breakthrough and burnout are a hair’s breadth from one another. Enter Tiffany Day, a Wichita-raised artist who first went viral in 2017 when a video of her singing Hallelujah on a school trip blew up online. She spent the subsequent years unsuccessfully chipping away at building on that virality, cycling through acoustic guitar covers and bedroom R&B. Only by channeling her frustrations into this year’s anxiety-ridden sugar rush Halo did Day finally regain her early momentum.Day’s music stands out for its robust balance of giddy hyperpop and frank vulnerability: think of it as the tears-on-the-dancefloor dynamic for the infinite scroll era. Halo opens with Everything I’ve Ever Wanted, a plainspoken ode to the coveted come-up and the dreaded fall-off, in which Day panics about success. “When something good comes crashing into me, it’s like I can’t breathe,” she frets through a smear of Auto-Tune.Halo is high energy but came from a place of exhaustion, with Day concluding that this album would be her last. Past caring about others’ opinions, she injected it with a crushing electroclash chaos that illuminates her insecurities in a bright neon hue. On songs like DoIt4me and Pretty4u she alternates between freaking out in front of the mirror and hiding in the corner at parties, exposing herself further from behind walls of yo-yo synths and hacksaw bass lines. It’s enough to make youthful insecurity feel manageable, or to make you thank god those days are a thing of the past.David RenshawThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenPitying … Coco and Clair Clair.Photograph: Coco & Clair ClairCoco and Clair Clair – One OneIf you loved squirming underSmerz’s withering gaze last year, let your skin prickle to this Atlanta, Georgia duo’s addictive, pitying dismissal of an ungrateful ex, as menace encroaches on their minimalist, stumbling percussion.LSHelen – Dead Shark IIEleven years after Helen’s debut, Liz Harris (AKA Grouper) unexpectedly reforms her dream-pop band. Full of silt, stardust and rumble, Dead Shark II is as good as the genre gets.LSLancer – 2LateAfter his ultra-emotional, 80s-sampling rap tracks Cry and Southpaw this year, the UK vocalist switches up to singing for his synthwave-ballad debut for XL, restless and upset in the choppy wake of a breakup.BBTBlack Bananas – Eddie’s AlbumThe side project from Royal Trux’s raw-voiced vocalist, Jennifer Herrema, is back and on supremely fun form, flexing taut disco-funk behind a beaded curtain of murky lo-fi chillwave production.BBTEden Aurelius – Entre NousThe NYC producer’s beautiful new album of ambient compositions and featherlight dub techno has a milky-sun blend of warm and cool, though its title track adds a touch more heat with a very subtle dancehall pulse.BBTHana Stretton – FromThe lo-fi, blanketed intimacy and the British-Australian songwriter’s heavy, layered vocals suggest peeping under the bed and finding a tiny choir laying in wait, from a new release on Phil Elverum’s label.LSNew Radicals – One Night Only (Break Loose Break Free!)The film it soundtracks, of the same name, looks weird (The Purge … for pre-marital sex?) but the first NR song since 1999 is cause for celebration, with Gregg Alexander’s knack for secular affirmations designed to lure hangdogs out of their holes.LSSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistElectronic musicPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Arun Sood and Angeline Morrison: Donn/Dubh review – British folk giants startlingly transform sacred histories | Music | The Guardian
description:
(Real World)
Leaning on their Hebridean heritage, the duo meld 10th-century Celtic cantos with distortion, dream-pop and post-rock, with shades of Twin Peaks and Boards of Canada
Author: Jude Rogers
Headline: (Real World)Leaning on their Hebridean heritage, the duo meld 10th-century Celtic cantos with distortion, dream-pop and post-rock, with shades of Twin Peaks and Boards of Canada
Content: Full of febrile layers … Angeline Morrison and Arun Sood.Photograph: Clare BaileyView image in fullscreenFull of febrile layers … Angeline Morrison and Arun Sood.Photograph: Clare BaileyFolk album of the monthMusicReviewArun Sood and Angeline Morrison: Donn/Dubh review – British folk giants startlingly transform sacred histories(Real World)Leaning on their Hebridean heritage, the duo meld 10th-century Celtic cantos with distortion, dream-pop and post-rock, with shades of Twin Peaks and Boards of CanadaJude RogersFri 7 Aug 2026 03.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo of Britain’s most exciting folk musicians, both of Hebridean heritage, are behind Donn/Dubh (Black/Brown), an album inspired by Saltair na Rann, a 10th-century Celtic collection of cantos in which sacred history is foretold, and winds are given colours. Angeline Morrison and Arun Sood expand its spectrum of northerly and westerly shades, soldering together traditional Gaelic texts and tunes with distortion, drone, dream-pop and post-rock.The pair have the chops for such a project. Morrison, co-founder of the Black British Folk Collective, has brilliantly brought forgotten Black histories into the folk canon for years, including on 2022’s The Sorrow Songs. That same year, Sood’s Searching Erskine used sonic collage and old recordings to conjure the lives of residents on his grandmother’s abandoned home island of Vallay. Their talents converge around Alastair Smith’s startling production: Morrison’s deep voice, ghostly one moment, lullaby-warm the next, inhabiting soundworlds recalling the shuddering shadows of late-90s Boards of Canada and Unkle.View image in fullscreenArun Sood and Angeline Morrison: Donn/Dubh.But Morrison opens A Rìbhinn a Bheil Cuimhn’ Agad (Young Maiden, Do You Remember?) over a softly played piano, and gentler moments like this anchor the pair’s giddy explorations. So does a 1952 recording of Sood’s uncle psalm-singing on Òran Molaidh (Praising Song), bowed cellos and synths buoying him, before Sood’s rich Scottish voice enters, speaking of a time “before God”.Sweeter moments include Mo Nighean Donn As Bòidhche (My Most Beautiful Brown-Haired Girl), rippling by on shimmering electronics, and Teann A-nall Mo Chailin Donn (Come Here, My Brown-Haired Maid), setting a Uist love song against gauzy, Twin Peaks-worthy walls of synthesisers. The album’s darker turns are powerful: Tha Mi Sgìth (Fairy Song) twists Sood’s daughters’ voices into Boards of Canada-adjacent folk horror. Full of febrile layers, this album’s ambitions unpeel with every tantalising listen.Also out this monthLive at Dingle’s 1974(self-released) is the first official release from London folk singerClive Woolf, whose career ended at 28 after a debilitating brain illness. Recorded just weeks before he stopped playing, it captures the singer and guitarist’s soulful spirit, especially on a stunning a cappella Low Down in the Broom (now in his 80s, he still attended the Cecil Sharp House folk club as a listener until the pandemic).Gobletsound like the wayward offspring of Milkweed and the Focus Group, and Elfgiffu House is their debut album on an exciting new London DIY label (Circle Dance). Led by Amy Lawrence, her project imagines a future Cornish utopia through eerie vocal ensembles, recorders, kelhorns and Breton bombardes.Cinder Well’sA Blooming Body(Hen House Studios) finds the US artist wading into starker waters following her successful theme tune for Small Prophets, although her grasp of Americana glows on the gorgeous Of Nettles and Roses.This article was amended on 7 August 2026. Cinder Well is American, not Irish as an earlier version said.Explore more on these topicsMusicFolk album of the monthFolk musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Flo: Therapy at the Club review – skirting the dancefloor and overly sweating the small stuff | Music | The Guardian
description: The British R&B girl group’s follow up to 2024’s Access All Areas is lyrically spicy and musically diverse but somewhat slow paced and lacking the euphoria and hedonism the title suggests
Author: Kate Solomon
Headline: The British R&B girl group’s follow up to 2024’s Access All Areas is lyrically spicy and musically diverse but somewhat slow paced and lacking the euphoria and hedonism the title suggests
Content: Unhurried … (from left) Renée Downer, Stella Quaresma and Jorja Douglas AKA Flo.Photograph: Alex J PiperView image in fullscreenUnhurried … (from left) Renée Downer, Stella Quaresma and Jorja Douglas AKA Flo.Photograph: Alex J PiperMusicReviewFlo: Therapy at the Club review – skirting the dancefloor and overly sweating the small stuff(EMI)The British R&B girl group’s follow up to 2024’s Access All Areas is lyrically spicy and musically diverse but lacks the hedonism the title suggestsKate SolomonFri 7 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Flo burst out in 2022, the trio were hailed as the second coming of the R&B girl group, and even paid homage to their harmonising forebears Destiny’s Child, Sugababes and SWV in the intro to debut albumAccess All Areas. They didn’t quite hit as expected – only one single scraped the Top 40 – but they sound undeterred on a vibey second album that adds lyrical spice and musical left turns.View image in fullscreenFlo: Therapy at the Club.Therapy at the Club follows the flow of a night out, but one rooted in the slight mania of romantic disappointment rather than euphoric release. Pose is a pared-back interpolation of Pump Up the Jam, skittering hi-hat hits echoing the clicks of confidence-boosting burst-mode selfies. On Remedied, Flo are distracted by the admin of getting a cab as big-band horns blast behind an anxious beat; with its 3/4 time signature, piano and dreamy melismatic vocals, the title track sounds more like sashaying through the park than the soundtrack to copping off with strangers.Like any self-respecting girl group, Flo have their balladry down: Floating is a belter, showcasing their chemistry as the three vocal lines soar around each other. But at 16 often mid-paced tracks, the album drags. Miss U Missing Me meanders through a ghosting situation that ends up feeling kind of justified. The overall disconnect between theme and energy is distracting: there’s self-assurance to Therapy at the Club’s unhurried pace, though more time sweating it out on the dancefloor would make it a more satisfying listen.Explore more on these topicsMusicR&Balbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Strange Loops: Clarinet Quintets album review – drama, imagination and sonic flair | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Clarinettist Mark Von de Wiel performs music by Anna Clyne, Ruth Gipps and Weber
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Clarinettist Mark Von de Wiel performs music by Anna Clyne, Ruth Gipps and Weber
Content: Performances of drama and beauty … clarinettist Mark van de Weil.Photograph: Peter van den BergView image in fullscreenPerformances of drama and beauty … clarinettist Mark van de Weil.Photograph: Peter van den BergClassical musicReviewStrange Loops: Clarinet Quintets album review – drama, imagination and sonic flairVan de Wiel/Soloists of the Philharmonia(Signum)Clarinettist Mark Von de Wiel performs music by Anna Clyne, Ruth Gipps and WeberClive PagetFri 7 Aug 2026 05.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark van de Wiel was principal clarinet of the Philharmonia from 2000 until 2025, during which time he gave the UK premiere of Anna Clyne’s Strange Loops. The title, derived from Douglas Hofstadter’s 1979 bestseller Gödel, Escher, Bach, describes a cyclic system where, by moving up or down through different hierarchical levels, you unexpectedly find yourself back at the beginning.View image in fullscreenStrange Loops: Clarinet Quintets.Composed during lockdown, Clyne’s klezmer-inflected musical loops do just that, multiplying and mutating with syncopations and sidesteps and yet somehow reaching a satisfying conclusion. It makes a buoyant, yet bittersweet opener, meticulously realised by Van de Wiel with violinists Zsolt-Tihamér Visontay and Fiona Cornall, Nicholas Bootiman on viola and cellist Karen Stephenson.Clyne’s slinky, 21st-century riffs couldn’t be further from the pastoral calm of Ruth Gipps’ 1942 Rhapsody in E-flat. The clarinet was her husband’s instrument and, along with the oboe, which she played herself, it always drew out the best in her. Van de Wiel is dark-toned and buttery in a performance that matches dramatic resolve with sonic beauty.Finally, Weber’s Clarinet Quintet gets a virtuoso outing with plenty of colour and pliable tempi. Van de Wiel shapes the solo clarinet lines with imagination and dramatic flair, but his fellow musicians also get their moments in the sun in a generous and collegiate account captured in warmly detailed sound.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: Pony Island 2 Panda Circus: gallop out of hell in this phantasmagorical follow-up to 2016’s indie hit | Games | The Guardian
description: Daniel Mullins explains how he plans to follow up his quirky classic without losing what made it stand out in the first place
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Daniel Mullins explains how he plans to follow up his quirky classic without losing what made it stand out in the first place
Content: Bamboozling … Pony Island 2: Panda Circus.Illustration: Daniel Mullins GamesView image in fullscreenBamboozling … Pony Island 2: Panda Circus.Illustration: Daniel Mullins GamesSummer games previewsGamesPony Island 2 Panda Circus: gallop out of hell in this phantasmagorical follow-up to 2016’s indie hitDaniel Mullins explains how he plans to follow up his quirky classic without losing what made it stand out in the first placeIgnas VieversysFri 7 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGlitchy aesthetics. Literally collapsing menu boxes. The game taunting you by “possessing” your Steam friends. Technical tricks of this nature may sound gimmicky in 2026, but they felt excitingly unorthodox a decade ago, when Pony Island came out to critical acclaim.Fans of Daniel Mullins, the celebrated indie developer of Inscryption, will be forgiven for forgetting that Pony Island 2: Panda Circus is in active development. After all, it’s been almost three years since the announcement – and a full decade since it was first teased as an Easter egg in Pony Island’s ARG (Alternate Reality Game) – with only a single trailer and a bunch of tunes from the soundtrack released to the public.View image in fullscreenItching to glitch … Pony Island 2: Panda Circus.Illustration: Daniel Mullins GamesWhile the announcement trailer teases the return of endless-runner sequences and glitchy menus, Panda Circus is seemingly a far bigger and more complicated project than its predecessor; hence the 3D landscapes, pixel art JRPG sequences and even apparent nods to games such asThe Case of the Golden Idol. Which is why Mullins claims that, at least in terms of gameplay variety, Panda Circus is closer to The Hex and Inscryption than the original game.“[Pony Island 2] is multifaceted in its gameplay and wide-ranging in its influences. But this time the disparate game systems are united by more common elements,” he says, referencing the drag-and-drop “hacking” puzzle. “That simple premise was extended into an endless amount of blocks and holes of various descriptions.”The plot sees a historical warrior who was slain on his crusade and was damned to hell, where he’s tormented by a video games-making Lucifer. This comically morbid tale “is the strongest link to its predecessor” from a narrative standpoint – although, we’re told, this warrior won’t be Theodore (Pony Island’s protagonist), but a different ancient crusader.In the gameplay that we do get to glimpse in the trailer, the player and his furry companion are traversing through the top-down map, visiting villages and places of interest. It plays like “Oregon Trail through medieval China”, Mullins says after I mention noticing hunger and thirst bars. All this is happening while you’re being tormented by lordly King Yan, the Chinese god of death, played by voice actor SungWon Cho in lavish full-motion interludes.View image in fullscreenBack in the ring … Pony Island 2: Panda Circus.Illustration: Daniel Mullins GamesOther sections promise different mythological themes and menacing deities – an overarching structure that will be familiar to those who played Inscryption. Then there is the Earth Prison, a three-dimensional hub that our hell-bound protagonist can explore, accessing different chapters by using what seems to be a mythical USB stick.If the devil is truly in the details, Mullins gives him plenty of places to hide: Panda Circus seems to be brimming with them. “There is an almost unmanageable number of bespoke, one-off game systems,” he says. “It’s too big to fit in my mind now and that is a new challenge.”The indie dev admits he would have “been troubled” if he knew just how long it would take to make Panda Circus – even with a handpicked team of collaborators. “I’m very lucky because it was a total chance that we started working together,” Mullins says about composer Jonah Senzel, whom he has worked with ever since the original Pony Island. “He turned out to be a genius.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile Mullins shies away from showing any new piece of gameplay, Panda Circus, now in its “final stretch” phase of development, is undergoing private beta. As for the release date: “it may become public knowledge soon,” he hints coyly.Bombastic boss battles, an ARG that will see fans dissecting previous games with archaeological zeal (“I bet they’ll crack it in a couple weeks,” Mullins quips), and meta moments that wink at you cheekily are all to be expected from the developer’s most ambitious project to date.“All the time has gone into making a big game that’s just downright turgid with secrets. There are worlds within worlds and layers upon layers.” Another classic Mullins joint, then, and we couldn’t be more ready.Pony Island 2: Panda Circus is in development forPCwith plans for Linux/Mac “not long after”.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Helen Goh’s giant shortcake with summer fruits and vanilla cream – recipe | Dessert | The Guardian
description: A jamboree of juicy stone fruit and summer berries with a crusty, sugary top brings a riot of textures and colour to your dessert table
Author: Helen Goh
Headline: A jamboree of juicy stone fruit and summer berries with a crusty, sugary top brings a riot of textures and colour to your dessert table
Content: Helen Goh’s giant shortcake with summer fruits and vanilla cream.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenHelen Goh’s giant shortcake with summer fruits and vanilla cream.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.The sweet spotDessertHelen Goh’s giant shortcake with summer fruits and vanilla cream – recipeA jamboree of juicy stone fruit and summer berries with a crusty, sugary top brings a riot of textures and colour to your dessert tableHelen GohFri 7 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAgiant American-style shortcake is one of summer’s great celebrations: tender, buttery shortcake, softly whipped cream and an extravagant tumble of fruit. Rather than prescribing a single combination, I like to let the market decide. Choose whatever looks and smells best: strawberries, raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, greengages, apricots, cherries, nectarines or peaches all work beautifully. Aim for a mix of juicy stone fruit and berries – it will bring different colours, textures and levels of sweetness to every bite. This is a dessert that embraces the glorious abundance of the season – a proper summer bonanza.Giant shortcake with summer fruits and vanilla creamWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep15 minChill1 hr+Cook1 hr 20 min, plus coolingServes8-10For the shortcake380g plain flour,plus extra for dusting70g caster sugar, plus 1 tbsp3 tsp baking powder½ tsp fine sea salt150g cold unsalted butter250ml cold double cream, plus 1 tbsp extra for brushing1 tsp vanilla extract1 tsp fennel seeds, lightly toasted and crushedA few small mintleaves, to garnishFor the fruit350g stone fruit of choice, stoned and cut into 5-7mm wedges350g berries of choice, halve or quarter strawberries, depending on size40g caster sugar, plus extra depending on the sweetness of the fruit2 tsp lemon juiceA pinch of fine sea saltFor the cream350ml double cream20g icing sugar1 tsp vanilla extractA pinch of fine sea saltCut a sheet of baking paper to fit a large baking tray, then, using a 20cm cake tin or dinner plate as a guide, draw a 20cm circle on it.Whisk the flour, caster sugar, baking powder and salt in a medium bowl to combine.Put the cold butter between two sheets of baking paper and give it a few firm whacks with a rolling pin, until it forms a rough sheet about 5mm thick. Tear the butter into irregular pieces and add to the flour mix, tossing to coat. Rub the butter lightly between your fingertips to flatten into smaller flakes of about 1-2cm across – some pieces will still be visible throughout the flour.Combine the cream and vanilla, then pour into the flour mix. Stir gently with a fork until the mix forms a shaggy dough, then use a flexible spatula to fold it over a few times, until there are no obvious dry patches. The dough will still look rough and that’s exactly what you want.Turn the dough out on to a lightly floured work surface, then flour your hands and gently pat and press the dough into a rough disc. Transfer to the baking paper, placing it on the side without the circle. Using the drawn circle as a guide, gently press the dough into an even 20cm round, about 2cm thick. Wrap the dough in the baking paper and chill for at least an hour, or up to three hours.To bake, heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Unwrap the dough, put it (still on the baking paper) on to a large baking tray and brush the surface with the remaining tablespoon of cream. Mix the crushed fennel seeds with the extra tablespoon of caster sugar and sprinkle evenly over the top.Bake for 30 minutes, then reduce the oven to 190C (170C fan)/375F/gas 5 and bake for a further 15 minutes, until deeply golden brown and cooked through. Transfer to a wire rack to cool completely.About 30 minutes before serving, combine the fruits, sugar, lemon juice and salt in a bowl. Toss gently and leave to macerate until the fruit has released some of its juices.Meanwhile, whip the cream with the icing sugar, vanilla and salt until it holds soft peaks.Put the shortcake on a serving plate. Using a serrated knife, slice horizontally to lift off the central crusty-domed cap (about 1cm in thickness). Don’t worry if it cracks into a few pieces – reserve on a plate for serving. Spoon the whipped cream over the shortcake and pile most of the fruit on top, along with a little of the syrupy juices. Finish with a few small mint leaves.To serve, cut the shortcake into wedges and transfer to plates. Spoon over the extra fruit and juices, then tuck pieces of the crisp fennel-sugar top alongside each serving.Explore more on these topicsDessertThe sweet spotCakeFoodBiscuitsSummer food and drinkFruitrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Jimi Famurewa’s deli-style chilli, chicken and parm meatball sandwiches – recipe | Recipes from FEED | The Guardian
description: New Guardian Food show FEED with Jimi Famurewa travels the UK in search of its favourite food trends. This epic ciabatta melt is Jimi’s ode to the American-Italian sub
Author: Jimi Famurewa
Headline: New Guardian Food show FEED with Jimi Famurewa travels the UK in search of its favourite food trends. This epic ciabatta melt is Jimi’s ode to the American-Italian sub
Content: Deli-style chilli, chicken and parm meatball sandwiches.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food stylist and recipe developer: Sonali Shah. Prop stylist: Davina MajiView image in fullscreenDeli-style chilli, chicken and parm meatball sandwiches.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food stylist and recipe developer: Sonali Shah. This epic ciabatta melt is Jimi’s ode to the American-Italian subPaid for byAbout this contentJimi FamurewaFri 7 Aug 2026 04.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 04.40 EDTShareThis recipe combines the influence of an enjoyably fiery Calabrian chilli chicken parm sandwich I had atBada Bingin Manchester and the meatball sub I enjoyed atBelly of the Beastin Newcastle.The key adaptations here are the flattening of the meatballs to sit snugly in the ciabatta; the smoked garlic butter that gives you a garlic bread lid; and the Jersey Shore deli-style combination of Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference Calabrian chilli and fennel pasta sauce with grilled mozzarella. Don’t skip the shredded lettuce as it adds much-needed freshness and texture.Prep10 minCook15 minServes4500g Sainsbury’s British 6% fat chicken mince50g panko breadcrumbs3 tsp Sainsbury’s Italian herb seasoning100g Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference parmigiano reggiano cheese,grated1-2 tsp chilli flakes(optional)Olive oil2 x 340g Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference Calabrian chilli and fennel pasta sauce2 x 400g Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference ciabattas80g unsalted butter,softened2 cloves Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference smoked garlic,peeled and finely chopped2 x 125g Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference buffalo mozzarella,drained½ Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference sweet romaine lettuce,finely shreddedDeli-style chilli, chicken and parm meatball sandwichesIn a large mixing bowl, add the chicken mince, panko breadcrumbs, two teaspoons of Italian herb seasoning, half of the grated parmigiano reggiano, chilli flakes if using and a pinch of salt and pepper. Mix until well combined, shape into 16 small balls then press down so they’re puck shaped.Heat a large wide-based pan over medium high heat with a generous drizzle of olive oil. Once hot, add the chicken meatballs and cook for 8-10 minutes or until golden all over and cooked through. Once cooked, stir in the pasta sauce and remove from the heat.Halve the ciabattas horizontally, then place all four pieces, cut-side up, on to a baking tray. Heat your grill to medium.Mix together the softened butter with the chopped garlic, one teaspoon of olive oil and the remaining teaspoon of Italian herb seasoning. Spread this butter on the cut sides of the two sandwich tops.Evenly spread the meatballs and sauce across the two bases. Top generously with torn mozzarella and the remaining parmigiano reggiano.Keeping the sandwiches open, grill for 3-4 minutes or until the cheese has melted and the garlic butter has browned.Carefully remove the open sandwiches from the grill then leave to cool for 1 minute.
